Hillsboro
Football – The Trojans played at Lyons on Friday, Oct. 18 where they won 32-0. The Trojans led 7-0 at halftime from a 35-yard run from Jesiah Gooch in the first quarter.
The floodgates opened in the second half where Gooch scored three times, all on runs, and Zayne Haslet got in the endzone as well on a 41-yard run in the fourth quarter.
Coming—The Trojans will play at home against Smoky Valley on Friday, Oct. 25.
Volleyball – In their last regular season action, Hillsboro traveled to Marion on Thursday, Oct. 17, for a showdown with the Lebo Wolves and the hometown Warriors.
Hillsboro started the night against the 1A state-ranked Lebo Wolves. The match was a battle from the start. The teams exchanged points throughout the first game. Lebo took the first set 26-24. The Trojans dominated from the start of the second game and won the second set easily 25-10. The last set, however, was a repeat of the first. Hillsboro did gain a small advantage toward the end of the set but could not close out the game, and Lebo came back to win the set and match. It was another tight one with Lebo winning 26-24.
In the second match, the Trojans played the Warriors. After a 25-19 first set win, the Trojans fell to Marion in the second 18-25. In the final game, Hillsboro slowly built a lead and won the final contest 25-18.
The Trojans finish out the regular season with a 23-12 record. In a quick turnaround, Hillsboro will begin postseason play on Monday, Oct. 21, when they travel to Blue Rapids for regional play. The new format set by KSHSAA splits the 2A schools into 4 regions. The teams in each region are ranked 1-16 by overall win-loss record. Teams in each region are assigned quads based on their seeding. With a 6 seed in their region, Hillsboro will play the number 11 seed, Hutch-Trinity; the number 14 seed, Ell-Saline; and the number 3 seed, Valley Heights. The winner and runner-up of the regional will advance to a sub-state on Saturday, Oct. 26. Sub-states will be formed after the regionals have been played and will be at the highest-seeded school.

title: Gooch a leader on and off the football field
author: Gary Van
description: By Gary Van Cleave/Special to Hillsboro Free Press Hillsboro Trojan junior Jesiah Gooch knows how to become an effective player on the football field. 'Demonstrating exceptional versatility, he took…
content:
By Gary Van Cleave/Special to Hillsboro Free Press
Hillsboro Trojan junior Jesiah Gooch knows how to become an effective player on the football field.
'Demonstrating exceptional versatility, he took on pivotal roles as a running back, linebacker and key special teams player, excelling as a kickoff returner,' Gooch said about himself in an electronic sports resume with his #32 uniform glistening in the watermark background.
'His remarkable on-field performance is a testament to his durability, dedication and strong work ethic,' the sports resume continued. 'Jesiah is characterized by his unwavering integrity, making him a valuable asset on the field and a commendable individual off the field.'
The 6-foot-1, 210-pound Gooch who runs a 4.8/40 accounted for 1,048 all-purpose yards as a sophomore, including 715 rushing yards.
'Great season, with great teammates,' Gooch said. 'We didn't make it as far into the playoffs as we should have or wanted to, but it was still a good season.'
Hillsboro went 5-4 last year which ended with a loss to Kingman in the playoffs. It didn't stop Gooch from having a super sophomore campaign.
'1000 yards, for me, means hard work pays off, and I had great players as teammates,' Gooch noted.
'Gooch has a work ethic that has pushed me to work harder,' said Zander Haslett, who's playing this fall at Southwestern. 'He came in as a little freshman when I was a junior. Fast forward a year and he is already the same size as me and is lifting just as much weight as I am.'
That includes 450 pounds of squat, 290 clean and 290 bench. He won the 198-pound class at the Conway Springs weightlifting tournament.
'Getting first in the Conway Springs meet made me realize that just as a sophomore I'm starting to be very competitive in weightlifting,' Gooch said. 'It shows how my hard work pays off and what I could do in the future with weightlifting and sports.'
He got his football genes naturally as his dad Jeremy and uncle Jason both played football at Friends. Jeremy was a RB/LB and Jason was a RB/safety.
'It's hard to describe myself, but I would say I have a really good work ethic. I try to be a good leader and role model,' Gooch said. 'I always go 100%. Hopefully, these things are what others feel about me.'
'He never misses a day in the gym or misses a field workout. I cannot say that I have ever seen him go easy on a workout and he's always working harder than everyone else in the room,' Haslett said. 'Dude is the real deal and has a bright future.'
Gooch was voted by his teammates to be a co-captain as a sophomore in which he registered 84 tackles that ranked him top five among sophomores in the state.
'It means to me that I am doing things right, like working hard, being consistent, giving it my all,' Gooch said. 'And they recognized this and put me in a co-captain position. I am super thankful to be a co-captain.'
As a freshman, Gooch was named Offensive Rookie of the Year by his team which vaulted him to greater things this past season.
'I love the team aspect of football and that it takes everyone working together, and towards the same goal, to be successful,' Gooch noted. 'I am VERY competitive and can't stand losing, and that competitiveness is one of the things that drives me.'
'Jesiah is nonstop on the field and a beast in the weight room,' Anders Weisbeck said.
His leadership goes well beyond the gridiron. Gooch was one of two students named to the two-month Marion County Leadership Program.
'Being selected for the Marion County Leadership Program gave me confidence in knowing that I can be a leader and help make a difference,' Gooch said.
Which has led to Gooch's greatness as a football player and a huge fan of the team concept.
'Team concept is everyone working towards a common goal, and by doing that, our guys have developed a brotherhood mentality that plays a big role in winning,' Gooch said. 'Having guys that can build you up and help you get better, it's important because a team that does not bond together and does not back each other up won't win or get anywhere.'
If you ask him about his longest kickoff return of 65 yards, he'll tell you why he got that yardage.
'I am successful in kickoffs because my team blocks well, and I wouldn't ever second guess. I would just go,' Gooch said.
Same thing how he legged out 715 rushing yards or 264 yards after contact.
'It means all the work that my team and I have put in was shown through that and our season,' Gooch said. 'Every day of practice counts. If you're not working consistently, then you're not going to see success or see progress.'
Gooch's overall goal in life is simple, his resume lamented.
'He would just like to continue to improve himself into a servant leader, where he can help others succeed wherever God puts him,' Gooch said on his resume. 'He would like to find a place where he can further his education in aviation, aerospace or engineering and play the sport he loves at an extremely high level.'

title: Science Saturday and Story Walk in Peabody on Nov. 2
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Peabody Township Library and the Peabody downtown shopping district will host Science Saturday and Story Walk on Saturday, Nov. 2. The library will wrap up the Summer Reading Program with a free…
content:
Peabody Township Library and the Peabody downtown shopping district will host Science Saturday and Story Walk on Saturday, Nov. 2.
The library will wrap up the Summer Reading Program with a free interactive program by Mad Science out of Kansas City at 1 p.m. at the Vintage Bank Park in Peabody.
According to the organization's website, Mad Science has developed science programs that are kid-tested and approved for over 30 years.
Following the 45-minute program, Mad Science will kick off the downtown Story Walk by reading the first few pages of the featured story 'How Do You Hug a Porcupine?' by Laurie Isop.
Additional science-related activities will take place from 11 a.m.-3 p.m:
*The Sunflower Theatre, 114 N. Walnut, will host virtual reality demonstrations provided by Army National Guard personnel. Participants can take a virtual tour through the human body or experience
working on the International Space Station.
*Dzz Spot Reptarium and Educational Center will have a variety of snakes, reptiles and turtles for hands-on learning. Exact location downtown is pending.
*Flint Hills Gypsies, 111 N. Walnut, has apothecary and natural history displays.
*Porcupine Tea Company, 215 N. Walnut, will have science activities.
The library will also be continuing its fall book sale in the basement.
'We are thrilled about this opportunity to get parents and children into our downtown businesses for the story walk. We received a library grant to pay for the Summer Reading Program wrap-up and decided to do everything at once for a really fun downtown event,' said Peabody Township Library Director Rodger Charles.

title: Lehigh woman becomes U.S. Citizen
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: While many Americans have threatened to leave the country if their presidential candidate doesn't win, one Marion County woman has been working to become an American. Ae Meyers, 67, was born and…
content:
Ae Meyers with her step-grandchildren Asher Price, 7, Elizabeth Price, 12, and Violet Price, 6. Meyers became a U.S. citizen on Oct. 18 after living in the U.S. for 46 years on permanent residence status.
While many Americans have threatened to leave the country if their presidential candidate doesn't win, one Marion County woman has been working to become an American.
Ae Meyers, 67, was born and raised in Seoul, South Korea where she lived until she was 21.
In 1974, she met and married a U.S. serviceman stationed in South Korea. Two years later, she left behind her family to move with her husband to the United States to L.A.
Meyers then applied and received her permanent residence status. Her husband was still on active duty. With a month-old child, little cash and a plane ticket to Des Moines, IA, the family went to stay with his family. Then they moved to Colorado Springs, CO.
After the husband's service, the family, which now had three small children, moved to Hutchinson and then to Lyons. Along the way, a separation and divorce happened. Meyers and her children later moved to McPherson. For the last 15 years, she has lived in Marion County.
Meyers has been a very hard worker her whole life. She worked as a seamstress in South Korea. She also worked 17 years in the salt mine in Lyons and worked for several years at Certainteed in McPherson until she was laid off.
'Somebody told me to go to AGCO in Hesston. I told them I'm gonna work hard and I'm gonna be here every day and I want this job. They asked how many times a person should call in sick a year. I tell them, 'Oh, I don't call in sick so I don't know',' said Meyers.
She got hired on Oct. 1, 2008, and met Rodney Franzen the following April. They moved in together shortly after into an old farmhouse outside Lehigh. She retired from AGCO in 2022 after working there for 14 years.
In 2018, her permanent residence card needed to be updated so she could get the real ID star on her driver's license.
'Every time you move or change your name, it's supposed to be updated. And it was out of compliance because her purse was stolen in the eighties. The lady at the DMV said they can ask you to leave when it's out of date. She told us 'You better get this fixed'. That's kinda what started it all,' said Franzen.
They went to the Hesston Library and a librarian found the forms they needed. The librarian also told them to talk to the postmaster who directed them to Catholic Charities.
The woman at Catholic Charities asked Meyers why she hadn't gotten citizenship yet.
'I had three kids I was raising by myself. And I was working at the factory. I didn't have time,' said Meyers.
The woman told her to wait until she was 65 because applicants who have been here 20 years and are over 65 have to answer a pool of 20 questions rather than 100 questions. The couple decided to wait at that point.
In August of 2023, Meyers enrolled in a civics class she heard about from a friend. The six-week class was taught by retired Wichita public school teachers at an organization called International Rescue located just south of Entrust Bank.
'You're sitting in that room with people from all over. And you learn a lot about the laws,' said Franzen. 'The class met at 5 on Friday afternoons, and there was a lot of traffic. Our friend Charlotte Maxwell drove her many weeks, helped her study and prayed for her.'
In January, the couple hired an immigration lawyer to go through the citizenship application which included giving work history, marriage and divorce documents, W2s and fingerprinting at the Homeland Security office in Augusta.
The application was submitted in April. In September, Meyers got a letter notifying her that her hearing was set for Oct. 8 at the I.C.E. (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) office in Wichita.
Meyers was very nervous for the hearing since it was just her and a lawyer who met with the judge, and Franzen could not go with her.
'I dressed in a dress and even put the makeup on. I answered all those questions, and the judge said 'You answered every word and no hesitation. You're done. You passed'. So I give them a hug.' Ae Myers was sworn in as a U.S. citizen on Oct. 18.
Meyers and 128 others, from 32 countries, were sworn in on Friday, Oct. 18, at a ceremony on the WSU campus. Her daughter and step-grandchildren surprised her and came to the ceremony.
'I just love them. You cannot ask for better kids. That is the sweetest that they came to the ceremony,' said Meyers.
Meyers said she had a lot of support throughout the involved process, and she credits Franzen the most for all of it.
'He's the one that made it happen,' said Meyers. 'If it wasn't for him, I would have never made it, because there's a lot of work.'
Franzen credits all the helpers along the way including Spring Valley Mennonite Church and First Baptist Church in Canton.
'You don't know all this stuff unless someone's helping you. God puts people in your path to help,' said Franzen. 'Now she has the protection from the constitution and the bill of rights and next election she can vote. Like most immigrants, she will vote for freedom, safety and economic opportunities for her children.'
When asked what she likes about America, Meyers said, 'That everything's okay. Everything's good. And freedom.'
Franzen hopes that Meyers' story will inspire others to get their citizenship.
'I'm so glad she did it, and maybe the point of it would be to encourage others. I'm proud of her and her kids are. I encourage other people to use what's out there,' said Franzen. 'Use your public library. And Catholic Charities is always there and it's free. I would just encourage them to take the steps and see what happens.'

title: Marion County election results
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: 67% of Marion County voters showed up for the General Election on Tuesday, Nov. 5 either by in-person voting or by advanced ballot and early voting. The preliminary results were not available until…
content:
67% of Marion County voters showed up for the General Election on Tuesday, Nov. 5 either by in-person voting or by advanced ballot and early voting. The preliminary results were not available until close to 2 a.m. on Nov. 6 due to the large turnout.
In the District 2 County Commissioner race, Republican Michael D. Beneke beat unaffiliated incumbent David Mueller, 610 to 500.
For District 3, Republican Clarke Dirks beat Democrat Randall M. Eitzen, 713 to 166. Republican incumbent Randy Dallke ran as a write-in candidate, but the results will not be available until after the canvass.
Republican Ashley Herpich, who ran unopposed, received 5,029 votes for County Clerk.
Unopposed Republican Tina L. Groening received 5,298 votes for County Treasurer.
Shelby Schroeder, Republican, who also ran unopposed, received 5,176 votes for Register of Deeds.
For County Sheriff, unopposed Republican Jeffrey T. Soyez had 4,830 votes.
All of the Court of Appeals and District Court judges retained their positions.
Republican Michelle Brown and Libertarian David Graham ran as write-ins for county attorney. The result of the race will not be available until after the canvass.
Hillsboro City Council Ward 1 candidate Jeffrey J. Jorgenson received 515 votes while Ward 2 candidate Byron C. McCarty, Jr. had 532 votes. Both ran unopposed.
For state offices, Republican Michael A. Fagg received 4,844 votes for State Senate, 14th District and Republican Scott Hill had 2,233 votes for State House, 70th District. Republican Mike King defeated Democrat Jenna Ratzlaff for the State House, 74th District, 2,273 to 753.
For national offices, Republicans Trump and Vance beat Democrats Harris and Walz, 4219 to 1380 and Republican Derek Schmidt defeated Democrat Nancy Boyda for US House of Representatives-District 2, 4,196 to 1,300.
For other results and more information, go to marioncoks.net and click Election Information. No results are final until the canvass on Friday, Nov. 15.

title: Hillsboro plans for the future
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council, along with several other city leaders, spent close to three hours in a strategic planning meeting on Tuesday, Nov 12. The meeting began with City Administrator Matt Stiles…
content:
The Hillsboro City Council, along with several other city leaders, spent close to three hours in a strategic planning meeting on Tuesday, Nov 12.
The meeting began with City Administrator Matt Stiles explaining that the strategic plan started in January 2020 and has been updated quarterly.
Stiles led the group through a review of the vision, values, goals and status of the past five years of the current strategic plan with a promise to work on a three-year plan in the rest of the meeting and another two or three meetings. He said the hope is to have marching orders to work on by the end of the meeting process.
'I think what we have accomplished is a little bit unique. We've done quite a bit,' said Stiles.
Stiles explained there were three tier-one goals: childcare, housing and workforce development. The city is getting ready to open a new childcare center in February. They are also working with Mennonite Housing on a housing development on 12 duplexes that will start sometime at the end of the year next year or the beginning of the following year. A few other housing options are also in the works.
'For our workforce development, we are trying to do some things to build workforce here. This includes our entrepreneurship agenda as well. We've got the partnership with Central Kansas Entrepreneurship Center at Tabor College (CKEC) so that's something that we've worked with them to do the side hustle challenge and the lecture series,' said Stiles.
The group learned that Tabor is also building a $12 million business building that will house CKEC.
Stiles said that the city has also connected with USD 410 and job shadowing and other opportunities.
'One of the things we have in this community is a lot of jobs, but we don't have a lot of people that will lead to jobs,' said Stiles. 'You can kinda start to see where everything gets connected because we don't have a place to put them if they wanna live here. They don't have childcare for them. They have a kid. They don't work. So they all gotta work together.'
The tier-two goals have been community development, financial stability and public safety.
'This is what I call the fun stuff. This included the gigabyte fiber premise in town. That was one of the first things that got knocked off the list. The community plaza project is in here, too. We built a trail out to the hospital and now we have another grant to build a trail out to Orchard Drive where the new housing is going to go—over on the north side of the street from the pharmacy there all the way up to Sonic,' said Stiles.
Colin Hansen, CEO of Kansas Power Pool led the second half of the meeting during which the group focused on the vision and values for the next three years.
The group started with their vision statement of Hillsboro being a prairie community focused on people, places and progress.
Thurston said, 'How do we identify ourselves? In the past, Hillsboro has really kind of approached that in a really disjointed way. We have a strong Russian Mennonite, German Mennonite heritage here, but that doesn't include everybody. That excludes a lot more people than it includes. That's just the way the community has developed over the years. So I thought about what is something that can describe us that is inclusive, that would include everybody? And I think about living on the prairie and what does it mean to live on the prairie? When we think of agriculture, for example, that's one of the first things you think about. The first settlers came here to farm and the Russian Mennonites brought the turkey red wheat and turned Kansas into the breadbasket of the world. But those things didn't happen just like that. There was a lot of winds they had blow against you—drought, hail, storms of life. We've all gone through those things, and I think it's something that we can all kind of identify with. So that was my thing about the prairie part. And I just feel strongly personally about that. I'm open to other people's input, but that's where it came from.'
The group discussed several key words including progress, innovation, resiliency, vision, communication, faith, community, values, people and family.
The idea of lifelong learning was also emphasized.
'We have a community where literally it's started at preschool and you can have in-person learning from preschool all the way through a master's degree,' said Councilman Jeff Jorgenson.
'One of the things that I said early on in in my tenure as mayor was I want Hillsboro to become a college town and not a town with a college. We want Tabor to feel welcome here and embraced and loved, but we also want Tabor to love the community as well and not just have students on the island of Tabor. We want them to be out and be part of the community,' said Thurston.
The group tentatively decided to move childcare to a tier-two goal while moving community development up to a tier-one goal. They will meet again to continue working on a vision statement, goals and values. A meeting date has not yet been set.

title: Officiating isn't perfect? Say it isn't so
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: Polls are taken on a lot of subjects, but I've never seen...
content:
Polls are taken on a lot of subjects, but I've never seen a poll asking, 'Do you think that officiating is perfect?' I've never seen a poll where the public agrees on anything, but this would likely be the first and only poll where 100 percent of the respondents would agree that officials make mistakes.
As a longtime former basketball official, I know firsthand that officiating isn't perfect. It's not an easy avocation when perfection is what people hope for, but is impossible.
Sports fans by nature are emotionally invested in the outcome of a sporting event. Hence, human nature flares up and causes fans to be frustrated, irate and worse after a bad or questionable call.
Here's why officiating is such a challenge. Officials are human. Players are human. Coaches are human. Fans are human. Therein lies the problem. We're all human, and we all make mistakes.
There are missed calls in every game, but questionable calls by officials near the end of close games receive extra scrutiny.
Officials do their best to enforce the rules of the game as consistently as possible. Once I heard a coach say, 'All we want is consistency.' To which an official replied, 'You want consistency. We want consistency. Everyone wants consistency. The problem is, they aren't always playing consistently out there.'
Last year, Kansas City wide receiver Kadarius Toney was flagged for an offside penalty. That call and play became one of the NFL season's flashpoint officiating moments. The penalty wiped out a remarkable go-ahead touchdown late in the game when Travis Kelce threw a long lateral pass to Toney, who ran the ball in for an apparent touchdown.
Although the officials ruled correctly, the question remained: Did Toney lining up offside by a foot give him an advantage when he didn't get the ball until eight seconds later during the play?
The call was technically correct, but should that call be made in a league that aims to create the most entertaining and thus lucrative product? But is it fair to ask an official to set aside a rule that appears to be black and white?
This season, a pass interference call against a Cincinnati defensive back put Kansas City in position to win the game on a last-second field goal. Most football experts agreed that the defensive pass interference penalty was legit, although one former coach said that penalty isn't always called.
There's the rub. Depending on the official and the angle of that official to the players on the field, a penalty may or may not be called. Not every official will judge each play the same way.
Someone on X (Twitter) thought the official waited to see if the pass was caught before throwing his flag. Truthfully though, it's better for an official to throw the flag a little late after processing what he saw, than react too quickly in making the call.
I recall a basketball coach complaining to an official about a so-called late whistle or call. To which the official responded, 'But was it right?' That is the bottom line after all.
When I was officiating a college men's basketball game, I recall anticipating a foul near the basket and immediately blew my whistle, only to realize the defensive player made a clean block. I would have gotten the call right if I had held my whistle for a second, rather than anticipate the foul.
I had been rightly taught to anticipate the play and not the call. I broke that rule more than I care to admit.
Officiating is mentally challenging. An official has to be firm, but not unapproachable. An official is often making unpopular decisions which can cause people to be upset in almost every single game. Being an official isn't for the faint of heart.
I read that the qualities of a good official are integrity, hustle, judgment, communication, consistency, courage, and common sense. That should be a piece of cake, right? Well, no.
As someone once told me, 'The trouble with common sense is that it's not that common anymore.'
I read a quote that's so true: 'Have no fear of perfection. You'll never reach it.'

title: County receives grants
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Marion County Board of Commissioners met on Monday, Dec. 16 and heard from Marion County Administrator Tina Spencer that the county received a Patterson Family Grant for $50,000 for two CPR…
content:
The Marion County Board of Commissioners met on Monday, Dec. 16 and heard from Marion County Administrator Tina Spencer that the county received a Patterson Family Grant for $50,000 for two CPR devices and accessories. Spencer also told the board that they have been awarded an Emergency Management Performance Grant (EMPG) of $25,000 for Emergency Management, an annual grant that the department can continue to apply for and receive as long as they keep meeting the requirements for it.
Spencer also told the board that the county received the insurance claim for the damage from the fire in the transfer station.
'The amount that we received was $3,631.25. That was based on the estimate for the work that you all approved to have done and less the deductible,' said Spencer.
The board also received department updates from Spencer. Spencer informed the board that the health department has lots of interior work happening. The parking lot is expected to be poured this week. The glass for the vestibule entry is delayed until after the first of the year.
For the Road & Bridge updates Spencer informed the board that written recommendations for 140th, 330th and Nighthawk are expected early in January. The department placed sand on 140th (Aulne Road) to help smooth out the surface. Drainage work and tree removal are current tasks that the department is working on.
Spencer also gave an update from the Department on Aging. Medicare open enrollment was busy and went well. Director Luretta Turk is working on logistical strategies to improve commodity distribution in some areas.
According to Spencer, the new ambulance is coming off the production line and going to quality control. The PA system projects in both stations are moving forward.
The update for Planning/Zoning is that income qualifications for the LEPP grant were changed, which should allow more individuals in Marion County to apply for this assistance.
Spencer updated the board that she spoke to the KDOT Engineer for Harvey County, and he indicated that he will submit a request for a traffic study of the intersection of Highway 50 and Eastlake Road. The commissioners had requested this be done in a previous meeting due to the high number of accidents that have occurred there.
Spencer reported that she is working on year-end budget projections with departments and preliminary work on financial statements is underway.
She has also approved salary sheets and fuel bids and attended KMAAG training in Wichita with County Clerk Ashley Herpich last week.
The board will meet for one more regular meeting on Monday, Dec. 23. There will not be a commission meeting on Monday, Dec. 30, but there will be a payday meeting on Tuesday, Dec. 31. Jan. 6 will be the first commission meeting in 2025.
In other business, the board:
* approved early checks for $198,450.11.
* commended Marion County Treasurer Tina Groening for her reports and for taking care of the county's money.
* approved the transfer of $116.666.66 from Road & Bridge to special equipment.
* approved the transfer of the ARPA interest earned from ARPA to Health Capital Project for $160,764.89.
* met in executive session for an employment interview.
* learned that newly elected officials will be sworn in at 11 a.m. on Jan. 13. At 12:30 p.m. that day there will be a reorganizational commission meeting.
* learned there will be a new commissioner training Jan. 15-17.

title: USD 410 BOE hears project updates
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The USD 410 Board of Education met on Monday, Dec. 9 where they heard bond project updates from Superintendent Clint Corby. 'We've been really pleased with the secure entry at the main entry at the…
content:
The USD 410 Board of Education met on Monday, Dec. 9 where they heard bond project updates from Superintendent Clint Corby.
'We've been really pleased with the secure entry at the main entry at the high school. I'm excited to get that next year at the elementary and get that moving. The curtain gym dividers are up and look sharp. They look really, really good. Pleased with how that project has gone,' said Corby.
Corby told the board about plans for an elementary school addition that will serve as both usable space and a tornado shelter. He explained that there would be two classrooms and an office for the family advocate position.
'There would be a hallway that the classrooms would share in between. You got sinks on the outside walls and individual toilets on the other side,' said Corby.
The addition would be added onto the end of the current kindergarten and first-grade hallway at the southwest corner of the school.
Corby recommends that the new space be used for preschoolers for a variety of reasons including the circle drive location for drop-off and pick-up, the constant need for two classrooms for preschool while other grades fluctuate and the ability to design the spaces for three and four-year-olds.
'So we're designing that space for them, and things are their size and then opening up our other spaces for other uses, whether it be social workers, speech, band, you name it—where we can use those other spaces and have more flexibility,' said Corby. 'Then last but certainly not least, in the event of a tornado, our slowest kiddos are gonna be our preschoolers. And so having them in the space that they're already there eliminates that need to have to move them elsewhere.'
The board discussed allowing football players to purchase used football helmets.
'We have had parents or guardians and students ask if they could purchase used football helmets, but, in the past, we have not permitted this. After discussions with the Kansas Association of School Boards (KASB) and our insurance agent, we are recommending two options for parents/guardians of football players and football players who are 18 or older to purchase used football helmets,' said Corby.
The first option is if the student wants a helmet still eligible for school team use. The student buying the helmet must pay the replacement cost of $375. The second option is for those helmets no longer eligible for school team use and cost $100.
The board decided that the helmets can only be used for display. Parents/guardians of football players and football players who are 18 or older would also be required to sign the Assumption of Risk and Waiver of Liability to complete the purchase. Only seniors and alumni can purchase the helmets for this purpose.
Board President Jared Jost gave a Marion County Special Education (MCSEC) report and shared that MCSEC is working with an apprentice program that allows a para working in a school to be recognized.
'They can go into that apprenticeship and take college classes, and get a Masters and become a SpEd (special education) teacher. It's another great way to try and find talent out there. Sometimes a teacher will say that person was a para for 10 years, and they would have been an awesome teacher. Well, hopefully, this will eliminate that kind of deal,' said Jost. 'I think we currently have three enrolled in the program with this deal. So we're excited about it.'
'The number one area in the state for education vacancies is special education,' said Corby.
The board approved the resignation of HMHS Vocal Music teacher and HHS Musical Coordinator Lynn Just effective the end of the 2024-2025 school year.
In other business, the board:
* accepted several donations from the HHS Athletics Booster Club and Shutterfly.
* approved the 2025-2026 calendar
*discussed activity bus options. Corby explained that they plan to retire a current bus that they use as a spare and will have a greater need for an activity bus than a route bus.
* approved the resignation of HHS Instructional Aide Juana Pritchard effective Dec. 13.
* approved the payment of bills totaling $348,360.72.

title: Department of Commerce denies Peabody grant funds, demands closure of local business
author: Jessie Wagoner
description: It seemed like a dream come true for Peabody Main Street Association (PMSA). In May of 2023, the organization and its volunteers learned they'd been awarded $1.5 million in grant funding to help…
content:
It seemed like a dream come true for Peabody Main Street Association (PMSA).
In May of 2023, the organization and its volunteers learned they'd been awarded $1.5 million in grant funding to help restore the city's historic downtown.
Yet in the year and a half that followed, scandal, death and a threat by the Department of Commerce to claw back half the funding and not release the other half has turned the situation into a bureaucratic nightmare.
'The exorbitant request for documentation, sometimes bordering on harassment, coupled with a stunning lack of communication after submission of said documentation has left me perplexed,' Morgan Marler, PMSA board member, said. 'The sheer lack of state department guidance and oversight should be disconcerting to every Kansan.'
Problems began when the Department of Commerce investigated former state employee Jonathan Clayton, who oversaw BASE Grant awards and funding. Clayton was dismissed from his position with Commerce after it came to light that he had been convicted of previous financial crimes over 10 years ago. When Clayton left the Department of Commerce, he began working for the City of Peabody in code enforcement and eventually as the interim city clerk. He also volunteered his time as the grant administrator for PMSA.
In July, PMSA received word from Commerce that their grant documentation had not been submitted properly and they were at risk of losing grant funds. Clayton stated he had submitted the documentation several times, and he agreed to a meeting with the PMSA board to get the documentation of off his computer so they could submit it themselves. However, Clayton did not arrive for the meeting and was reported missing by his husband, Christopher King. Clayton was later found deceased, the victim of an apparent motor vehicle crash.
Following Clayton's disappearance, a previously scheduled email was sent from Clayton's email address to various government and media sources, accusing Lieutenant Governor and Secretary of Commerce David Toland of altering BASE Grant applications in an effort to sway how grants were distributed. The Department of Commerce denied the allegations and advised Clayton was being investigated for the possible misuse of BASE Grant funds in Mullinville, his hometown.
PMSA, the City of Peabody and the Peabody Chief of Police have reviewed their finances and say no misuse of funds occurred in Peabody. They have been able to account for all funds and have no concerns. The Kansas Bureau of Investigation continues to investigate the claims of misused funds in Mullinville.
PMSA, an organization operated by a fully volunteer board, with no paid employees has invested thousands of hours over the last several months attempting to meet the demands of Commerce to no avail. Now, CK Vintage, a popular downtown business owned by King, is being forced to close its doors. The Department of Commerce has required PMSA to terminate its lease with King to receive the second disbursement of funds. Commerce says the lease is a 'conflict of interest.'
'On Sept. 4, when Matt Hanson with Witt O'Brien came for the site visit, he made it clear to us that Commerce was going to request us to terminate the lease with Christopher if we were going to be allowed to receive the second disbursement,' Marler said.
Witt O'Brien is the company hired by the Department of Commerce to perform an audit of Commerce's handling of BASE Grant funds and look into the allegations made by Clayton and the allegations of financial misuse by Clayton.
'He told us Commerce considered it a conflict of interest,' Marler said. 'We were devastated. Christopher had already lost so much, and we knew it would be financially and emotionally devastating to lose his shop, too.'
Marler said other than the bad news about the lease termination, the meeting with Hanson went well. They were able to provide him with all the documentation he requested. Following the meeting, Hanson sent them an email with a punch list of items to complete, which PMSA has done.
The Hillsboro Free Press has obtained a copy of Hanson's email with the list of requirements. The requirements included meeting with a lawyer about the lease between PMSA and King and determining the next steps for the property.
PMSA has requested a copy of Witt O'Brien's final report and recommendations from Commerce, but they have not received it. Hanson stopped replying to their emails and phone calls in November. The Hillsboro Free Press has also requested a copy of the final report from Hanson, who has not responded to those calls or emails, either.
PMSA provided King with a notice of termination of his lease with an effective date of Dec. 27. It was another blow to him, following so much loss already. King is now in his final days at CK Vintage. He is selling everything in the store for 50 percent off and bidding farewell to his loyal customers.
'Everyone in Peabody has been so supportive of me through all this,' King said. 'They have kept my fridge full, encouraged me, been kind. I couldn't have made it through without the support of my friends here.'
After providing Commerce with all the required grant documentation and following their direction to terminate the lease with King, PMSA was under the assumption Commerce would issue the remaining $750,000 of funding. However, Commerce has not, and on Dec. 9, PMSA received a letter, signed by Toland, directing them to evict King by Dec. 20 or Commerce would begin the process to take back the first $750,000 of grant funds, money already spent on projects.
'In the event Grantee fails to terminate the lease at the 109 N. Walnut property as requested under Section VII (Q), Commerce at its option may terminate the agreement and require all grant funds previously provided by Commerce be repaid by Grantee and/or not provide any remaining grant funds to Grantee,' the letter stated.
PMSA members say they have done everything they possibly can to comply with all of Commerce's requests. Ultimately, when Commerce told them to evict King by Dec. 20, which violates tenant-landlord laws, they said no more. PMSA has retained an attorney to help guide them in the next steps forward. They will not be terminating King's lease earlier, and his store will remain open until Dec. 27.
PMSA board members provided the following list of projects completed with the first disbursement of grant funds:
•Five roof replacements
•Three interior framing jobs
•Six HVAC systems
•Four electrical upgrades
•Two major structural and masonry repair jobs
•Two-door entry structures
•Three major exterior wall limestone wall stabilization projects
•Coal chute termination and structural repairs
•Asbestos removal
•Window replacements
•City hall and library repairs
•Rotten flooring replacement
'Almost all of these projects are related to improvements that are going to extend the lifespan of our historic buildings,' Marler said.
The second disbursement of funds was earmarked for a downtown waterline and sidewalk replacement project in conjunction with the City of Peabody. PMSA said the 'delays that Commerce's actions have caused' to the start of the project are a 'devastating blow' for the community.
The Department of Commerce has not replied to requests for comment on these issues, other than to issue a denial about all claims made by Clayton. The Hillsboro Free Press submitted an extensive open records request to Commerce to which they replied they needed more time to gather the requested documentation, including the Witt O'Brien report.

title: Wind farm concerns
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Dear Editor: The Hillsboro airport is in jeopardy of being shut down permanently. This should get the attention of all citizens of Hillsboro. What is needed is more information. Those who pay close…
content:
Dear Editor:
The Hillsboro airport is in jeopardy of being shut down permanently. This should get the attention of all citizens of Hillsboro. What is needed is more information.
Those who pay close attention to the news know that in October 2023, it was reported that Orsted, the builder of the Sunflower wind farm between Peabody and Florence, was planning to expand to the west part of Marion County, to the townships of West Branch (Goessel), East Branch, Menno, and Liberty. Liberty, as you know, is directly south of Hillsboro.
In my conversations with two licensed pilots, they tell me that pilots don't want to fly within 5 miles of wind turbines because of the air turbulence that comes behind the turbines. Within 3 miles, it can flip over a small plane. Light turbulence can be felt 20 miles away. Towns like Moundridge and Newton have established 5-mile zones around their airport. Hillsboro has not.
Two different sources are trying to find out more from the FAA, but so far they have not returned calls. If the pilots are right, imagine a south wind. If there are any wind turbines placed almost anywhere in Liberty Township, this would make it hazardous, if not impossible for airplane take-offs and landings at the Hillsboro Airport. Thus, if wind turbines go in, the Hillsboro Airport will effectively be shut down.
Is that what the citizens of Hillsboro want? If not, you need to let the powers that be know this.
Yes, what we need is more information. You can contact your City Administrator or the County Planning and Zoning Board or Director or the Marion County Commission. You need to get their attention and let your wishes be known. Otherwise, the days of the Hillsboro Airport may soon be over.
Brian D. Stucky
Goessel

title: Goessel City Council hears street complaints
author: Cynthia Goerzen
description: Goessel City Council met on Dec. 9 and heard a complaint about potholes in the street by the gas pumps. However the city does not maintain that section since it is not city property and not a city…
content:
Goessel City Council met on Dec. 9 and heard a complaint about potholes in the street by the gas pumps. However the city does not maintain that section since it is not city property and not a city street. Those who drive there are actually trespassing. It was also pointed out that those who exit the gas pumps the other way, to the west behind the grocery store, are also trespassing; that is also private property.
The council also heard a complaint about traffic driving too fast on Centennial Drive. A golf cart was mentioned too, with no break lights and not licensed.
On another matter, the council expressed gratitude to Funk Electric for putting up the city's Christmas decorations at no cost to the city.
New public works director Alex Goossen attended the meeting. His first day of work for the city was Dec. 9.
In other business, the council:
* discussed police equipment and voted to replace the body camera for a cost of $525. They also approved quotes to upgrade the radios to encrypted channels for a cost of $788.06 and $2,618.00.
* talked about cats again. They listened to a complaint about stray cats and the harm they do. Concern about rabies was also mentioned.
* discussed a cat ordinance but made no decision at this meeting.
* scheduled a work session for Jan. 28 to discuss housing needs in Goessel.
* planned for snow removal.
* discussed the need for a meeting with the fire board to coordinate use of water, the city-owned building and fire hydrants.
* discussed the issue of dead trees. Owners had been notified but took no action. They could be asked to appear in court for not complying.
* talked about the disc golf area at the city park. Council member John Stucky said the average use is about 30 rounds a month.
* briefly discussed the creek clean-up project.
* heard a complaint about dogs barking.
* listened to a request for an extension on a request for three dogs. The council denied the extension. One dog will need to be removed.
* heard appreciation that potholes had been filled.
* heard appreciation for the requirement for house numbers, which will help in possible emergency situations.
* heard a complaint about a hole that fills with water in the compost area at the burn site. The muddy area makes it harder to access the compost.
* heard appreciation for the new street signs.

title: Be a chip off the old block and bake a family pie
author: Lindsey Young
description: One of my favorite parts of December this year has been the honor of being able to try out four different reader-submitted recipes—one for each week. I have often said that I think sharing…
content:
Chocolate chip pie takes the flavors of a good chocolate chip cookie and puts it into pie form, featuring little pockets of chocolate throughout every bite and a nice, thick layer of whipped topping to cap it off.
One of my favorite parts of December this year has been the honor of being able to try out four different reader-submitted recipes—one for each week.
I have often said that I think sharing food—whether in physical or recipe form—is a kind of love we show to each other. I think that's especially true of the foods we make year after year to share with family and friends.
I had to laugh at the note Deb Preheim of Hesston included with her chocolate chip pie recipe.
'My grandmother and mother were famous for this pie at holidays,' she said. 'They always wanted to make different desserts, but our families insisted on chocolate chip pie.'
I'm feeling fairly certain every family has at least one of these recipes. For my mom, it was always deviled eggs, which, ironically, has become the most requested side dish for me at Young family gatherings, as well.
The tradition continues.
As for this chocolate chip pie, I can definitely see why it's popular with Deb's family. It's really yummy, and despite the steps initially seeming just a little intimidating, I can confidently tell you that it's actually pretty easy to do.
'I make this for my family, as well,' Deb wrote. 'Maybe it will become a tradition for you, too!'
Chocolate Chip Pie
Ingredients
2 cups scalded milk
1/4 cup brown sugar
1/2 cup white sugar
1/3 cup flour
1/2 tsp salt
2 whole eggs
1/2 tsp vanilla
2 Tbsp butter
1/2 cup chocolate chips (I use milk chocolate)
Extra chocolate chips for topping
Cool Whip
Baked pie shell
Directions
Combine sugars, salt, flour and well-beaten eggs in a saucepan.
Add scalded milk slowly, stirring constantly. Add butter. Heat until thick and smooth, stirring constantly.
Remove from heat and stir in vanilla.
Allow to cool until just warm. Add chocolate chips and stir. The chocolate chips should remain intact with just a hint of a swirl.
Pour into a baked pie shell and refrigerate until chilled. Top with Cool Whip and sprinkle more chocolate chips on top. You've created a masterpiece!
Not only was this a pretty pie, but I thought it had the perfect balance in its sweetness. I was worried it would be way too rich, but it was just a very pleasant, tasty dessert. It's a good one to pair with a cup of coffee.
Thank you to all of you who shared recipes with me during the holidays this year and to those who sometimes surprise me with them throughout the year, too.
May your 2025 be a year full of love, laughter and of course, wonderful food.
Spice Up Your Life is a weekly recipe column by Lindsey Young, who describes herself as an enthusiastic amateur cook and can be reached through her website at spiceupkitchen.net.

title: Program spreading kindness one lasagna at a time
author: Jessie Wagoner
description: There are times in life when everyone struggles. It could be a lost job, a death in the family, struggles with depression, or simply having a very bad day. While there is no quick fix for any problem,…
content:
There are times in life when everyone struggles. It could be a lost job, a death in the family, struggles with depression, or simply having a very bad day. While there is no quick fix for any problem, a devoted group of volunteers has found one thing that helps: a home-cooked meal. This desire to help others birthed Lasagna Love.
' Lasagna Love is a global nonprofit and grassroots movement that aims to positively impact communities by connecting neighbors with neighbors through homemade meal delivery,' Micala Teetzen, south central Kansas local leader for Lasagna Love, said. 'We also seek to eliminate stigmas associated with asking for help when it is needed most. Our mission is simple: feed families, spread kindness, and strengthen communities.'
Lasagna Love began in 2020 when a mom in California was making lasagna for her family. She made a second one and posted it in a Facebook group, offering a free meal to anyone who wanted or needed it, no questions asked. Teetzen said the response was overwhelming.
' So many people wanted the free meal, and so many other people stepped up to offer to make lasagna so everyone could have one,' Teetzen said. 'So it really started grassroots like that, with 10 volunteers and an Excel spreadsheet.'
The Excel spreadsheet has now turned into a website devoted to Lasagna Love, lasangalove.org, and thousands of volunteers. Lasagna Love now delivers 3,500 meals per week in every state and four countries. The volunteer count is now at 56,000 and growing. Lasagna Love is a program that delivers lasagnas to families in need for some extra love and kindness.
' We have delivered more than two million lasagnas,' Teetzen said.
People can go to the website, lasagnalove.org, and either request to receive a lasagna or volunteer to make and deliver a lasagna. Teetzen has a couple of volunteers in the area looking to make lasagnas for those in need, and she also hopes to grow the volunteer base in the area so more people can benefit from the lasagna love.
People can request lasagna for any reason, with absolutely no judgment. Teetzen said the reasons for requests vary. Sometimes people have a new baby at home and are overwhelmed, and other times it is a college student, desperate for a home-cooked meal. Financial strains, mental health struggles and health problems wear people down, and sometimes just not having to worry about what to make for dinner can be a huge help.
' We don't know people's situations or conditions, so we are all about no judgment,' Teetzen said. 'But it is a wonderful opportunity, very rewarding. The people giving are receiving just as much.'
Teetzen said there is always room for more volunteers with Lasagna Love. She said some families use the volunteer time as a learning activity for their children, teaching them how to cook and then making the deliveries together. Lasagna Love has partnered with Girl Scouts to offer a badge, leading to Girl Scout troops doing food drives for lasagna ingredients and then cooking and delivering the lasagnas as a service project.
' In Wichita, we have about 75 requests a month and 15 volunteers,' Teetzen said. 'We would like to spread out and get more volunteers and more requests so we can reach more people.'
To volunteer or to request a lasagna visit, www.lasagnalove.org.

title: Area Sports Roundup 1.29.25
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Goessel Boys basketball - The Bluebird Boys competed in the Centre Tournament Jan. 21-25. On Tuesday, Jan. 21, the boys led early, fell behind by 13, battled back to tie the game three times, but came…
content:
Hillboro's Easton Shahan shoots the ball in the game against Remington on Tuesday during the Trojan Classic. Shahan had 22 points in the game helping secure the Trojan's 61-28 victory. Photo by Karrie Rathbone.
Hillsboro's Talia Jost moves in to score for the Trojans in the game against Clay Center during last week's Trojan Classic. The Trojans won 36-34 in overtime.
Goessel
Boys basketball – The Bluebird Boys competed in the Centre Tournament Jan. 21-25. On Tuesday, Jan. 21, the boys led early, fell behind by 13, battled back to tie the game three times, but came up short in the end losing to Douglass with a final score of 63-59.
Next up, the Bluebirds had a heartbreaking overtime loss to Herington. They led big early, fell behind in the fourth and tied it back up 40-40 to force overtime, but came up short losing 43-45.
The Bluebirds finished up the tournament with a game against Centre on Saturday, Jan. 25. The Bluebirds fell behind and Centre won 64-45.
Coming—The Bluebirds will compete on Jan. 31 at Udall.
Girls basketball – The Bluebird Girls competed in the Centre Tournament Jan. 21-25. On Tuesday, Jan. 21, the girls opened the Cougar Classic with a 50-27 winover Rural Vista.
Next up, the Bluebirds played Marion on Friday, Jan. 24. The game was close with Marion edging out Goessel with a final score of 38-35.
The Bluebirds finished up the tournament with a close game against Wakefield on Saturday, Jan. 25. The Bluebirds won 35-30.
Coming—The Bluebirds will compete on Jan. 31 at Udall.
Hillsboro
Boys basketball – The Trojan boys competed in the Trojan Classic Tournament Jan. 21-25. On Tuesday, Jan. 21, the 6th-seeded Trojan boys beat 3rd-seeded Remington.
'Our first round was against an undefeated Remington. We led most of the game, but really extended our lead in the fourth quarter when we caught fire and scored 29 as a team. Easton Shahan had 22 points. Lincoln Wichert and Seth Driggers followed with 12 each. Noah Beavers cleaned up the boards all night with 13. Seth also led the team in assists with seven. We were very efficient due to our ability to find great looks and share the ball. We won 61-28,' said Coach Kyle Kroeker.
Next up, the boys played Hesston on Friday, Jan. 24. Hesston won 56-40.
'In the semi-finals, we had a rematch from a week ago against Hesston. We had a rough stretch during the 2nd and 3rd quarters. We weren't able to make the comeback. We were led in scoring by Easton Shahan with 17. Anders Weisbeck led us in rebounding with 5. The final score was 58-40,' said Kroeker.
The Trojans finished up the tournament with a close game against Holcomb on Saturday, Jan. 25.
'We played Holcomb in the 3rd place game. It was a tight game all night long. It ended 53-49. We had a balanced attack with Lincoln Wichert and Easton Shahan scoring 13 each and Noah Beavers scoring 10 for the game. We were able to battle with some great teams throughout the week. The Trojan Classic field was full of great talent. During these tough games, we continue to improve. We are looking forward to the rest of the season,' said Kroeker.
Coming—The Trojans will compete next on Jan. 31 at home against Minneapolis.
Girls basketball – The Trojan Girls competed in the Trojan Classic Tournament Jan. 21-25. On Tuesday, Jan. 21, the 8th-seeded Trojans played a close game against first-seeded Clay Center securing a 36-34 victory in overtime.
'I thought we started out well on both ends of the floor. Finding ways to score and playing really solid defense in that first quarter. The rest of the game was just a battle. The game went back and forth throughout the rest of the game without a lot of rhythm from either team. We did a good job keeping our composure and just continuing to play hard. We were able to make just enough plays to grab the overtime victory. Proud of the girls,' said Coach Micah Ratzlaff.
Next up, the girls played Moundridge on Friday, Jan. 24. The Trojans couldn't quite pull off a win and Moundridge won 42-33.
The Trojans finished up the tournament with a game against Riley County. Riley County won with a final score of 34-22.
'This was one of the best tournaments I have coached in. It was loaded with talent and a great environment for the players and fans. Our girls played hard finishing fourth. On Saturday, we really struggled to get into any rhythm and Riley County was able to make more plays down the stretch. We made a comeback in the 3rd quarter but seemed to run out gas in the 4th. Hats off to a solid Riley County team,' said Ratzlaff.
Coming—The Trojans will compete next on Jan. 31 at home against Minneapolis.
Wrestling – The Hillsboro/Canton-Galva Trojan Wrestling team competed in Eureka on Saturday, Jan. 25.
Aimee Kelley, Anna King and Claire Morey competed in the 5th Annual Eureka Women's Invitational. All three did not place.
Five boys competed in the 31st Annual Eureka Invitational but failed to place.
'The Eureka Men's and Women's Invitational on Saturday proved to be a tough tournament as always. We held out several younger wrestlers that competed on Tuesday instead. Unfortunately, we had some of our more experienced wrestlers out of the lineup as well due to illness and injuries. Therefore, we only had five guys and three girls competing on Saturday. They all got some quality matchups that provided a good gauge of where they are and what they need to continue to improve on,' said Coach Scott O'Hare.
Coming—The Trojans will compete on Thursday, Jan. 30 at Council Grove.

title: Goessel Council meets despite the snow
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Goessel City Council met on Tuesday, Feb. 18, despite the snow and frigid temperatures. Council meetings are usually the third Monday of the month. However, the regular February meeting date would…
content:
Goessel City Council met on Tuesday, Feb. 18, despite the snow and frigid temperatures. Council meetings are usually the third Monday of the month. However, the regular February meeting date would have been on Presidents' Day, a federal holiday. The city office is not open on federal holidays.
Schools were closed on Tuesday the 18th because of the weather. But the council met for four hours that evening, from 6-10 p.m.
The council discussed several issues with Darin Neufeld of EBH Engineering. He has worked with Goessel on various projects.
He talked with the council about extending utilities to the lots purchased by Tim Wiebe's family, which includes a lot on North Buller and four lots to the north on Kansas Avenue. They talked about a wastewater ordinance and installing water lines. The discussion will be continued at the next council meeting.
On another matter, Neufeld talked with the council about the flood-control project. Trees that still need to be removed have been marked. The council noted tree removal progress that has already been made along the creek to help alleviate flooding in town. One more property has issues that need attention to help control flooding.
In other business, the council:
* heard from public works director Alex Goossen that he had received a new light for the water tower.
* heard that Goossen had spent time removing snow and planned to do some work on the city's road grader.
* discussed maintenance of private roads. It was noted that there was not enough interest on B Road for an easement, so the city will not maintain that one. However an easement was created for A Road. Therefore, the city will maintain that road.
* considered a TAAS (Technology as a Service) quote from Nex-Tech but decided not to pursue the offer.
* heard that the court session had been postponed to March.
* heard that nuisance properties had been inspected.
* talked about stray cats and a TNR (trap, neuter and return) program. The cost would be approximately $100 per cat. Although the council discussed the possibility of obtaining a grant to help with the cost, they decided not to pursue the TNR issue.
* voted to adopt Resolution 25-08, GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) Waiver, which allows a different accounting method.
* discussed pursuing a grant for a television for the community room in the city building.
* discussed recreational vehicle regulations in town. The council looked at the city of Walton's RV ordinance.
* held a work session on Jan. 28 to discuss expansion, the fire department, a sump pump survey and water leaks.
* talked about the recent water leak at the Jan. 28 work session. A boil order had been issued due to the leak. It was rescinded when it was determined that the water was safe to drink.
* noted that Courtney Demaray is currently the city treasurer.
* approved the month's expenses for a total of $62,695.72.

title: Marion County on list for $26M for water projects and technical assistance
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: TOPEKA–Governor Laura Kelly and the Kansas Water Office announced Thursday the award winners for the second round of the Senate Substitute for House Bill 2302 Grant Programs, which provide over $26…
content:
TOPEKA–Governor Laura Kelly and the Kansas Water Office announced Thursday the award winners for the second round of the Senate Substitute for House Bill 2302 Grant Programs, which provide over $26 million in funding for water projects and technical assistance to communities across Kansas.
'Water is vital to the livelihood of our communities and Kansans,' Governor Laura Kelly said. 'This funding is a crucial step in addressing pressing water issues to safeguard our water supply for generations to come.'
In 2023, Senate Substitute for House Bill 2302 increased the amount of state funding for the State Water Plan Fund (SWPF) and created two new water-related grant funds: the Technical Assistance Grant Fund and Water Projects Grant Fund. In the first year, 34 municipalities and special districts related to water were rewarded $18 million.
'The expansion of the State Water Plan to include support for municipalities and water districts continues to be a critical component towards ensuring communities across the state have access to a reliable supply of clean water,' said Senator Kenny Titus, Kansas Senate District 18.
The grant program received over 300 applications in its first year, and an additional $10 million was provided in 2024 through the Legislature to address the high demand for funding.
'We are grateful for the Legislature and Governor Kelly for approving this additional funding,' said Connie Owen, Director of the Kansas Water Office. 'We received a large number of applications again this year. This funding is necessary to Kansas communities.'
Over 270 communities applied for the 2024 funding period, requesting a total of $237 million. Thirty-nine technical assistance grants and 24 water projects grants were awarded to 70 communities and special districts related to water.
'Our small agricultural towns are the lifeblood of our state,' said Senator Rick Billinger, Kansas Senate District 40. 'And this funding will help these communities have the clean and affordable water access they need to thrive.'
A total of $26,287,103 was awarded and some of that money is going to Marion County.
Goessel will receive $50,000 from the Technical Assistance Grant Fund.
Marion County Improvement District 2 will receive $458,880 from the Water Projects Grant Fund.
Marion County Rural Water District No. 4 (MCRWD4) will receive $1,414,760 from the Water Projects Grant Fund. Last fall, MCRWD4 applied for needed replacements and upgrades to mitigate water loss throughout its system. The funds will be used to replace the forty-five-year-old pumping station to ensure 889 rural customers of Marion and McPherson counties continue to be provided with reliable and safe drinking water. Their office is located in Hillsboro.
'I am so pleased to see the list of rural communities and rural water districts across Kansas that have been awarded grants to mitigate their specific water issues,' said Representative Lisa Moser, Kansas House District 106. 'Water is the lifeblood of our state. Without it, nothing else matters.'

title: County discusses wind farm lighting system
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Marion County Board of Commissioners met on Monday, March 10 to discuss the Aircraft Detection Lighting System (ADLS) lighting in the Sunflower Wind project area, which is located between Marion,…
content:
The Marion County Board of Commissioners met on Monday, March 10 to discuss the Aircraft Detection Lighting System (ADLS) lighting in the Sunflower Wind project area, which is located between Marion, Peabody and Florence.
Planning/Zoning/Environmental Health Director Sharon Omstead opened the session by giving background to the packed room which included the board, Marion County Administrator Tina Spencer, Country Attorney Brad Janz, Orsted (the company that handled the Sunflower Wind project) representatives Danny Sears-Greer, Jase Sherwood, Joshua Svaty and Zoe Weinstein and members of the public.
Omstead explained that the wind farm was required to install the ADLS lights and use them, which they did.
'However there was a warranty issue, and the lights weren't working as we had hoped. And so they default to blink so that's a safety factor,' said Omstead. 'This has been going on for a while, and Orsted has been kind of battling out this warranty issue. It's a new technology, it's just taken a long time to work out the kinks. So the commission requested that Orsted come in and talk about why it has taken so long.'
According to Omstead, Orsted was required to install ADLS lighting as a condition of their conditional use permit (CUP).
'It was not in the regulations at the time. Since that time, legislation has enacted a law that all existing wind farms in Kansas have to implement that system. But they were given a certain amount of time to comply with that regulation,' said Omstead.
Orsted Manager Jase Sherwood explained that there's been an issue with contractors in getting them to mobilize and get to working on this issue as well as working through various technical issues with it being a newer technology.
'All of that said, here over the last couple of months, we've actually got folks deployed out to the site,' said Sherwood. 'So it's kind of a two to three part system.'
Sherwood explained that they have one manufacturer that operates the radar system and one that does the lights, as well as the construction company.
'So we got our system reconfigured, which does require shutting each unit down, going to each individual unit and then accessing the network switch at each individual user unit up tower. We've been able to configure, change a few communication protocols and get the equipment where it is actually communicating with the system. The system itself is functioning, but the communication between that system and the lighting is kind of what's been causing all the problems. So, in short, there's a few that have a few errors. We have a couple more that we need to get taken care of as far as getting a few lights replaced, like anything electrical or mechanical, those subject to failure, those just got wrapped up this Friday,' said Sherwood. 'I'll be submitting a few more warranty claims to get some of these remaining lights taken care of. I get communications from both the lights and from the ADLS tower. I can also help manage and monitor the functionality of our system in case we start to lose any communications with them in the future.'
Sherwood explained that there are a few triggers, and the system is more sensitive than anybody would like.
'Weather low cloud cover can initiate the radar. Large blocks of migrating birds can set it off, and it can also pick up traffic on Sunflower or Nighthawk, so it's a little sensitive. They'll take it back as far as they can without it posing a risk to any aircraft,' said Sherwood.
'I'll just add that the CUP did say that the system needed to be installed, and it is installed. So we are satisfying that portion of the CUP, and while it is not currently operating as we would like it to, we are making every effort to do so. We are working with the contractors and doing this at each individual turbine, which does take time. So there are some extenuating circumstances that are just out of our control,' said Orsted Asset Manager Sears-Greer.
Orsted reported that 96% of the lights are working on the ADLS system so they are compliant with what is expected. They said they will continue to work on the lighting issues.
Commissioner Dirks stated that he has received numerous complaints about wind farm issues from people and asked who he needed to have people contact. He was told that the representatives would leave contact information with Spencer.
The board also heard from Marion County Sheriff Jeff Soyez that nine cattle—ranging from old cows to a couple cows with calves to 600-pound intact bulls—were found roaming over the weekend on Remington Road.
'Just straight up Remington Road like you're going to Pilsen, between 230th and 240th. We have been in contact with every cattle owner up there that we can find and nobody is laying claim to these cattle at all. And today's prices—that's a shocker. So I wanted to give you the heads up. We tried to gather them yesterday. We got four of them caught, and yeah, they're wild,' said Soyez.
Soyez said he has made arrangements to have them held in El Dorado.
'I've talked to the El Dorado sale barn. They'll house them for us for 21 days. The state statute is we'll have to advertise them seven days prior to the sale,' he said.
Soyez hopes to catch them all, even if it means hiring cowboys.
'Our landowners are upset up there because their wheat's green enough and these cattle are destroying their wheat so we need to get them off their wheat. That's our responsibility,' said Soyez.
He said they would check the cattle for identification to see if they can trace who they belong to. If not, the money will go into the stray cow fund in the county to repay the people who helped gather and haul the cattle and for damages on the wheat. Any money left over will be held for six months and then released back to the state if not claimed.
In other business, the board:
*approved early checks in the amount of $43,198.41.
*learned that the Marion County Health Department ribbon cutting will be at 10 a.m. on March 31.
*approved a laptop replacement for the Emergency Management Deputy Director for $5,383.50. The laptop has a higher level of capability than the normal office computers and is more capable of working in the field and serving as a mobile operations center. The laptop had been budgeted for by Emergency Management.
*approved EMS write-offs for $1,452.47.
*approved a burn resolution for the county 4-1 with Dirks opposing.
