title: Galloping Goose from Goessel Day is Aug. 4
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: TOPEKA, Kan. – Galloping Goose from Goessel Day in Kansas will be celebrated Aug. 4, honoring the adventurous life of the late Kansan Randolph 'Randy' Woelk. Governor Laura Kelly's Office released the…
content:
TOPEKA, Kan. – Galloping Goose from Goessel Day in Kansas will be celebrated Aug. 4, honoring the adventurous life of the late Kansan Randolph 'Randy' Woelk. Governor Laura Kelly's Office released the official proclamation today in Topeka.
Woelk was born Aug. 4, 1921, in Goessel and raised in a farmhouse north of Newton with no electricity or running water. A second-generation Mennonite immigrant, Woelk knew only two words of English – lunchpail and toilet – when he started attending classes at a one-room schoolhouse in Harvey County. Woelk earned his nickname –the Galloping Goose from Goessel – by excelling in athletics during high school years in the 1930s.
Woelk's defining moment on the running track came in the spring of 1939 when he broke the legendary Glenn Cunnigham's mile-run record for high schoolers at the University of Kansas Relays. His KU Relays time was among the top 20 high school performances in the country in 1939. Later that season, he became Goessel High School's first state champion in any sport when he won the Class AA mile title, recording a time that would have easily won both the small and large school classes. Following a solid running career at Kansas State Teachers College in Emporia, Woelk enlisted in the Army in response to the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. As a Mennonite, Woelk could have claimed conscientious objector status but chose instead to defend his country. He attended officer training school in New Jersey and then was a member of the Army Signal Corps in the Pacific Theater.
After returning home from WWII, Woelk began a teaching career that included stops in Montezuma, Wichita and Beloit. He was part of the CHEM Study project that remade the way chemistry was taught in American high schools in the 1960s and 1970s. Woelk was the rare high school teacher to receive a Fulbright Educational Exchange Grant, which led to him teaching for a year at Kakamega Secondary School in Kenya. Woelk was also a natural-born salesman, first going door to door peddling Compton's encyclopedias and later Fuller Brush housewares. He was also an avid ham radio operator, earning the coveted National County Hunter Certificate seven times.

title: Country Threshing Days features food, history
author: Adam Strunk
description: Country Threshing Days this year in Goessel isn't just a celebration about the town and agriculture but the community's Mennonite heritage. The celebration in Goessel coincides with the 150th…
content:
A photo promoting the Country Threshing Days event shows a crowd gathered, looking at a demonstration of old tractors and farm equipment. The event takes place Friday through Sunday, Aug. 2 to 4 in Goessel. Contributed.
Country Threshing Days this year in Goessel isn't just a celebration about the town and agriculture but the community's Mennonite heritage.
The celebration in Goessel coincides with the 150th-Anniversary of Mennonite farmers coming to the area and beginning to settle in central Kansas. It lasts Friday through Saturday, Aug. 2 to 4, and will feature displays of old-time farm equipment and a wide variety of activities.
At 7 p.m. on Aug. 2, there will be a heritage presentation, telling the story about the 1874 Mennonite immigration that helped settle the area. The event includes a narrated pictorial presentation and reading of first-hand accounts of the immigrants, who left south Russia and found a home in and around Goessel. The event takes place in the Goessel High School Gymnasium, 100 E Main St.
A parade starts in Goessel's downtown at 9:30 a.m.
A 'Low German' meal with an a la carte menu will be served Aug. 3 at the elementary school from 10:30 a.m. to 1 p.m.
The menu includes verenika, bierocks, sausage, zwieback, cherry moos, New Year's cookies and drinks.
From 10:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., there will also be food to purchase at the preparatory school on museum grounds. Those items include bierocks, BBQ sandwiches, bean salad, chips, monster cookies and New Year's cookies.
Both events take cash or check only, with the proceeds going to benefit the Mennonite Heritage and Agricultural Museum.
Throughout the event, there will be demonstrations from Hart Parr, Oliver and White farm equipment, as well as extensive antique farm machinery displays.
There will also be threshing, steam tractor, sawmill, draft horse and engine demonstrations.
There will also be activities for children on Saturday and Sunday at the Uncle Milt's Shed event in Goessel. The events allow children to try their hands at corn shelling, horseshoes, marble games, beanbag toss and floating wooden boats.
They'll also be able to make their own milk carton immigrant houses, wooden boats, adobe brick blocks and tombstone rubbings, among other things.
As of press time, an exact listing and schedule for all the activities and events had yet to be posted. If you're looking for more information on the event, check its website at wheatco.org for updates.
Admission to Country Threshing Days is $7, and admission lasts all three days of the event.

title: Summer Interns at MB Foundation
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Three community-connected college students worked at MB Foundation as interns and temporary help this summer. Emersyn Funk and Frank Wichert, who grew up in Hillsboro, Kansas, and Barry Ma who was…
content:
Emersyn Funk, Frank Wichert and Barry Ma served as interns this summer at MB Foundation in Hillsboro.
Three community-connected college students worked at MB Foundation as interns and temporary help this summer.
Emersyn Funk and Frank Wichert, who grew up in Hillsboro, Kansas, and Barry Ma who was born and raised in Shanghai, Mainland China and moved to Hillsboro to attend Tabor College, made valuable contributions to MB Foundation.
Through their internships, they worked in a variety of departments and learned new skills that will benefit their future careers.
Funk worked on marketing projects, performed data analytics and assisted the accounting and IT departments.
Wichert contributed to a variety of departments by assessing Financial Health data in the loan department, working with accounting and operations on special projects and scheduling visits from MB Foundation's ministry partners.
Ma assisted the office by verifying data records, arranging files and applications and performing other organizational tasks for the HR and operations teams.
When asked about the experience, Funk said, 'My internship at MB Foundation gave me valuable
experiences through many different departments that have prepared me well for future classes and a career. One of the best parts about working here has been getting to work in a place that shares my values and mission for building the Kingdom of God.'
As summer comes to an end, the three will return to college at Taylor University, MidAmerica Nazarene University and Tabor College.

title: Author to visit Marion County
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Storytelling is an engaging way to pass on to next generations who we are as families and individuals. Author Carolyn Zeisset will speak on 'Keeping Your Heritage Story Alive' at 7 p.m. on Wednesday,…
content:
Storytelling is an engaging way to pass on to next generations who we are as families and individuals. Author Carolyn Zeisset will speak on 'Keeping Your Heritage Story Alive' at 7 p.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 2 at the Marion City Library and then at 12:30 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 3 at the Hillsboro Senior Center at 212 N. Main St. (sponsored by the Hillsboro Public Library and the Hillsboro Senior Center).
Everyone is welcome to attend this informative program at either location.
What stories do you have about your own and your family's heritage? How do you keep those stories alive?
Zeisset will describe the differences between storytelling and the more formal biography, history or memoir. She likens the latter to an obituary read at a funeral and storytelling to the reminiscences people share.
'It's usually the told stories that people remember,' she says.
Zeisset is the author of the historical fiction novel 'Then the Rules Changed' which is set in Ukraine and Marion County. One of her family heritage stories became the idea that developed into the novel, which has been enjoyed by readers ages nine to ninety-nine. Copies of the book will be available for purchase. Cash and checks accepted.
She has roots in central Kansas, graduated from Newton High School and had grandparents in Marion County. She has been an educator at preschool, elementary, middle school and adult levels in public school, religious education, and business settings. Her husband lived in Marion for two years when he was a preschooler.
'Coming to central Kansas is coming home,' she says.
Zeisset has long been interested in stories and history. She says one of her greatest satisfactions comes from readers who say her novel opened conversations in their families about their heritage. During her presentation, she will relate a few stories from her heritage and include time for the audience to recall some of the stories they would like to pass on to younger people in their families.
For more information, call the Marion City Library at 620-382-2442 or the Hillsboro Public Library at 620-947-3827. No reservation is needed.

title: Hillsboro approves metering upgrade
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Oct. 1 and approved upgrading to an advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) on water and electric meters in early spring of next year. City Administrator Matt…
content:
The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Oct. 1 and approved upgrading to an advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) on water and electric meters in early spring of next year.
City Administrator Matt Stiles explained that the city updated all its water meters to the Sensus AMR (automated meter reading) system in 2019 and the electric meters in 2022 with the assistance of Kansas Power Pool (KPP).
'The Sensus AMR system allows a handheld unit to be driven around to read the meters. Currently we
place the handheld in the trash truck and can typically read all but a handful of meters each cycle,' said Stiles.
Implementing that system dramatically reduced staff time needed for reading meters since staff
are only deployed to re-read meters or on service calls.
'The AMR system works well, but we are missing out on some significant advantages to upgrading
to the AMI. When meters were upgraded, we chose Sensus because the meters installed for AMR are also AMI capable with a software upgrade,' said Stiles.
Stiles explained that with the AMI system, a base unit tower is installed that communicates with the meters via secure radio frequency. Meters can be read remotely at any time, alarms can be set to alert different events and pinpoint where service is interrupted and service can be turned off remotely. Data from readings is securely stored in the cloud and can be accessed by staff and customers with a portal option.
'The biggest benefit is for the electric system. Mapping and outage alerts can move our response to
be proactive rather than waiting for customers to call in to report outages. Troubleshooting and
repairs are quicker and safer, restoring service to customers in an efficient manner. Billing and
meter reading is also streamlined. City hall staff can read customers in and out, retrieve real-time
data and potentially disconnect electric customers for nonpayment without having to use a public
works employee,' said Stiles.
The proposed cost for the installation of the base station on top of the large water tower is $50,066.75. The initial setup fees and first-year licensing costs total $76,241.66, making the first-year investment $126,308.41. Each year there are additional licensing fees that will be split between water and electric. 'The cost in 2024 would be the initial $50,066.75 for the equipment and $8,240 for the RNI SaaS Setup Fee. The remaining $68,001.66 would be due in 2025. The initial cost would be paid by the electric department with the ongoing costs being split by electric and water and sewer,' said Stiles.
The relatively small size of the project and the fact that it is not a unique application of technology has
disqualified it for any grant opportunities.
'There are many benefits on the billing and account management side, with AMI reducing the labor and improving our customer service.
The council approved the capital outlay of $50,066.75 for the electrical fund in 2024. The remaining costs will be addressed in 2025.
In other business, the council:
* approved vouchers totaling $315,323.15.
* approved CDBG vouchers totaling $280,300.00.
* heard a department update from City Clerk Danielle Bartel.
* approved the release of the Parkside Homes property with dilapidated duplexes on Ash Street. Stiles explained Parkside Homes entered multiple bond financing arrangements to refund, construct and renovate their facility since 1987. This made the city a titled landowner until the bonds are paid and released. To sell the property, the city and all parties that are partners to the agreement on the bonds must consent.
'There is little financial risk to the city in allowing the property to be released and sold. In fact, it is likely to have more value for the city if the duplexes are removed and new housing is constructed,' said Stiles.
* heard updates about the project for improvements to the water treatment facility approved in the $1.1 million forgivable loan with KDHE to treat iron and manganese. The initial phase of the project consisted of a full-scale pilot study to evaluate the use of chlorine dioxide to treat the raw water. Initial results indicate that chlorine dioxide alone cannot fully treat the raw water when conditions are at their worst. An alternate treatment method such as Ozone (an inorganic molecule formed from dioxygen by the action of ultraviolet light and electrical discharges within the Earth's atmosphere) may need to be evaluated, which is outside the scope and budget of the current project.
The second phase of the project is constructing permanent upgrades at the plant. EBH Engineering completed and KDHE approved plans to install a new permanganate feed system at the plant and to install piping and valving in the plant to allow both clarifiers to be utilized during treatment. Both items aid in treatment during blue-green algae and manganese events and qualify for forgiveness.

title: Hillsboro celebrates public power
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: This week is Public Power Week, a national celebration of the benefits of public power. The week provides the opportunity for locally-owned, not-for-profit public power utilities like Hillsboro to…
content:
This week is Public Power Week, a national celebration of the benefits of public power. The week provides the opportunity for locally-owned, not-for-profit public power utilities like Hillsboro to highlight the benefits and values of public power and hopefully foster a deeper understanding among customers and stakeholders about their local utilities.
'It's a time for communities like ours to recognize the importance of owning and managing our own utilities. It's a way to connect with the community and share the value of having local control over our energy resources,' said Hillsboro Mayor Lou Thurston. 'It's an opportunity to showcase the work our local utility staff does every day to serve Hillsboro. It also strengthens trust between our local government and residents, helping people understand how public power makes Hillsboro a better place to live and do business.'
The week consists of friendly competition where cities can earn points for various activities. The points are then tallied up and the winner gets the traveling trophy. Hillsboro won the competition last year and is going all out to try to win again this year with various activities planned throughout the week such as a cereal food drive, an electric car show, Public Appreciation Wednesday at city hall and more.
About KPP
One of Hillsboro's goals for the week, is to help the community learn more about the Kansas Power Pool (KPP). KPP, one of two municipal energy agencies in Kansas, is the not-for-profit municipal joint action agency that provides all the electricity used in Hillsboro and 23 other Kansas communities.
'Our mission at KPP is to provide affordable and reliable electric service to our members. By working together through KPP, our 24 Kansas cities can be more efficient and cost-effective and succeed in what has become a very complex electric industry,' said CEO and General Manager of KPP Energy Colin Hansen who has worked in the utilities field for over 22 years.
'What makes KPP especially important is that it allows smaller cities like Hillsboro to have a say in how power is generated, purchased and managed,' said Thurston who serves on the KPP Board of Directors. 'Unlike privately-owned utilities, KPP is owned by the member cities it serves. That means decisions are made with the community's best interests in mind, not for the benefit of shareholders. It also fosters collaboration between member cities, sharing best practices and resources. Public power keeps our focus where it should be—on reliability, affordability and community well-being.'
Hillsboro became a member of KPP in November 2005 in the same year that the company formed.
'Being part of KPP has brought many advantages to Hillsboro. First and foremost, it has allowed us to secure stable energy prices, which means our residents and businesses don't face wild fluctuations in their utility bills. It has also given us access to technical expertise and resources for maintaining and improving our local grid. Winter Storm Uri showed us that during extreme weather events, KPP's pooled resources ensure we can manage energy demands more effectively than if we were on our own,' said Thurston.
Hansen said there there are many benefits to being a member, but the most important one is affordable and reliable electric supply.
'KPP electric rates are at the second lowest level that they have been since 2014. It would be significantly more costly for Hillsboro to secure power supply on its own outside of KPP,' said Hansen.
Solar Project
KPP is currently working on a project for a one-megawatt solar array that would span seven acres in Hillsboro. The project site will be out near the wastewater lagoons and will inject power into the Hillsboro distribution system.
According to KPP Director of Engineering Services James Ging, KPP is installing 18 megawatts total throughout the entire membership in addition to the one megawatt in Hillsboro. The other communities included in the project are Clay Center, Ellinwood, Greensburg, Marion, Wellington and Winfield. The entire project aims to generate sufficient electricity to meet the needs of approximately 4,000 homes and businesses.
Ging said the support of USDA PACE (Powering Affordable Clean Energy) loan financing, as well as some investment tax credit, has made the $49 million project economical for KPP members to install.
'KPP and Hillsboro are the only PACE awardee in Kansas so far and one of very few public power systems in the U.S. to be selected. It's exciting to be able to bring low-cost renewable energy to our members through this USDA Rural Utilities Service program. The solar array will be a great addition to our existing portfolio of electric generating sources and serve Hillsboro well,' said Hansen.
'This project is about bringing more renewable energy into the mix, which is something we've been
working toward for years. By participating in this initiative, Hillsboro is demonstrating its commitment to both environmental stewardship and long-term energy security. It helps keep costs stable and reduces our carbon footprint. This means we are acting now to ensure a more sustainable future,' said Thurston. 'I'm proud that we are a part of this project, and I believe it aligns us perfectly with our vision of respecting our past while building strength for the future.'
KPP is still waiting for the terms and conditions on the USDA loan to get to them so the board can approve them.
'Once that happens, then we can start procuring equipment and picking our contractors to do the work. We're expecting it to take about a year to get all 18 megawatts done,' said Ging. 'I think it's gonna be great to have those those solar arrays in communities. We're used to seeing wind windmills everywhere, but not so much solar. I think it'd be kinda cool to have that in your backyard where you can see it. Then we'll also be able to educate the community with that—to do school tours and and do educational events with the schools.'
For more information on Public Power Week activities, check out the City of Hillsboro Facebook page or call the city office at 620-947-3162.

title: Fire destroys Hillsboro home
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: A Hillsboro family is in need of donations after experiencing a house fire on Saturday, Oct. 5. The house, located in the 700 block of Washington St., and all of the family's belongings were…
content:
A fire destroyed a home on Washington St. in Hillsboro on Saturday. The family living there is in need of donations.
A Hillsboro family is in need of donations after experiencing a house fire on Saturday, Oct. 5.
The house, located in the 700 block of Washington St., and all of the family's belongings were completely destroyed.
'Hillsboro, Marion and Durham Fire Departments got dispatched to a structure fire at 703 S. Washington at about ten minutes after 6 p.m. Saturday evening. Hearing the call, Hillsboro Police responded as well and arrived first,' said Hillsboro Fire Chief Ben Steketee.
A police officer informed fire crews that everyone was out of the house.
'I was the first firefighter to arrive on the scene and saw the southeast corner of the house fully involved with flames pushing out approximately 12'. Engine 1952 arrived next with Captain Matt Hein, who quickly directed his crew to perform the initial attack to the exterior using tank water, knowing that Engine 1951 was en route and would provide water supply from the hydrant. And that's what happened. The initial attack was successful, and the exterior fire was knocked down quickly. Then Assistant Fire Chief Todd Helmer led crews from Hillsboro and Marion inside to perform interior firefighting operations, search for fire spread and pets that were reported to be inside. Of the five that were reported, three were found alive,' said Steketee.
Assisting on the scene also were Marion County Sheriff Deputies, Marion County EMS, Marion County Emergency Management and Marion County Communications (dispatch) who were all instrumental to the successful outcome according to Steketee.
The family of Zac and Sarah Gutierrez, 17-year-old daughter and 3-year-old son, have found temporary housing at Country Haven Inn.
They will receive some funds from the American Red Cross to help with housing, but they will need additional funding help to pay for the hotel and find a new place to live in Hillsboro.
Word about the family spread quickly, and donations have already started pouring in.
'We love Hillsboro and want to stay here,' said Sarah. 'We are so grateful for the community support and want to thank everybody that has already reached out to us.'
They are especially in need of clothing, Christian CDs and a CD player for their daughter, bath or other small toys for their son and an air mattress while they figure out housing. They will need household items including furniture once they find housing. They also need notebooks and school supplies for their daughter who they homeschool.
For clothing they need men's shoes size 10.5, 38/40 pants and 2X shirts; women's plus size leggings, 2X t-shirts, size 10.5 shoes; women's large leggings and pants, size 11 shoes; and little boys 4T clothing, size 12 shoes and 5T pulls ups.

title: Sometimes reality is stranger than fiction
author: Shana Thornhill
description: Some people like horror stories. Some people like to be scared out of their wits by fiction. I never much needed that kind of fiction: I had real-life accounts of mishaps and accidents on the farm.…
content:
Some people like horror stories. Some people like to be scared out of their wits by fiction. I never much needed that kind of fiction: I had real-life accounts of mishaps and accidents on the farm. There was the time Grandpa tipped the car or the reason he wouldn't let Mom feed the pigs by herself. There were stories of Grandpa getting a staple stuck in his eye while fixing the chicken coop, or the rats jumping at Grandpa and Uncle Harry from the walls of the granary. There are plenty of stories of people dying
underneath overturned tractors, especially the 'suicide' front ends (like the one we have). Add in the gruesome tales of others' chainsaw accidents, and you have some real nightmare fuel when it comes to possible deadly events out here on our place. Freddy, Michael, and Jason have nothing on us.
One beautiful evening recently, I was getting ready to head into town for a birthday party. I loaded up the cake and tried to holler to Darling Hubby ( like I usually do) that I was getting ready to leave. I always feel like Frau Farbissina from that Austin Powers movie when I call my husband—yelling 'SCAAAAAAAAAHT' at the top of my lungs, feeling like my jaw is unhinging—I'm just glad there's usually nobody around to actually see me do it.
That particular day, I hadn't seen him since about an hour earlier when he put on his shoes and headed outside. I figured he was doing some yard work and just couldn't hear me, so I hollered a few more times before I gave up, left a text and fired up the car. I saw that the tractor was gone, so I figured he must be out working on firewood. As I was driving out of the driveway, I heard a resounding CRUNCHrattlerattlecrunch. At first, I thought nothing of it and pulled out into the road.
Then, I remembered the stories. What if the chainsaw had jerked? What if the TRACTOR had jerked, pulling him down into the creek underneath it, and my darling hubby was, even now, trapped beneath it, unable to call for help? Or worse yet, able to hear his phone ring but unable to reach it as I happily tripped off to a birthday party? YIKES!! I flipped around and barreled towards our south pasture.
I turned in and listened to see if I could hear the tractor running. I couldn't. Heart in my
throat, I rolled the windows down and started bellering for Darling Hubby. 'SCAAAAAAAAAAAAAHT!', then creeping forward and listening, examining the treeline for any skid marks or smoke, simultaneously hoping for and dreading the thought of hearing a scream. No answer. I headed back towards the house.
I navigated the farmyard (just how many used and/or abandoned vehicles do we need, anyway?) and drove down towards the back side of the creek. That leftover stump from last year tried to stop me going round the corner, but my trusty SUV won. I drove down towards the trees, yelling my fool head off.
When I got to the trees, it dawned on me that the horn might be louder than I was, if not by much. I laid on the horn with fervor, wishing desperately for a train horn. No sound, no marks, no smoke. I was beginning to think I'd have to walk the creek bottom on foot. But wait . . .CRUNCH.
There, off to my right, in the walnuts. Blessing the inventor of backup cameras, I reversed as quickly as I dared, and barreled off towards the sound, and the faint sight of smoke. Soon I could hear a familiar growling, chopping sound.
Imagine if you will, a crazed woman in an SUV careening towards you through a pasture. She's hanging out the window, mouth wide open, possibly unhinging her jaw. That's what Scott, my Darling Hubby, saw when he happened to look up from the tractor with the mower attached. I gesticulated wildly, and eventually he understood the vital need to turn off the tractor so he could hear me honk the horn and scream about how I thought he was dead and pinned under the tractor somewhere.
His version of this story will no doubt include the fact that I almost gave him a heart attack, showing up out in the pasture that way. My account includes the fact that I almost strangled him in my sheer relief that he was alive, uninjured and (most importantly) untrapped under the tractor with a chainsaw in the creek.
We both managed to survive that day, and the cake made it to the party unblemished. It just goes to prove that sometimes reality is stranger than fiction! Stay safe out there!

title: USD 410 BOE approves bids and personnel changes
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The USD 410 Board of Education met for their regular monthly meeting on Monday, Oct. 14 and approved base and alternate bids from DCS Services for the Hillsboro Elementary School (HES) sewer lines,…
content:
The USD 410 Board of Education met for their regular monthly meeting on Monday, Oct. 14 and approved base and alternate bids from DCS Services for the Hillsboro Elementary School (HES) sewer lines, Hillsboro Middle High School (HMHS) domestic water line, HMHS HVAC and HES HVAC projects.
'So far, we're up $670,000 under budget, which sounds tremendous. And it's good, but tremendous might be a stretch because in the grand scheme of our projects, that's 5% of the total amount we're going to spend. That means there are more projects and things that we can get done. But in the grand scheme of things, a 5% swing can happen quickly with a lot of projects,' said USD 410 Superintendent Clint Corby. 'It's something to feel good about, but it's not something to think we'll have no matter what happens or that we're in the clear. I wish that were the case, but it does give us a little bit of cushion. I feel good about that. Because most school districts at this point are already playing the game of 'what are we gonna have to cut?' and we are not there yet. So far so good.'
For the HES sewer line repairs project, the board approved subcontractors Five Star Mechanical and Echo GPR services for $ 36,145.92. For the HMHS domestic water line project, the board approved subcontractors Five Star Mechanical for $ 45,515.06. For the HMHS HVAC project, the board approved subcontractors Carrier, Don's Heating and Air, Elcon Services Inc. and EPM Inc. for $2,037,999.92. The board approved the same contractors for the HES HVAC project for $ 513,050.78.
Corby said he is pushing for the middle school gym HVAC portion to be finished before summer.
'With all of our camps this summer, having a gym space is going to be important. If it is feasible for the companies, I would like to do some of that work during school so that way, at least we do have some gym-based space this summer for our teams because the big gym will be unavailable due to the HVAC work going on there,' said Corby.
The board unanimously made the following personnel changes:
*approved the resignation of Tyler Clements from his position as Hillsboro Middle School Assistant Football Coach effective Sept. 26.
*approved the resignation of Anthony Epp from his position as Hillsboro Middle/High School Custodian effective Oct. 11.
*approved the resignation of Rustyn Kerbs from his position as Hillsboro Elementary School Preschool Aide effective Oct. 18.
*approved the resignation of Rustyn Kerbs from his position as Hillsboro Middle School Boys' Head Basketball Coach effective Oct. 18.
*approved the resignation of Tyler Clements from his position as Hillsboro Middle School Boys' Assistant Basketball Coach effective Oct. 18.
*approved the issuance of a contract to Phil Oelke to serve as Hillsboro Middle School Assistant Football Coach (0.33 FTE) effective Sept. 30.
*approved the issuance of a contract to Tyler Clements to serve as Hillsboro Middle School Boys' Head Basketball Coach for the 2024-2025 school year.
*approved the issuance of a contract to Rustyn Kerbs to serve as Hillsboro Middle School Boys' Assistant Basketball Coach for the 2024-2025 school year.
*changed Juana Pritchard's schedule from 7.25 to 5.50 hours per day of serving as Hillsboro High School Instructional Aide effective Sept. 3.
*changed Charles Page's schedule from five to eight hours per day to serve as Hillsboro Elementary School Custodian effective Sept. 16.
*changed Daryl Kliewer's schedule from four to eight hours per day effective Sept. 16 to serve as Hillsboro Middle/High School Custodian in addition to his work as USD 410 Route Bus Driver.
In other business, the board:
*accepted several donations including a $15,500 donation for the HHS GAP program and an $8,000 donation to the HHS CTE programs from St. Stephen's Kansas Charitable Trust. 'They've given us several similar levels of donations for the past several years,' said Corby. 'It's a very big deal. Their generosity over the years has been tremendous and our kids have greatly benefited from it.
*heard reports from HMHS Principal Tyler Weinbrenner and HES Principal Nathan Hiebert on the beginning of school at each of their buildings.
*heard information presented from Layne Frick of Fee Insurance Group about the district's property and casualty insurance.
*met in executive session to conduct Corby's evaluation. No action was taken.

title: Goessel City Council approves chicken ordinance
author: Cynthia Goerzen
description: The Goessel city council met on Oct. 21 and approved Ordinance #311, concerning the number of hens that are allowed. Specifically, the ordinance states: "The maximum number of female chickens…
content:
The Goessel city council met on Oct. 21 and approved Ordinance #311, concerning the number of hens that are allowed. Specifically, the ordinance states: 'The maximum number of female chickens allowable under this provision shall not exceed ten (10).' Roosters are not allowed.
Speaking of animals, the council also discussed the matter of 15 dog owners who do not have tags and collars for their dogs.
The city has also received complaints about cats in town. Pet cats and stray cats are an issue. It was mentioned that some people in town feed groups of cats. Some people with pet cats do not keep them inside but allow them to wander. The comment was made, 'If your cat is important to you, keep it inside,' mentioning that some cities require tagging and limits on the number of cats. Recognizing that cats can carry diseases, the council discussed vaccinations for cats. Some cities require cat vaccinations. Some on the council favor tagging and vaccination, while some on the council do not.
Turning their attention to another matter, the council also passed Ordinance #312, which pertains to house numbers. All houses should be numbered. The numbers should be at least three inches high and two inches wide. The ordinance states that they 'shall be legible and conspicuously placed on the front of each house'.
The ordinance states that the city is divided into an east and west side; Church Street is the dividing line. Houses and buildings on the east side of a street need to have even numbers and odd numbers on the west side. Likewise, houses and buildings on the north side of a street need to have even numbers and odd numbers on the south side.
In other business, the council:
* heard that letters had been sent to the county Wind Farm Planning and Zoning Commission. Esau mentioned an Oct. 24 meeting that was scheduled to discuss a wind and solar moratorium.
* talked about trash that has been dumped at the burn site three weeks in a row. Trash is not allowed there; it is a violation.
* discussed clean-up along the creek. Three properties still need to be cleaned up to avoid flooding in town.
* discussed Harvest Festival, noting that Bethel College Fall Festival was on the same day, as well as a high school volleyball event. Council members talked about the inflatables for children and safety guidelines that had been in place.
* heard from Public Works Director Paxton Van Rossun that street signs have been replaced. The old posts will be sold at a consignment auction.
* heard that the light on top of the water tower needs to be fixed.
* briefly discussed a pickleball court for the city park. Esau had received advice from Newton Public Works.
* discussed the need for a sewer project and talked about money for it. The council would like a CD to save money for the project.
* talked about the need for a fence ordinance. City clerk Jennifer Bliss will research ordinances of other cities.
* reviewed the police report from Anthony Voth, which stated that court had been held the previous week. He had also dealt with driving complaints and nuisance properties.
* discussed the property at 312 South Buller Street. Building inspector James Masters said it is not in compliance.
* discussed a dead tree on a property, noting that the tree could fall on wires or onto the street. The tree needs to be removed, but the owner of the property does not claim certified letters.
* talked about homes that were built before 1982 and could have copper piping.

title: Pomp's Tire Service takes over Rod's Tires
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Pomp's Tire Service, which started in 1939, has 257 locations in 17 states stretching from Ohio to Washington State including a Hillsboro location after taking over Rod's Tires on Oct. 1. Rod Koons…
content:
Pomp's Tire Service, which started in 1939, has 257 locations in 17 states stretching from Ohio to Washington State including a Hillsboro location after taking over Rod's Tires on Oct. 1.
Rod Koons and his wife Carrie established Rod's Tires over 25 years ago in 1999. But they recently decided to make a change and sold the business. The couple had thought about it for a few years and decided it was time.
'As we've progressed through time, one of Carrie's and my goals in life is we need to clean up behind ourselves. We are both 61 years old, and we knew that we were one health issue away from potentially having to lock the doors if something would happen to either one of us,' said Koons. 'That's reality. You can't go through life worrying about the what ifs in life, but you also gotta be aware of the what ifs in life and be prepared and make plans to deal with those in one way or another. So a couple of years ago, we reached out to Pomp's Tire, which is a major corporation, because we knew with our size and the value of our assets and the physical plant that we had here, our options of people to sell to were very limited just because of the sheer amount of dollars. An individual isn't gonna have that kind of resources available to complete the transaction.'
Koons said that Pomps hasn't grown so much through building brick-and-mortar buildings but through acquisition.
'Just people like us that reached out. They're a 3rd-generation, family-owned company based out of Green Bay, Wisconsin. Just a solid bunch. It's just a very good people-friendly, employee-minded company. Here in the 1st couple weeks, we've seen employees are important to them,' said Koons. 'The employees are important, not only their well-being but their safety at work. That's a big part of what Pomp's is about. Not that we were unsafe, but they've got people and resources to make sure that happens and there's some value in that.'
While many things will stay the same, there will be changes with the new ownership, but Koons feels there will be positive changes.
'There will still be a place here providing the services that we provided, but it isn't gonna be the same. I'm not gonna sit here and say that because that's foolishness when people say that when there's change. Because if it was gonna be the same, you wouldn't have made the change. It's going to be different,' said Koons. 'There's probably better opportunities for our employees for advancement. There's probably overall a better benefit package, a few more perks and things like that.'
All of the employees have been maintained and long-time employee Dallas Bartel is the new manager.
One thing that will change is the Koons' presence.
'Carrie is busy right now closing out our books and those types of things. But then she is stepping back and doing some things that she hasn't gotten to do for 25-plus years because of this place,' said Koons. 'And I'm actually gonna take a position out of the store but within the company. It's an agricultural sales development position throughout a three-state region of Kansas, Nebraska and Missouri to provide some support and resources and knowledge to some of the other stores to help grow the Ag side of their business. One of the things that we talked about from day one with the Pomp's representatives was that for it to become a Pomp's location I really need to be out of here. It's just how it is for it to transition on.'
Koons is pleased with the experience they had.
'We've had a great 25-plus years. It's been a wonderful experience, and it's kind of weird to move out of something that you really enjoy doing and still had a passion for. A lot of times when you cease doing something, it says you're tired of doing it or whatnot. And that was never our reasoning. We just knew that we had to take advantage of this opportunity because we weren't gonna get many other opportunities,' said Koons. 'We can all look around and see all the empty steel buildings in this community and know how that book ends. We made a decision so we could avoid being a part of that. Opportunity arose, and we made that decision and moved ahead. We're happy and blessed that we could be in the driver's seat of that opportunity rather than being in the back seat and having to react because things change.'
And now, he is looking forward to what is next.
'It's simply a new season in our lives. We're looking forward to the new season. We really are excited about the things that are ahead for us and the store and the community,' said Koons.
Pomp's Tire Service is open 8 a.m.-5:30 p.m. Monday through Friday and 8 a.m.-12 p.m. Saturday and is located at 401 Orchard Dr. The phone number is 620-947-5789. For more information, visit pompstire.com.

title: Brookens to retire from 46-year law career
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: After 46 years of practicing law, Bob Brookens has decided to retire. 'At the end of the month, I will be shutting the doors. October 31st will be the last day for my office,' said Brookens. 'Part of…
content:
Bob Brookens will retire at the end of the month. He has been a lawyer in Marion County since 1978.
After 46 years of practicing law, Bob Brookens has decided to retire.
'At the end of the month, I will be shutting the doors. October 31st will be the last day for my office,' said Brookens. 'Part of me says I need to continue, but another side says I need to not and that's the hard part.'
Brookens is well known around Marion County, particularly in Marion and Hillsboro where he has practiced law in offices in each town. He is also familiar with other towns in Marion County.
'I was city attorney all the way up to Lost Springs, and I was either the prosecutor or the city attorney in Peabody, Burns and Goessel. I got to know a lot of people and enjoyed wherever I was. I had good relationships with all the people I worked with,' said Brookens.
Brookens has practiced in Marion County his entire career since moving here in 1978. In 1981, he joined the firm of Morse and Batt in Marion. He also joined the Hillsboro office a few years later. That office opened up in Hillsboro in 1956.
'I started going to the Hillsboro office in '85. I continuously did that until reality hit. I had to shut the Hillsboro office down in 2023. Between rent, having a phone that forwards calls, computer access and more, it just became unrealistic for me to maintain both offices. I decided to keep the office in Marion since the courthouse is there,' said Brookens.
Now he is closing up the Marion office since there is no one to take over.
'I have tried for someone to come in. I had a couple that came from law school but obviously wanted to be in a different place because they left and went to a vastly different location. It wasn't like they went to another small county. Throughout the state of Kansas, there is a shortage of attorneys,' said Brookens.
Brookens, who is an Eagle Scout and raised four boys with his wife Anita in the Marion area, is sad to be ending his career but believes it is the best decision.
'An attorney needs to be comfortable with what they're doing, and I want to leave while I'm comfortable with what I do. I don't want to be looking over my shoulder to see if I'm doing things wrong. I want the people that are seeing me even now to know that we're doing things the right way,' said Brookens.
He has many great memories of his time as a lawyer.
'My favorite part was dealing with a variety of people. This county has an incredible variety of people, all of whom I've enjoyed. I even enjoyed some of the criminal cases that I had because, in several of the cases where somebody got convicted, they stayed in touch through the years afterward and reported to me how they were doing once they got out of prison. So we obviously had some kind of relationship,' said Brookens. 'One man that I remember went into prison, and I sent a very simple version of the Bible with him because he had trouble reading. I heard from him about two and a half years later that he had completed it and he was in a men's group. He was still going back to the scriptures that I had highlighted for him. He said, 'They got me through, and I will never ever do the things that I did before'. That was worth everything.'
He also served as a state representative for two terms.
'My law partner went on the bench as a judge, and I had to get back to work full time so I didn't run again. The community and being an attorney for Marion County was far more important than being in the legislature,' said Brookens.
Brookens isn't exactly sure yet what retirement will look like for him.
'I've spent enough time just getting things ready to shut down that I haven't done a lot of planning what we will do. I'd like to think we'll do a little traveling. I've been to 46 of the states and would like to go to the last four but whether we do it or not depends on how tired we feel,' said Brookens.
There will be a retirement reception for Brookens from 3-5 p.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 30 at his office at 403 E. Main in Marion. All are welcome.

title: Tabor student creates art for local businesses
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: London Eichelberger, a senior at Tabor College, stumbled into a side hustle that she calls Highclass Doodles. 'It's still very much in that baby process of just doing things here and there. I kind of…
content:
London Eichelberger poses in front of a mural she created for Villa Bella Boutique in Hillsboro. She has also painted large murals on the windows of Level Up in Hillsboro.
London Eichelberger, a senior at Tabor College, stumbled into a side hustle that she calls Highclass Doodles.
'It's still very much in that baby process of just doing things here and there. I kind of started it by asking Shannon (Parsons, co-owner of Level Up in Hillsboro) if I could do her window,' said Eichelberger. 'I just really enjoyed the new mural in town. And I'd always seen artwork done on windows. So I asked if I could do it. Just kind of off-shooting, wondering if I could just try it out. I've never done it before and she said sure.'
Eichelberger really enjoyed doing that first mural and has since continued to create one each season. Her newest fall mural is up currently at Level Up.
'I just started with hers and really enjoyed it. Then she had me keep coming back, and by the second one I felt like I could start doing this more often and for more people because I really enjoyed it.'
'London is amazing. Everything that she's done for me has been freehand. She creates two or three different scenarios, and then we sit down and decide which one we're going to do, said Parsons. 'She's just a very creative young lady, and she's got a lot going for her. I love that she's done this for us and creates these different themes for different times of the year. It's really helped our business as well. So it's kind of a win for her because she gets to do something that she enjoys, and it also helps for our business as well.'
After getting a few murals at Level Up under her belt, Eichelberger started reaching out to other people and businesses. Villa Bella boutique owner Mallory Ediger hired her to do a permanent mural outside on the north wall of the building.
'London was great to work with throughout the entire mural process. She was able to take our vision and made multiple sketches so we had some great options to look at. She was able to create a great mural that represents our brand well, and we are so excited to have people take photos in front of it,' said Ediger.
Eichelberger said her favorite part of doing the murals is painting on a large scale.
'It's something you don't get to do very often. It's very intimidating and challenging but in a good way. I find it very relaxing and kinda soothing. It's very calming. Being outside is really nice, too,' said Eichelberger. 'It's just a simple process that isn't too tedious to think about especially if you go in with a plan. Then you just get to do the painting which is the fun part.'
She found doing the Villa Bella mural was a little more difficult since it is permanent.
'I was challenge with making sure it's perfect and everything's measured properly,' said Eichelberger. 'With the murals at Level Up, I had a plan going in but free-handed it. I didn't really do a lot of measuring because it allowed for a bit more freedom since it was gonna be taken off. With it being on glass, it's easier to remove during the process.'
The artist has some more projects in the works.
'I have made some connections in Marion. I have also been in talks of doing one for my friend back home in the Kansas City, MO area who has her own business as well as some signage for her,' said Eichelberger.
As she wraps up her senior year at Tabor with an individualized theater major and a psychology minor, she hopes to build up more of her portfolio of past projects and expand, because she's enjoyed painting the murals.
'I would like to continue doing more of it. I will probably keep it as more of a side hustle just because it's not something that I would do full-time. I feel like that'd also be kind of difficult since it's very niche and requires good weather which the Midwest isn't really known for. I'll do it more as a fun hobby but something that I'd like to pursue and continue as I graduate and go on to get my master's. Just a little way to make extra money and have some fun,' said Eichelberger.
Eichelberger said she is not only aimed toward small businesses but to anybody who's interested in any type of artwork.
'I've had people talk to me about doing a nursery or things like that. I can do inside or outside,' said Eichelberger.
'If there's anybody that wants to just add a little creativity to the front of their business, London's a great option for that. People see us a little bit clearer now when they drive by and they're like, 'Oh, what is that fun stuff?' So I think that's helped us, too,' said Parsons.
For more information or to hire Eichelberger, go to her Instagram @high_doodles, email
londonme5586@gmail.com or call or text 816-912-8012.

title: Marion County Health Fair will be Nov. 2
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Live music will launch the annual Marion County Health Fair on Saturday, Nov. 2. Bob Delk & Friends, sponsored by Tampa State Bank, will entertain from 8-9:30 a.m. The fair is from 8-11 a.m. at the…
content:
Susan Mayo, Bob Delk and Steve Hanneman will be providing live music for the Marion County Health Fair in Marion on Saturday, Nov. 2 at the Marion Sports and Aquatics Center.
Live music will launch the annual Marion County Health Fair on Saturday, Nov. 2. Bob Delk & Friends, sponsored by Tampa State Bank, will entertain from 8-9:30 a.m. The fair is from 8-11 a.m. at the Marion Sports and Aquatics Center at 104 S. Thorp Street in Marion.
HealthX Talks—where 'eXperts' have 15 minutes to share tips for staying alive and well—follow from 9:30-10:30 a.m. This year's experts are:
Kickboxing Demonstrations with Keri Collett of St. Luke Hospital
Trending Weather Apps with Marcy Hostetler, Marion Co. Emergency Management
Medical Spa Wellness Services with Katie Perry of S&S MEDSPA
Healthy Nutrition for all Ages with Shannan Parsons of Level Up & Next Level Nutrition
The inexpensive lab tests—offered throughout the morning by St. Luke Hospital and Hillsboro Community Hospital—are the big attraction at the Health Fair. Four tests for just $35: Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), lipid panel, complete blood count (CBC) with differential, and thyroid-stimulating hormone test (TSH). Cash, check or credit card will be accepted.
Additional tests, such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) for men 40 and older, hemoglobin A1C, and free thyroxine test (FT4), are also available for $15 each. Lab results are mailed within one to two weeks after the Health Fair.
The latest Moderna COVID-19 vaccine, for ages 12 and older, will be offered by the Marion County Health Department, along with Fluzone, Flublok (ages 50-64) and High Dose (65+) flu vaccines. The Marion County Health Department bills most major insurance companies. Please bring your primary insurance card and driver's license. Uninsured? No worries—we have options available for those without insurance.
Over 25 exhibitors will be present and offer prize drawings. Prizes include gift cards, free services, gift baskets and other tantalizing merchandise.
Kids' Corner will feature activities and prizes for the younger visitors. Susan Mueller will be on hand with bunny rabbits for the children to meet at 9 a.m. She'll also share some short bunny stories while teaching children how to care for and be kind to pets.
Three massage therapists, Rachel Gfeller, Shirley Davis and Jerusalem Driggers, will offer free, 15-minute massages throughout the Fair. Marion County Ambulance will perform blood pressure checks. Legacy Eyecare will clean and adjust your glasses. Safe Hope will have a popcorn machine going. This is just a taste of what exhibitors will offer on Nov. 2.
Scoops & Sweets of Marion will add a sweet note to the event. Madison Vinduska will sell warm drinks and her delicious pastries.
'The annual health fair is a great chance to meet local health providers, get lab work at a discounted
rate and get your flu shot or COVID-19 vaccine all in one stop,' said Marion County Health Department Director Krista Schneider.
This fun and informative event is sponsored by the Marion County Health Department, St. Luke Hospital and Hillsboro Community Hospital.

Temmuz-eylül döneminde THY'nin toplam geliri geçen yılın aynı döneminin yüksek baz etkisine rağmen yıllık olarak yüzde 4,9 yükseldi ve 6,6 milyar dolara ulaştı. Toplam gelirin yüzde 84'ünü oluşturan yolcu gelirleri Uzak Doğu bölgesinin güçlü katkısıyla 5,6 milyar dolar olarak gerçekleşirken, kargo gelirleri geçen yılın aynı dönemine göre yüzde 47 artarak 911 milyon dolar oldu.
Turkish Cargo üçüncü çeyrekte taşıdığı kargo miktarını yüzde 16,8 artırırken, Uluslararası Hava Taşımacılığı Birliği'nin (IATA) eylül ayı verilerine göre yüzde 5,7 pazar payıyla dünyanın en büyük üçüncü hava kargo taşıyıcısı oldu.
Üçüncü çeyrekte toplam yolcu ve kargo gelirinin yaklaşık 4,9 milyar doları ihracat geliri olarak kaydedilirken, 9 ayda THY'nin ülkeye kazandırdığı toplam ihracat tutarı 12,9 milyar dolara ulaştı. Ortaklığın 2002 yılından bu yana 18 katına çıkarak yaklaşık 40 milyar dolara ulaşan toplam varlığı Türkiye ekonomisi için önemli bir değer kaynağı oluşturmaya devam etti. Esas faaliyet karı 1,3 milyar dolar oldu
Yolcu birim gelirlerindeki rekabet kaynaklı baskı, motor problemleri ve küresel enflasyonun maliyetler üzerindeki olumsuz etkileri nedeniyle esas faaliyet karı üçüncü çeyrekte 1,3 milyar dolar seviyesinde gerçekleşti. Ortaklığın operasyonel nakit yaratma gücünü gösteren FAVKÖK (faiz, vergi, amortisman ve kira öncesi kar) ise 2,3 milyar dolar oldu. Aynı dönemde FAVKÖK marjı yüzde 35,2'ye ulaşarak hem tarihsel ortalamasının hem de emsallerinin üzerinde kaydedildi.
THY'nin etkin ve dinamik portföy yönetimi sayesinde ürettiği finansal gelirleri ise net karını destekleyen önemli bir unsur oldu. Uçak sayısı 467'ye çıktı
100. Yıl Stratejisi çerçevesinde 2033 yılında 800 uçağı aşan bir filoya sahip olmayı hedefleyen Ortaklık, uçak üretiminde yaşanan darboğaza rağmen yılın 9 ayında filosunu yıllık yüzde 9 büyüterek uçak sayısını 467'ye çıkarttı.
Filosunu genişletirken uçak finansmanında uyguladığı çeşitlendirme stratejisiyle finansman maliyetini ve kur risklerini en aza indirmeyi hedefleyen Türk Hava Yolları, üçüncü çeyrekte 3 adet Airbus A350 uçağı için Çin Yuanı ile borçlanarak bu döviz cinsinde Çin anakarası dışında ilk kez finansman sağlayan hava yolu oldu.
Aynı dönemde yakıt verimliliği yüksek 2 adet A321-Neo uçağının finansmanı için ilk kez sürdürülebilirlik bağlantılı kredi kullanan Ortaklık, sürdürülebilir finansman alanında da yer edindi. Havacılık sektörünün her alanında başarılarıyla adından sıkça söz ettiren THY, öncü niteliğindeki finansman işlemleriyle de dikkatleri üzerine çekti ve Airline Economics tarafından üç ayrı finansman ödülüne layık görüldü.

title: Pet groomer loves working with animals in new business
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Karina LaPerle Torres has always loved animals and has now found a way to spend more time with them while getting paid. 'My dad purchased a home on North Lincoln that he rebuilt from the ground up. My…
content:
Karina LaPerle Torres recently opened Pretty Paws Pet Grooming & boutique in Hillsboro.
Karina LaPerle Torres has always loved animals and has now found a way to spend more time with them while getting paid.
'My dad purchased a home on North Lincoln that he rebuilt from the ground up. My mom, dad and I turned it into a pet grooming business. So once we got it all set up, we got a permit from the city. And once it was approved, I began accepting clients,' said Torres.
Pretty Paws Pet Grooming and Boutique, located in Hillsboro, offers grooming for small animals by appointment.
'I bathe, shave and trim nails for dogs. I do nails for small animals like kitty cats, guinea pigs and such,' said Torres.
The shop also has a boutique area with animal-themed items, like dog ear-cleaning wipes, bows, leashes and more available for purchase.
'It's been fun. I'm enjoying it,' said Torres.
While the shop just recently opened, Torres has been doing pet grooming for three years. She got started in the business after learning how to care for her dog.
'I have a husky, and she requires a lot of care with cleaning and stuff. I started trimming her paws and then I would do her nails. My mom got some more pups too, and she needed someone to bathe them so I started helping her,' said Torres.
She then started a business called Zen Dog where she would walk dogs and do dog sitting at people's houses who couldn't travel.
'Or I would travel to the vet clinic and drop the dogs off at their house and people would pay me to do that. And I would get asked if I bathe dogs. Eventually I just took the plunge and started doing it. I did a mobile grooming service. And then I finally got my own spot,' said Torres. 'It's been so great. I love meeting the dogs and getting a connection with them. With dogs, they'll get to know you and when they see you and they like you, they make it known. It's so cute to see them come in and wiggle instead of sometimes when they first come in, they'll cower and be nervous. But usually after the first time they come, their owners will bring them back and they just get so excited. It makes me feel like I accomplished something when I build a trusting relationship with them,' said Torres. Karina LaPerle Torres recently opened Pretty Paws Pet Grooming & boutique in Hillsboro.
Her parents, Erik and Trini Torres who own Pueblo Viejo in Hillsboro, also help with the new business.
'My mom and I just adore animals, so this has been in the works for quite some time. I'm the only one that does the grooming, but she helps manage the location. She and my dad were the ones that put it all together and I helped with inventory and stuff. We all work together on it just about as equal. I just groom them,' said Torres. 'It's a family business. If anything needs to be repaired, my dad's there. If I need help, my mom comes in, and she'll love on them because she really loves animals, too. This was something that she was pushing for me. She believed in the dream and that we needed to do this and it happened.'
Torres said the business has been going great and has people coming in from all over Marion County. And for those who can't make it on their own, Torres can help out.
'I try really hard to help people who don't have the ability to take their pets during the week so I'll be available for them when it's best for them. When you're a business owner, you can't really take your animals during the week. So if they tell me 'My schedule is crazy, I own this business or I'm disabled', I will go pick them up. I will walk them to their homes. I will meet them on an off day or at a later time and just try to squeeze everybody in as best as I can,' said Torres.
While Torres has a lot of flexibility, she does not take walk-ins and operates by appointment only.
Pretty Paws Pet Grooming & Boutique is located at 207 N. Lincoln in Hillsboro. To schedule an appointment for your pet, call or text 620-504-2237 or visit their Facebook page at Pretty Paws Pet Grooming & Boutique.

title: Harvey County United Way adds Marion County to coverage
author: Sarah Beauchamp
description: By Sarah Beauchamp After residents of Marion County weren't being served by the surrounding United Way organizations, Harvey County Director Dalton Black began working to take it on. 'I'm really…
content:
By Sarah Beauchamp
After residents of Marion County weren't being served by the surrounding United Way organizations, Harvey County Director Dalton Black began working to take it on.
'I'm really excited,' Black said. 'I've been working on this for three-plus years. I'm excited to see it moving forward.'
The organization recently announced that it was now the United Way of Harvey and Marion Counties.
Part of Marion County had been assigned to Harvey County, but parts were assigned to McPherson and Flint Hills United Way in Emporia. Black reached out to Flint Hills to see if they were interested in taking over the Marion County coverage area.
With Emporia being so far away, they weren't interested and relinquished their coverage area to Harvey County. For awhile, the county was split between Harvey and McPherson.
'We had a longer conversation about our futures, and they ultimately decided it was not something they wanted to pursue,' Black said about McPherson.
Black said many of United Way's partners, like Heart to Heart, Safehope and Trinity Heights Respite, all serve Marion County, as well.
'It seemed like a natural fit for us,' Black said.
After taking over from McPherson, Black said they spent time reaching out to the Marion County community to see what the needs were and if there was interest in a United Way there.
Right now, Black said they plan to focus on supporting the partner agencies that serve Marion County while they build a foundation.
'We're building a base of support and getting involved in task forces there,' Black said. 'As we get more entrenched in Marion, we'll see different needs.'
While overall funding will benefit both counties, Black said they were keeping the finances separate. He said all fundraising efforts would be kept in the county the money was raised in.
'That was a big concern people had as we reached out to them,' Black said.
Black said the focus areas for Marion County would be different. He referenced Marion County's established child care task force, compared to Harvey's new one and said it wouldn't make sense to get involved there.
For now, an employee who lives in Marion County is working there one day a week to start getting more established. Black said as time goes on, he hopes to have a full-time Marion County employee. Right now, he said they were relying on her to lay the foundation but acknowledged there was a disconnect with physically traveling back and forth between the counties.
'I feel like that's the turning point, when you have a person that's fully dedicated in the community,' Black said.

title: How weather affects outdoor sporting events
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: Back in the late 70s and early 80s, I was an announcer at a Newton radio station. One person I had the pleasure of knowing there was Gene Price. In addition to selling advertising, he also gave…
content:
Back in the late 70s and early 80s, I was an announcer at a Newton radio station. One person I had the pleasure of knowing there was Gene Price. In addition to selling advertising, he also gave weather reports.
He generally used forecasts from the National Weather Service, but he occasionally had his own perspective on what to expect. For example, on occasion, he forecasted heavy rain in the coming days, because he observed that a number of turtles were seen crossing roads.
Being skeptical, I asked him, 'How do you know the turtles aren't crossing the road just to get to the other side?'
However, more often than not, his forecast methods were accurate.
Once I gave Gene a gag gift — a weather rock to help with his forecasting. The rock was attached to a piece of string and connected to a piece of wood.
Words etched onto the wood said something like this: 'If rock is wet, it's raining; if white, it's snowing; if moving, it's windy; if spinning, it's a tornado.' He received the gift in good humor.
We experience weather every day, and it often plays a significant role in outdoor sporting events. But which sports are most affected by wind, rain, heat, cold, and snow? Anyone who has played golf or tennis knows how wind can wreak havoc with the sports.
Auto racing on oval tracks is almost always canceled or delayed when it rains. Heavy rain also affects football games, soccer, and track and field meets. But lightning is the game-stopper in almost every situation.
Typically, the high school athletic or activities director will have a lightning detector to monitor how close lightning strikes are to the stadium. In general, a significant lightning threat extends about 6 to 10 miles from the base of a thunderstorm cloud.
According to the National Federation of State High School Associations, the area must remain lightning-free for 30 minutes before play can resume.
For college football games, if lightning strikes within an eight-mile radius of a game, the NCAA requires a minimum of 30 minutes to pass without lightning before play can resume. An additional 30 minutes is added to the clock for each lightning strike occurring within that radius.
Playing a game in the rain makes football games more sloppy, even on artificial turf, because traction becomes an issue, as does holding onto a wet, slippery football.
If it rains for very long or hard in baseball, the game will get delayed or postponed. A wet field and wet baseball is a problem. It's dangerous for a pitcher to throw a ball when it's hard to get a grip.
As a former soccer official, I can testify that rain is a problem, especially if you wear glasses. I recall officiating a college soccer game in Hesston during a steady and sometimes hard rain. I can't really remember or tell you what happened because I honestly didn't see much of what happened.
Wind also can affect the quality of play. Of course, in most cases, both teams are helped or hindered by a strong wind at their backs or in their faces. Field position can change dramatically in windy conditions.
I personally experienced a case where the wind only helped one team in a soccer match.
Our team (Tabor College) played the first half going into a stiff wind. You hope to keep the score tied or close until half, when you change directions and have the wind at your backs in the second half. Unfortunately, about five minutes before the first half ended, a front blew through and the wind shifted 180 degrees in the opposite direction.
The result? We played virtually the entire game into the wind, which was a bummer. It was doubly a bummer because the other team was more talented than we were to begin with. Suffice it to say, the final score wasn't close.
Even with our advanced technology, forecasting the weather is challenging. Perhaps the most accurate one I've heard is: 'Weather forecast for tonight: dark. Continued dark overnight, with widely scattered light by morning.

title: Hillsboro discusses plans for fire station
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Nov. 5 where they heard from Hillsboro Fire Chief and Building Inspector Ben Steketee. Steketee presented the annual department head report with a PowerPoint…
content:
The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Nov. 5 where they heard from Hillsboro Fire Chief and Building Inspector Ben Steketee. Steketee presented the annual department head report with a PowerPoint report on the building department and fire department activities.
He highlighted the contributions of Caren Funk who assists with contractor licensing, permit process and fire department secretary duties. Steketee also gave statistics including 59 building permits issued, 94 contractors licensed and $1730,764.38 in project value.
Steketee also updated the council on training activities, including wildland fire training and rescue tool comparison events. He reported that training events include physical exertion tests and EMS assist calls, with firefighters undergoing rigorous training to ensure readiness. Steketee informed the council that the fire department has responded to 13 wildland fires, 11 vehicle accidents and nine rescues this year.
Steketee emphasized the importance of a new fire station to accommodate the growing number of firefighters and equipment to serve the city and the greater area.
'As we grow to keep up with the needs of the public, we have compressed ourselves into our existing facilities as tightly as we can. We have outgrown the space. Having firefighters don their gear in the same spaces where the trucks are exiting is a recipe for an injury or worse. So we placed some of our apparatus in the old AMPI building, which creates a delay responding with those pieces of equipment. With roof leaks that persist despite repairs being attempted, we have double-stacked the apparatus,' said Steketee.
The increasing number of volunteer firefighters is another reason a new building is needed.
'We have a glut of volunteer firefighters. In fact, too many. That's very unusual,' said Steketee.
'That speaks very clearly to the culture that you have amongst your team, and people want to be part of something that's successful and that feels good to be part of. They know that they've got a brother and sisterhood and that you guys have each other's back,' said Mayor Lou Thurston.
Thurston also emphasized the urgency of addressing fire station needs to ensure public safety and future growth.
'I think that the issue has never been the need for this. It's just the cost associated with it. And listening to Ben, I think he's made a pretty good case that we need to do this sooner rather than later. You know the need for this is not getting less, and we can't keep counting on luck or fate to keep somebody alive,' said Thurston.
Hillsboro City Administrator Matt Stiles provided a financing analysis including a $6.1 million project cost and various financing options including temporary note financing, USDA Rural Development financing and potential grant money. He also discussed the benefits and challenges of each financing option, emphasizing the importance of acting now to secure funding.
'We're going to have to borrow the money. We don't, unfortunately, have that money sitting around. We're looking at a $6.1 million project cost, thinking that by the time we do it, things may go up a little bit, and we have to outfit this thing. So it's not just building the building. We've got to put things in it,' said Stiles. 'It's never going to get cheaper from today. If it's something that we're really wanting to do, we would want to now. Now is as good a time as any. As far as the construction cost goes and how you pay for it—that's the $6 million question.'
Thurston emphasized the significance of the decision and the need for the council to step up and serve the community.
'Unfortunately, those things aren't getting cheaper, but it's extremely important. This may be one of the most important decisions as a council that we're gonna make while those of us that are on the council are serving. It's not easy, but that's why you got elected to serve. This is that time to step up and serve,' said Thurston. 'We cover 119 square miles. It's also important to think about not just protecting what we have but protecting what we're going to have. We are going to have 12 new duplexes, 24 new living units with the potential to double that to protect and a lot more people coming. The new childcare center will need protection. We have got to be on top of our game to protect. It's not just who we are today, but we gotta think about who we're gonna be in the future.'
Stiles outlined the next steps, including securing temporary note financing and working with architects and builders.
The council agreed to move forward to secure the new fire station.
In other business, the council:
* approved vouchers totaling $300,007.12.
* approved the appointment Alicia Lopez to the Hillsboro Housing Authority board.
* recognized Matt Hein, Hillsboro Street Department, for 10 years of service. Hein expressed his gratitude and thanked the City of Hillsboro for the recognition.
* approved a $215,600 bid from APAC Shears for water plant improvements.
* approved increasing the Christmas bonus for city employees to $75 and keeping the bonus at $50 for council members.
