title: Goessel hires new public works director
author: Cynthia Goerzen
description: Goessel City Council held a special meeting on Nov. 11 to interview a candidate for the full-time public works position since the current public works director, Paxton Van Rossun, has requested part…
content:
Goessel City Council held a special meeting on Nov. 11 to interview a candidate for the full-time public works position since the current public works director, Paxton Van Rossun, has requested part-time hours. He will continue working for the city 16 hours a week.
Alex Goossen was the only applicant for the job. Goossen grew up in the Goessel community and currently works as a park ranger at Meade State Park. Goossen accepted the public works job for $29 per hour, with the expectation that he will become water and wastewater certified. He will begin the public works job on Dec. 9.
The council voted to spend up to $300 a year on clothing for public works, with the name and logo on the front of the shirts and public works on the back. Mayor Evan Esau thought it was important to identify who is coming onto a resident's yard.
On another matter, the council spent considerable time at the regular Nov. 18 meeting discussing cats. Some on the council favor requiring cats to be vaccinated for rabies. Others do not. Some would like cats to wear a collar with a tag. Others said cats will not wear a collar.
Some on the council prefer that cats not be allowed to roam but kept on the owner's property. Some thought cats should be allowed to roam. Some keep their cats inside during the day and allow them to roam at night. Others keep their cats inside and do not allow them to roam. Comments were made that dog owners are required to scoop up after their pets, but there is no stipulation for cats that make a mess on property other than their own. The council talked about the matter of cats trespassing onto someone else's property and fighting the pet cats there. The comment was made, 'Your cat is trespassing if it is on my property.'
The council also discussed the number of cats that should be allowed but made no decision. Some on the council would like to limit the number of cats per household. It was noted that many cats live in a building near the gas pumps, and someone comes to feed them.
The council considered a cat ordinance but did not vote on it.
In other business, the council:
* talked about a Christmas light contest. The public will vote to determine the winner.
* thanked council member Ariel Krause for the mum plants she had purchased for the planters outside the front doors of the city building.
* considered a request for a recreational vehicle in the mobile home park. Krause mentioned the two temporary camper hook-ups at the city park and noted that several people in town use an RV as their permanent home. The council talked about an RV that has been parked on a street and mentioned concern about blocking emergency vehicles.
* spent some time listening to David Pyle of McPherson talk about rental housing he would like to build in Goessel. Formerly, he built church sanctuaries and big commercial buildings. Pyle's sons work with him. However he would like to stay within an hour's drive of McPherson and currently prefers to build smaller buildings such as rental duplexes. A one-bedroom duplex costs $620 per month. He is currently building some duplexes in Marion. Some of his duplexes have garages, and some do not. Council members will look into the matter but felt like Goessel has more need for family housing.
* talked about rock for the streets.
* talked about a dead tree on private property that needs to be removed and will be dealt with in municipal court.
* talked about water and sewer issues at the 112 South Buller property.
* passed Ordinance #313 which requires building permits when putting up fences and establishes setback requirements.
* approved the month's expenses of $39,668.06.

title: HCF continues under new leader
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Over the past two decades, the Hillsboro Community Foundation (HCF) has grown into a trusted partner for local donors and nonprofits alike. HCF has facilitated the establishment of numerous charitable…
content:
Chad Hughbanks
Over the past two decades, the Hillsboro Community Foundation (HCF) has grown into a trusted partner for local donors and nonprofits alike. HCF has facilitated the establishment of numerous charitable funds, enabling individuals and families to leave a lasting legacy for Hillsboro and the surrounding community. These funds have supported a wide range of initiatives, including scholarships, community projects, nonprofit support, health, arts and culture.
The organization recently celebrated its 20th anniversary with a huge Dollars-4-Scholars campaign.
Hillsboro's generous community donated $83,685, which was then matched by an additional $70,000 from the Patterson Family Foundation.
This significant increase in funding will directly benefit 12 scholarships, empowering deserving students to pursue their dreams.
'It was gratifying to see the community and donor support for our students during the campaign. These contributions are a big step towards growing the scholarships awarded through the foundation. We thank all the donors who helped make this campaign successful,' said HCF Board Treasurer Kelly Groening.
On Oct. 7, the Hillsboro Community Foundation strengthened its future by hiring Chad Hughbanks as its new full-time director. Hughbanks's hiring replaced the part-time director position previously held by Max Heinrichs, made possible by a Capacity Building grant from the Patterson Family Foundation.
A lifelong resident of the area, Hughbanks grew up north of Lehigh and graduated from Hillsboro High in 2006. He is proud to serve the community he has called home since he was a kid.
Since 2020, Hughbanks has been a dedicated volunteer with the Hillsboro Community Foundation.
'I started off as a volunteer graphic designer. I did that and then became part of the grant cycle committee as a community member. I was involved with that for two years prior to coming on as a board member in December of 2023,' said Hughbanks.
It was during the campaign planning that Hughbanks realized he might be ready to take on the director role.
'That was about the time when I started having conversations internally with the foundation board members and had a lot of support going forward,' said Hughbanks.
He is excited to contribute to the Foundation's mission and continue making a positive impact on the community he loves.
'Dedicating my time and energy to the community I grew up in was a simple decision to make. Hillsboro is my home. Being able to help contribute to its future is something I've wanted to do for a long time,' said Hughbanks. 'Growing up, my parents instilled in my brother and me that your family and community will take care of you, but you need to take care of your family and community, as well.'
'In less than two months as director, Chad has already had a very positive impact on the foundation, bringing energy, vision, and fresh ideas. Under his direction, we believe the foundation's role of facilitating charitable giving in the Hillsboro area is in good hands,' said Groening.
'I'm excited to build on the legacy of the dedicated individuals who founded and shaped the Hillsboro Community Foundation. From the original five visionaries to the 54 board members who've served, and from past directors like Kathy, Cynthia, Bonnie, Virginia, Max and Erin, their hard work has laid a strong foundation. My goal is to propel HCF into the next twenty years and beyond,' said Hughbanks.
The next focus for Hughbanks is Giving Tuesday.
'Giving Tuesday is our next event. That's going to be December 3rd, and we're hosting it at Pizza Hut from 5-8 p.m. Pizza Hut is going to be donating back 20% of their sales that night to the Foundation. But it's a time when people can come in. They can donate in person if they want to. They can get a meal. They can meet Foundation staff members and volunteers and ask questions about the foundation, about what we do, what we got going on. So it's a time when people can come in and get more information about what the Foundation does to help Hillsboro, Lehigh and Durham,' said Hughbanks.
Donations can also be made online at www.hcfoundationks.org/giving-tuesday. Giving Tuesday donations are tax-deductible.
HCF is also now leasing space inside the Hillsboro Chamber of Commerce at 110 N. Main St. in Hillsboro if people want to stop in to make a donation or visit with Hughbanks and get more information about what is going on at HCF. More information is also available at their newly updated website at www.hcfoundationsks.org

title: PCF announces matching gift opportunity from PFF
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Peabody – The Peabody Community Foundation (PCF) is excited to announce that between now and Dec. 26 all donations to the foundation will be matched dollar for dollar, up to $70,000, thanks to the…
content:
Peabody – The Peabody Community Foundation (PCF) is excited to announce that between now and Dec. 26 all donations to the foundation will be matched dollar for dollar, up to $70,000, thanks to the generosity of the Patterson Family Foundation (PFF). This incredible opportunity builds upon the success of last year's matching campaign, where PCF met the full $70,000 match.
The PFF has graciously provided this matching gift opportunity to help further local philanthropy and strengthen rural community foundations like PCF. Gifts made to the PCF between Nov. 26 and Dec. 26 will be eligible for this match, which is designed to encourage and amplify giving within the Peabody community.
'We are incredibly grateful to the Patterson Family Foundation for their ongoing support,' said
Paige Barnes, Associate Director. 'This matching opportunity helps to ensure the sustainability of our foundation and provides much-needed funding to benefit a variety of initiatives that support our community. We encourage everyone to contribute, as every dollar donated will have double the impact.'
While gifts to all of PCF's 30 component funds will be matched, the board has identified several
key priorities for this year's match campaign. These include funds dedicated to Community Improvement and Housing, endowments that allow for the distribution of grants, and funds that
support the Peabody City Pool. For maximum local impact, the PCF board is encouraging donations to these key priorities and to funds held by local charities. Donations to scholarship fund will not be available.
PCF will host Giving Tuesday/Winterfest from 5:30-8 p.m. on Dec. 3 at the Peabody Burns Jr. Sr. High School. Giving Tuesday provides an opportunity to learn more about local charities and how to support them. The Winterfest event includes a student art show, a choir performance, a cheerleader and basketball team spirit show, a free throw contest and an alumni basketball scrimmage.
For more information on how to contribute to the Peabody Community Foundation, or to inquire about local charities and opportunities to support them, please contact PCF Associate Director Paige Barnes at 316-243-6799 or via email at paige@centralkansascf.org.

title: MCL presents A Nutcracker Christmas Home Tours on Dec. 8
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: The Marion City Library will host their annual Christmas Home Tour from 1-4 p.m. on Sunday, Dec. 8. This year's 'A Nutcracker Christmas' has four homes on the tour. They are as follows: Bryan and…
content:
The Marion City Library will host their annual Christmas Home Tour from 1-4 p.m. on Sunday, Dec. 8. This year's 'A Nutcracker Christmas' has four homes on the tour. They are as follows:
Bryan and Angela Hess
The Hess home sits on a quiet corner lot. It's a ranch-style home that was built in the early 90s. Their house is simple but filled with Christmas decor. Every room is decorated. Angela got a love for decorating at a very early age. At Christmas time her mom decorated every inch of their house. Angela remembers how it made her feel when all the decorations were up. It gave her such a sense of peace. Angela's mother passed the love of decorating on to her.
Christmas to their family is the celebration of the birth of their Savior. When she decorates, it is to show her love for Christ and also her love for her family with the beautiful surroundings. There is a peacefulness just to sit at night, turn the lights on and contemplate it all. It's taking in the beauty of the Christmas decorations.
Glen and Pam Hett
The Hett's Christmas decorations reflect their love of farm life and their time spent in the Seattle area, the mix is eclectic, but very much them. They have been married for almost 48 years and have lived and farmed on the family farm for most of those years until 2005 when Glen started traveling for Boeing. For 13 years they lived in the Seattle area and two of their three children followed them up there and have started their own lives in the northwest. Glen retired from Boeing four years ago, and they moved back to their farm and built a new home.
The old farmhouse was the same farmhouse that Glen's grandparents bought around 1920 where his father was raised and where they raised their kids. The old place had seen better days so they tore it down and built a more energy efficient one. They salvaged pieces from the old house and incorporated them into the new home. They have many treasured antique pieces, including three nativity sets, from both of their families, and they are used throughout their home.
Pam has been collecting Santa's for 47 years and most are on display. Half of their decorations are country farmhouse and half are their love for the northwest and the Seattle area. In their granddaughter's room, they have fun kid decorations and a Lego Christmas elf house they built.
JD Bauman and Phoebe Janzen
Their house was built around the early 1920s, and it has all of the original trim and molding. They purchased the house in 2022 and added a carport, sunroom and a deck off the back of the house. They have added a garage (unattached). Also, JD painted the entire house on the outside and all of the rooms in the house except for the addition.
Tracey Long
Long's home is a bungalow-style house that was built in the 50s. At some point in the 60s, the original owner had a shoe repair shop in the back garage. There is a glass brick wall that divides the living room and kitchen which is in its original state as designed when the house was built. And this year the hardwood floors were restored to their red oak beauty.
A train village will be on display at the Marion City Library in the Santa Fe Room during the Home Tours.
Refreshments will be served at the library.
Tickets are $5.00 and must be purchased at the Marion City Library only on the day of the event or before.

title: 'It feels like a total loss'
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Coneburg Grill ownership, staff shift through ashes after Sunday fire An early...
content:
Coneburg Grill ownership, staff shift through ashes after Sunday fire
An early Sunday morning fire tore through The Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody and has left the popular restaurant and bar charred and unusable.
Around 4:40 a.m. a person contacted 911 to report seeing smoke coming from the building located at 904 Peabody St, off U.S. Highway 50.
Peabody Fire Chief Colton Glenn said the department made it out to the fire at 4:44 a.m.
'There was a lot of fire coming from the kitchen area of the building,' he said. 'We had a couple guys immediately put an attack on that and gained access to the building through that back kitchen door. We had it knocked down pretty quick. Hillsboro and Marion both also showed up for mutual aid.'
While the building is still standing, the amount of damage is vast. The kitchen appears completely destroyed. The inside of the building is burned and blackened. Insolation and wires hang from the ceiling. The booths that often held hungry customers burned and melted.
'We are not sure of the extent of the damage at this point, though looking through the lens from an 'ownership perspective', it feels like a total loss,' owner Lindsey Marshall said.
She said she first learned of the fire, after receiving an alert from the building's security company early Sunday morning.
'The patio and sturdy fireplace are still in great shape, and we have four walls supporting the structure. Beyond that, the damage to the interior looks fairly bleak,' she said.
Glenn said the state fire marshal's office is working to find the cause of the fire, and no cause was known yet. The state fire marshal's office has not returned phone calls to the Free Press at this time. Glenn said it could be a few weeks before anyone gets a copy of the report.
Marshall said she has hope about rebuilding as she navigates through it all.
'The Coneburg staff and I have worked way too hard over the past 13 1/2 years to let this take us down,' she said. 'I would love to see a rebuild happen. There are so many people who treasure this place. It houses so much nostalgia, memories, laughter, tears. And our community needs something like this.'
Marshall said the restaurants served as a frequent local and regional destination, a stop for travelers on the highway and a halfway point for families in neighboring communities to meet.
'So, as soon as we sort through the rubble, we will start putting one foot in front of the other and get the ball rolling with a more definitive answer and plan for our supporters,' she said.
Marshall's biggest concern is for her staff.
'We work as a team, we are family,' she said. 'Not being able to greet our guests on a daily basis is going to take its toll. We will miss them immensely, but look forward to seeing them, and serving them again as soon as possible.'
She said no one is sure what to do with their time as they work through the process of the restaurant's destruction.
'We are all so dedicated to the Burg, we spend our off time here with each other, and we stand together through all of the super good and super bad parts of life,' she said. 'At the end of our shifts, we gather together and ruminate about it all: life, love, customers, dreams, the environment we're creating for others to enjoy. We talk about our day, about our lives, we brainstorm, we connect, we find solutions to keep getting better.'
Marshall is thankful to so many for all the support, condolences, humor, help and more that they have offered.
'I would like to acknowledge the Peabody Fire Department and Fire Chief Colton Glenn, as well as the City of Hillsboro Fire Department, our local police force and the passerby who took the time to notify Marion County Dispatch of the fire,' said Marshall. 'Colton has done well with the fire department with recruiting and training and I'm especially proud of his determination to move our community forward. My sister, Morgan Marler, answered the phone immediately when I called, and was available to help me answer and ask all of the questions in the midst of absolute chaos. The two fire marshals that made the trip to Peabody, on a Sunday, and were able to answer all the hard questions for me. I absolutely have to thank my staff for standing solidly beside me, as I navigate my way through this catastrophic event. They are my rock. I love them so much, we are a family, and we cannot wait to get together as a team, again. I've worked so many years to find the 'right pieces to the puzzle' for staffing the Coneburg, and they are absolutely, exactly that.'
Glenn credits his guys who showed up and helped.
'I have a great group of guys that are young and willing, who have dedicated the time to training and getting their qualifications,' said Glenn. 'That's why the Burg is still standing and not just a pile of rubble at this point.'
In an effort to support Marshall, her staff and the restoration of the Coneburg, an official GoFundMe has been set up at https://gofund.me/68efbc37.
Donations can also be made at any Vintage Bank in Kansas. Reference the Coneburg Inn in Peabody.
The Peabody Association of Churches has set up a tax-exempt fund where people can donate larger amounts. They are also collecting gifts for the children of employees for Christmas. All of these funds will first be used to assist employees with wage assistance until more permanent assistance can be set up. Whatever is remaining will be used to supplement what is not covered by insurance for the rebuilding of the Coneburg.
Ashley King is offering her baked goods of sourdough loaves, English muffins, sandwich loaves and more by donation and her daughter is selling handmade necklaces. King has a few baked items available for pick up at Porcupine Tea Company and Mercantile.
'I'll be doing more baking this week and will post more items next weekend to support the same cause,' said King.
Orders can also be made through her website https://seeds-to-sourdough.square.site.
'All baked goods orders that people would like to place for the cause will be made to order so it will take between 24 to 72 hours. I will include a way for people to let me know that these orders are for the Coneburg. I'll probably do this for the next 7 days,' said King. 'As an alternative, I will be creating a donation link on my website and will also have a donation jar available at the Porcupine Tea Company and Mercantile.'
Peabody resident Samantha Wilson wanted to help the Coneburg employees during this time so she set up a GoFundMe for them. At press time, the fund had already raised almost $2500.
'Not only is this a business our community knows and loves but also a business that provides for many families on a daily basis. It's an extremely unfortunate situation and it makes it even
worse that it happened during the holidays,' she said. 'I'll be sure it gets divided and given to the correct people.'
To contribute, go to https://gofund.me/431ba15d.
'We have literally received hundreds and hundreds of calls, texts and messages from our
Coneburg Family near and far,' Marshall said. 'Right now, it's hard for me to respond to them all because of the work that immediately needs to happen. But, it is comforting to know that we have such a large customer base that cares about us and how we are faring. It is overwhelming, but we feel the love and are grateful for it. So extremely grateful. We will need all the help and love, all the prayers and good vibes, all the support from those who have fallen in love with the Coneburg over the years.'

title: Hillsboro discusses utility rate increases
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Dec. 3 to discuss utility rate adjustments. Rates for water, trash and recycling are reviewed annually by the council in November with any changes taking…
content:
The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Dec. 3 to discuss utility rate adjustments. Rates for water, trash and recycling are reviewed annually by the council in November with any changes taking place at the beginning of the following year. After discussing the rates in a November meeting, the council requested more information from Hillsboro City Administrator Matt Stiles to determine the impact of the proposed rates. Stiles presented the information to the council in this meeting.
'Trash rates are proposed to increase for residential users from $14.75 to $16.75 per month. Recycling would also increase from $3.50 to $5.00 per month,' said Stiles.
Stiles explained that the largest change would be in the water rates.
'There is an increase in the base rate proposed along with the conversion to a conservation rate tier structure. The current rates for both residential and commercial/multiple dwellings are a $29 base charge with a price per 1,000 gallons of $6.58,' said Stiles.
The proposed increase in the base rate would be $34 for residential and $36 for commercial. The proposed conservation tiers for residential would be $6.71 for 0-7,000 gallons; $6.85 for 7,001-15,000; $6.98 for 15,001-30,000; and $7.12 for 30,001 +. The proposed conservation tiers for commercial uses would be $6.71 for 0-15,000; $6.85 for 15,001-40,000; $6.98 for 40,001-80,000; and $7.12 for 80,000 +.
Stiles presented data on residential water consumption showing seasonal variations and the impact of the new conservation tier. He explained that the impact of the water conservation tier does make a difference between high-end users and everyone else.
'That is the goal of the conservation tier—to provide a financial incentive to reduce water use,' said Stiles. 'The average monthly increase for low water users is $8.75. The middle water user should see a monthly increase of $9.22 while the high water users can expect $12.53 on average.'
'Well, I would just like to say thank you for going through and pulling all this. I know it wasn't easy to go and do all of this, but I definitely appreciate it. It's nice to see how the different tiers would fall with the adjustments. This does help me to conceptualize it,' said Councilman Ronald Wilkins.
The council encouraged Stiles to move forward with preparing an ordinance for the utility changes.
'The challenge that we have is how much and how often. And what we're trying to avoid is going years without an adjustment and then making a huge adjustment which really hits people hard. And so as much as it hurts to have to raise rates, I feel like it's more doable if we do it consistently, more frequently, than if we hold off and then have to take a big chunk,' said Mayor Lou Thurston.
'I do agree with the incremental adjustment. It's just easier for people to swallow that vs. a one big lump sum hitting them out of nowhere,' said Wilkins.
They will vote on the ordinance at the Dec. 17 meeting while rate changes will begin in January 2025.
Assistant City Administrator Callie Arnold updated the council on a grant the city received.
'The City of Hillsboro was granted an award of $15,735 from K-State 105 Entrepreneurial Blueprint Initiative to renovate the northernmost room of Bluejay Lanes which is that room that holds the pool table. We are going to turn that room into a versatile consignment space for community retail opportunity,' said Arnold.
Arnold explained that the money from the grant will be used for renovating the space.
They are still waiting for the exact terms of the grant and then they will make plans for the space.
The grant will pay for new signage so the council discussed a name change for the bowling alley. They decided to hold a contest for the public to name the bowling alley. The city staff will set up the parameters for the contest and bring it to the board for approval.
In other business, the council:
* approved vouchers totaling $160,211.65.
* approved agreements with Core and Main and Sensus for the AMI project
* approved a Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) of 3% per hour for eligible full-time and regular part-time employees effective Jan. 5, 2025.
* learned that the awardee of the Mission, Values and Purpose (MVP) recognition for November is Hillsboro Police Chief Jessey Hiebert. According to Stiles, Hiebert was nominated by a member of his department for work intervening on a mental health call where the person was suicidal.
'Chief Hiebert backed up the officer on scene and was able to talk the individual in crisis to seek mental health service rather than harm himself. It was an outstanding example of how our people live out the mission, values and purpose of our organization. That recognition is available quarterly to any employee who is nominated by another employee or by the public,' said Stiles.

title: Goessel School Board hears about service day
author: Cynthia Goerzen
description: The Goessel School Board met on Dec. 9 and heard from junior high/high school principal Scott Boden about service day, which had been on Nov. 26. Service projects for high school students included…
content:
The Goessel School Board met on Dec. 9 and heard from junior high/high school principal Scott Boden about service day, which had been on Nov. 26. Service projects for high school students included helping at Bethesda Home, New Hope Shelter, and Caring Hands Humane Society, plus projects at the school. Students also did farm and home projects and raked leaves in the community. FCCLA (Family, Career and Community Leaders of America) students went to the elementary school to make Christmas ornaments with those students.
Junior high students decorated at the school in the morning and raked leaves in the afternoon.
Fifth-grade students organized a food drive for the Tabor Mennonite Church Food Pantry. Elementary school principal Jody Schmidt said that elementary students donated 652 food items.
Turning their attention to another matter, the board discussed the possibility of adding cross country as a fall athletic option for junior high students. The board is following procedures to consider when adding a new KSHSAA (Kansas State High School Activities Association) sport. Board members had talked with staff about the matter on Nov. 19. The board is considering the benefit to the school and the impact it might have on other sports. They are considering the expense and staffing needs. The board might vote on the matter at the January board meeting.
In other business, the board:
* voted to hire Carrie Soukup as forensics sponsor.
* heard from Schmidt that students have been taking AimswebPlus Winter Benchmark Assessments in reading and math.
* heard that 2nd grade teacher Amy Flaming mentors new 5th grade teacher, Elizabeth Alderfer. Amy Rosfeld moved into the Resource teacher position.
* heard that grade school students had learned about gratitude as a character trait.
* heard about a grade school assembly that introduced empathy as the character trait for December.
* expressed appreciation to staff and community volunteers for their efforts at the Bluebird Classic basketball tournament.
* discussed updating the vehicle handbook to include a schedule for bus replacement and a list of all school district vehicles plus their mileage and current condition.
* approved a vehicle bid for a 2020 Ford Fusion Hybrid from Hillsboro Ford, at a cost not to exceed $16,000. Driver's education funding would be used to pay for it, and it could be used for other needs when not being used for driver's education. The school's current vehicle has 175,00 miles and has ongoing repair issues.
* voted to approve the low bid for a Carrier rooftop heating, ventilation, and air conditioning unit for a cost of $29,540.98 from Goering Hardware. This will replace the faulty unit at the junior high/high school auditorium.
* learned from Schmidt about the Student Improvement Team (SIT) that identifies and addresses student needs and creates goals for meeting those needs. Currently, plans have been written for 13 students. The team meets every six to eight weeks to assess progress. Parents of the students are included.
* heard that holiday breaks can be difficult for some students, and elementary staff have dealt with some behavior issues in an effort to let students know they are cared for.
* voted to approve Knudsen, Monroe & Company for the annual financial audit.
* is considering March 29 as a possibility for the employee banquet. Typically, this has been held in December, but this year no December dates were available.

title: Hillsboro man selected for 2024 Service Academy Selection Board
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: WASHINGTON– U.S. Senator Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) recently announced the members of his 2024 Service Academy Selection Board. The board will review applications and interview candidates who are applying…
content:
WASHINGTON– U.S. Senator Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) recently announced the members of his 2024 Service Academy Selection Board. The board will review applications and interview candidates who are applying for admission to the U.S. Service Academies.
Applicants will be interviewed by the selection board on Saturday, Nov. 16, at Fort Hays State University in the Robbins Center. The U.S. Service Academies include the U.S. Military Academy, U.S. Naval Academy, U.S. Air Force Academy and U.S. Merchant Marine Academy.
'Selecting Kansas students for our service academies is one of my greatest privileges as a U.S. Senator, and I am grateful to the dedicated individuals serving on the Service Academy Board who assist in this process,' said Sen. Moran. 'The young men and women applying from Kansas show not only academic excellence but also a commitment to serving our nation. I appreciate the board's investment of time in these students and in our country's future and look forward to receiving their recommendations.'
Moran's 2024 Service Academy Selection Board includes Michael James, Ph.D. of Hillsboro. James serves as the Executive Director of Administration and Finance at Kansas State University Salina Aerospace and Technology and is a U.S. Naval Academy graduate.
'It is an honor to be asked by Senator Moran to represent my alma mater and rural Kansas on the selection board amongst some distinguished Kansas citizens. I am looking forward to meeting some of the best and brightest students in the class of 2025. I made it to the Naval Academy from a very small rural school and I hope my presence on the selection board will inspire other students from Marion and other rural counties to pursue an Academy appointment and service to their country,' said James.

title: Teen performs in The Nutcracker
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Hillsboro's Ashtyn Matlock, 13, has been taking dance lessons at Studio 23, her family's dance studio in Hillsboro, since it opened in 2018. All of her years of lessons, performances and hard work…
content:
Hillsboro's Ashtyn Matlock performed in Ballet Wichita's The Nutcracker Dec. 12-14 in the lead role of Clara. Photo by Bill Collins.
Hillsboro's Ashtyn Matlock, 13, has been taking dance lessons at Studio 23, her family's dance studio in Hillsboro, since it opened in 2018. All of her years of lessons, performances and hard work paid off when she auditioned in August and landed the lead role of Clara in the Ballet Wichita production of The Nutcracker. She also danced in the Arabian Corp in the production.
'Last year, she had a very small role as a soldier with very little dancing. She decided she wanted to study at Ballet Wichita so she started taking dance classes there in January. She worked really hard,' said dad Jeremy Matlock.
Ashtyn knew she wanted to be Clara. She auditioned with a whole group of people hoping for the role of Clara.
'She came out and said 'I hope I get Clara'. I said, 'You're taller than a lot of girls. We know you can dance. We know you can act, but you never know what they're looking for.' Our expectations were real low, but our hopes were real high. When we got the news that she was going to be Clara. We were all excited,' said Jeremy.
The Nutcracker was performed at Century 2 under the direction of Logan Pachiarz and Assistant Director Jamie Simmons. The 120 dancer cast performed six shows total with two of those being student matinees with over 4,000 kids from the Wichita schools.
Ashton had close to 100 family and friends come to support her.
'We're really grateful to the town and the support that they gave,' said Jeremy.
Her dad and mom Krista were her biggest fans.
'We were in tears throughout the show,' said Jeremy. 'I told her when she first got this thing, 'You need to bring us, the audience, into seeing all the acts, all the dances from your perspective,' and that is totally what she did. She helped us appreciate the Nutcracker through Clara's eyes. She's just really fantastic with that.'
Ashtyn said she had fun, but she also worked hard. Rehearsals started at the end of August.
'We were driving to Wichita about four days a week. For some rehearsals, depending on if it was Act 1 or Act 2 or just whatever scene it was, the range would be two to eight hours. Plus ballet classes on top of that,' said Ashtyn. 'Some days we would have two shows. It was hard but definitely worth it. I enjoyed every moment of it.'
She said her favorite part was the performances.
'I also did a dance called a pas de deux, which is a partner dance, for the first time. That was definitely one of the highlights,' said Ashtyn.
She also enjoyed getting to meet new people.
'I really like my friends that I've made in Wichita. I could not have done this journey without my friends, my teachers, Mr. Logan, our director, and Miss Jamie, his assistant,' said Ashtyn.
Asthyn plans to continue taking classes at Ballet Wichita and Studio 23 but will have winter break for Christmas. She also plans to audition for shows next year.
'It's very fun. I enjoy every minute of it all,' said Ashtyn.

title: HCH Physical Therapy provides patient-focused care
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Hillsboro Community Hospital is made up of several departments including Physical Therapy Rehabilitation Services which offers a variety of treatments for a large range of diagnoses. The highly…
content:
Front: DeVona Roble, OTR, Miranda Reed, CPTA. Back Row: Hillsboro Community Hospital Director of Rehabilitation Services Jenica Weaver, DPT, ATC, Michelle Winter, SLP, Tera Hiebert, CPTA. Not Pictured: Megan Lowe, OTR. They make up the Physical Therapy Rehabilitation Services at Hillsboro Community Hospital.
Hillsboro Community Hospital is made up of several departments including Physical Therapy Rehabilitation Services which offers a variety of treatments for a large range of diagnoses.
The highly-qualified staff works with hospital, post-acute care (swing bed) and outpatient patients.
'The biggest thing is we offer one-on-one treatment. The industry standard nowadays is for multiple patients to be seeing a therapist at once and you just don't get super personalized care. But we still hold to the traditional model of one-to-one treatments. We allow an hour per patient, so lots of one-on-one quality time treating patients. And we get a lot of good feedback from the community and comments from patients that they really appreciate that personalized one-on-one time especially if they've gone other places and and not had that experience,' said HCH Director of Rehabilitation Services Jenica Weaver.
Weaver graduated from Wichita State University with a Doctor of Physical Therapy degree and from Washburn University with a Bachelor of Science in Athletic Training. She is a BOC-certified athletic trainer and a Certified Strength and Conditioning Specialist through the NSCA. She enjoys working with patients of all ages and abilities from high-level athletes to geriatric patients with balance and gait deficits. She also enjoys educating patients on healthy lifestyle choices and assisting patients in achieving their functional goals.
'I was certified in dry needling in 2019. I actually got to go to Rhode Island and get certified over a three-day course there. I'm able to treat all the extremities as well as the lower cervical spine. I can treat patients for headaches and any other musculoskeletal injuries like hip pain, shoulder pain, back pain, etc,' said Weaver.
In addition to dry needling, Weaver and her staff can provide treatments such as electric stimulation, ultrasound, Iontophoresis, cranial/sacral, ISTM/ASTM, Kinesio taping, myokinesthetics, muscle-energy techniques and more.
'We also do a lot of myofascial relief techniques. One of my assistants has taken numerous courses to be certified in myofascial release. We've got outpatient occupational therapy, too. And she likes to use a technique called MNRI which basically takes your primitive reflexes that you're born with—not all of those integrate normally in everyone. So she helps work on getting those reflexes to integrate which helps with function and pain. She's currently treating some patients with multiple sclerosis. They're responding really well. They've gone from being wheelchair-bound to now they walk into their appointments. So that's pretty cool,' said Weaver.
The department also offers outpatient speech therapy.
'Our therapist works with patients with speaking disorders and also cognitive and memory function,' said Weaver. 'And she treats adolescents to the elderly.'
In fact, the whole department can see any age.
'We see anywhere from freshly born babies, we can treat for PT up to elderly, 105-year-old patients. We treat the entire lifespan of patients,' said Weaver.
Weaver said the hospital also recently brought on a respiratory therapist who does pulmonary rehabilitation.
'She's here three times a week, and she's already got a pretty good caseload going. We don't work directly with her, but there is some crossover of patients with her program and hours,' said Weaver.
Patients are typically referred by local doctors as well as doctors from surrounding areas.
'We accept every insurance plan. That's not what I would consider to be the norm right now. That's pretty convenient for patients and the community to know as well,' said Weaver.
For more information or to schedule services, please call 620-877-4279 or 620-947-3114 or go to https://www.hillsborohospital.com/getpage.php?name=Physical_Therapy⊂=Medical%20Services. They are located at Hillsboro Community Hospital at 101 Industrial Road in Hillsboro.

title: Tabor's Gardner breaks tackle record
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: By Tabor College Sports Information Director Nathan Howard and Laura Fowler Paulus Brooks Gardner is a familiar name around Hillsboro. As the son of Tabor College Head Football Coach Mike Gardner, it…
content:
Brooks Gardner recently broke the Tabor College all-time tackle record.
By Tabor College Sports Information Director Nathan Howard and Laura Fowler Paulus
Brooks Gardner is a familiar name around Hillsboro. As the son of Tabor College Head Football Coach Mike Gardner, it might have been easy for Brooks to be known based on the successes of his father, but he blazed his own trail, making a name for himself as a three-sport athlete playing baseball, basketball and football at Hillsboro High School before enrolling at Tabor in the fall of 2019.
When Brooks joined the Bluejay football program in the fall of 2019, he mainly played special teams, before switching to defense as a sophomore, taking on a new role as a linebacker. 'My journey started as a freshman on a fairly older team where we had a lot of returners on defense, so I didn't get to see much action as far as defense goes,' explained Brooks. 'However I played all special teams my freshman year and had really good production in that role. In my sophomore year, I started defense having made major improvements to my size and speed that summer in the weight room and on the field.'
His career wasn't without adversity.
'My junior year was supposed to be the year that I broke out and started my campaign for All-American as a linebacker. I remember very vividly that fall camp seemed easier, and I understood our defense and was reading everything the offenses were doing nearly perfectly. It was until halfway through our first game of that 2021 season that I tore both my ACL and meniscus. I was heartbroken, to say the least, but I had to be strong for my teammates who were still playing and still had to be a good teammate to them. In 2022 coming off a knee surgery, I questioned if I would still be the same player I was before with a fully reconstructed knee this time around,' said Brooks.
But then, in the first game he played in after his knee surgery, he had a game-sealing forced fumble that allowed the team to put the game away.
'After that moment all the worries and doubt in my mind left and I had one goal, and that was to be the best version of myself on and off the field. That season resulted in me getting an Honorable Mention all-conference bid. I'd say that's pretty good after knee surgery. 2023 came around and I had another great year even though I had to miss four games with broken ribs, but playing in that last game and getting the win against Ottawa was pretty sweet. I ended the season off with getting a 2nd team all-conference honor for linebacker, 1st team all-conference special teams at long snapper and being named a 1st team NAIA All-American Long Snapper. As I prepared for my final season, I knew I'd have a lot of expectations riding on my shoulders, I never once let that affect me mentally and just kept one foot in front of the other as I have my whole career,' said Brooks.
Coming into this last season, Coach Mike Gardner didn't expect Jake Schenk's all-time tackle record to be broken anytime soon. Schenk played for the Bluejays from 2002-05 and recorded 342 tackles over his career, an impressive number and not an easy one to attain. It wasn't until after the first game of the 2024 campaign that Coach Gardner thought there could be a chance for the record to be broken.
Brooks came into the 2024 season with 258 tackles, so 342 was definitely within reach. Things looked even clearer going into the Bluejays game on Nov. 9, as Saint Mary came to town and Brooks needed 14 tackles. The press box crew started counting during the game, the number kept growing—10, 11……15, 16. He had done it. Brooks Gardner broke Jake Schenk's almost two-decade-old record, after tackling adversity after adversity.
'I didn't even know how close I was. The tackle record was not within our Tabor Football Record Book so I had no idea what the number of tackles was until I broke the record with 346,' said Brooks. 'It's surreal. I never thought that that was something I was going to surpass. Throughout my career, I never thought about the overall record. I just played one week at a time and cared/focused more on the opponent at hand.'
Ending his career as a staple in the Bluejay defense, Brooks could probably fill his own trophy case with the number of individual awards he has earned throughout his career; awards like First Team All-KCAC, NAIA All-American, etc., but his name will forever be immortalized in the Tabor College record books.
'His persistence, competitive spirit and love for his teammates speak volumes. As his coach, I looked at his career as being all over the map. He played hurt, never complained about anything. If he would've been healthier who knows how many more tackles he would've had,' said Coach Gardner. 'He played all three linebacker spots, nickel at times and a hybrid safety we created due to injuries with our defense. Coach Hill (Assisant Coach) did an amazing job of placing him where we needed him. He also had teams run plays and shift formations away from his side which actually helped our overall defense. He led us in tackling in '20, '22 and '23. To do what he did playing in a system where he was utilized in five different spots and still was around the ball all the time makes him one of the best players we've had here.'
Mike Gardner is proud of Brooks as both a coach and a father.
'He did an amazing job of not making excuses and was a great teammate. He separated being a player, a teammate and a coach's son. Bottom line is he's as humble as he is tough. He never asked me about the record and it wasn't until he was within five, I even brought it up. All he wanted to do was compete and win. The way he has carried himself over his career is what has made it even more special to see him do this,' said Coach Gardner.
As to what's next for Brooks, he plans to finish up his Masters in Education in Neuroscience and Trauma in August. Following earning his Masters degree, Brooks is weighing several options, including pursuing a professional football career overseas and going into law enforcement.
But he will always treasure his time playing football at Tabor.
'My career as a Tabor Bluejay is something that I will forever hold near to my heart and something that I will be able to share with my kids and grandkids when that time comes,' said Brooks. 'I am beyond thankful for all my former teammates, and for Coach Hill being more than just a coach, but a mentor, friend, enemy at times, and also a family member for life.'

title: Department on Aging offers many services
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: While the Marion County Department on Aging has been around for many years, not everyone realizes just how many services the department offers to the older residents of Marion County. The department's…
content:
While the Marion County Department on Aging has been around for many years, not everyone realizes just how many services the department offers to the older residents of Marion County.
The department's mission is 'to provide information, support and advocacy to our residents 60 years of age and older, their family and caregivers. To promote older adults independence and improve their quality of life'.
The mission is carried out through the work of Director Luretta (Lu) Turk and Secretary and Transportation Coordinator Lanell Hett. Hett has worked for the department for 42 years.
'I want people to know Department of Aging is out there. We care,' said Turk.
The department provides information and referrals to services and agencies that work with 60+ individuals and assists in helping fill out paperwork for programs 60+ individuals are eligible for in the county and state.
They assist with energy assistance (such as LIEAP Jan 1-March 31), USDA grants and loans, housing vouchers, Durable Power of Attorney, signing up for Social Security and more.
'I come from the nursing home field. I spent 13 years working in the nursing home in social service,' said Turk. 'I can also help people with completing their Medicaid papers. I can also do the faxing for them. It doesn't cost them anything.'
Another large need that the department meets for Marion County is transportation.
'We take people to the doctor's office. We take people to Walmart. The only thing we cannot do is dialysis and chemo even though that is a huge need,' said Turk. 'We go all over Marion County and to Wichita, Emporia, Salina, Newton—kind of a big old circle.'
They ask for 24-hour notice and that a trip be scheduled during office hours. There is a suggested contribution. It is also first come/first serve and dependent on having a volunteer and a van available for when it is needed.
'I have two vans. I don't always have the resources or the people to drive them. We could always use more volunteers to drive the vans,' said Turk. 'One of the vans is wheelchair accessible.'
The department is also in charge of distributing USDA Commodities—free food—to the following communities in the county: Burns, Florence, Goessel, Hillsboro, Lost Springs, Lincolnville, Marion, Peabody, Pilsen, Ramona and Tampa. The commodities are given out on the third Wednesday of the month.
The program is first come/first serve. Residents are to go to their community to pick up their commodities. Income guidelines must be met for households of 1-$1,580; households of 2-$2,137; households of 3-$2,694; households of 4-$3,250; households of 5-$3,807; households of 6-$4,364; households of 7-$4,921; household of 8-$5,478.
'If you are not physically able to pick up your commodities you can assign someone to pick them up for you. Just let us know,' said Turk. 'All the food is delivered to the senior centers around the county.'
Turk does her best to advertise the dates through the senior centers and the newspapers.
'There are people that rely on it. You don't fill any forms out. You just sign saying that you're below this level,' said Turk. 'I have volunteers. That's when I reach out to the schools and see if the kids can come help load up vehicles. There are drivers that come and pick up food, and the state tells us how much and how many items to put.'
Turk is a Senior Health Insurance Counselor of Kansas (SHIC) and has just wrapped up Medicare enrollment. The department offers assistance to anyone getting ready to retire or already enrolled in Medicare during open enrollment from Oct. 15 through Dec. 7.
This year she worked with many to help them change their insurance plans for drug plans.
'There's been a lot of changes with drug plans this year. I look at the plans with them. I put their drugs in the system, and the local pharmacies have been wonderful, Eric (Driggers) and Tracy (Lanning). They do the comparisons. So you put all the drugs in there and you click compare,' said Turk.
Soon, Turk will start focusing on Homestead and Federal and State income tax returns. She can assist 60+ individuals/families in filing returns with incomes less than $60,000. If one makes under $25,000 a year, they do not have to file taxes.
And if there is something else someone needs help with, they just need to call. Turk or Hett may have the answer or know someone who does. They love to help out however they can.
'I have so much respect for our older population. I don't feel like I'm going to work. I go in there. I'm me. I don't try to be anything I'm not. I'm honest with them, and I'm gonna do my best to get the needs they need,' said Turk. 'I am all for Marion County, and I'll do whatever I can to help. It's important that people realize that,' said Turk.
For more information or assistance, go to https://www.marioncoks.net/marion-co-dept-aging or call 620-382-3580 or 620-323-0806. The office hours are 8 a.m.-4:30 p.m. Monday-Friday but call first since Turk is often out around the county at various locations. The office is located at 309 S. Third (located inside the Marion Senior Center) in Marion.

title: County meets with new members on board
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Marion County Board of Commissioners met on Monday, Jan. 13 for...
content:
The Marion County Board of Commissioners met on Monday, Jan. 13 for the first meeting with newly elected and sworn-in board members Michael Beneke and Clark Dirks. Returning Commissioners Kent Becker, Dave Crofoot and Jonah Gehring were also present along with Marion County Administrator Tina Spencer, Marion County Clerk Ashley Herpich, County Counselor Brad Jantz, members of the public and the press.
The meeting began with a reorganization of the board. The board unanimously voted for Commissioner Jonah Gehring as chairman and Commissioner Dave Crofoot as vice-chairman. Spencer will send out committee descriptions in next week's packets for board members to familiarize themselves with and the board will revisit the topic at next week's meeting on Tuesday, Jan. 21.
Spencer gave project updates. The expected punch list walk-through date for the Marion County Health Department is now moved to Jan. 24 due to weather-related delays.
'It's looking almost finished. It looks pretty good in there. There's still a lot happening. There's electrical work happening, technologies happening. They're finalizing the flooring and the cabinets and things like that. So now we're looking at January 24th as the architect's date to do the walkthrough for the punch list. And generally we would expect any required repairs to be made within seven days after that. Then we'll be doing all the final cleanup and be able to start the move-in process,' said Spencer.
Spencer reported that Road & Bridge's primary focus has been clearing snow and ice/storm response. She also told the board they had a dump truck roll on its side on Saturday.
'They were plowing and hit the edge of the road and corrected, but then they hit a culvert and so they ended up going over on the other side. We think it's repairable. They were able to set it up and no injuries. But it is going to take some work on the truck. The individual was not able to climb out through the passenger or through the driver's side. So they actually had to bring them out through the windshield,' said Spencer.
Gehring expressed relief that no one was hurt.
The meeting ended with commissioner comments during which Becker thanked the courthouse groundskeeper and welcomed the new commissioners.
'I think we need to thank our groundskeeper, Kevin. He had a monumental job out here trying to get all that ice off. So I think we need to give him a big shout-out and pat on the back for outstanding work trying to keep the public safe. And I want to welcome Mike. I wanna welcome Clark, give you the best,' said Becker. 'My prayer is we all work together as a team to further this county down the road.'
Dirks stated he would like to introduce a subject for discussion for next week's meeting.
'I kind of ran on improving efficiencies and reducing the tax burden on Marion County residents. And to that end, I'd like to initiate discussions with the board about reducing our salaries. Back in 2018, we went from three commissioners to five, and last year we hired Tina. I think that is a good step. But the next step I would like to discuss with the board is about reducing our salaries by 20% and compensating a little bit for those increased costs,' said Dirks. 'When I decided to run for this position, I thought it was a volunteer position. I didn't even realize we got paid. I don't know that we need to make a decision right now, but I'd like to put that on the agenda to discuss. As a commission, we look at reducing our salaries to make a commitment to the people of this county that we're trying to do our part to reduce costs that they're paying for.'
Gehring said, 'My comment is with the new commissioners I think we got enough in our handbag to do our own strategic planning. We hit a lot of our past goals. It's time to make new ones. So we've got some new guys that have a lot of ideas that I think we need to hear and address and move forward. So we work on strategic planning and potential dates and make sure everybody's okay with it. And we're probably gonna take about three meetings, two to three hours apiece of work sessions. Get enough ideas on the walls, determine which ones are high priority, which ones are low priority—we've done this before.'
There will be new commissioner training in Topeka Jan. 15-17.
The next meeting will be at 12:30 p.m. on Tuesday, Jan. 21 since the courthouse will be closed on Monday, Jan. 20 for the MLK holiday.
In other business, the board:
* Spencer explained change orders to the new board members. The board approved change orders.
* ratified the verbal disaster declaration for winter weather that Chairman Mueller declared last week.
* approved pay application for the health department in the amount of $365,351.12.
* approved looking for charitable causes to donate former commissioner laptops to if applicable.
* met in executive session for personal matters of non-elective personnel. No action taken.
* met in executive session for attorney/client privilege. No action taken.

title: Law enforcement tips for driving in snow and ice
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: We are not very far into winter yet and have already had a large amount of snow. And along with snow comes one of the biggest issues which is driving in snow. What most law enforcement recommends when…
content:
We are not very far into winter yet and have already had a large amount of snow.
And along with snow comes one of the biggest issues which is driving in snow.
What most law enforcement recommends when it comes to driving on snow is: don't do it if you can avoid it.
'If you don't have to travel—don't travel. Emergency services work so many accidents involving people traveling for reasons that would not be considered essential,' said Hillsboro Chief of Police Jessey Hiebert.
If you have to travel, windshields and windows must be completely clear of snow and ice.
The law specifically states, 'No person shall drive any motor vehicle with any sign, poster or other nontransparent material upon the front windshield, side wings or side or rear windows of such vehicle which substantially obstructs, obscures or impairs the driver's clear view of the highway or any intersecting highway.'
'Driving with the windows covered is the worst and most common thing we see,' said Hiebert.
It's important to take the time to clear the whole windshield off.
'Your windshield must be completely cleared, not just a spot so you can see out,' said Marion Chief of Police Zach Hudlin.
And focus on all the windows, not just the front windshield.
'I've seen people not using the rear defroster to clear frost from the rear window. This can cause vision impairment; you need to see what's behind you also,' said Peabody Chief of Police Phillip Crom.
There is no law that you can't leave snow on your roof, hood or trunk, but law enforcement highly recommends against it for several reasons.
'Many people neglect clearing the snow from the top of their vehicles. This can pose a traffic hazard once the vehicle gets on the highway and the snow or ice flies off their vehicle in front of or onto another vehicle,' said Hiebert.
'You need to clear the snow off the hood and roof of your vehicle. As I'm sure you've witnessed, the snow melts a little and flies off creating a giant snowball flying at 50 mph coming directly at you,' said Hudlin.
Heavy snow or ice can also affect your car's center of gravity and impact your car's handling and stability.
Hudlin says to clean off your lights as most newer vehicles have LED lights that don't warm up and melt the snow off for you.
Hiebert points out that people with 4-wheel drive vehicles sometimes forget that their vehicles don't stop as well as they go.
'When a tire runs across the ice it doesn't matter if it's a 2-wheel or 4-wheel drive. It's still a tire on the ice with the same difficulty slowing or stopping,' said Hiebert.
And Crom said that low-profile cars should stay clear of deeper snow.
'We have pushed numerous low-profile cars out that have got stuck in deeper drifts,' said Crom.
For any vehicle, if there are mechanical issues, get it off the road if possible. This is common sense in any driving climate.
And don't forget those pesky ice patches that hang around forever after the rest of the roadway is clear and dry.
'If you see an ice patch ahead slow your speed before you are on top of it, sudden braking upon ice at high speeds usually doesn't end well,' said Hiebert.
Hiebert also suggests planning before you even get out and drive in the snow.
'In the winter months, I would say when the fuel gauge gets to ½, get fuel. One never knows when they will be stuck in their vehicle for extended periods of time, and it's a lot more comfortable if a person can have the engine running with the heater on,' said Hiebert. 'And always dress as if you have to walk—even if you are driving. You never know when you might end up having to leave your vehicle for emergency reasons such as an accident or being stranded.'
The best advice for driving in snow and ice? Slow down, use caution and common sense.
'It's really just common sense when driving in the snow and ice. Everyone's in a hurry and they forget to use common sense,' said Crom.
Have patience. The levels of caution and driving experience amongst all drivers vary. That slower vehicle in front of you might be your lifesaver in disguise,' said Hiebert.

title: USD 410 BOE approves board appointments and personnel changes
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The USD 410 Board of Education met on Monday, Jan. 13 where they elected Jared Jost to serve as Board President and Rod Koons as Vice President for 2025. The board also made board appointments for the…
content:
The USD 410 Board of Education met on Monday, Jan. 13 where they elected Jared Jost to serve as Board President and Rod Koons as Vice President for 2025. The board also made board appointments for the 2025 year. They appointed Jared Jost to MCSEC Representative; Sara Wichert to MCSEC Alternate Representative; Jessey Hiebert to TEEN Representative; Sarah Fenske to TEEN Alternate Representative; Rod Koons to Chief Negotiator; Scott Winter to Assistant Negotiator; Jared Jost to KASB Governmental Relations Representative; Jimmy Janzen to USD 410 Technology Committee Representative.
The board also made the following personnel changes:
*approved the issuance of a contract to Dillon Boldt to serve as HMHS Vocal Music Teacher for the 2025-2026 school year.
*approved a supplemental contract to Dillon Boldt for Grades 6-12 Vocal Music for the 2025-2026 school year.
*approved a supplemental contract to Dillon Boldt to serve as HHS Musical Coordinator for the 2025-2026 school year.
*approved a contract to Jim Millman to serve as HHS Assistant Baseball Coach for the 2024-2025 school year.
*approved a contract to Dave Kroeker to serve as HMHS Assistant Track Coach for the 2024-2025 school year.
*approved the resignation of David Funk from HMHS Assistant Track Coach.
*approved the extension of a two-year contract for Clint Corby to serve as USD 410 Superintendent of Schools through June 30, 2027.
Corby updated the board on bond projects including the second and final phase of the roof projects.
'The total amount is $992,258.40. When you put all of our roofing projects together, that puts us about $350,000 under budget from where we thought we would be—very, very happy with that. That's probably the thing I'm most excited about is not chasing leaks,' said Corby.
Corby also gave an update on the HMHS art room windows. He explained that originally when they budgeted for the windows, they did not include the art room windows.
'So while the number is more than we anticipated, it's not more because prices went up, it's more because there was more work. The wall material that's going in that art room—it's really gonna be a state-of-the-art space when we are done. It's gonna look really, really nice,' said Corby.
The cost for the project is $345,517.76.
The board approved both projects.
In other business, the board:
*accepted various donations including $2,400 for USD 410 Family Food Service Account Balance Payments from Harold and Darla Loewen and $3,750 for USD 410 Food Service Local Beef Program.
*learned that there are 11 total snow days built in before the district would need to worry about making up any school days. There have only been two snow days so far this year.
*approved the purchase of seven switches including corresponding management licenses and the renewal of 42 wireless management licenses from Twotrees Technologies, LLC for $17,535 contingent upon the approval of USD 410 E-Rate funding (which covers 70% of the cost).
*approved nonresident capacity recommendations as presented.
*approved the payment of bills totaling $604,426.02.

title: Former Tabor student charged in 2022 crash that killed two
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: A former Tabor College football player was charged last week in the fatal crash that killed two of his teammates in 2022. Jonathan Medina was driving a 2001 Toyota 4 Runner with a California license…
content:
Johnethon Aviles Christopher Aviles
A former Tabor College football player was charged last week in the fatal crash that killed two of his teammates in 2022.
Jonathan Medina was driving a 2001 Toyota 4 Runner with a California license plate. He was 19 at the time of the accident. The accident occurred on Sunday, Feb. 27, around 3:50 a.m. on Indigo Road near the intersection of 130th Road.
According to the Kansas Highway Patrol report, Medina was listed with a suspected serious injury and taken to Wesley Medical Center.
Two other occupants were listed, and both were listed as having fatal injuries. The first occupant was 23-year-old Johnethon J. Aviles of Paso Robles, CA., and Christopher Jesus Castillo of Tustin, CA.
The report also stated that no one was wearing a seat belt.
'The Tabor College community is devastated by the tragic loss of Christopher Castillo, Johnethon Aviles, and of the significant injuries sustained by Jonathan Medina,' President David Janzen said at the time of the accident. 'We extend our prayers to the Castillo, Aviles and Medina families, asking for comfort, peace and God's presence during this unimaginable time.'
Aviles and Castillo arrived on campus in August 2020, finding a home both on and off the field. Castillo, a criminal justice major, was set to graduate in May 2022, while Aviles was studying agri-business in preparation for finishing in May 2023.
Tabor awarded both posthumous degrees at Commencement in the spring of 2022.
'Both of these guys meant so much to our team,' said Coach Mike Gardner in March 2022. 'They were two of the most unselfish players I've ever had. They played their roles very, very well. I could ask either one of them to do anything on any week and they were more than happy to do that. They are going to be greatly missed.'
On Monday, Jan. 27, Medina was charged with two counts of involuntary manslaughter while driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs.
A first appearance for Medina was scheduled for Monday, Feb. 3 in Marion County District Court, but no updates were available at press time.

title: Recipe proves that, actually, it is easy bein' cheesy
author: Lindsey Young
description: Editor's Note: This column was first published on Jan. 28, 2016. Is...
content:
Editor's Note: This column was first published on Jan. 28, 2016.
Is it summer yet? I'm in need of some serious sun and some serious warmth right now, and I can't wait to toss my sweaters into a plastic tub and forget they exist for a while.
I know I still have time, but I am so ready.
My only consolation this time of year is warm, comforting food, and this week, I found a chowder recipe that almost makes me glad it's winter.
Almost.
This recipe comes from 'A Night Owl Blog' and was published by Jenny Bullistron. You can find the original at http://www.anightowlblog.com/2015/10/cheesy-italiansausage-potatochowder.html. Rather than using Italian sausage as her ingredients list calls for, I put all the spices I listed below in my version, and I also felt no Italian soup was complete without garlic, so I tossed that in, as well.
Cheesy Italian Sausage Potato Chowder
Ingredients
1 small yellow onion, diced
1/2 teaspoon oil (I used olive)
1 pound sausage (I used mild)
4 to 5 cloves of garlic, minced
a liberal pinch of red pepper flakes
1/4 to 1/2 teaspoon
cayenne pepper
1/2 teaspoon paprika
1 1/2 teaspoon basil
1 teaspoon oregano
1/2 teaspoon black pepper
salt to taste
4 cups potatoes, peeled and diced (I used Russet)
3 cups chicken stock or broth
1 cup diced celery
1 cup milk (I used whole)
1 cup shredded sharp cheddar cheese
Directions
In a pan, heat the oil over medium and add the onions. Saute until they are translucent.
Add in the sausage and break apart while cooking.
When the sausage is almost done, add in the garlic, red pepper flakes, cayenne, paprika, basil, oregano, black pepper and salt. Continue cooking until the sausage is cooked through, and drain off any grease that accumulates in the pan.
While the onions and sausage are cooking, place the chicken stock, potatoes and celery into a Dutch oven and bring to a slow boil. Turn the heat to medium, and let the vegetables simmer for about 20 minutes or until the potatoes are fork tender.
Add the sausage to the Dutch oven, along with the milk and cheese. Stir to combine. Serve once all ingredients are warmed through.
Joey praised this recipe as one of the best things I've ever made, and I did spice it up enough that it has a bit of a kick to it, so if that's not your style, you might leave out the pepper flakes and cayenne. It will still be delicious.
And as for winter, I suppose I'll just hunker down and deal with it for a few more months.
At least I have some leftover chowder to keep me warm for the time being.
Spice Up Your Life is a weekly recipe column by Lindsey Young, who describes herself as an enthusiastic amateur cook and can be reached through her website at spiceupkitchen.net.

title: Say what? Not everyone loves a winner
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: For years, the prevailing thought has been that everyone loves a winner. But if you stop and think about it, you know that's not true in many areas of life, including sports. Over the years, Hillsboro…
content:
For years, the prevailing thought has been that everyone loves a winner. But if you stop and think about it, you know that's not true in many areas of life, including sports.
Over the years, Hillsboro has experienced a lot of winning and athletic success stories between the high school and Tabor College. Most of us appreciate their successes because we personally know many of the student-athletes and coaches.
It's also true and not surprising that not everyone outside of Hillsboro loves the success of the Trojans and Bluejays.
There are various reasons why people love winners. Among them, it's associated with positive qualities like determination, hard work, resilience, and accomplishment. Winners are generally admired for their success.
But as we've noted, not everyone loves a winner.
A few years ago, most of the country cheered for the Kansas City Chiefs to win the Super Bowl. But after the Chiefs appeared in four of the last five Super Bowls (not including this year), winning three of them with quarterback Patrick Mahomes, there appears to be a lot of fan fatigue. Except for Chiefs fans, most of the country was rooting for the Buffalo Bills to beat KC in the AFC Championship game this year.
So what changed? After appearing in seven consecutive AFC championship games, the first answer is obvious. The Chiefs win too much. Others are simply jealous.
Another factor is that the Chiefs have been accused of referee favoritism. Some fans believe a lot of the controversial calls go in the Chiefs' favor. Many believe the refs go out of their way to protect Mahomes and are quick to call a personal foul if someone breathes on him.
There's no doubt that officials miss calls in every game, but are these accusations about favoritism true?
Since Mahomes took over the starting QB job in Kansas City for the 2018 season, the Chiefs have been the sixth-most penalized team in the NFL, with 659 penalties called against them, according to statmuse.com.
According to a Kansas City FOX 4 news story, the theory that the NFL was 'rigged' in the Chiefs' favor peaked last season, with the Chiefs winning back-to-back Super Bowls, Taylor Swift joining the fanbase, and much more. In 12 out of 17 games, though, the Chiefs were flagged more than their opponents and they were well over the league average for penalties per game.
One stat reveals six quarterbacks benefited more from roughing the passer calls per 100 attempts than Mahomes. The No. 1 beneficiary of those calls was Bills QB Josh Allen, and it's not particularly close.
One player who knows what it's like to have fans root against you is former New England Patriots wide receiver Julian Edelman. When the Patriots were the team to beat, fans thought that referees made calls that benefited them. So he knows what the Chiefs are going through right now.
Asked on the Rich Eisen Show if he thought the Chiefs were receiving preferential treatment from officials at key spots, Edelman said: 'It's a bunch of bull-oney that the league is helping the Kansas City Chiefs. If you've got a problem with it, go beat them.
'The refs aren't involved, and when you throw interceptions, when you fumble the ball, when you jump offsides, when you don't convert third downs or fourth downs … they can't control that. If you want to beat them, go beat them. Don't talk about it, be about it.
'I'm so sick and tired of hearing people say that about the Chiefs,' said Edelman.
According to the FOX 4 story, whether it is the Patriots, the Steelers of the 1970s, Jimmy Johnson's Dallas Cowboys, or the dynastic New York Yankees of Major League Baseball, people grow tired of winners very quickly.
CBS sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson said it well: 'I feel for Josh Allen and the Bills, but also don't enjoy hearing all the hate on the Chiefs,' she wrote on X (formerly Twitter) following the AFC Championship. 'I witnessed Brady and the Pats' dominance firsthand, and what KC is doing feels just like that. Let's take a moment and appreciate what Mahomes and the Chiefs have accomplished.'
In the Super Bowl, the Eagles demolition of the Chiefs showed that while KC had a great run, they're still human.
