title: Raising awareness on teen dating violence
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Dating violence is common among teens and young adults. According to loveisrespect.org, 1 in 3 U.S. teens will experience physical, sexual or emotional abuse from someone they're in a relationship…
content:
Dating violence is common among teens and young adults. According to loveisrespect.org, 1 in 3 U.S. teens will experience physical, sexual or emotional abuse from someone they're in a relationship with before becoming adults. And nearly half (43%) of U.S. college women report experiencing violent or abusive dating behaviors.
And it happens here in Marion County as well.
Safehope, an organization that provides domestic and sexual violence advocacy services to Marion, McPherson and Harvey Counties, served 134 youth last year across the three counties for 2024. Of those, approximately 19 are teen dating violence victims according to Safehope Community Engagement Coordinator Heather Murrow.
Due to the relatively low number of teen dating violence victims served, Safehope doesn't separate that statistic by individual county to protect the confidentiality of the victims.
It's important to remember that many teens are not comfortable reporting in smaller communities thus it is uncertain exactly how many teens in the three counties have been victims of dating violence.
It's also important to remember that while females experience higher rates of physical and sexual dating violence than males according to the CDC, males can and do experience dating violence.
Each February, young adults and their loved ones nationwide raise awareness about teen dating violence through Teen Dating Violence Awareness Month (TDVAM). This annual, month-long effort focuses on advocacy and education to stop dating abuse before it starts.
According to teendvmonth.org, unhealthy or abusive relationships take many forms. Some behaviors that should raise a red flag include: Excessive jealousy or insecurity
Invasions of privacy
Unexpected bouts of anger or rage
Unusual moodiness
Pressuring unwanted sexual activity
Blaming them for problems in the relationship and not taking any responsibility for the same
Controlling tendencies
Explosive temper
Preventing them from going out with or talking to other people
Constantly monitoring whereabouts and checking in to see what they are doing/who they are with
Falsely accusing them of things
Vandalizing or ruining personal property
Taunting or bullying
Threatening or causing physical violence
Parenting a teen through dating can be difficult. But that is where a teen can be set up to avoid falling into a relationship that leads to teen violence.
Allyson N. Krehbiel, LSCSW, LCAC, who works at Prairie View in Hillsboro, said, 'One of the biggest challenges of parenting is balancing setting limits with giving kids freedom and autonomy. Making mistakes in a supportive environment is where true self-confidence comes from. I believe that what teenagers really want from their parents is for their parents to trust that they, the teen, can make good decisions for themselves. Start talking to your pre-teens and teens early about aspects of a healthy vs unhealthy relationship.'
She warns parents to use caution.
'If your teen is in a relationship that you have a feeling is not healthy, it is important to not jump to forbidding the relationship. What is prohibited is more desired, and then the relationship will likely continue behind the parent's back. As a parent it is much better to know what is going on than to be in the dark,' said Krehbiel.
Most of all, keep communicating with your teen.
'Talk to your teen about what they value about their relationship and validate those reasons. Use statements like, 'I wonder how you will know if this relationship is not good for you?' or 'I notice that you seem to be upset after spending a lot of time with this person.',' said Krehbiel.
'Gently outline what is acceptable and unacceptable for you and the point that you as their parent will need to intervene.'
Studies have found that abusive behaviors in unhealthy relationships are more unlikely to increase over time.
For teens or anyone who thinks they are in an abusive relationship, reach out to someone you trust such as a friend, teacher, parent or other trusted adult. You can also ask for help from a school counselor or therapist.
Or call your local police, Safehope at (800) 487-0510, Prairie View at (800) 992-6292 or call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-SAFE (7233). Teenage dating violence is more common than you know—you are not alone.

title: Youth present budding businesses at Youth Entrepreneurship Challenge
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Central Kansas Entrepreneurship Center (CKEC), City of Hillsboro, Marion Economic Development Incorporated and K-State Research and Extension hosted the 2025 Youth Entrepreneurship Challenge on…
content:
Alexis Hostetler took 1st place in the high school division in the Marion County Youth Entrepreneurship Challenge sponsored by the Central Kansas Entrepreneurship Center (CKEC), City of Hillsboro, Marion Economic Development Incorporated and K-State Research and Extension. The challenge was held at Tabor College on Saturday. Benjamin Hein 1st place in the middle school division in the Marion County Youth Entrepreneurship Challenge sponsored by the Central Kansas Entrepreneurship Center (CKEC), City of Hillsboro, Marion Economic Development Incorporated and K-State Research and Extension.
The Central Kansas Entrepreneurship Center (CKEC), City of Hillsboro, Marion Economic Development Incorporated and K-State Research and Extension hosted the 2025 Youth Entrepreneurship Challenge on Saturday at the Franz Family Heritage Lobby at Tabor in Hillsboro.
Seven young Marion County entrepreneurs, three from Marion and four from Hillsboro, showed up and presented their businesses, hoping to win the top prizes.
Tristen Cope, K-State Research and Extension, said that the prizes came from a partnership between Marion's E Community and the City of Hillsboro in partnership with Network Kansas.
'Each of them gave $1,500 in order for us to give the prices for the event which is huge,' said Cope. 'Then Tabor College and the extension office helped to host and prepare the event for them.'
There were three components to the challenge.
'They have an executive summary that they submitted first. The executive summaries are kind of formal summaries of your business. What I explained to each of the youth—it's like a resume for your business. So you're highlighting your different points, your marketing. You're highlighting your target audience and then how your projections are for your business in the next three years,' said Cope. 'Then they have the trade show portion. And then they have the formal presentation. So each of them are weighted between the three different things to give them their final score.'
All of the participants showed up dressed to impress and gave thorough and well-prepared presentations to guests and judges.
'I loved being able to hear each of the passions of our youth about what they're doing. They were all so good,' said Cope.
There were two divisions: high school and middle school.
At the end of the morning, the winners were announced.
Marion High School senior Alexis Hostetler took 1st place for high school and a prize of $750 for her business Community Cooking, a fun and interactive cooking class for anyone in Marion County with an interest in cooking and/or baking.
'We will host cooking classes at the Marion High School FACS room. I would send out an ingredient list at the beginning of the month with all the dishes we're making and ingredients as well as alternatives in case anybody is allergic or you don't like a certain food. And then the people who sign up for the classes would go and buy it themselves,' said Hostetler.
Hostetler said she hopes to give the community someplace where they can go and have a good time with their friends or family.
'50% of young adults feel as though they're under-prepared when it comes to at-home cooking, especially for living independently. I just want them to have the skills to be able to make healthy meals that'll keep you energetic on a budget, too. So the weeks would be set up to do it weekly with an appetizer, an entree, a dessert and then an on-the-go dish. Something you could make in 20 minutes or less,' said Hostetler.
For more information on the class, email Hostetler at hosteale@students.usd408.com.
Marion High School senior Olivia Carlson took second place for high school and won $500 for her business Photos by Olivia Carlson.
'I started taking photos in 2022, and I mostly started with sports action photos specifically at my Centre High School games. And then as I got better at taking photos, I started taking them of the other team, like people that I knew,' said Carlson.
Carlson also does senior and family portraits.
'But the way that I make money is by the team and individual (sports) photo orders. What people most commonly order is memory mates. So they get one team and then one of their child,' said Carlson. 'And then another thing that I started doing for Centre was senior banners.'
Hillsboro Middle School 6th grader Benjamin Hein won first place for middle school and $750 for his business Benjamin's Butt Nuggets which sells farm-fresh eggs.
'The current price is $5 per dozen. I'm planning maybe to increase them in 2026 to $6 per dozen if the market holds up to that. I specialize in farm-to-table business and I'm kind of marketing to people that want a farm-fresh egg. They want to know where their food's coming from, what's being fed, where it lived for most of its life,' said Hein.
Hein plans to expand his business down the road.
'Some of the goals that I'm looking forward to and saving up for is I want to buy a cow calf and hopefully move into the meat industry. Butcher them. Something like that. Some other goals I can do with the chicken business is I wanna sell fertilized eggs and maybe chicks,' said Hein. 'This is more like a gateway business to other agricultural things.'
In addition to hand stamping the cartons, Hein offers egg delivery to his customers. To order, call Hein at 620-381-0601 or email benjhein13@gmail.com.
Marion Middle School 7th grader Kaya Tajchman took second place for middle school and $500 for her business, Little Paws at Home Pet Care, a pet-sitting service.
'I'm doing this business because more animals are comfortable at their home, in their own environment and they just feel safer there. And people have been just so busy lately with school activities, work and even vacation travel. And so that's why I'm setting this up. And I have two pets, a cat and a dog. So I have lots of experience with this. And ever since I've been growing up, I've had other animals over the years to sit,' said Tajchman.
She offers several services such as feeding watering, belly rubs, walking and more.
'It is required for animals to have their updated rabies shots and vaccines for my own safety too. And as long as your animals aren't aggressive. People have asked me if I do farm animals. I'll do chickens, feed them and spend time with them. And I just hope this works out for me,' said Tajchman. 'I can't drive yet so I'm trying to keep it local in Marion. When I get older, I'll probably drive out to Hillsboro sometimes.'
To schedule, call 818-292-6578.
Hillsboro Middle School 8th grader Emerson Corby took third place and $250 for his business E's Hobby Shop which produces 3D printed hobby products.
'I can print anything from a golf tee to a puzzle box holder for when you're doing your puzzle to see the picture better. I can also customize things with people's names. I can do different colors. I have tons of different color options. I can even size it depending on what you want it to do,' said Corby. 'Most of my products are priced under $10, so it is more affordable than like Amazon. And also it's easier to get it in if you're here in town and like you're going golfing tomorrow, but you don't have any tees. I'm already here in town. It's easier.'
Corby, who already owns a business making vanilla, decided to expand into 3D printing this past summer.
'I really started liking it. Christmas rolled around, and I got a 3D printer. And then I made some products and some of my friends were like, 'I want those.' And so I was like, 'Maybe I can make money off of this.' And here I am,' said Corby.
Corby said there is no limit to what he can make and he is open to suggestions.
'My favorite part is finding all the models or designing the model. 'It's cool to see what other people have made, and it's really fun to like make your model and then it's just on the computer. All of a sudden you can touch it. It's really crazy. 3D printers can do stuff that like normal machines could never do,' said Corby,
To order, call 620-381-3752 or email eshobbyshop@gmail.com.
Hillsboro's 8th grader Kathy Hein's business Safiskin lotion and lipgloss and Hillsboro's 6th grader Quin Janzen's business Sunrise Scratch chicken feed were runner-ups in the middle school division.

title: Hillsboro hosts legislative update
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Kansas State Representative Mike King and Kansas State Senator Michael Fagg attended...
content:
Kansas State Representative Mike King and Kansas State Senator Michael Fagg attended a legislative update at city hall in Hillsboro Saturday morning where a small handful of citizens showed up along with Hillsboro Mayor Lou Thurston and City Administrator Matt Stiles.
Thurston started the time thanking the politicians for coming.
'It's not for the faint of heart to step up and do the job that both of you guys do. And I appreciate that tremendously because in the state of Kansas, how long are you on the job, in Topeka, what is it, three months out of the year? Right? And so who can afford to do what you do or in essence volunteering their time to serve the people under that basis. It just makes it really tough. I just want you to know how much I appreciate what you guys do,' said Thurston.
Fagg opened up his time sharing about his background explaining that he was in banking for 47 years. He told the group a bit about his work in Topeka for the 90 days that he is there.
'I've enjoyed the work. I really have met a lot of new people. It's not what you think it is when you get up there. It's about relationships. I don't run the state. I'm one of 40. And if you burn relationships, you're not gonna be effective. So it's building those relationships, because once you get something (a bill) out, it's gotta go to the other side of the house and you gotta have somebody helping you on the other side too. So it's kind of an interesting thing that goes on.'
Fagg told those in attendance that he does want to hear from people about bills that concern them but to know that there are a large number of bills and many of them he has not come across.
'If you say,'Well Mike, what about 318?' Well, a lot of times these bills are assigned to a committee and until it gets to the floor, you don't see some of that. You kind of hear rumors of it, but you don't really get in that part of it. I've had people call me up and say, 'Oh my gosh, you need to kill this bill.' And I said, 'Well, where's it at?' 'Well, I think it's on the house side.' 'Well, which committee is it in?' And sometimes they haven't even been heard,' said Fagg. 'There are so many bills out there. I don't worry about them until they come within my scope. I can't worry about something I can't control.'
Fagg said he is on four committees that meet every day: Agriculture/Natural Resources; Financial Services/Insurance; Utilities; Ways and Means.
'And then we go to floor at 2:30. So this is every day. So I would ask that you call me, don't email me. That's a whole lot easier. A five-minute conversation—we'll do more than any excellent email is what I would say because there's so many of them,' said Fagg.
Fagg said his day starts at 7:30 a.m. with people in the hallway and it ends at 9 p.m. His assistant lines up dinners every night for him with different senators.
'I don't wanna go with the same group all the time. I want to be working relationships. I find that interesting, and I think you can be proud of what we're trying to do so far,' said Fagg.
Fagg shared that he is focusing on cutting spending and helped save the state $41 million with water rights issues. He is continuing to focus on water issues in the state of Kansas. He is also interested in what will happen on the energy side with utilities with the new administration.
Fagg closed his time of sharing talking about the Senate.
'A lot of times we don't fight as much as you think we do. We probably agree 75/80% of the time with what we do. You never hear that part of it, the good stuff, but you always make a big deal of the things that you are disagreeing on,' he said.
King said that he is also on several committees: Financial Institutions and Pensions (includes banking and KPERS); Commerce, Labor and Economic Development; Social Services Budget ($7 billion budget that has KDHE, CDAs, Department of Aging and Disabilities, Department of Children and Families and state mental hospitals).
'And then I'm on a couple of joint committees with some senators and some representatives on there. And those will meet throughout the year as needed. They put me on budget because of my past experience as KDOT Secretary. I'm used to a big state budget and trying to understand everything that goes into those,' said King.
King said that he finds the work hard.
'People say I'm a Republican with a heart and so that's another reason why they put me on a social services budget. There's so much need out there. There's so many opportunities that we have to our fellow Kansans and those that need just a little extra help and effort to be really productive in life,' said King.
He also starts his day at 7:30 a.m.
'I've told my assistant to start scheduling meetings at 7:30 and up until 5:30. So it's a full day, but we're only up there for 90 days,' said King.
King said they get daily emails from leadership on what happened in every committee.
'I lead a freshman group, because my wife and I have lived there for four and a half years. So we'll do something twice a week. We had the State Department of Education come in where we can ask those stupid questions in a little bit more of a safer setting. Kansas Electric Co-op is hosting us for an event. We toured Mirror Inc. which is a behavioral health center to Topeka. So I host that and then just have different lobbyists come in and talk about different issues that's been told to us,' said King.
King, who represents the 74th district, said that his district includes 11 cities and 15 school districts.
'One little stat that was kind of fun, I wanted to know how long do people stay in the House of Representatives? So the average Republican is in the House 4.1 years. The average Democrat is in the House 8.5 years. Republicans have no one with over 20 years in the House. And the Democrats have four of over 20 years,' said King.
King also gave some numbers on bills.
'So the big things that we've been working on, on the house side, and we've kicked out unfortunately, I think too many bills. I think we've kicked out 500 bills. So in total, we're getting close to 800 between the House and the Senate,' said King. 'But to me, the amazing thing is, everybody that has an idea and to go up there and who writes the bills. It gets introduced to the committee and I'm really proud of that. So doesn't matter if you're Democrat, Republican, doesn't matter if you're a lobbyist or if you're a citizen, you have the opportunity to say, 'This is important to me and I would like for you to talk about that.' So of these 800, maybe 10% of them actually go through a voting process.'
Both Fagg and King recommend checking out kslegislator.org to follow committee hearings and bills.
'You can look up a bill on there, and it will tell you exactly where it's at in the process,' said Fagg.
You can reach Senator Fagg at 316-377-7987 or email michael.fagg@senate.ks.gov. He does prefer a phone call. Representative Mike King can be reached at 620-242-8977, mike.king@house.ks.gov or msking51@swbell.net.

title: Hillsboro announces new name of bowling alley
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council met on Wednesday, Feb. 19 where they voted on the new name of the bowling alley from the submissions of the bowling alley naming contest. The Hillsboro Rec staff narrowed…
content:
The Hillsboro City Council met on Wednesday, Feb. 19 where they voted on the new name of the bowling alley from the submissions of the bowling alley naming contest.
The Hillsboro Rec staff narrowed the entries to two choices: The Spare Time Lanes and The Gutter Ball.
Those who submitted the names for Spare Time Lanes were Becky Gage, Dominic Cardinell and Jeff Haslett. Those who submitted the names for The Gutter Ball were Kerry Hein and Trent Jones. They will be given bowling memberships for making it through to the finals.
The council voted and chose to go with Gutter Ball.
The council also discussed changes made to the snow and ice removal code.
City Administrator Matt Stiles explained that many of the existing provisions were outdated or incomplete regarding traffic flow and responsibilities.
'These updates align with current practices and aim to improve safety while streamlining snow removal efforts. If adopted, these changes would make the current municipal policy obsolete, as it
contains outdated equipment listings from 2003. There would be a minimal financial impact,' said Stiles.
Key changes include:
• Business responsibility: All businesses must clear ice and snow from walkways within 24 hours.
• Snow emergency declaration: The police chief retains authority to declare a winter storm emergency, with an automatic trigger added for snowfall of three inches or more.
• No parking routes: The designated 'No Parking' routes during snow emergencies have been slightly reduced.
• Trash placement: Residents must place trash in accessible areas for safety.
• Clearing process: The specific clearing procedure was replaced with a priority street list, allowing the Street Department flexibility in addressing key areas efficiently.
• Private property imitation: City crews will not clear private property unless necessary for public safety.
• Sidewalk clearing fee: A $100 fee will be charged to property owners who willfully neglect sidewalk clearing, ensuring the city does not become a default service provider.
• Commercial trash & recycling: Businesses must clear snow and ice blocking dumpsters. Failure to do so may result in service disruption. If excessive trash accumulates and requires city pickup, the appropriate dumpster fee will apply.
Councilman Ronald Wilkins asked about business owners who physically cannot get into town to clear sidewalks and residents who cannot physically clear their sidewalks.
'Would the city just charge them a hundred dollars to go and clear it out for them? Or is there any type of process for it,' asked Wilkins.
'So what would typically happen if it was a situation like that where we have this much snow on the ground, we are not gonna mess with sidewalks. We're going to focus on getting the streets done. You just would have that ability to make that charge and clean that off if you had to. It's really more designed to be somebody who's willfully negligent about doing that. We're reasonable people. We don't want to go in there and write tickets to people. It's just there to say, 'Hey you have a responsibility to do this.' And if you don't then, and you do this multiple times, we have some sort of recourse for that,' said Stiles.
The purpose for the meeting was discussion. The council agreed to move forward with making a new ordinance for adoption and will approve an ordinance at a meeting in the future.
In other business, the council:
*approved vouchers totaling $429,599.88.
*heard from Kansas County Association Multiline Pool (KCAMP) CEO/Administrator David Luke about the KCAMP organization and membership benefits.
*heard annual department update from Director of Parks and Recreation Director David Ediger.
*approved the adoption of Ordinance 1404 which is a zoning change for lots 1-4 of the Parkside Addition, the duplexes on the northeast corner of Ash Street and Willow Road. The property was previously owned by Parkside Homes but was sold to Flint Hills Management LLC, a company owned by Darrell Driggers, for the construction of new duplexes or townhomes on the property.
*approved zoning change for 501 S. Main from a duplex to office space use.
*approved a memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Tabor College for the continuation of the Central Kansas Entrepreneurship Center (CKEC).
*approved contract with Plenert Mowing Service for contract mowing.
*met in executive session to discuss personnel matters on non-elected personnel. No action taken.
*learned that the city applied for a $29,782 APPA DEED Board grant to create an Electric Education Academy and a mobile app for residents. The city will contribute $6,000 in purchased items and $15,000 in in-kind staff time, with additional unconfirmed support from KPP Energy staff.
'In partnership with Tabor and KPP Energy, we would develop educational content for the Academy and deliver it through the app, which will also feature city-specific resources. The app is designed for potential expansion to other KPP communities and the broader APPA membership,' said Stiles.
*heard that the latest episode of Coffee with the Mayor with David Ediger and Andrea Sneed about the upcoming summer schedule will be released on Friday, Feb. 28.
*learned that the city received a $2,000 grant from the Hillsboro Community Foundation (HCF) to replace the lion water fountain in the park.
'This project was initially proposed by a Senior Government Class in 2023, and our grant application aligned with their original design. The funding will cover 30-40% of the total project cost,' said Stiles. 'Additionally, the Rec Department received a $1,500 HCF grant to support afterschool programming. The department continues to expand its offerings and is actively seeking volunteers to help lead courses and clubs.'

title: Area Sports Roundup 3.5.25
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Goessel Boys basketball – The Bluebirds boys basketball season came to an end on Tuesday, Feb. 25when they lost to Little River in the first round of 1A substate. The final score was 65-29. Girls…
content:
Seth Driggers jumps for the ball in the Hillsboro game against Marion on Thursday, Feb. 27. The Trojans beat the Warriors 61-27 in the first round of sub-state. Photo by Karrie Rathbone. Hillsboro's Talia Jost fights for the ball against Sacred Heart in the first substate game on Friday, Feb. 28. The Trojans won 34-23. They play against Moundridge on Wednesday, March 5. Photo by Karrie Rathbone.
Goessel
Boys basketball – The Bluebirds boys basketball season came to an end on Tuesday, Feb. 25when they lost to Little River in the first round of 1A substate. The final score was 65-29.
Girls basketball – The Bluebird girls played the 1st round of 1A substate on Monday, Feb. 24 against Northern Heights. The Bluebirds won 51-21.
The girls next played against Madison on Saturday, March 1. Their basketball season came to an end when they lost to the Bulldogs with a final score of 47-32.
Hillsboro
Boys basketball – The Trojan boys played at home against Pratt on Tuesday, Feb. 25. They fell just short of a win with a final score of Pratt 43- Hillsboro 41.
'This game was a tale of two halves. We played very well on both end in the first half and were able to create an 11 point lead. The second half it was much harder on both ends. It was an incredibly physical game. Lincoln Wichert led us with 22 points and Nash Dickinson added 10. Anders Weisbeck collected a team high nine rebounds and three assists. Pratt was able to make a last second layup to win the game by two. It was a tough loss, but the boys battled all night and never backed down,' said Coach Kyle Kroeker.
The boys played at home against Marion in the first round of sub-state on Thursday, Feb. 27 where they won 61-27.
'We were able to put together a solid game offensively and defensively. This led to shooting 72% from 2 and 35% from 3. The boys played a very solid game defensively creating 20 turnovers and scoring 26 points off those turnovers. Lincoln Wichert and Easton Shahan both had 14 points. Owen Dalke led us in rebounds with five and Nash Dickinson led us in assists with four. This team brings the energy on defense every night which translates to great looks offensively,' said Kroeker.
Girls basketball – The Trojan girls played at home against Pratt on Tuesday, Feb. 25. The girls won with a final score of 44-39.
The girls next played at home against Sacred Heart in the first round of substate on Friday, Feb. 28. They won 34-23.
'We had a really good match up Friday night against Sacred Heart. I knew our first round match-up was going to be a tough game and that it was sad that one of us was going to be done right away. Sacred Heart played a really tough schedule like we did this year. I thought the difference was our defense. I was proud of our girls for carrying out the game plan and grinding out another tough win. We know we have a tough game ahead against Moundridge who has beaten us twice and I believe is the best 2A team in the state. We will embrace the challenge and be ready to compete on Wednesday,' said Coach Micah Ratzlaff.
Wrestling – The Canton-Galva wrestlers competed in the KSHSAA 3-2-1A Boys State Championship in Hays on Friday and Saturday, Feb 28-March 1.
William Andrea (11-26) wrestled in the 106 weight class. His place is unknown and he scored 0 team points. The results were as follows: Champ. Round 1 – Xzander Donner (Russell HS) 38-5 won by fall over Andreas (Fall 0:47); Cons. Round 1 – Mason Bottorff (Effingham-Atchison Co Community HS) 25-14 won by fall over Andreas (Fall 5:25)
Jaxon Chrislip (20-14) wrestled in the 144 weight class. His place is unknown and he scored 0 team points.The results were as follows: Champ. Round 1 – Reid Griffiths (Herington HS) 37-6 won by major decision over Chrislip (MD 14-2); Cons. Round 1 – Trey Zorn (Russell Hs) 18-14 won by decision over Chrislip (Dec 4-2).
'Obviously the weekend at Hays did not go as we had hoped. However it was an important experience for them, as they will both be back with the team next season with another opportunity to return to compete at the state tournament. Honestly William making it to state in only his second season of participating in wrestling, after not winning a single match last year, was a huge testament to the progress he made this season and the experience he has gained. It seemed like some things started to click for him the last month of the season. I think he will take the experience he got by qualifying for state and will be poised to return for a solid senior season,' said Coach Scott O'Hare. 'Jaxon has had a rough time staying healthy since returning from Christmas break, as he was out of the lineup for a couple weeks dealing with illness, causing him to miss out on some important tournaments. He then suffered an ankle/achilles injury the night before Regionals that hampered his ability to compete the way he is capable. This set him up for a tough draw at the state tournament. We are looking forward to Jaxon returning next season to provide great experienced leadership for our team. We expect him to get on track for an awesome junior season.'

title: Marion couple enjoys working with people
author: Wendy Nugent
description: Learning people's stories is what Patricia Enos of Marion enjoys about her job. Patricia and her husband Daryl own River Mill Woods at the Chisholm Trail Center (CTC) in Newton. She gets to know…
content:
Patricia Enos, right, helps a customer decide on framing and matting of something she brought to River Mill Woods at Chisholm Trail Center in Newton. Photo by Wendy Nugent. Daryl Enos of Marion works at his and his wife's store, River Mill Woods, at the Chisholm Trail Center in Newton. Photo by Wendy Nugent. Patricia and Daryl Enos sit on a giant chair Daryl made and takes to the Kansas State Fair. Photo by Wendy Nugent.
Learning people's stories is what Patricia Enos of Marion enjoys about her job.
Patricia and her husband Daryl own River Mill Woods at the Chisholm Trail Center (CTC) in Newton. She gets to know people's stories through her side of the business, which is framing pictures and taking orders for shadow boxes used to display various items like snakeskins or family heirlooms.
Other items they bring to Patricia include family photos, memorabilia from trips and their kids' high school sports medals.
She said she gets to know the people through their items.
'We have people bring that stuff in,' she said. 'You gotta ask—where did you wear this?'
People may wonder where the couple got the name for their business. The name is from the property on which they reside in Marion, which used to have a river running through it that powered a flour mill that still stands on the property, and there are woods there, as well.
Daryl said his family bought the property with a mill on it. The house harkens back to 1870 and the mill to 1871.
'We had the river that theoretically ran the mill,' he said, adding that the river was moved in 1919.
'Marion flooded horribly,' Patricia said. 'It always has.'
At the time, the powers that be thought if they straightened out the river, it wouldn't flood so much. That wasn't true. When the river was moved, the mill owners sued the county.
The Ehrlichs owned the mill and lost their power, so they converted to diesel. The mill was in operation until the early 1960s. Grinding feed was the last part of their operation.
The home is 150 feet from the mill, and between the house and the mill was a railroad track.
'It felt like a train was going through your house,' Daryl said. 'Mom and Dad moved there in 1965. Dad was the elementary principal, and Mom was a physical education teacher at Marion Elementary.'
Daryl and Patricia moved there in June 2000.
There are two houses by the mill. Daryl said he grew up in one of those, and the other was the Ehrlich home. Now they rent out the Ehrlich home.
Before that, Daryl taught industrial arts for 24.5 years. He taught in Lewis and Baldwin City, the latter of which was where he had his first job.
He also instructed welding, metalwork and drafting.
'I taught drafting for 25 years,' he said.
He also did a lot of coaching, about 30 years' worth. It was mostly girls basketball. In Lewis, he was the head high school and junior high girls basketball coach. He also assisted in football and track.
Patricia was a homemaker until they moved to Marion. They started their business in Lewis in 1987. It was part-time, and they ran it out of their home. When they moved to Marion, it was full-time for both of them.
'We've been self-employed longer than I taught school—even Steven, basically,' Daryl said.
There's a reason they moved the business to Newton.
'Because we were dying on the vine in Marion,' he said.
Daryl makes and sells custom furniture.
'When you deal with custom furniture and custom furniture making, not everybody wants that,' he said. 'You need to have people who want to pay for that.'
Doing custom work is time-consuming.
'You're doing one-off work,' he said, adding that people bring in a concept, he designs it and then he gets the design approved.
He designs it on the computer with computer-aided drafting (CAD), which is what he taught.
'[CAD] does everything I need to do,' he said.
Their first intention was to run the business on their homesite, and they built a 42-by-60-foot shop. They found out no one wanted to drive to the country to get a custom frame.
'They'd drive to Newton,' he said. 'They'd drive to Wichita before they'd do that.'
Patricia opened shop in downtown Marion. They outgrew that, so Patricia moved to 'the Hill' since downtown was in the Valley. They were on the Hill for about five years.
'I've been in my shop since 2000,' Daryl said.
Their supplier came through and told the couple a custom framer above Copies & More in Newton was closing shop, so they bought equipment from him. He also gave them his client list, but they didn't go to Marion. The Enoses then decided to come to Newton and were on the south end of the CTC for three years.
'We ran out of space there in a hurry,' Daryl said. 'The owners of the mall were very helpful getting us moved.'
They've been in their current location on the west side for about a decade.
They tried selling art but didn't sell much.
'I started building wooden frames for her,' Daryl said about Patricia.
They sell quite a bit of wooden furniture he makes. He also creates whatever someone wants to pay for. One of the largest things he's made was the 27-foot Hesston City Council table, which is U-shaped. That was a two-month-long project.
He's also made hutches, custom framing boxes like shadow boxes for Patricia's side of the business, a Marion High School trophy case and an 18-foot dining table for his mother-in-law.
'As a custom furniture builder, I'm pretty cheap,' Daryl said, adding that he charges $40 an hour.
'Pat's found a lot of interesting things over the years.'
For instance, a man brought her a cigar tin and told her he had something for her. Turned out it was a 30- or 40-year-old rattlesnake skin.
'He killed it when he was a kid in the western states,' Daryl said.
Patricia soaked it in glycerin for several weeks, and the skin was at least 4 feet long.
'She framed that,' Daryl said.
She's also framed a lot of World War II uniforms for people.
'I ended up doing the casework a lot of times,' Daryl said, adding that she also frames jerseys.
Patricia has a lot of repeat customers and customers from out of state and all over Kansas.
Daryl also makes outdoor furniture from plastic, and he builds wooden caskets, which people ask for.
He enjoys building things.
'I've always liked creating something, and wood is what I grew up with,' he said. 'I like the different grains and the different woods.'
He also likes seeing people's ideas come to fruition, and he and the customer design items together.
'We try to do the best for people,' he said. 'God's given us talent.'

title: Hillsboro approves container housing additions
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council unanimously approved the addition of four duplex shipping container homes and one single family shipping container home to be built on 3rd Street. City Administrator Matt…
content: The Hillsboro City Council unanimously approved the addition of four duplex shipping container homes and one single family shipping container home to be built on 3rd Street. City Administrator Matt Stiles explained that the Planning Commission heard all the cases first on Feb. 29 in a public hearing where developer Dustin Burke presented the plans. 'We did have one member of the public come in, but he really was more interested in just gathering information and did provide some comments with regards to parking. So we received no negative comments, and we reviewed the full set of plans,' said Stiles. Stiles said the Planning Commission looked at the parking concerns at the meeting. 'I think most of the issue that was discussed there was with regard to parking. The plans do meet the requirements. You're supposed to have two offsite, off street space per living unit and the way it's set up, it would do that,' said Stiles. Stiles said that the Planning Commission discussed similar projects happening in Lindsborg and the quality of those projects. 'Originally, the Planning Commission was hesitant to allow further container home construction before the developer finished the initially requested single family home. However, based on the construction in Lindsborg and discussion with the developer, the Planning Commission was comfortable in allowing the proposed projects to move forward,' said Stiles. Stiles and his staff also toured the Lindsborg project and found it favorable. 'We went and toured one that was under construction in Lindsborg—similar floor plan to one half of this duplex. It felt like that construction was as promised. Everything looked to be in accordance, and Ben [Steketee, Hillsboro Building Inspector] and I didn't have any issues with how it was being built,' said Stiles. 'We toured one that was finished over in an existing neighborhood. It's actually half a block south of Bethany College right next to a park. They're both situated right in the middle of more traditional existing homes. Didn't really feel out of place to me. Didn't seem to be an issue at all as far as what that would look like.' The single family shipping container home has the same plans previously approved by the council in a meeting in January and will be built at 108 E. 3rd Street. The four duplex shipping container homes will be at 204, 206, 208 and 302 E. 3rd Street. There are 15 lots total that could potentially hold shipping container homes on 3rd Street. 'The developer has indicated that he would prefer to build the duplex units first. Those would be developer owned and rented. For the project to move forward there would need to be extension of some utilities not originally done by the previous developer. Electrical service extension would be more than $20,000 as well as the installation of a new fire hydrant at approximately $15,000. Both those costs would be borne by the developer as utility extensions,' said Stiles. Stiles said the city's housing incentive policy would require the city to provide sewer taps and water connection fees which would be close to $16,000 for materials in installation. The developer plans to get started as soon as the utility extensions are figured out and materials are secured. 'Four duplexes—that's eight living units plus two singles—that's 10. And you add in the Mennonite Housing proposed project, which would add another 24. So we're talking about development this town's not seen in a very, very long time. When we think about our strategic plan with childcare, housing and workforce, we're well on our way,' said Mayor Lou Thurston. The full sets of plans for the shipping container homes are available to review at https://www.cityofhillsboro.net/site-home/news/february-2024-planning-commission-agenda. In other business, the council: *approved vouchers totaling $186,748.88. *heard the Adams Brown 2023 audit for the City of Hillsboro. *heard an annual report from Director of Central Kansas Entrepreneurship Center Jeremy Ensey. *rejected all bids from bid opening for the Hillsboro Childcare Center (H4C) on Feb. 29 and set new bid opening for 2 p.m. on Wednesday, April 10. *set a public hearing for 6:30 p.m. on April 16 for adoption of the revised flood plain management ordinance for new FEMA Flood Plain maps.

title: Warriors track strong in numbers and talent
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: The Warriors track team is led by two senior athletes, Gabby Newell and Jonathan Frese. 'Gabby has been a very good hurdler for us for the past three years and she will assume that role again this…
content: The Warriors track team is led by two senior athletes, Gabby Newell and Jonathan Frese. 'Gabby has been a very good hurdler for us for the past three years and she will assume that role again this year. She will help out with our relays and she is a great mentor for our young hurdlers. Jonathan has worked so hard to get to this point in his career and we know he will have a great year on the track. He will lead our sprint group and be an important part of the 4x100M and 4x400M Relay teams. We can't wait to see these two in action,' said Coach Grant Thierolf who returns for another year as head coach. The team returns with some great depth and competition. 'In our throwing events we return most of our entries from last year's team. Brian Nguyen, Sophia Dye, Jackson Bitonti and Madisyn Hulett all return and all of them are finalists from last year's HOA meet or the Regional meet we hosted at Marion. We think all of them have positioned themselves to throw better this year and they will help lead our throw group. Jackson Howard, Silas Nickel, Cheyenne Wilson and Madison Beery are all freshmen who will have a chance to make the varsity team this season,' said Thierolf. In jumps, the Warriors have a few veterans that will lead the crew but they are young in this area. 'Addison Cooper and Kenna Wesner lead our jump group and they will be looking to improve on last season's marks. They are both working hard and we are expecting great seasons from both of them,' said Thierolf. Jesse Snyder and Wyatt Soyez are back for the boys' team and they are bigger and faster than they were last year. All four of these jumpers can long jump and triple jump so the team has good depth with their juniors and sophomores in these events. 'We have a large group of freshmen who will challenge for varsity sports. Cooper Jirak, Tripp Peterson, Jordy Raymer and Hitch Soyez all will get some jumps in and they are a talented group of young men. Our lady jumpers include Delaney Hostetler, Jessica Methvin, Kate Wessel and Vyolett Dawson and just like the freshmen boys, this is a talented group of athletes. Our pole vaulters will once again be a strength of our team,' said Thierolf. Kellen Waner was one spot away from making the State meet last year and Hailey Harshman was in the final group at Regionals as well. 'We look forward to improved seasons from both of them. They are joined by two very good freshmen. Isaac Wesner and Dylan Kraus have great upsides in vaulting and it will be fun to watch them grow into the event. We will have at least one high jumper this year and we look forward to watching Sam Loomis in that event as he joins our track and field team this season,' said Thierolf. On the track, the team has some young talent that will just get better and better as the season rolls along. Jonathan Frese will be joined in the sprint group by Jesse Snyder, Sam Calvert, Wyatt Soyez, Tripp Peterson, Hitch Soyez, Isaac Wesner and Leroy Wessel. All are working hard and all will get faster each week. 'Cooper Jirak will run the hurdle races for us, and we may talk Kellen Waner into the 300 hurdles again this year. On the girls side of things, Gabby Newell will lead our sprint group with the help of Taryn Kraus. Taryn runs the hurdles as well and is focused on the 300M hurdles this season. These two will be joined by Alycia Jones, Kaelynn Metro, Eliza Richardson and all of the jump squad members. We will get some good relay work from all members of the sprint and hurdle group and getting on to the varsity relay teams will be quite an accomplishment for any of these young runners,' said Thierolf. The final group is made up of the hardest workers on the team according to Thierolf. 'Our distance runners have put in a great winter, running through the cold to be ready for the season. Luke Wessel and Eli Klenda lead a great group of young runners. Luke will specialize in the 800M this season as we think he will be one of the best runners in the state. Eli is healthy this season and has had a great winter of building miles and miles as he gets ready to challenge the best in the 3200M. Harrison Beery and Owen White are ready for breakout seasons and Keenan Lange, Jaxon Salsbury, Zayden Janzen, and Vlad Harris will give us great depth in our boys distance crew. Maria Carlson, Gabrielle Stuchlik, and Carmen Cuevas will all run the 800M for us this year and we think this group will show a lot of improvement. Maria will also give us a strong option in the 400M and the 4x400M relay. This is a fun group of athletes to work with and we will enjoy watching them improve as we head into May,' said Thierolf.

title: DEATH: Harriet Klaassen Suderman
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Harriet (Klaassen) Suderman's life story Mom loved attending funerals more than anyone I know, and she always said that each one was 'the best funeral ever!' On behalf of the family, I thank you for…
content: Harriet (Klaassen) Suderman's life story Mom loved attending funerals more than anyone I know, and she always said that each one was 'the best funeral ever!' On behalf of the family, I thank you for celebrating the life of our mom with us today. Harriet Joan Klaassen was born on September 21, 1936, to David and Frieda Klaassen in a small house they built in rural Inola, Oklahoma. She was the oldest of five children and exemplified many traits of a first born child. Sisters Luci and Jenny were also born in Oklahoma, and Mom had many fond memories of her childhood. She wrote how the family headed for the back woods to pick blackberries into their gallon syrup buckets to be eaten with cream and sugar. She adds that the family often went skinny dipping after that, as there could be too many days to wait for their Saturday night baths. Mom attended Pleasant View, a country school of eight grades, until she was twelve. She started 1st grade at the age of five and rode her horse named Happy to school, with her school bag and dinner bucket tied to the saddle with binder twine. It was a three mile trip each way and ended with the challenge of how to tie up her big horse, so sometimes she asked the older kids for help. Mom spoke three languages at the age of five—English was the language of her school, High German was the language of her church, and Low German was spoken with family and friends. Mom was baptized in a coal pit near her Inola Mennonite Brethren Church by Reverend Henry J. Enns. Her verse for that day was I John 1:9 which says, 'If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness.' This remained her favorite verse. At the age of 12, Mom and her family moved from Oklahoma to a farm just northwest of Hillsboro since both of her parents were originally from this area. Mom often described herself as her 'daddy's girl.' The two of them shared similar personalities, and he taught her many things including how to buck bales and how to ice skate on their pond. When Mom was 15, twins Doug and Jolene were born, rounding out the family with five children. Mom always claimed she helped raise the twins because her 42-year-old mother was understandably tired. Mom graduated from Hillsboro High School in 1954 at the age of 17. The one-mile drive into town didn't take long–as Mom liked to say, 'Why drive 45 when you could drive 90?' Mom and Dad were married in 1954 and had four children over the next nine years: Glenn (1955), Debi (1956), Lori (1959) and David (1963). Dad worked in the oil fields, and the family lived in a house between Hillsboro and Peabody rightly referred to as 'the middle of the section.' Dad eventually started grain farming. They built a new home six miles south of Hillsboro and a half mile east in 1962. When David, the youngest, was nearly 13, Dad and Mom announced they were expecting a baby. That was me (1975). This announcement was quite a surprise to everyone! Life on my parents' farm was busy and sometimes quite hectic. We all had our roles: Dad drove the combine and tractors and ran the finances, the boys drove the tractors, the girls drove the grain trucks, gardened, cleaned, cooked and delivered meals to the field. Mom organized almost everything, and she was good at it—even if her approach could have used some softening. She had a knack for knowing how to move vehicles from field to field in the fewest trips. Furthermore, she prided herself on cooking well for both the family and the hired men, and we regularly packed roast beef, mashed potatoes and gravy and homemade rhubarb mulberry pie in the large styrofoam ice chest. Grandkids began joining the family four years after my arrival—six girls in a row followed by four boys—and eventually my three girls, totaling 13 grandchildren. This initial group was followed by 18 great-grandchildren and two great-great-grandchildren–and Mom was a shamelessly proud grandma! My parents' car sported a license plate that read, 'Let me tell you about my grandchildren.' (Unfortunately, this was the same car that I drove to high school.) Mom also sewed baby blankets for each newborn grandchild as long as her arthritis allowed, making two blue blankets and two pink blankets when David and Connie announced that twins were on the way. Mom also wore a gold necklace from which hung many small birthstone rings, each one representing one of the 13 grandchildren, and she was always so excited about a new addition. Writing frequent postcards to her grandchildren allowed mom to maintain connections and record snippets of information about her life. Finally, Mom would want me to mention the stockings. Every Christmas (up until the last few years) she hung a stocking for each of us, and this was an impressive display of the blessings of family. The 57th family member is expected to be born soon. My brothers and sisters have happy memories of family cross-country camping trips that sometimes lasted three weeks. As they grew up and moved away, however, travel for my parents and me consisted of visiting the families of Glenn in eastern Kansas, Debi in California, Lori in Texas and David in Wisconsin. Cooking was a significant part of mom's daily life. Breakfasts were grounded in eggs and bacon, dinner was at noon and often delivered to the field, lunch might include a 4 p.m. sandwich made with her 'homemade' Rhodes bread, and supper was later in the evening. Her specialties included zwieback, waffles and white sauce, square biscuits, cherry tarts, lemon sponge cake, watermelon rind pickles, cinnamon rolls topped with maple frosting and chopped cashews, and at least 12 kinds of pie. (Mom frequently donated a pie-a-month-for-a year at the Ebenfeld Mission's Sale. She always made two at a time, so we could enjoy one at home.) She loved sharing her treats, and often said things like, 'It looks better on you than me!' or 'Life is short—eat dessert first!' Church was a priority for my parents. It seemed like we attended every Sunday morning and evening service, Wednesday night Bible study and mid-week Sewing Circle. Mom taught Sunday School and VBS, bringing energy, creativity, and a love for children. She told how one boy memorized the books of the Bible so easily that she had him memorize them backwards! Mom loved being a part of the Ebenfeld Mennonite Brethren Church and eventually the Hillsboro Mennonite Brethren Church. All of us kids remember how she rounded up neighbor kids who didn't have a church home and drove them to church, and this continued until not many years ago. She also exemplified the gift of hospitality, and it was common practice for Mom to invite church visitors to our home for the Sunday noon meal, even if we'd just met for the first time. As a farm wife, Mom got her fill of mousy grain trucks and meals on the tail gate, but she never lost her love for the outdoors. Each season brought its own thrills. Dad cut cedar Christmas trees from our woods, and she made wreaths to match. When I was young, Mom lined the creek bed across the road with daffodils so we could see them every spring from our front window. Summer (and the hard work of her children!) brought fresh tomatoes, potatoes, and green beans along with a plethora of hollyhocks. And fall was about hayrack rides, bittersweet from the woods and Thanksgiving stuffing heavy with sage. The small cabin situated by the family pond was a favorite getaway for mom–and more recently for Glenn, David and other family members not afraid to live without electricity or plumbing. Dad and Mom chose to retire to a duplex on Lincoln Street in 2005. We thought life might become simpler for them, but Mom made sure they attended just about everything the town had to offer. She couldn't get enough of Hillsboro's school sports and music and drama productions along with anything that had to do with Tabor College. Having a grandchild on stage made it even better, but it wasn't a prerequisite. Dad passed away in 2012, and some difficult years followed with Mom's gradual loss of independence. Dementia and other health challenges eventually meant it was wise for Mom to move to Parkside's assisted living at the congregate and then to full care in the main building. The latter is where Mom passed away at the age of 87 on the evening of Wednesday, March 27, 2024, surrounded by many children and grandchildren. There is so much more that Mom loved: pearly-white fingernails, church choir, singing while driving the grain truck, green shag carpet, the poem 'Footprints in the Sand,' anything leopard print, the pink playhouse, John Denver (she would want you to know we are distantly related), every pastor she ever met and every sermon she ever heard, white 4-H rabbits, shopping in Wichita, the Marion County Fair, her 60 first cousins, Rice Krispies treats (the original recipe), bottle lambs and kittens, tea parties for birthdays, the musical Oklahoma!, the Adobe House (her mother was born there!), the Et Cetera Shop, birds and her bird clock that chirped every hour, the Living Bible translation, 'talking telephone,' strawberry shortcake, all the holidays, and, of course, funerals. And maybe funerals aren't so bad. The funerals Mom attended were a lot like this one–a time of remembering all the best in a person. It's also a time when we're reminded that even if life on earth is so very, very full of wonderful things (and she always spelled 'wonderful' with 2 L's), our faith in the story of Jesus means the most 'wonderfull' are yet to come.

title: Marion author releases sixth book
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Marion author Thane M. Schwartz has been at it again. He recently released a new book called 'Paper Wolves: A High County Thriller.' According to Amazon, Paper Wolves is the story of Lonnie who…
content: Paper Wolves is the most recent book by Marion author Thane Schwartz. Marion author Thane M. Schwartz has been at it again. He recently released a new book called ‘Paper Wolves: A High County Thriller.' According to Amazon, Paper Wolves is the story of Lonnie who 'should have stayed on the straight and narrow beam that the priest had suggested; but he succumbed to his own lusts and temptations after finding a black leather briefcase containing the files of a top-secret satellite weapons program, and soon found himself being chased around the Rocky Mountains by those that he tried to extort: A corrupt little mountain town and her casino, The Department of Defense, NORAD, and The Israeli Secret Service…just to name a few. Keep your head down Lonnie and stay off the skyline…the children of Palestine are counting on you. …Not for the faint of heart.' Schwartz, who has already written five other books, sets his most recent book in both Marion County and Cripple Creek, CO. 'I'm here. I'm both places. I've got a couple of houses in Cripple Creek and I'm out there a few months out of the year, and then I'm here a few months out of the year,' said Schwartz. Schwartz describes his latest book as 'kind of a science fiction political thriller'. 'The main character Lonnie is a janitor in a casino in Colorado. He used to be a real famous anchorman in Denver on the news that he got into alcohol and cocaine, and he ended up as an unrecognizable janitor at a casino. So the people don't know who he is, that he used to be famous and he finds a briefcase as he is cleaning the rooms and it's Department of Defense, stuff like that,' said Schwartz. 'It's about spraying the soybean fields in Brazil to kill their crops down there from satellites using this thing to dispense a virus. And those viruses are being made inside the newly constructed soybean facility just east of Hillsboro, KS.' Schwartz was motivated with the plot line from several real-life events including a soybean facility recently built in Marion County. 'And then the windmill farms supply the energy to run the facility,' said Schwartz. 'And that was just a sham. The windmill farms were just a sham to bring down lower costs for the state of Kansas, but it was really just a front through this bio-weapons program. Within this program, there's another black op program going on, and it has to do with thinking if we can kill soybean crop, we can probably kill people with this thing.' Schwartz explains that the book covers a variety of topics. 'The book is gonna cover politics, it covers religion. It touches on some touchy issues. My character tries to extort the Department of Defense and they find out and they chase him around the Rockies. And my character Lonnie, ends up with a priest and a couple of alcoholics in his journey, and the priest is trying to talk him out of doing certain things,' said Schwartz. 'It's an interesting book. It's fun. There's a lot of different plot lines.' Schwartz said that he expects the book to upset some people, especially those in Marion County. 'So what an ending. I'm sure I'm not gonna make many friends,' said Schwartz. 'I touch on some religious topics that are contrary to what's being taught, but that's just my opinion and welcome to America. I'm sure there will be places that won't wanna have my book in their store. I've got a character with a foul mouth and there's some nudity. But it's also funny at times.' Like his other books, Schwartz has followed the same writing process with his most current project. 'You know what happens is I'll get a couple of characters in my mind. I won't even think about writing books. I'll just be sitting around doing something and a couple of characters that come into mind. And the next thing I know I get kind of immersed in these characters. Most of the time if I want it to come out right, I follow the character around with my notepad, so to speak, and I'm writing down what I see and who he meets. I know that sounds odd. He'll meet other characters along the way. And then I'll try to immerse myself in what those people are like. And then I'll just follow them along through the journey and they take me through the book and I'm just writing it down,' said Schwartz. Schwartz said his books usually take him five months to write and then he takes a break for a couple of weeks. 'I'll go back, read the book and go, ‘there's no way I wrote this',' said Schwartz. 'And then I think to myself, ‘well, really, I didn't, I just followed these characters around with a pen and pencil'.' Schwartz plans to take some time off to take a break, but he knows he will be working on his next project before long. 'I'm already starting to write again because if I don't, things get awfully squirrely. I got too much time on my hands,' said Schwartz. 'I'm best writing. That's kind of what I like doing.' The book is available at a few places in Marion County, but the easiest way to get it is through Amazon. For more information or to order the book, go to https://www.amazon.com/PAPER-WOLVES-High-Country-Thriller/dp/B0CSX6VGSM/ref=mp_s_a_1_2?crid=PN085JFVX9A0&keywords=thane+schwartz+books&qid=1706132497&sprefix=%2Caps%2C206&sr=8-2.

title: New owners take over Marion gym
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Brian and Kodi Crofoot were not planning on adding any more work...
content:
Brian and Kodi Crofoot were not planning on adding any more work to their already full plates, let alone operating a fitness gym in Marion, but they quickly changed their minds when it fell into their laps.
The gym, formerly known as Diamond H Fitness was set to close and be handed over to the county for storage. But Marion County Commissioner David Crofoot knew there was another option for the gym—his son and daughter-in-law.
'About four months ago, my dad came to us and explained that the gym was going to the county, gutted and used for storage. A lot of people were stressed about it and wanted to keep the gym so they would have a place to work out. My dad thought we could buy it, take over and restore it to a place for people to work out. It made sense to me since I was already here every day working out and Kodi was trying to find a place to call home. It just made sense,' said Brian Crofoot. 'It all came out of nowhere and fell into place. I said I didn't want to lose my gym from a selfish standpoint. So I just bought it.'
Kodi, who used to own Panzer Chiropractic in Hillsboro until she sold it to Fox Chiropractic last year, said, 'Part of it too was it was winter and we were just being lazy in the evenings. And I was like, ‘well, we need something else to do. Get us something to do at night. Get us out. Get us off the couch'.'
The couple made an offer and eventually the former owner accepted it and the couple took over.
'We already had some customers that came with the gym when we bought it. There was more in the past, but we're slowly trying to build it back up,' said Brian.
Kodi said there were some obstacles they needed to overcome such as broken-down machines and entry issues, but they were able to get those taken care of.
'Us being more accessible and able to be here in three minutes for people who have key fob issues or want to sign up has been helpful. And Brian called someone and had them here immediately to repair the inoperable machines. Many have been fixed and the rest have parts on the way to get them operable,' said Kodi.
The whole endeavor has become mainly Kodi's project since she not only has the extra time to put into it, but she has started doing Department of Transportation physicals for truck drivers out of the office. She is also coming up with groups and activities including a fun run for Chingawassa Days.
'I've been coming up with ideas for that. I miss being involved,' said Kodi.
'We've been running for a month officially and already adding stuff. We're go-getters so we will keep adding things and expanding,' said Brian.
Brian is doing the gym in addition to working full-time at Western Associates in Marion.
The couple hopes to add classes such as yoga, pilates and more down the road since they have the space for that. But for now, they are just focused on getting things running and in good order.
'I will be starting classes. It's kind of one little thing at a time. I'm taking a class for group fitness instructor. I want people to know I'm taking the time to get certified and have that behind my belt. I'll start them off probably in April,' said Kodi. 'For now, when people do sign up for memberships, I can show them around the gym and help get them started in a workout program. They are not just thrown to the wolves.'
The gym is open 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
'The gym has two showers so people can come in before work or after work, whatever they want do. And we have 6,000 square feet of weights and cardio,' said Brian. 'You could go to Dallas or New York or anywhere and put this gym there and people would think it was a nice gym.'
Kodi added, 'I worked out Genesis while I was covering for a chiropractor in Lawrence for two weeks. So I'd go and it was nice and everything, but I mean they have 30 treadmills all crammed together and tight. This is more spacey, and I feel more comfortable here, if that makes sense.
So far the couple has enjoyed their new endeavor.
'It's been fun to meet everybody,' said Kodi. 'It's been good. I enjoy coming up here and everybody's just so much happier. I mean, we're keeping it clean. It's not a hundred percent perfect, but it's getting there. We've done a lot with the short amount of time we've had it. And we have plans for lots more. Just the relationships you build with people here are pretty cool.'
The gym offers a variety of fitness plans to suit the customer just right. The couple are usually both there on Saturday mornings to answer questions customers have. And Kodi is in and out throughout the week for questions about membership or anything else. They respond to messages on Facebook and are also available by phone at 316-282-2731. They also have a website diamondcfitness.com. Or customers can email them at DiamondCFitness@gmail.com.

content:
Victor Lloyd Jost, 90, Hillsboro, died on April 6, 2024 at Parkside Homes.

title: Area Sports Round-up 4-10-24
author: Hillsboro Free Press

content:
Centre
Centre Track – The Cougars competed at the Burrton CKTL meet on Tuesday, April 2.
For the boys, Micah Carlson took 2nd place in the 400M with a time of 59.30. Michael Herrera can in 3rd with a time of 1.00.05. Carlson took 4th in the 800M with a time of 2.59.23.
Robert Spohn came in 5th for the 300M intermediate hurdles at 50.69. He got 1st place for high jump with a 5'4' and 2nd place in triple jump with 36′ 4.5'.
The boys placed 6th overall out of 6 teams.
For the girls, Jenaya Plett took 2nd in the 400M with a time of 1:10.86 while Jimena Sanchez took fourth place with a time of 1:14.79. Kaitlynn Bina took 1st in both the 800M race and the 1600M race. Allie Stuchlik came in 2nd for the 1600M race with a time of 6:32.06. She took 1st place in the 3200M at 14.11.17.
Ryleigh Jones took 6th place in shot put at 24′ 1.5', 6th place at discus with 67′ 3' and 4th in javelin with 73′ 1'.
Olivia Carlson took 1st in triple jump at 31′ 7.5', 2nd place in long jump at 14′ 8.5' and placed 5th in 100M high hurdles at 18.93.
The girls came in second overall out of 6 teams.
Hillsboro
Hillsboro Golf – The Trojans got their season started on Tuesday, April 2 at the Herington Invitational. There were a total of 65 golfers participating in the tournament. Hillsboro was not able to post a Team Score due to only having three golfers participate, and team scores are based on the scores of the best four golfers.
Junior Lincoln Wichert took 6th place with a score of 87. Senior Annaliese Jorgenson came in 25 th with a 103. Freshmen Braxton Hiebert tied for 39 th place with a 113.

Wichert took 10th place with 97. Jorgenson hit 105 earning her 17 th place. Hiebert came in at 24 th with 109. Senior Monroe James took 39 th with 127.

'It was good to get a couple competitions in this week to give us a chance to evaluate where we are and what things each of them need to begin working and focusing on. It was great to see Lincoln get off to a good start for his junior season, picking up two Top 10 finishes. His score of 87 at Herington was a new personal best in competition, and outside of a couple bad holes, he played much better than that score indicates. He was pretty disappointed in his score at Hillsboro on Friday, but it was still good enough to earn a medal. Senior Annaliese Jorgenson has gotten off to a bit of a slow start by her standards, but she is getting back on track and hitting some really good golf shots. She just needs to put it all together to post scores that we feel we can expect from her. Freshman Braxton Hiebert has been a pleasant surprise. He has just taken up golf this year and Tuesday was his first ever 18 hole round. Posting a 113 was very respectable onTuesday and he improved to a 109 on Friday with a back nine of 52. Being fairly athletic and very coachable, we expect Hiebert to make drastic improvements as he gains more consistency, confidence and experience,' said Coach Scott O'Hare.
The coach is hopeful that with more practice and a few more JV tournaments that a few of their other golfers will gain some experience, confidence and consistency to enable the team to get a full group of six golfers participating in future varsity tournaments.
Coming—The team will compete next at 1 p.m. on Monday, April 15 at Sterling.
Marion
Marion Girls track – The Warriors got started with their season on Friday, April 5 at home with the Marion Relays.
'We had a very good meet for our first big invitational of the year,' said Coach Grant Thierolf.
The hurdlers lead the way with wins in both hurdle events. Gabby Newell is so steady in the 100H and got us off to a great early start. Taryn Kraus looked strong in the 300H and gutted her way to a win in this tough event.
'Dylan Kraus had a very good night for us, placing 3rd in the 400M with a great time and placing 4th in a strong pole vault field. We really liked the way our throwers competed with Madisyn Hulett and Sofia Dye scoring points in all three throws,' said Thierolf. 'We are getting better week by week in this area.'
The jumpers didn't score any points but had a good day in a really tough competition. Maria Carlson ran the best early season 800M of her career and scored some points in that event.
'Our 4x400M Relay ran an exciting race and finished just behind Smoky Valley in a great early season time of 4:28.9. Overall, this meet was a great way to start our invitational season,' said Thierolf.
Coming—The team competes next at 3 p.m. on Thursday, April 11 at Chase County.
Boys track – The Warriors got started with their season on Friday, April 5 at home with the Marion Relays.
'Very fun night for a young Warriors Track and Field team. We had contributions from every part of our team and that makes for a special day of competition,' said Coach Grant Thierolf.
The runners on the track led the day with Luke Wessel establishing himself as one of the top 800M runners in Class 2A.
'He dominated a good field of runners and ran a great tactical race,' said Thierolf.
The sprint crew did things they haven't done in a few seasons. Jonathan Frese, Wyatt Soyez, Jesse Snyder and Tripp Peterson ran great open events and really looked strong in the 4x100M Relay.
'Add Luke into the mix for Tripp in the 4x400M Relay and we finished the night on the track with a great race in that final relay,' said Thierolf.
The throwers had a big day in the field with PRs in six of the nine slots that we had.
'Jackson Bitonti, Brian Nguyen and Jackson Howard all had good days throwing and offered a great glimpse of what our throw unit can become by the end of the season. We had a strong day on the jumps, led by Kellen Waner's PR in the pole vault. He will keep going higher as the season progresses and we think the rest of our jump crew will just keep getting stronger and stronger throughout the year. Overall a great night for the Warriors as we finished second in the 16 team meet,' said Thierolf.
Coming—The team competes next at 3 p.m. on Thursday, April 11 at Chase County.

title: Marion County EMS holds open house
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: The Marion County EMS Station 2 held an Open House on Saturday, April 13 to welcome the public in to view the new facility and enjoy lunch, a bounce house and games. The Marion County Emergency…
content:
EMS Director Chuck Kenney (in front) grills hot dogs for guests at the Marion County EMS Station 2 Open House on Saturday, April 13. Kenney and his staff grilled 500 hot dogs.
The Marion County EMS Station 2 held an Open House on Saturday, April 13 to welcome the public in to view the new facility and enjoy lunch, a bounce house and games. Marion County EMS Director Chuck Kenney visits with his brother Daniel Kenney while supervising kids on the bounce house at the Marion County EMS Station 2 Open House on Saturday, April 13. Many from the public attended to check out the facility and enjoy lunch and games. The Marion County Emergency Medical Services (EMS) Station 2 in Hillsboro hosted an open house on Saturday, April 13 from 10 a.m.-2 p.m. for the public to check out the facility and enjoy a meal, bounce house and games.
'We've had quite a few people come in and sit down and eat and visit. It's been a good time. A lot of primarily Hillsboro folks passing by to grab a free lunch,' said Marion County EMS Director Chuck Kenney. 'We had all the county commissioners stop by. We also had some out of the Hillsboro area, rural farmers stop by, visit and chit chat and just kind of ask questions about how do you guys get to my house when it's wet and rainy and stuff like that. Just concerning questions that they had.'
The station has been open and operating since the spring of 2022, but the department was waiting for the sign to be completed and installed before holding an open house for the public to attend and check out the facility. The facility is located at 410 N. Ash in Hillsboro next to the Hillsboro Police Department.

title: Stay sober behind the wheel on 4/20
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Driving high can be just as dangerous as drinking and driving is the message the Kansas Department of Transportation (KDOT) and the Drive To Zero (DTZ) Coalition want to share during the 'If You Feel…
content:
Driving high can be just as dangerous as drinking and driving is the message the Kansas Department of Transportation (KDOT) and the Drive To Zero (DTZ) Coalition want to share during the 'If You Feel Different You Drive Different' safety campaign.
Hillsboro Police Chief Jessey Hiebert agrees.
'Most of the Driving Under the Influence (DUI) cases worked within Hillsboro are drug-related. I think with the increased social acceptance, and in some states legalization, of marijuana and THC products, we will continue to see an increase in drug-related DUI arrests and fatality motor vehicle accidents,' said Hiebert. 'In Hillsboro, in about 50% of drug-related DUI cases involving THC, there were also additional illicit substances involved.'
According to a KDOT press release, Cannabis culture slang recognizes April 20, commonly called 420, as a 'marijuana holiday,' resulting in greater potential for illegal driving while drug-impaired. Law enforcement agencies across Kansas will participate in the effort to improve safety by increasing enforcement from April 18-22.
'Nobody should ever drive while under the influence of any impairing substance, it's illegal, and it could be deadly,' said Gary Herman, KDOT Behavior Safety Manager. 'The effects of drugs such as marijuana are no less dangerous than driving after drinking alcohol. Judgment and reaction time is compromised, putting everyone at risk on the road with a driver potentially driving high.'
A Feb. 6 article in the Wall Street Journal titled, ‘Marijuana Impairs Driving for Longer than you think', summarized research conducted by multiple universities and noted marijuana affects people differently than alcohol and can remain in the body longer than once thought.
'Users of THC may experience impaired body movement or control, altered sense of time, impaired memory and changes in mood which all could change the way a person operates a motor vehicle,' said Hiebert. 'The percentage of THC has risen drastically in the marijuana that is currently being used in relation to what was used back in the 60s.'
According to KDOT 2023 preliminary data, 59 people died last year in Kansas crashes where drugs were involved. Another 265 people sustained reported injuries in drug-related crashes. To help save lives and prevent drug-related crashes, KDOT and the DTZ Coalition are sharing these tips:
·Never ride with an impaired driver.
·If you have ingested an impairing substance, hand your keys over to a sober driver.
·Take the keys from someone impaired and help them get home safely.
·Contact law enforcement if you see an impaired driver on the road.
To learn more about the If You Feel Different You Drive Different campaign, visit https://www.trafficsafetymarketing.gov/safety-topics/drug-impaired-driving.
