title: County clarifies EMS transfer policy
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Marion County Board of Commissioners heard from EMS Director Chuck Kenney about the Interfacility Transfer Policy. 'There's been several different policies over the last couple years. Some…
content:
The Marion County Board of Commissioners heard from EMS Director Chuck Kenney about the Interfacility Transfer Policy.
'There's been several different policies over the last couple years. Some conflicting with other agreements,' said Kenney.
'We had a transfer policy that was adopted in August of '22. And then we had the policy that the board adopted in December of '22 that had some charges associated with it, like fees and everything that Brad [Jantz, county attorney] drafted. And then after that we had the service agreements with the hospitals. And so some of the things that are in those service agreements are in conflict with the standard policy and the most recently adopted transfer policy,' said Marion County Administrator Tina Spencer.
Some of the conflicts have revolved around mileage and costs for ambulances.
'What I've been doing is basically the 60 mile thing, working with both hospitals. I've been taking bits and pieces out of the previous policies and agreements and kind of just working as a patient advocate really. So this is tidbits from all the policies and agreements summarized into one form so we have something in reference to go and actually look at and kind of clear the pond a little bit,' said Kenney. 'This policy still has the 60 mile radius, but the center of the radius is the intersection of 190th and Nighthawk.'
I've been taking bits and pieces out of the previous policies and agreements and kind of just working as a patient advocate really. So this is tidbits from all the policies and agreements summarized into one form so we have something in reference to go and actually look at and kind of clear the pond a little bit,' said Kenney. 'This policy still has the 60 mile radius, but the center of the radius is the intersection of 190th and Nighthawk.' The policy states that at no time can requests for transfers take precedence over the ability of Marion County EMS to provide services for the county. There must be appropriate staffing – personnel and vehicles- left to cover 911 calls.
'It's stating that when we are adequately staffed, we can look at these other types of transfers on a case by case basis that are listed there. So it's maybe a little bit more flexible than what we had and have been following,' said Kenney.
'It gives some leniency to let the director kind of work with the hospitals instead of this is it,' said Spencer.
'And it does put in a statement that says that you have to have a certification from the physician for the need of the transfer, which has been a practice that staff has been doing, but it hasn't actually been officially in the policy. So just codifying our current practice,' said Kenney.
The board approved the new policy which will now supersede any previous policies.
'I appreciate all the work you and Tina have put together on having everything together in one place, in one policy,' said Chairman Dave Mueller.
The board also heard from Kansas Legal Services (KLS) Managing Attorney Ty Wheeler who spoke with the board about a budget request for $5,000 for 2025.
Wheeler explained that KLS has focused its efforts on special needs individuals, such as victims of domestic violence, the homeless, children in foster care, the elderly, farmers, those with disabling conditions, individuals seeking access to health care, those seeking mediation services and persons who need basic life skills and employment training. The primary mission of KLS is to provide equal access to justice for persons not able to pay for legal and other essential services.
While KLS is located in Emporia, they serve Marion County as well.
'We are a high-paced, high-volume office. We try to be there for people who have no other access to the civil or criminal justice system and in Emporia, we do some criminal cases. We do them in Morris and Marion. The reason we've come over here and done some is because Judge Powers asked me to—actually begged me to. The only problem is when I was down to one staff, we did tell Marion County, stop appointing us; let us get our breath caught,' said Wheeler.
KLS has closed several cases in Marion County but continues to work on a few cases and will work on more in the future when they hire more staff.
'We represented 82 people from Marion County, 13 of them in civil cases and 64 under the public defender contract. We had nine people that we advised in office. Generally our advices now are done,' said Wheeler.

title: Golf isn't the identity for No. 1 golfer in the world
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: How would you answer this question: What defines you as a person? Is it your career, your personality, your character, how you treat others, your sense of humor, your integrity, your family, your…
content:
How would you answer this question: What defines you as a person?
Is it your career, your personality, your character, how you treat others, your sense of humor, your integrity, your family, your service, your generosity, your money?
When professional golfer Scottie Scheffler, age 27, was asked that question recently, he gave an answer that's worth hearing. Spoiler alert – it's not golf, even though Scheffler is currently the No. 1-ranked golfer in the world.
He has won two of the last three Masters Tournaments. Since Jan. 1, 2022, Scheffler has gained nearly 575 strokes against the field. He has been 100 shots better than the second-best player in the world over the last two years — Rory McIlroy.
Since World War II, only Tiger Woods, Jack Nicklaus, and Seve Ballesteros have won two Masters by age 27. Scheffler is now on that short list.
Before this year's Masters, Scheffler talked about how he is not defined by his golf score or his success, but rather his Christian faith. When you hear an athlete talk about his faith, maybe your eyes roll, like, 'yeah, whatever.' But for Scheffler, his faith is simply his belief system. It's who he is.
In fact, his Christian faith doesn't diminish his competitive drive. If anything, it gives him a healthier perspective.
He told his buddies he wishes he didn't want to win as badly as he did. 'But I love winning. I hate losing. I really do,' said Scheffler. 'And when you're here in the biggest moments, when I'm sitting there with the lead on Sunday, I really, really want to win badly.
'And my buddies told me this morning my victory was secure on the cross (of Jesus Christ). And that's a pretty special feeling to know that I'm secure forever and it doesn't matter if I win this tournament or lost this tournament. My identity is secure forever.'
He was then asked about how he used his faith on the golf course.
'I believe that today's plans were already laid out many years ago, and I could do nothing to mess up those plans,' said Scheffler. 'I have been given a gift of this talent, and I use it for God's glory. That's pretty much it.
'Like I said, my identity is secure already, and I get to come out here and compete, have fun, enjoy it; and then at the end of the day, win or lose, my identity is secure,' said Scheffler.
While Scheffler was competing in the Masters, his wife was expecting the birth of their first child. Scheffler was even prepared to immediately leave the Masters during the tournament, unless the call that his wife was going into labor came after he had started the final round.
Kyle Porter of CBS Sports, wrote: 'The freedom Scheffler's faith provides – allowing him to be secure in himself knowing that's all that's required is doing the best he can any given week – is a trait professional golfers strive to achieve through myriad psychological tricks, coaches and techniques.
'That this belief system is built into the best player on the planet is an extraordinary benefit. In fact, it's among the reasons why he's the best player on the planet.
'In a sport that pushes the relentless pursuit – more wins, more money, more fame – his worldview of contentment as a Christian, as a husband and as a soon-to-be father is a gift.'
Over time, staying grounded in his faith may be the ultimate challenge, because, as Scheffler noted, 'Golf definitely is a selfish sport.'
For now though, he seems very well grounded. As Scheffler said: 'This golf tournament does not change my identity. My identity is secure, and I cannot emphasize that enough.'

title: Driggers keeps on ticking
author: Haddie Breugem
description: by Haddie Breugem By Gary Van Cleave Special to Hillsboro Free Press Like Timex watches, Hillsboro Trojan junior Seth Driggers takes a licking but more importantly keeps on ticking as the Timex…
content:
by Haddie Breugem
by Haddie Breugem By Gary Van Cleave
Special to Hillsboro Free Press
Like Timex watches, Hillsboro Trojan junior Seth Driggers takes a licking but more importantly keeps on ticking as the Timex commercials once said.
Last year he injured his hip in the back half of the track season while triple jumping. That injury only worsened by regionals.
'At the regional meet, even though I should have had the marks to make state, I fractured my hip coming out of the blocks for the 200 and the season ended there,' Driggers said.
No state championship as a sophomore. Not even an opportunity to showcase his skills to other Class 2A competitors.
'Well immediately after, I was just devastated the season was over,' Driggers noted. 'I didn't really think about the injury, I was just upset because I felt I should've made state.
'Mentally I just wanted to get going again. I couldn't stand to not work out or run so I just stayed motivated for football and went to all the workouts until I was cleared. I don't believe I was ever in a bad head space, I just wanted to be at 100% for the next season. I just put all my focus into my recovery so I had no time to feel bad for myself.'
He's back to being a tormentor after putting up notable numbers in football, basketball and now track. He's now ready to make a statement.
On Friday, April 26 in a meet at Hillsboro, he won the 100 and 200, helped the 4×1 to a third place finish and took fourth in the long jump. He set a new pr of 11.10 in the 100.
'Well I am proud of the marks I've been able to hit this far, but I've always had high expectations for myself,' Driggers said. 'I am impressed by being able to hit these marks in the early parts of the season. My coach and I had better marks in mind for me, but if I keep improving and the rate I'm supposed to, I will get there in no time.'
Until the Bob Nightingale Invitational at Halstead recently, he took first in every individual event that he participated in.
'Our (4×1) relay has been getting consistently better throughout the year so far,' Driggers said. 'In our first meet we were disqualified for our handoffs, but we have been placing consistently in top three since then, getting fourth at the Nightingale.'
Jesiah Gooch, Preston D'Albini and Peter Farha – two freshmen and a sophomore – have teamed up with Driggers to run a 45.70.
'I would say he is someone a lot of younger kids on the team look up to for the fact that he pushes himself so hard and helps others in practice,' D'Albini said. 'I learned to be a better teammate from him.'
Overall Driggers has 10 golds on the season (nine individual events, one relay); three silvers (two individual events); a bronze and two fourth-place.
'The Nightingale had my first losses in individual events this year, but I ended up setting my pr in both long jump and the 100 in that meet,' he said. 'So I am definitely happy with that performance despite getting second.'
Driggers' success began his freshman year.
'My freshman year I definitely did well for my age,' he said. 'I was a 400 runner and did long and triple jump as well. I had some decent marks with a 55 in the 400, in the 19-foot range for long jump and a 40-foot triple jump. I sadly didn't have the marks to make state, but I was able to consistently get better and learn from some of our experienced jumpers to get to where I am now.'
As a sophomore, he started to anchor the 4×1 and replaced the 400 with the 200.
'I had a great year setting new marks with a 21-5 long jump, 42-6 triple jump and 22.91 200,' he noted. 'I hurt my hip sometime in the back half of the season while doing triple jump and that hurt my performance the rest of the year. I was still able to take first in my league for long jump despite the pain, but I had to scratch the rest of my events that meet.'
He's back for a vengeance in his junior campaign.
'It feels really good to come back from an injury even stronger than I was before it had happened,' he said. 'It means a lot to be up there with some of the best in my qualification and I can't wait to see if I can take the top spots for all three of those events.'
'Seth is a hard worker in the classroom and in athletics. Seth doesn't take a single practice off,' junior Anders Weisbeck said. 'If you can't find him at the track or working out he is probably at a football camp. He is always on that grind and loves the competition. Seth does not like to lose.'
'It will take a lot to win state this year,' Driggers said. 'I've been working hard all year just to be where I am at, but I will need to work harder than ever to be able to compete with these guys in the biggest meet of the year. For my races specifically I am going to need to really work on my start so that I can start as well or better than I have been finishing my races.'
As for college, he's exploring his options at the moment. He caught five touchdown passes, picked off six passes and finished with 613 all-purpose yards as well as a punt return for a TD and a pick six.
'I hope to compete in football, track or both at the collegiate level but also getting an engineering degree is very important to me because I know I won't have sports forever,' Driggers said. 'Whether it is track or football I just want to be able to compete at the highest level possible while also getting a great education to set me up for my future.'
A state championship would springboard him to that promising future.
'It would mean the world to me. I have been striving for it for years and it has been one of my biggest goals that I have set for myself throughout high school,' Driggers said. 'While it is a dream of mine to be a state champion in my personal events, I also want us as a team to have a plaque to show for all of our hard work this year because my teammates are the ones who constantly push me to be better.'

title: Are standards higher for coaches than most politicians?
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: Coaches at every level, from kids to professional athletes, deal with unrealistic expectations. That's arguably true for politicians, too. On paper the expectations for junior high and high school…
content:
Coaches at every level, from kids to professional athletes, deal with unrealistic expectations. That's arguably true for politicians, too.
On paper the expectations for junior high and high school coaches sound reasonable.
One document states: That every individual who coaches high school sports will view him/herself as a teacher first, and will value the concept that interscholastic athletics are an extension of the educational process of [school name]. It is in the relationship between coaches and athletes that life lessons are learned. The values of wellness, citizenship, sportsmanship, integrity, and ethics most affect students in interscholastic athletics when coaches emphasize those values.
Here's another good aspiration: That since the percentage of students who end their participation in organized sports is well over 90%, coaches focus their attention on developing students who can become contributing members of society by focusing on each student being expected to do his/her best and not focusing totally on whether the school, the activity, or the team ultimately finishes with the most points in the contest.
While these coaching ideals are admirable, anyone joining the coaching profession soon learns that parents and fans expect more – like winning X number of games and championships.
In fact, it could be argued that expectations for coaches exceed many occupations in society, especially politicians. 'We hold high school, college and pro football coaches to a higher job performance standard than we do our politicians,' said Clay Travis, an American writer, lawyer, radio host and television analyst, and founder of OutKick. 'Football coaches get fired all the time. How often do incumbent politicians? Almost never. Pretty wild to think about.
'Seventy-five percent of American voters were unhappy with the direction of the country in 2022, yet only one incumbent statewide politician lost – Gov. Steve Sisolak of Nevada. Every other incumbent running for office statewide in the US won, D or R. Easy to blame the politicians, but voters reward poor performance. We are way tougher as a nation on football coaches than politicians,' said Travis.
One could easily conclude that coaches of any team sport are held to a higher standard than politicians. It's win or else.
In 2014, Ian Foster of Australia said on LinkedIn: 'In choosing which aspiring politicians (or parties) to support I try to work out what they believe, rather than what they promise. I then try to ascertain which ones' beliefs best mirror my own, and support them. Policies and promises are fairly transient and are often ignored, forgotten or discarded by those making them, let alone the media and the electorate. Beliefs, on the other hand, define a person and often give a clearer indication of where they're heading and what they intend for us.
'Politicians are salesmen and saleswomen, trading in ideas, hopes and fears. Ideally they believe in the value of their product, but don't count on it, as they may also be seeking personal advantage as much as any other trader. Far too many become prisoners of powerful, fearsome or very wealthy lobby groups that provide valuable support in return for ‘favors'. They lose their moral compass, and the attraction for short-term gains or personal comforts displaces the original motives of public service that drew them into politics in the beginning,' said Foster.
Nevertheless, Foster believes a surprising number of politicians have a sincere desire to advance the interests of their entire society, and retain this throughout their political lives.
It's fair to ask if winning games overrides consistently poor behavior by a coach. We should continue to aim high to hire coaches who aspire to truly teach and provide lessons that prepare student-athletes for life. It's impossible for every coach to win championships, but that doesn't mean they can't be winners in other ways.
As for politicians, we should aim high to elect those who want to enter the political arena with a priority of public service, not self-service. All too often it feels like the best we can do is to keep our expectations low, so we won't be disappointed.

title: No two days are the same for Marion County EMS Director
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: For Marion County Emergency Medical Services (EMS) Director Chuck Kenney and those under him, no two days are the same. 'It's very, very complex, and I wouldn't have it any other way. It keeps you on…
content:
Chuck Kenney serves as Marion County EMS Director. For Marion County Emergency Medical Services (EMS) Director Chuck Kenney and those under him, no two days are the same.
'It's very, very complex, and I wouldn't have it any other way. It keeps you on your toes,' said Kenney.
According to Kenney, EMS is still very new in the grand scheme of things.
'Police have been around for hundreds of years. Fire departments have been around since the dawn of time. EMS has been around since the 1960s. So we are very young in the public servant realm. We're getting our feet wet,' said Kenney. 'And then Marion County is even younger because we've only been full-time about seven years.'
Prior to that Marion County EMS was strictly volunteer service.
'So we're infants in the public servant area for Marion County as a full-time dedicated service,' said Kenney. 'But EMS in Marion County has been around for a very long time as volunteers.'
Some of the volunteers still on the roster have been serving since the early 1990s.
'We still got a few of them hanging around. It's their hearts. They have huge hearts—servant's hearts for sure,' said Kenney.
The department currently has 12 full-time staff and 29 volunteer and part-time staff.
Kenney, married with four children and one on the way, spends his time outdoors when he is not working. He and his family spends most summers camping at the lake and the early fall and spring with their English Setters in hunting competitions. Kenney started in the department in 2019. He served as Interim Director from July-November of 2022 and then again as Interim Director from September of 2023-February of 2024 when he became full-time director.
Kenney said the question he gets most from members of the public is about how ambulances can get to rural houses when roads are difficult due to mud or bad weather.
'All of our ambulances have a map book. We have a fair weather map in each ambulance that shows if it's been raining, these are the roads you avoid. Roads can be junky in spots, but to each residence during a rain event, there's usually some good pathway to get to a house. We might have to circle this mile section instead of following Google Maps which would take you to the most direct route since more than not, the most direct route is not the safest—not the best route. So we carry map books, and then the crews are encouraged on nice days to stay in their response area but go drive around,' said Kenney. 'I tell them to familiarize yourselves with the roads because that map book is a little bit old. They might have re-rocked an older mud route. Or somebody might have built a new house and then what once was a mud route now might have a nice road.'
While the department is selling an ambulance that needs much work done and waiting on a new 4-wheel-drive chassis pickup-style ambulance to arrive this fall, they currently have six ambulances.
'We have them in Marion, Hillsboro, Peabody and Tampa. It's almost a perfect quadrant. With Hillsboro and Marion only 10 miles apart it is evenly spread out. It's 10-15 miles for one of those ambulances to get down to cover Peabody in case that ambulance has gone out. And vice versa up to Tampa. So we all work together to cover the county but each major area has an ambulance for that particular area with back-ups in Hillsboro and Marion,' said Kenney.
The new ambulance was purchased with COVID-19 money but is on backorder due to the high demand for ambulances all over the county. It will be a huge help to the county.
'It's gonna be very beneficial for roads in the winter. We've been very lucky to have a road and bridge department. This particular last couple of snowstorms we had over the winter they plowed roads for us to get our 2 wheel drive ambulances through, and now this new ambulance will help even more,' said Kenney. 'We've had a couple of ambulances get stuck over the years where a 4-wheel-drive chassis pickup probably could have gotten them out.'
Kenney has also come up with a new transfer policy which was an issue in the past.
'It's nice to have a clear-cut policy in place. There was quite a bit of tension between EMS and the hospitals for the last couple of years, particularly revolving around transfers. I would like to work with the hospitals coming up because there are new bills in the Senate and in the House specifically talking about ambulances. There's certain criteria, population density, number of calls frequency and some other criteria to where it will list an ambulance can transport a patient with only one of the people being an EMT or above,' said Kenney. 'Whereas right now, the way the statute reads is that we have at least two qualified persons on the truck. So everybody has to be a trained technician.'
The new bill would allow for less staffing on the ambulance so that Kenney can send a crew member and a truck, and then a hospital can send a nurse with their patient to facilitate a transfer.
The new bill would allow for less staffing on the ambulance so that Kenney can send a crew member and a truck, and then a hospital can send a nurse with their patient to facilitate a transfer. 'That would be extremely beneficial for us, especially for those transfers that are going outside that 60-mile radius,' said Kenney. 'Now I can take our backup truck and send a captain who would normally provide ALS backup assistance and say a nurse from the hospital and then transport that patient to Topeka or KU Med. But that is a goal I would love to work with all the hospitals. We're all about patient advocacy and doing what's the best for the patient.'
Kenney is happy with the job and enjoys what he does. There is one thing he would change though.
'I wish people knew that there are more resources out there for them—the health department has so many options for citizens to go through such as senior living, senior centers, etc. Marion County has so many options that people can get help through. Like today, we had an instance where I was on the phone with the hospital trying to find a nursing home bed for a particular individual. It's by no fault of their family. It's just that they might not have known that there are options out there for rehab for individuals. So resource management, resource options—there are so many more out there than people think,' said Kenney. 'We enter houses that I would be ashamed that my family member was living in this particular way. And I personally would try to help.'
Kenney encourages people to look around the county and find the resources they need.
'If you need any help, there are things out there for you,' said Kenney.
They will keep doing their complex roles as EMS workers.
'As EMS we've gotta play the role of therapists. We have to play the role of an ER provider. We have to play the role of sometimes you have to be a parent and have that stern full talk that no one really wants to have with somebody. There's so many hats that we have to wear that it can become emotional especially if you start to see the same people progress through the months to years, seeing them age and just get worse and worse and worse. There are resources out there for people,' said Kenney.

rd in the 3200m and will go on to compete at state. Sophomore Addison Jost finished 2 nd in the 800m and broke a 40-year-old Hillsboro High School record with her time of 2:21.59.

title: Tombstone tour on May 26 at Alexanderwohl
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: The 1874 Mennonite migration experience was vastly different for each person who made the trip from south Russia to Kansas. The difficulties of the early settlement period were also experienced very…
content:
The 1874 Mennonite migration experience was vastly different for each person who made the trip from south Russia to Kansas. The difficulties of the early settlement period were also experienced very differently. Some, like Elder Jacob Buller, had the heavy responsibility of guiding the whole group on his shoulders. For a few, like Anna Richert Wedel, they remembered a prior migration from Prussia to Russia. Anna Funk Unruh lost her mother within six months of arriving in Kansas. How did they cope and continue to persevere?
On Sunday, May 26, we will hear their stories, along with five others, through first-person accounts presented at their tombstone.
Talking Tombstones Tour will begin at 3 p.m. at the Alexanderwohl Mennonite Church Cemetery. Three stories will be presented, and then participants will drive to Tabor Mennonite Church Cemetery for three stories. Following that, we will go to Goessel Cemetery and Blumenfeld Cemetery.
We encourage people to carpool between cemeteries.
The Immigrant Flags also will be up at each cemetery to mark the graves of the immigrants in 1874.
In case of bad weather, the event will be inside Alexanderwohl Mennonite Church. If the road to the Blumenfeld Cemetery is inaccessible, Anna Richert Wedel's story will be told at another cemetery.

title: Candidates are in for 2024 elections
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Preliminary filings for the 2024 elections were due by noon on Monday, June 3. The primary election will be Tuesday, Aug. 6, and the general election will be Tuesday, Nov. 5. County races For Marion…
content:
Preliminary filings for the 2024 elections were due by noon on Monday, June 3. The primary election will be Tuesday, Aug. 6, and the general election will be Tuesday, Nov. 5.
County races
County races For Marion County offices, there are several positions on the ballot.
Incumbent David Mueller, unaffiliated, is running for county commissioner second district. Michael Beneke (R) and former Commissioner Dianne Novak (R) have filed to run.
Incumbent Randy Dallke (R) has filed for county commissioner third district. Clarke Dirks (R) and Randy Eitzen (D) have also filed to run.
Both of the commissioner district races will be narrowed down to one Republican in each race during the primary election. The remaining Republican and other candidate will run in the general election.
No one has filed to fill the office of county attorney. The office has been held by Joel Ensey.
Incumbent Ashley Herpich (R) has filed for county clerk. She took over as county clerk in February when former County Clerk Tina Spencer became Marion County Administrator.
Incumbent Tina Groening (R) filed for county treasurer. She took over the position in November when Susan Berg died.
Hannah Branson (R) and Shelby Schroeder (R) have filed for register of deeds to replace the retiring Rebecca Wingfield.
Incumbent Jeffrey T. Soyez (R) has filed for county sheriff. Travis L. Wilson (R) has also filed for county sheriff.
City races
City races For city offices, there are several positions on the ballot, and all but one are uncontested.
The Burns City Council has five candidates for three positions. They are Rehea I. Huts (R), David J. Pearson (R), Darn Hacker (R), Zeb Hatfield (D) and Bill Needham(R).
For Hillsboro Ward 1 City Council, Jeffrey J. Jorgenson (R) has filed.
For Hillsboro Ward 2 City Council, Byron C. McCarty, Jr. (R) has filed.
Carl Gehrke has filed for Ramona Mayor.
Mark G. Lockhart (R) and Paul Tucker (R) have filed for Ramona City Council.
There were many openings and no contests for the township offices.
The Republican Committeeman race for Marion City South will be contested for the primary election. J. Robert Brookens and Gene Winkler have both filed for the position.
Deadlines
Deadlines 'The filing deadline for unaffiliated voters to file for election is the day before the primary at noon,' said Election Clerk Michelle Looper.
Monday, July 15, is the deadline to file an affidavit of write-in candidacy for national, state, county and first class cities (Marion County does not have any first class cities).
Tuesday, July 16, is the last day to register to vote. Registration books close at 5 p.m.
Tuesday, Aug. 6, is the primary election.
On Wednesday, Aug. 7, voter registration books reopen.
All of the candidates and filings can be found online at https://www.marioncoks.net/sites/g/files/vyhlif6456/f/uploads/candidate_list_website.pdf.

title: Ediger steps down as Tabor College Director of Athletics
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: HILLSBORO, Kan. Tabor College Director of Athletics, David Ediger, has announced he will be stepping down from his role effective June 30. Ediger will continue to play a role in the Hillsboro…
content:
David Ediger will be stepping down from his Tabor role to be the new City of Hillsboro's Director of Parks and Recreation.
HILLSBORO, Kan. Tabor College Director of Athletics, David Ediger, has announced he will be stepping down from his role effective June 30. Ediger will continue to play a role in the Hillsboro community as he has been named the City of Hillsboro's Director of Parks and Recreation. This role will allow him to work more closely with the Hillsboro and Marion County residents, providing them with experiences and opportunities for all ages. Ediger looks forward to expanding the slate of recreation options offered for the adults in the community and continue to provide a robust menu of activities for the children and youth of the community. 'I have enjoyed serving Tabor College as the Director of Athletics. I look forward to keeping a positive relationship with Tabor in my new role. I wish Tabor only the absolute best as it continues to prepare people for a life of learning, work and service for Christ and His Kingdom', remarked Ediger. A 1995 graduate of Tabor College with a Bachelor of Arts in Health and Physical Education, Ediger played tennis and served as a student-assistant coach with the men's basketball program and continued to serve as an assistant men's basketball coach and tennis coach after graduating. Most recently, Ediger spent the last two years as the Director of Athletics at Tabor, after serving as Sports Information Director for one year and Associate Director of Athletic Communication for three years. Between his stints at Tabor, Ediger served as the Assistant Principal, Athletic Director and Head Girls Basketball Coach at Cimarron High School in western Kansas for almost 15 years. Ediger earned KCAC All-Conference recognition as a member of the Bluejay Men's Tennis team, was a four-year letter winner for Bluejay Tennis and a three-year team captain. He was also inducted into the Tabor College Athletic Hall of Fame as a member of the 1997 Men's Basketball team that reached the NAIA Fab Four.
Ediger will continue to serve in a volunteer capacity, serving as an occasional play-by-play analyst and public address announcer for the Bluejay Sports Information Department.

title: USD 410 gives bond updates
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The USD 410 Board of Education talked bond updates at their monthly meeting on Monday, June 10. Board member, Superintendent Clint Corby and Hillsboro Elementary School Principal Nathan Hiebert, who…
content:
The USD 410 Board of Education talked bond updates at their monthly meeting on Monday, June 10. Board member, Superintendent Clint Corby and Hillsboro Elementary School Principal Nathan Hiebert, who was filling in for Business Manager Jerry Hinerman, were in attendance. Scott Winter was absent.
'The guy doing the brickwork on our high school, he's earning every penny,' said Board President Jared Jost.
'It's a huge job. It's a huge difference of what you can see. I'm excited for that front of the high school to get done. I'm kind of chomping at the bit for that,' said Corby.
Corby passed around various swatches and samples to the board to show them what things will look like in the new projects.
He showed them the wooden material that will go on the auditorium stage. The auditorium seats will be maroon.
The bleachers in the high school gym will be maroon.
Corby said there were rumors that the bleachers would be black since they had been missing causing a gaping hole that looked black. But once the bleachers are on, they will be maroon.
Carpet has been selected for the auditorium as well as the tech center and the media center and all will soon be installed.
Curtains will also be installed in the auditorium and in the gym. The curtains in the gym will be vinyl, drop-down curtains with mesh on top and full color on the bottom. There will be a logo on the main court in the middle school basketball gym.
Corby said the contractors had started polishing the concrete in the auditorium where the seating will be. They had delivered all of the elevator materials and would be starting on that project next.
'The concrete is mostly completed except for the front of HMHS drainage and part of another entrance. They'll be back later this week. The materials for that heated concrete are supposed to be in Thursday, so they will be able to finish that. They're hoping Thursday afternoon or even Friday. The stage floor will be installed next week,' said Corby. They have one more week on the HES roof and then they will be at HMHS by the end of next week. And then in July, we get started on the carpet. Media center, tech center, drop down curtains, auditorium seats, doors, secure entrance, all in July.'
The board also made the following personnel changes:
*approved the resignation of Michele Berens from her position as Hillsboro Elementary School
Teacher effective at the end of the 2023-2024 school year.
*approved the issuance of a contract to Alyson Voran serve as Hillsboro Elementary School
Elementary Teacher for the 2024-2025 school year.
*approved the hiring of Dennis Boldt to serve as USD 410 Summer Painter for 40 hours per week for up to 8 weeks beginning May 20, 2024, at $13.50 per hour
*approved the reduction of one Hillsboro Elementary School Teacher Aide position originally funded with ESSER funds effective at the end of the 2023-2024 school year.
In other business, the board:
*approved the Hillsboro Elementary School Handbook as presented.
*approved the Hillsboro Middle High School Handbook as presented which included the new high school cell phone policy. It was approved 5-1 with Hiebert voting against.
*approved meal increases for the 2024-2025 school year. All but the reduced meals will increase by $0.10. The prices can be found on the USD 410 website.
*approved the bid from ImageQuest Inc. for 20 interactive displays, 19 wall-mounted brackets and
one mobile stand including installation for $46,050.88.
*approved the payment of bills totaling $1,221,696.19

title: Newly ordained pastor enjoys learning and serving others
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Frank Johnson is what many call a lifelong learner. 'I'm a student. I like to always be learning,' said Johnson. The Hillsboro man, who has been the Executive Vice President of Academics and…
content:
Rev. Dr. Frank Johnson (on right) poses with his wife, Terri. Johnson was ordained and installed as a worker priest at Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church in Hillsboro on Sunday. He also works at Tabor College as a Vice President.
Frank Johnson is what many call a lifelong learner.
'I'm a student. I like to always be learning,' said Johnson.
The Hillsboro man, who has been the Executive Vice President of Academics and Compliance at Tabor College where he has worked for 14 years, will now be adding the role of pastor to his list of things he has learned.
He is now ordained and installed as a reverend at Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church in Hillsboro. His ordination service happened on Sunday, July 14. The process to get to his ordination has been quite the journey and it is still ongoing.
'I'm at Concordia Theological Seminary in St. Louis, Missouri which was founded in 1837. So that's where I go twice a year. There are two intensives. It's a four-year program, and I'm halfway through, basically. It's what they call an alternate route,' said Johnson.
He explains that a seminary student typically attends seminary for three years and then takes a year off to go serve as a vicar. Then the final year is completed.
'With this program, you're immediately assigned a vicarage. So I've been a vicar here at Zion Lutheran for two years,' said Johnson. 'It culminates now—with the midpoint ordination. And then two more years of study for a certificate. It's a big deal in the Lutheran church.'
Johnson explained that his ordination and installation service was about his calling and calling is a big deal for Lutherans.
'In contrast to evangelicals who contend that there's an internal call—'God asked me to be a pastor, so I guess I must be a pastor'—There's still that for sure, but that's confirmed by the church. So that's what the Sunday's all about. This is the official church saying, 'Yep. God through us and us through God. He and we picked you'. So that's pretty cool,' said Johnson.
At his ordination service, many pastors attended and spoke.
'It was as much the pastors speaking to me as it was the people speaking to me,' Johnson said.
He is honored to be at Zion which recently celebrated its 140th anniversary.
'It's the oldest, continuously-operating, Christian fellowship in Hillsboro. It started services in 1884 with quite a lineage,' said Johnson.
Johnson will be on staff as a worker priest and will continue to work at Tabor until he retires from there. He will serve along with John Werner who continues to be the lead pastor at Zion.
'I'm just here to help him. My specific ministry will be pulpit supply—basically serving. There are nearly 160 Lutheran churches in the state of Kansas. I wouldn't serve all of those by any stretch, but I will travel around a little bit and speak to some of them and just give people a break, give vacations, somebody's sick, you name it,' said Johnson.
He is also considering doing some nursing home chaplaincy work since his wife works in the nursing home industry once seminary classes end and he has more free time.
'Classes are every Monday night from 6-8 p.m. We just had this one intensive so I've got two weeks to get a paper done. There'll be a couple week break, and then on to the next one. There are 10-week classes three times a year,' he said.
While Johnson enjoys being a pastor, he takes it very seriously. He also sees it as a gift to be able to help serve others.
'It actually comes with a lot of responsibility, a lot of burden, but it's a gift to serve people and preach. That's an important tradition in the Lutheran church. They expect us to do our work and come prepared, but then the people come to listen, so that's pretty cool,' said Johnson. 'Walking with people is a gift—sometimes sharing their story, sharing their cares, their triumphs and sometimes the hard days. It's a privilege to be able to do that.'
Johnson said anyone is welcome to visit and attend the church.
'We would welcome visitors and anybody that's not sure if they would like to come back to church. Zion is a great place. It has a rich, rich history,' said Johnson. 'It's a joy to serve there.'
Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church is located in Hillsboro at 106 N. Lincoln. The number is 620-947-3522.

title: County hears wind farm concerns
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Marion County Board of Commissioners heard concerns about wind energy expansion from Goessel residents led by Brian Stucky. 'I represent other concerned people in western Marion County who are…
content:
The Marion County Board of Commissioners heard concerns about wind energy expansion from Goessel residents led by Brian Stucky.
'I represent other concerned people in western Marion County who are here today, and although I am not an official representative of the Goessel City Council, they have asked me to be a courier to bring you information,' said Stucky.
He explained that in October 2023, a story appeared in the Marion County Record to say that the Orsted Energy company was now looking to expand to the west part of the County, in the townships of West Branch, East Branch, Menno and Liberty.
'Now we face the real possibility that 500-foot tall wind turbines will be near Goessel. There are positives and negatives. There are some who see wind turbines as a good thing, but there are some who absolutely do not want to live anywhere close to them for a variety of reasons. Turbines should be placed in areas with sparse population. Just not here,' said Stucky.
He said that on May 20 he made a presentation to the Goessel City Council calling for a 3-mile radius ban of wind turbines around Goessel.
'They then proceeded to run an online survey of Goessel town and rural citizens, which you have in your packet. The results were made public in their July 15 meeting. It is an overwhelming response of 70% being opposed to wind turbines anywhere near Goessel. The city council also indicated that they were unanimously opposed to wind turbines anywhere near the city,' said Stucky.
He said that the city attorney advised them that the city had no jurisdiction outside the city limits of Goessel which is what led him to turn to the board of commissioners to speak and give a packet of information to. The packet included a letter of support from the Goessel City Council indicating their opposition to wind turbines in western Marion County, two letters from Goessel business persons, six pages of results of the survey, four pages of maps of the four townships in question—with 1500 ft setback circles drawn around each residence that would indicate the population density, and a map from the Harvey County Planning and Zoning Director consisting of counties around Marion which have either had a complete ban or a permanent Moratorium.
'The obvious question here is what do they know that we don't know,' asked Stucky.
Also included in the packet was a call for an Amendment to the County regulations in Article 27 for a permanent ban to commercial wind turbines in West Branch, East Branch, Menno and Liberty townships.
'This is short, clear and clearly in line with what the vast majority of residents want. So I am asking to begin a conversation to take a new look at the County wind regulations,' said Stucky.
Chairman David Mueller asked Planning & Zoning Director Sharon Omstead about the current buffer zone around the City of Goessel.
'So currently, they have an area of influence. That means that any (wind farm) applications that would come through to the Planning & Zoning Board, the city would be provided notice of that application, and they would have the ability to respond to that application as well as the Marion County Planning Commission. The city does not currently have extra-territorial jurisdiction, which is a different type of zoning altogether where the City of Goessel would have more abilities in controlling what goes in and around their city,' said Omstead. 'The extra territorial jurisdiction definitely comes with more responsibilities from the city itself. It can be very expensive because they would be required to provide wastewater systems or water to the area that they choose to have jurisdiction over among other things. But the area of influence gives the city the ability to have more of a safe zone without necessarily having those responsibilities to provide infrastructure.'
The board, Goessel residents, County Counselor Brad Jantz and Omsted discussed the topic more but did not reach any conclusions due to the need for more information. It was decided that County Counselor Brad Jantz and Planning & Zoning Director Sharon Omstead will do research and the topic will be further explored at the Sept. 3 meeting.
In other business, the board:
* heard comments from the public regarding vandalism on Marion County Park & Lake docks. Superintendent Isaac Hett also spoke to the board about the vandalism issues. There was discussion regarding possible solutions including signage, privatizing docks and building more county-owned docks. Commissioner Kent Becker made a motion to allow the privatization of all docks with a fee attached to it, but the motion died for lack of a second. A motion was passed 4-1 (Commissioner Jonah Gehring opposed) to explore privatization.
*heard concerns about Marion County Park & Lake road maintenance from lake residents.
*met with EMS Director Chuck Kenney to discuss a Peabody ambulance station.
Spencer told Kenney, 'I just think it's good to be clear that the commission is committed to that (a Peabody ambulance station). The goal of the commission is to put full time service there, because it makes sense for the county and you have put money in the budget. We're looking to move forward. I think that's important for you to let people know that.'
It was decided to form a committee to work on the station plans.
*Jantz presented an updated draft of a resolution opposing the federal government's 30×30 land preservation goal. The board approved the draft 4-1 (Mueller opposed) for a public meeting for the public to give their input on the resolution. The meeting will be at 6 p.m. on Sept. 30.

title: Clayton identity confirmed, review underway says Department Of Commerce
author: Jessie Wagoner
description: By Jessie Wagoner, Adam Strunk The Kansas Department of Commerce on Aug. 29, issued a denial of allegations by a past employee that he was made to alter grant scores to funnel COVID funds to…
content:
By Jessie Wagoner, Adam Strunk
The Kansas Department of Commerce on Aug. 29, issued a denial of allegations by a past employee that he was made to alter grant scores to funnel COVID funds to legislative leader's districts.
It also stated an independent third-party contractor would do a full review of its American Recovery and Protection Act grants.
The statement comes after more than two weeks of news coverage and questions following the disappearance of interim Peabody City Clerk Jonathan Clayton.
Clayton's truck was discovered near Newton, north of Highway 50 on Aug. 25. On Aug. 29, the Kansas Bureau of Investigation notified Christopher King, Clayton's husband that an identification of the remains had been made through dental records. Jonathan Clayton
'I have had nothing but the best experience with KBI, the Harvey County Coroners Office and Harvey County Sheriff's Office,' King said. 'They have been sensitive and professional the entire time.'
Clayton, who was director of overseeing the Kansas Department of Commerce's COVID-19 funds until late 2023, disappeared Aug. 3. At the time he was working as the interim city clerk for Peabody.
Five days after Clayton's disappearance a previously scheduled email was sent to numerous media outlets and government agencies from an account appearing to belong to Clayton.
The email alleges that Clayton was made to alter grant application scores for BASE grants in order to funnel them to certain legislative constituencies like Butler and Johnson counties. These grants were aimed at spurring economic recovery in Kansas during the pandemic. The two counties Clayton mentioned received $48.6 million out of the total $100 million awarded for the first round of BASE grants.
The Department of Commerce issued a press release on the matter.
'Clayton's allegations of wrongdoing by the Department of Commerce related to the awarding of BASE grants, along with his allegation that he was forced to serve on a volunteer theatre board, are categorically false,' the Department of Commerce said in a release Thursday.
They also claim they were unaware of Clayton's previous conviction for financial crimes in Pennsylvania in 2018. Clayton was convicted of a scheme that involved stealing $200,000 from a ride-share company where he worked.
The Department of Commerce says they are unable to perform national-level background checks for the position he held. Therefore, their vetting process for potential employees only involves online searches, social media reviews and reference checks.
'He would not have been hired by Commerce had we been aware of these convictions,' the release says.
The release also stated that there was no evidence of impropriety at the Department of Commerce but as a precaution 'an independent third-party contractor is doing a full review of all ARPA grants.'
The name of the contractor was not stated in the release.
'Commerce has also requested and is assisting local, state and federal agencies investigating Clayton's volunteer work with community-based organizations in Kiowa and Marion counties who may be victims of fraud.'
Clayton's disappearance coincided with the Department of Commerce's denial of the second $750,000 portion of a $1.5 million BASE grant to the Peabody Main Street Association. He was scheduled to meet with PMSA on the day he went missing to transfer grant data from his laptop.
In May 2023, the Department of Commerce awarded PMSA $1.5 million to revitalize Peabody's historic district, with Clayton playing a key role in securing the grant as the then director of economic recovery.
Since then the Department of Commerce has provided PMSA an extension to provide the required documentation.
In previous interviews with Peabody's mayor and police chief, both reiterated multiple times that there is no criminal investigation related to Clayton in Peabody.
There is an active investigation into Clayton in Kiowa County. The Kiowa County Sheriff's Department and the Kansas Bureau of Investigation are investigating possible financial crimes related to BASE grant funds issued to the Mullinville Community Foundation. Clayton served as an unpaid volunteer who assisted the Mullinville Community Foundation in applying for and managing a BASE Grant. According to King, the Department of Commerce has terminated the grant to the Mullinville Community Foundation and is asking for $425,000 to be returned, however, the Mullinville Community Foundation has said the funds are missing, requesting the Kiowa County Sheriff to investigate.
'I can confirm that the Kiowa County Sheriff's Office is conducting criminal investigations that involve Jonathan Clayton,' Kiowa County Sheriff Kendal Lothman reported to the Harvey County News/Hillsboro Free Press Tuesday. 'Due to the fact that these investigations are ongoing, I will not release or discuss any of the details related to these cases at this time.'
By Thursday afternoon Governor Laura Kelly's office also put out a press release on the matter. The release said the statement was attributable to Kelly's chief of staff Will Lawrence.
The release defended Lt. Gov. David Toland, who oversees the Department of Commerce and was mentioned in Clayton's email. It describes Toland as someone who conducts himself with the highest ethical standards. The release stated Toland had initiated an independent review of grant awards, which were announced Thursday, two weeks prior.
'Clearly, Jonathan Clayton was able to avoid the discovery of his criminal convictions. His financial crimes coming to light, and questions about his involvement with local organizations that received ARPA grants, appear to have set off the chain of events that have occurred over the last several weeks,' the release stated.
'The governor and lieutenant governor will be pursuing changes to the background check statutes this upcoming legislative session. In the meantime, they will be working to sort out issues with those impacted at the local level and will provide whatever support they can to those communities.'

title: Marion business closes after 49 years
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Paul Swan has been a hard worker all his life especially once he started Swan's Refrigeration & Air Conditioning 49 years ago. When Swan and wife Kathy married in 1973, he worked at a grocery store in…
content:
Paul Swan poses with his wife Kathy. He recently retired from the refrigeration, air conditioning and heating company that he ran for 49 years.
Paul Swan has been a hard worker all his life especially once he started Swan's Refrigeration & Air Conditioning 49 years ago.
When Swan and wife Kathy married in 1973, he worked at a grocery store in Marion called Quality Food Market. Two years later he started his refrigeration, air conditioning and heating business.
'Working at the grocery store is what got me interested in doing refrigeration, heating and cooling. So I read a lot of books. I went to a lot of seminars. Pretty much self-taught,' said Swan. 'The refrigeration at the grocery store is what I wanted to do. So I was still working anywhere from 60 to 80 hours a week at the grocery store, and then I did air conditioning work and furnace work in my spare time, which I didn't have much of.'
He worked both jobs until switching over to full-time at his business only in 1993 when the grocery store closed down. But the company was more than enough to keep him working all the time even though he no longer worked at the store.
'I just liked fixing things. I used to work nights, weekends, holidays—didn't matter,' said Swan. 'I got calls in commercial refrigeration, and I would be there until the wee hours in the morning—midnight, 2 o'clock, 4 o'clock.'
Swan slowed down a bit in the past five years and quit doing weekends and nights.
'I pretty much worked 8 to 5 and then I quit for the day. If someone would call me in the evening, I would still offer advice, but they had to wait till the next day for me to come,' said Swan.
Swan has slowly been working toward retirement the past few years.
'My body kinda quit me three years ago. I had back issues. I had a hip replacement. That was part of why I can't get up and down off the floor. That's kinda one of the things that made me decide to quit,' said Swan.
Swan had hoped to turn the business over to his grandson once he retired. His grandson worked with him in the business for over 10 years.
'He worked through high school and quite a few years afterward. I wanted him to take over the business. He already knew how to do everything, how to fix things and he enjoyed the work, but he didn't want the business end of it. And I understood that completely,' said Swan. 'Since he didn't wanna do this, he got another job. And that was when I decided it was time to retire. I turned 70. It was time to quit.'
So Swan decided to close up shop and sell his extra inventory. He closed the business on Aug. 17 of this year.
He said there are a few aspects of the job that he will not miss, especially all of the paperwork.
'That's always been my downfall. I was slow on getting tickets out because you're either out working or you're doing bookwork. I enjoyed the work. Just didn't like the bookkeeping part of it,' said Swan.
He also won't miss being on ladders and the extreme weather conditions.
'I won't miss working on a roof when it's 105 degrees. And it never failed in our business. It's 105 outside—you're outside fixing an air conditioner. When it's minus 30—same thing. You're outside fixing whatever it is. That's just part of the game,' said Swan.
But he will miss his customers.
'The people were always the fun part. A lot of them would stand over me and watch, and we'd visit unless I was concentrating,' said Swan. 'I did enjoy all the people.'
He has fond memories of his customers over the years. He said one of the funny things that happened often was when he would work on refrigerators.
'Refrigerators are not something people normally move so there was a cloud of dust and sometimes dead mice and other things. The 80 and 90-year-old ladies would make me wait. They would make me get out of the way. They wanted to clean it even though it didn't bother me. It was one of the funny things of my job,' said Swan.
Swan and his wife Kathy, who retired last year, have lots of retirement plans. Most of all, they look forward to spending time with daughters Katrina and Becky, their grandchildren and great- grandchildren.
'Family has always been number one. Between working all the hours at the grocery store and then doing my business in my spare time, I kinda missed our daughters growing up. So I make a major effort to make sure that the grandchildren and the great-grandchildren are number one now,' said Swan.
He also plans on catching up with all the things and projects he has been unable to do for the past 50 years because of work. And both he and his wife have a camper and plan to go camping a lot.
'We've already done that. And we're gonna do more of it,' Swan said.
He is excited for the future but cherishes his 49 years in the refrigeration, air conditioning and heating business.
'It went fast,' said Swan.

title: Writer enjoys collecting irises
author: Shana Thornhill
description: I've always been fond of irises. My mom had a dozen or so various colors when I was a kid, and I can still remember the lemony, spicy scent of the reds, the grape scent of the purples, and the petals…
content:
I've always been fond of irises. My mom had a dozen or so various colors when I was a kid, and I can still remember the lemony, spicy scent of the reds, the grape scent of the purples, and the petals so dark they looked black. No matter what else we grew in the garden, the irises were always a fixture.
Growing up, I really learned to appreciate how low-maintenance irises are. And, just for clarification on today's column, I'm referring to Tall Bearded Irises. I have since learned that Siberian Irises, Japanese Irises and Louisiana Irises are all a bit more involved in the care department. Tall Beardeds, Intermediate Beardeds, Dwarf Beardeds and Border Beardeds seem to be a better fit for me, since they're pretty tough, once established. I did try my hand at Lousianas recently, but I didn't have an adequate water feature . . .and, as it turns out, barn cats think they're a comfortable place to lay, so rather doomed out here.
In my early adulthood, irises were always a welcome sight, but I certainly didn't go out of my way to obtain them. During the pandemic, we started looking for outdoor entertainment, even searching for what we called 'feral irises,' or irises growing wild by roadsides or abandoned homesteads. 'Feral yellows' and 'feral purples' (Flavescens and Pallida) were the most common, but we did manage to locate a few fancier colors and shapes. At the time, we just planted them all willy-nilly in a small plot, too close together, with no idea what color was where.
Social media algorithms probably began my descent into iris madness. I started noticing iris sales (some local, some not). A friend from TaeKwonDo was active in her local iris club, and I started seeing iris varieties more gorgeous than my wildest imaginations. Her gardens were a masterpiece of planning and maintenance, with hundreds of irises blazing brightly against the lawns. I hate to admit it, but I was rather envious of the colors, if not of the sheer amount of labor involved.
In my early attempts to obtain more specimens of my own, I started trading locally. Some of you might be familiar with the Marion County Iris Swap page I run on Facebook, connecting fellow fanciers with available irises. I met some fantastic people and got some fantastic irises that way. I was absolutely thrilled to help a friend clean out and thin some of her plantings as well. She had some absolute beauties that, I knew, would look stellar in my little iris garden! I even picked up random irises from the burn pile. Any iris is a good iris, I think.
And of course, I learned that it's not only possible, it's fairly easy to hybridize your own irises and create your own varieties! How could I not want to do that? Amazing!! And, of course, it helps to start with varieties you know and can trace the genetic heritage of. So began the intentional acquisition phase of my insanity.
Meanwhile, Darling Husband, being the wonderfully pragmatic man that he is, hit upon the perfect way to plant irises. He picked a sunny spot in the yard, ran a rototiller in a straight line, drove the mower down the line, and put in another rototilled bed. His impeccable reasoning was that it's easier to weed a bed when you can mow through it. Heck, with all that free labor, who was I to argue? He even filled the first few beds with the nameless irises we already had (pro tip, they're called NoIDs—I always think of the Domino's Pizza Noid, ha ha). Sure, they're planted too close and don't have names, but
when they flower, we can consolidate them and hopefully figure out who they are.
I went a little crazy at one of the online auctions, but I was learning about neat things like historicals, space agers, and color patterns. Ever supportive, Darling Hubs gave me a birthday present: money to spend at the Hutchinson Iris Club sale where I could buy whatever my little heart desired, and he'd plant them for me! Well, of course, I had to join the club after that, and the members are amazingly knowledgeable and helpful.
Irises seem to have made me organized. All of the new babies have name tags. I have locations mapped out, and lists of each variety by type, date, and source. Maybe that's why Hubs is so supportive. Thanks to him, we've made most of my iris ventures into dates. Going to Garnett to pick up my auction flowers was a neat road trip. Of course, we had to hit the Wichita Iris Club sale too . . .and Hubs was even in there picking up things he knew I was looking for. If he doesn't like irises, he certainly hides it well. He's out there planning and planting with me, and even rigs sprinklers for maximum coverage. Hopefully I can start selling some of these myself to recoup some of his investment.
As of this writing, I think I have my last irises in for the year. I think. Of course, I had to go charging off to pick up some lovely historical irises from a very kind lady in Marion this evening, so I guess there's always a possibility of more, but I'm going to have to stop before frost hits. I guess you just never know when Iris fever will strike next!

title: Lifelong Bluebird settles into new role
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Jody Schmidt has been a Bluebird for much of her life. The new principal at Goessel Elementary School grew up in the USD 411 Goessel School District and graduated from Goessel High School. She also…
content:
Jayce, Javin, Jody, Craig, Jayley and Jerah Schmidt. Jody is the new principal at Goessel Elementary School.
Jody Schmidt has been a Bluebird for much of her life. The new principal at Goessel Elementary School grew up in the USD 411 Goessel School District and graduated from Goessel High School. She also spent the last 23 years teaching at Goessel Elementary School before becoming the principal there this fall.
'Shortly after the birth of our first child, my husband and I decided to move home to Goessel as we wanted our children to experience the opportunities a small school has to offer. Goessel schools provide students with a well-rounded education while offering students many opportunities to be involved. The wonderful students, outstanding families, exceptional staff and supportive community is amazing,' said Schmidt.
After graduating from Goessel High School. Schmidt attended Tabor College where she earned her Elementary Education and Special Education degrees. She then earned a Masters of Science in Educational Administration from Emporia State University.
Schmidt began her career in education as an employee of the Harvey County Special Education Cooperative.
'My teaching assignment was at Halstead Middle School as one of the 4th through 8th grade special education teachers in the building,' said Schmidt.
After three years at Halstead Middle School, she began working for the Marion County Special Education Cooperative teaching special education at Goessel Elementary and did that for the next 23 years before moving to the role of principal.
Schmidt thoroughly enjoyed her time as a special education teacher and wasn't looking to leave the role.
'I enjoyed facilitating student growth and the positive relationships I built with students, parents and staff. I am passionate about advocating for students and their families to ensure the best education for all. However, when the elementary principalship opened up, I realized this opportunity would allow me to positively impact a greater number of students and families, support the outstanding staff and give back to a community that has given so much to me,' said Schmidt.
The position became open when Superintendent Mark Crawford shifted to only doing the superintendent role.
'I was the elementary principal and superintendent for three years at Goessel. I am now a half-time superintendent. Our BOE wanted this to be a cost-neutral initiative. My salary was cut by more than 50% to provide a fair principal wage for Mrs. Schmidt. Our district-level work force is very bare bones, even compared to other 1A districts. This empowers us to have a healthy number of teachers and staff dedicated to the classroom,' said Crawford.
Even with all of her experience in education, Schmidt has found there is a lot to learn in her new position.
'As a veteran special education teacher, I was quite comfortable and knowledgeable in my role and responsibilities. As a first-year administrator, it's like being a first-year teacher all over again,' said Schmidt. 'However I have thoroughly enjoyed the new learning and have worked hard to positively impact those around me. I am blessed to work with amazing people here at Goessel. I am particularly thankful for the support I've received from my fellow Goessel administrators, the Goessel Elementary staff, the office team and the USD 411 Board of Education.'
She has been surprised at the sheer number of decisions there are to make in a typical school day as principal but she enjoys the job.
'As principal, I enjoy building relationships with students, helping students succeed, celebrating success and promoting a positive school culture. I also enjoy supporting and positively impacting staff members. Working with parents and community members is also extremely rewarding,' said Schmidt.
'Mrs. Jody Schmidt is an instructional leader. Her many years as a teacher providing specialized instruction gives her a unique skill set as a new building leader. She understands the science of reading and what high-quality pedagogy looks like in all subjects. The most powerful, yet simple leadership trait she has earned is the trust of her teachers. She is a great listener and she knows what the staff and students need,' said Crawford.
Schmidt has several goals for the year.
'This school year I want to continue the tradition of excellence at Goessel Elementary. I plan to work to ensure students excel academically and socially. It is important that each student and staff member feel valued and supported in our school community. I also plan to continue to develop my leadership skills and engage in new learning as we are all lifelong learners,' said Schmidt.
Schmidt has been happily married for 26 years to her husband Craig. They have four children Jayce, Javin, Jayley and Jerah and a daughter-in-law named Danielle.
'We are both Goessel grads and attended Goessel Schools from Kindergarten through 12th grade. Together we have four children. Three of our four children are Goessel grads and our youngest is currently attending Goessel High School,' said Schmidt.
When not at school, Schmidt enjoys spending time with her family.
'Supporting my children as they participate in school activities has been a hobby over the years. I also enjoy reading and baking,' said Schmidt.

title: Peabody creates community art
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Peabody community members were invited to leave their mark on a silk banner on Saturday at the Art in the Park Banner Painting booth at the Peabody Fall Festival. Some drew intricate creations while…
content:
Brothers Madden and Mack Johns add their creativity to an art project on Saturday during the Peabody Fall Festival. Peabody community members of all ages contributed to the drawings that will be made into banners for downtown Peabody.
Peabody community members were invited to leave their mark on a silk banner on Saturday at the Art in the Park Banner Painting booth at the Peabody Fall Festival. Some drew intricate creations while others made dots and other doodles, but all seemed to enjoy adding their creative touches to the project.
Several additional banners were on display as well at the booth. Peabody-Burns elementary, middle and high school students created the banners during the week.
'The elementary school students did drawings about the community, middle schoolers added their touch by outlining the drawings and then the high schoolers came in and filled in the background which just really made it all stand out. It was amazing to see them work on it together,' said Sunflower Theatre Executive Director Susan Mayo.
The banner project is designed to be a community portrait and is sponsored by the Sunflower Theatre in Peabody. The theatre received a Kansas Arts Commission (KAC) Touring Roster Grant so they brought in KAC Touring Roster Artist Carol Bradbury to help make 8 crowd-sourced collaborative banners that create a big-picture portrayal of individual and community connection for downtown Peabody.
Bradbury is the founder of Bloomerang Studios, Inc., a collaborative art experience that celebrates community connection. Her process builds awareness of a community's diversity while helping to shape its creative identity. Her facilitation helps participants tap into their imagination more readily and experience flow.
Bradbury's work is informed by her diverse experience in art, design, branding, psychology and restorative practices. She holds degrees in design and painting from the Kansas City Art Institute and the University of Kansas and is the recipient of multiple awards and scholarships. She has been honored with the Kansas Arts Commission Emerging Artist Award and Go Topeka's Women of Influence Award.
To create the final designs, Bradbury works with the collective contributions of participants as a foundational medium, like a musician sampling sounds for making music. She helps communities, startups and small businesses bring their visions and brands to life.
'Now that we have created these banners, Carol will take pictures of these and digitally create composite illustrations to create the banners,' said Mayo.
Bradbury said working with Peabody members on the project, both at the Fall Festival and with the students, has gone really well.
'There has been a lot of great energy. It's wonderful to see the project grow and evolve. These are reflections of who we are together. It's a community garden,' said Bradbury.
The project is also supported by a Peabody classroom project called Haiku Dream. Haiku Dream uses different approaches to writing to explore another side of the community— its vision for the future.
'The whole school is involved in the Haiku project. They write the Haikus, and then Carol will take them and put them on the backs of the banners to go with the artwork on the front,' said Mayo.
'So the kids will be coming up with their own dream haikus. We gotta get into the minds of the babes—the wisdom of the babes. I've given them prompts. They will choose the top eight that will be on the backside of the banner. It's another extension of identity of who we are together,' said Bradbury. 'Combining the Haikus with the art is like the wisdom of the crowd coming together.'
The banners will be done in December.
'We will wait until the spring and nice weather to have an installation celebration. We haven't set a date for that yet, but we will let everyone know once we do,' said Mayo.

title: Hillsboro celebrates another reunion dinner
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: The Annual Hillsboro High School All School Reunion Dinner was held on Saturday, Sept. 29, at the Hillsboro Mennonite Brethren Church. Approximately 96 former students and spouses attended this year's…
content:
The Annual Hillsboro High School All School Reunion Dinner was held on Saturday, Sept. 29, at the Hillsboro Mennonite Brethren Church.
Approximately 96 former students and spouses attended this year's event. Brad Penner, class of '74, once again served as emcee for the evening. After a welcome and invocation by Penner, the guests were treated to a delicious buffet-style meal provided by Pioneer College Caterers from Tabor College.
Following the dinner, several classes were recognized for celebrating milestone anniversaries of their graduations. These included the classes of 1954, 1964, 1974, 1984 and 1994. Some of these classes also held individual reunions on the same weekend or on previous dates.
USD 410 Superintendent Clint Corby introduced Chad Hughbanks, the new director of the Hillsboro Community Foundation. Hughbanks shared some of the most recent contributions and functions of the foundation, in addition to his vision for the future.
Corby then gave a short update on USD 410 and its importance to the surrounding community.
The evening ended with everyone singing the school song 'Boost For Our Old High'.
In his closing comments, Penner recognized three members of the All School Reunion Planning Committee who will be stepping down, Cynthia Fleming, Kathy Decker and Jim Hiebert have served this endeavor for many years, and feel that it's time for others to carry the mantle for this event to continue, Penner challenged the guests to consider filling the void for future years.
