title: NEXT level nutrition now open in Marion
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Todd and Shannan Parsons recently decided to open up NEXT level nutrition in Marion after doing so well with their Hillsboro store, Level Up Nutrition. 'The Hillsboro store is doing amazing. It was…
content:
Callie Penner and Jessica Hajek were the first customers at NEXT level nutrition in Marion. This is the second location in Marion County for the business with the first shop, Level Up Nutrition, in Hillsboro.
Todd and Shannan Parsons recently decided to open up NEXT level nutrition in Marion after doing so well with their Hillsboro store, Level Up Nutrition.
'The Hillsboro store is doing amazing. It was good enough that we could open up another one here in Marion,' said Shannan. 'Both stores are doing really well—even the Marion one which has not been open very long.'
The couple opened the Hillsboro store in January of 2023 when they saw a need for a smoothie and juice bar in Marion County. Their goal then and now is to help people of all ages get results.
'We're doing specialty drinks and shakes just like we do over in Hillsboro. We're just offering healthy nutrition for everyone. It's not just for young kids. It's for any age person that wants to just live a healthier lifestyle or have something healthy to eat once in a while,' said Shannan.
The couple has been on their own health journey and has found that they 'love helping others' with their health journeys from weight loss to weight gain, muscle gain and more. Shannan has spent much of her time over the years caregiving and helping people and is now looking to do more of the same in this new venue.
They both previously worked at a nutrition club and decided they wanted to do their own thing. They knew they wanted to open one up where there was a need.
'We started looking around at small towns nearby and we really fell in love with how cute Hillsboro is,' said Shannan. 'And now we have a store in Marion.'
Like the Hillsboro store, NEXT level nutrition in Marion does protein shakes, workout and post-workout drinks, energy drinks and hydration drinks.
'You don't always have to have a sugary drink or soda or something like that from somewhere. I think sometimes we just live in such a fast-paced world and people like the convenience. They're just coming in and getting something quick, and it's nice to have an option to do it healthy too if we want to. And it doesn't always have to be unhealthy. There's lots of different things we can offer. We can offer a weight loss program if somebody is looking to lose some weight,' said Shannan.
The menu is vast with options to please any palate from sweet to sour. There are clever names such as Boss Babe, Chiefs, The Trojan, Blue Jays and more. Some shakes/smoothies double as meal replacements (great for seniors or those with digestive issues) with 21 essential vitamins and minerals and over 50 flavors or teas that boost your metabolism and help provide clean energy and focus. They offer energy bombs and iced coffee as well. And you can also choose add-ons for additional benefits for all of the drinks.
'Our drinks are safe for all ages. We can make any drink into a kid-size and make any drink non-caffeinated as well,' said Shannan. Shaina Schafer and her girls Sage and Sutton order nutritious drinks from NEXT level nutrition in Marion.
The couple wants people to know the drinks aren't just for the high school and college-age customers who frequent both stores.
'It's for all ages. And, honestly, most of our clientele is middle-aged people just looking for a healthier route,' said Shannan.
The new store is hosting a grand opening on Friday, Nov. 15 and Saturday, Nov. 16, and they invite everyone to come check it out.
NEXT level nutrition, located at 626 E. Main in Marion, is open 7 a.m.-4 p.m. on Monday-Friday, 9 a.m.-2 p.m. on Saturdays and 12-3 p.m. on Sundays. For more information, check out Next Level Marion on Facebook and Instagram. NEXT level nutrition is now open in Marion. The business offers nutrition shakes and energy drinks. The grand opening for the business will be this weekend.

title: Much to be thankful for this year
author: Shana Thornhill
description: Well, it's that time again when the days are shorter, the nights are chillier, and the year is winding down. Thanksgiving is coming up, and it's time to look back and count my blessings. I try to live…
content:
Well, it's that time again when the days are shorter, the nights are chillier, and the year is winding down. Thanksgiving is coming up, and it's time to look back and count my blessings.
I try to live with an attitude of gratitude on the daily, but several things really stand out this year. I'm thankful for this little grey kitty that's keeping me company as I write. As you may remember, a very kind neighbor gave her to me about a year ago, and I cannot imagine life without her now. I'm also thankful to the vets over at Spur Ridge for their care for all of my critters, most recently my aging male kitty. They helped him feel much better. Of course I'm thankful that my husband and children survived another year with me, if for no other reason than I don't look good in orange jumpsuits. And you know, the usual stuff for us—a roof over our head that usually doesn't leak, food to eat, and fun times together.
Some of the things I'm most thankful for might seem a bit odd to some people. Well, if you've read this column for any amount of time, you're expecting that, so here goes.
I'm glad Darling Daughter got her own apartment. She moved to the big city and stayed with my amazing big brother for a while, but she just got her own place. She's been eyeing these apartments since she was in middle school, so it's a big dream come true for her. I'm so glad she's spreading her wings and flying. I'm so thankful that we share a good relationship and that she still asks for my advice (and even pretends to take it sometimes). I'm thankful for the ways God has moved in her life, even down to finding her a table and chairs for her new place. The house is pretty quiet without her around, but she's got worlds to conquer. It also means I get to pester Darling Son more—because I'm pretty thankful for him too.
I'm especially thankful for modern medicine. My doc at Saint Luke has been amazing at listening and helping me figure out why things 'just don't feel right' lately. Granted, when I was wearing a heart monitor for a month in July, I didn't feel overly thankful, but I definitely am glad that the tests came back normal. Yes, I have it in writing, ha ha.
This week, I'm thankful for my brand spanking new bipap machine. I'll give some of you time to pick your jaws up off the floor. You see, one of the things that the good docs discovered is that my brain forgets to tell me to breathe about nineteen times an hour when I'm asleep. The kids also used to make jokes about what an awful snorer I was. Turns out it was because I was fighting to breathe. Go figure.
The first sleep study was at home. The coordinator was very instructive and helpful, and I got to wire myself up for two nights, with firm orders to sleep on my back. Oddly enough, that was some of the best sleep I'd had in months, contraptions or not.
The second sleep study was in-house, and again, the facilitator was a sweetheart. It didn't really feel like I ever got to sleep though, and the feeling of having air forced through a mask definitely wasn't helping. To top it off, this time I had extra wires stuck to my head, my legs, you name it. I felt like a bowl of very tired spaghetti. As it turns out, you CAN fail a sleep study—apparently they couldn't find a setting that actually helped.
After meeting a new pulmonologist, I got scheduled for yet another sleep study, this one in Wichita. The ladies there were so much fun, I almost wished I didn't have to try to sleep. Apparently, this one took, because they found a setting that actually kept my oxygen levels in the mid-90s. YAY!
Earlier this week, I went to pick up the machine. Mind you, I'm trying to stay optimistic—the whole idea is a massive pain in the posterior, but theoretically it will help me stay alive and possibly have a little more energy during the day. My equipment coordinator was fabulous. I hope I didn't make her late for her next appointment, since we were so chatty. She actually found me a smaller mask, showed me how to use the machine, and told me that Menard's has the cheapest distilled water.
So here I am, not quite a week into the whole bipap thing. I'm still getting used to strapping the mask on when I have to get up at night. The whole facehugger thing is still a definite inconvenience. But, Darling Hubby tells me that I haven't snored for days (he's definitely thankful for THAT), and I notice I'm not quite as tired in the afternoons. Not waking up with a headache is a rather new experience for me too. I'm not sure what to think about all this extra oxygen—apparently it hasn't had a noticeable effect on my goofiness, so that's a plus. It's all easier from here, I guess.
So, my friends, I hope your Thanksgiving is filled with joy, love, and unexpected blessings. Sometimes it's the weird stuff that we need the most!

title: Lifelong Learning on Dec. 9

description: Lifelong Learning at Parkside will feature author Beverley Olson Buller at 10 a.m. on Monday, Dec. 9, at the Parkside Apartments at 1 Park Avenue in Hillsboro. The public is invited. Buller will speak…
content:
Lifelong Learning at Parkside will feature author Beverley Olson Buller at 10 a.m. on Monday, Dec. 9, at the Parkside Apartments at 1 Park Avenue in Hillsboro. The public is invited.
Buller will speak about her book and research on William Allen White. White was a small-town newspaper editor who counted presidents and famous authors among his friends. He rose to worldwide fame before his death in 1944 but never left his hometown of Emporia. One of White's most interesting endeavors was his run for governor in the 1920s to rid Kansas of the Ku Klux Klan.
Buller loves books and kids but especially matching kids with the right book. As a long-time librarian, her professional motto is 'Anyone can like to read if they find the right book.' She grew up in Wellington and currently resides in Newton.

title: Hillsboro discusses fire station project
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council heard about financing for the fire station project from Greg Vahrenberg, Financial Adviser at Raymond James, at the Tuesday, Nov. 19 meeting. Vahrenberg explained the USDA's…
content:
The Hillsboro City Council heard about financing for the fire station project from Greg Vahrenberg, Financial Adviser at Raymond James, at the Tuesday, Nov. 19 meeting.
Vahrenberg explained the USDA's community facilities program which provides permanent takeout financing for projects like the fire station project. The USDA program involves a short-term construction financing with capitalized interest to cover interest payments during construction.
Vahrenberg discussed the USDA letter of conditions which outlines the requirements for long-term financing approval. The current interest rate for the USDA program is around 3.75% to 4.75%, with a 40-year financing term. Vahrenberg explained the steps involved in the financing process, including community input meetings, USDA approvals and the timeline for construction and financing.
Vahrenberg said the turnaround time for the USDA letter of conditions varies but usually takes a few months.
Several council members expressed concerns about the timing of the project and the potential impact of interest rate changes, but Vahrenberg reassured the council that the USDA program offers a stable interest rate and the option to refinance if rates drop.
Mayor Lou Thurston emphasized the importance of addressing the project now to avoid increased costs in the future.
The council agreed to proceed with the project and approved a special meeting for community input at 7 p.m. on Dec. 9 at city hall.
Water and Sewer Supervisor Morgan Marler and Kaleb Spencer gave a sewer inspection and repair proposal focusing on addressing inflow and infiltration issues. The proposal included camera inspection, cleaning and rehabilitation of manholes and the primary lift station. Marler and Spencer provided details on the condition of the manholes and the need for immediate repairs.
'These manholes are made with old brick and mortar, and the mortar has washed out of them over the years. So these manholes are at the top of our list because they're almost too far gone. If we don't do something with them pretty quickly, then we'll be replacing them,' said Marler.
The council discussed the benefits of the proposed work including a 50% reduction in inflow and infiltration issues and compliance with EPA requirements.
They also reviewed the cost breakdown for the sewer repair project totaling $75,400.
The council voted to approve the bid of $75,400 from Johnson Services and thanked the sewer department for their efforts.
In other business, the council:
* approved vouchers totaling $292,295.56.
* approved Resolution 2024-09 establishing a Reinvestment Housing Incentive District (RHID) for the Orchard Ridge Project being built by Mennonite Housing. An RHID collects the increment of property taxes generated by the development to offset the cost of the public infrastructure. In this case the roadway will be a private drive owned and maintained by Mennonite Housing. The public infrastructure that will be paid with the RHID is the water and sewer infrastructure. Electric infrastructure is exempted from these programs and will be paid by Mennonite Housing. The RHID payback, based on the modeling, appears to be nine years. Once the infrastructure is paid back, those tax increments go to the taxing jurisdictions including USD 410 and Marion County. An RHID does defer the collection of property taxes generated by the project, but in this case, facilitates the construction. The total RHID costs are projected at $964,292.21, but the actual final costs will be used. Mennonite Housing will put in the infrastructure and then collect a rebate of the taxes (city, county and local portion of USD410) until the actual costs are recouped.

title: Area Wide Sports Roundup 12-11-24
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Hillsboro Boys basketball – The Trojan boys kicked off the season at home against Sterling. Sterling won 60-40. 'We had a rough game from the field. We were able to get open looks throughout the whole…
content:
HHS wrestler Sutton Redger wrestles and pins Halstead's Riley Queen on Thursday, Dec. 5. The Hillsboro/Canton-Galva Trojans started off their season with a double dual against Minneapolis and Halstead. Photo by Karrie Rathbone.
Hillsboro
Boys basketball – The Trojan boys kicked off the season at home against Sterling. Sterling won 60-40.
'We had a rough game from the field. We were able to get open looks throughout the whole game, but weren't able to capital- ize on the opportunities. We played with energy but need to clean some things up defensively. This next week we play Lyons, Inman and Moundridge in the Moundridge Tournament. This will be a great opportunity to right the ship,' said Coach Kyle Kroeker.
Lincoln Wichert led a balanced attack by the Trojans with 15 points, two rebounds, and a steal for the game.
Coming—The Trojans will play in the Moundridge Tournament Dec. 10-13 at Moundridge.
Girls Basketball – The Trojan girls kicked off the season with a win at home against Sterling with a final score of 62-17.
'I was very pleased with the team on Friday night. I thought we executed well on both ends of the court and played with a lot of confidence and poise. We had good ball movement and consis- tently hit shots on offense, and we were able to apply enough pressure on defense to make it difficult for Sterling to score. We have a quick turnaround next week with the Moundridge tour- nament against some very good opponents. We will continue to work hard and get better. Proud of the team,' said Coach Micah Ratzlaff.
Amyah Werth led the way with 21 points, three assists, and four steals for the game. Both Ella Potucek, 13 points, two rebounds and two steals; and Daisy Klien, 11 points, one rebound, and one steal; were the other Trojans in double-digits scoring for the game.
Coming—The Trojans will play in the Moundridge Tournament Dec. 10-13 at Moundridge.
Hillsboro/Canton-Galva Wrestling – The Trojan wrestlers got their season started on Thursday, Dec. 5 with a double dual at home vs. Minneapolis and Halstead.
Khloe Willis-Dirks, Aimee Kelley and Anna King competed in matches vs. Minneapolis for the girls where Aimee Kelley beat Amiyah Sharp of Minneapolis in a match. There were no girls matches vs. Halstead.
Minneapolis beat Hillsboro in the boys dual with a final score of 39-27, but the boys rallied and won the Halstead dual with a final score of 45-22.
'It's always nice getting the first competition under our belt to get a gauge of where we are and what we need to start to focus on, as a team and individually. The Thursday duals only allowed for limited contested matches as all three teams were hampered by some illness and injuries. Therefore, we did not get nearly as many matches as I hoped for. The six matches we had in the boys dual against Minneapolis were not favorable from a team standpoint, as three of them were Hillsboro wrestlers getting their first ever high school varsity action. However, I am glad they got those match ups, as they need to gain that experience. We only had four contested matches against Halstead and I thought the guys competed better in those matches,' said Coach Scott O'Hare. 'Fortunately, between the girls matches against Minneapolis and the two boys duals, we were able to get several of our wrestlers some important mat time to gain experience and learn from.'
The girls competed in the Doug Kretzer Klassic Girls Tournament on Saturday, Dec. 7. Dirks, Kelley and King all competed but did not place.
'Three of our four girls wrestlers had the opportunity to compete in their first tournament of the season at the Kretzer Klassic in McPherson on Saturday. This is a very competitive tournament with several larger 4-5-6A schools. Although it is not showing up yet in the win-loss columns, these girls are battling tough, learning, and with each match, they showed progress,' said O'Hare.
Both the boys and girls will continue to work hard to improve.
'Across the board, we definitely will continue to work on new techniques and improve on what we have already worked on. We definitely need to get tougher, both mentally and physically. This is a tough sport already, and when things get hard in practice and in competition, the only way to expect to come out on top is to remain tough and grind through it. I am excited to see how this group steps up and continues to improve as the season progresses,' said O'Hare.
Coming — The Trojans will compete next on Friday, Dec. 13 at Ellis.
Marion
Girls basketball – The Marion girls kicked off the season with a win at home against Goessel on Friday night with a final score of 45-33.
'Our girls came out tonight focused and they played hard. It was a great team win to open the season. I thought we defended well. We fouled too much, but the girls stepped up and made big plays to close out the ball game. I was proud of how we handled the ball tonight and the energy we had throughout the game. We have some things to clean up and get better at, but it was effort basketball and grit basketball, and when we do those two things, good things happen,' said Coach Jason Hett.
Coming—The girls will play at Berean Academy on Friday, Dec. 13.

title: SAPC awarded federal grant for youth substance use prevention
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Hillsboro - Marion County Substance Abuse Prevention Coalition (SAPC) has been selected as a recipient of a $125,000 federal grant from the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP)…
content:
Hillsboro – Marion County Substance Abuse Prevention Coalition (SAPC) has been selected as a recipient of a $125,000 federal grant from the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy
(ONDCP) under the Drug-Free Communities (DFC) Support Program. This grant program, managed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), represents an opportunity to strengthen ongoing efforts in preventing youth substance use in our community.
ONDCP's DFC program is the nation's leading effort to mobilize communities to prevent and reduce substance use among youth. The DFC program provides federal grants to community coalitions to identify and respond to the issues unique to their community and change community conditions tied to youth substance use. With this grant, Marion County SAPC will be able to continue building a safe, healthy, and drug-free community.
'I wanted to personally congratulate your team on being awarded a Drug-Free Communities Support Program grant for $125,000,' said United States Senator Roger Marshall, M.D. 'I have continually supported this program and I am so proud these dollars are coming to Kansas. I know you will put the funds to good use educating the Marion County community on substance use and preventing substance abuse in our young people. Substance use in Kansas continues to be one of my biggest concerns
and it is rewarding to see people stepping up to help our communities fight this epidemic. The dedication that you have displayed to this goal is truly commendable. Thank you again for all the great work you do to keep our kids and communities safe.'
Marion County SAPC is very excited and grateful to have been awarded this grant, totaling $125,000 each year for the next five years. They look forward to utilizing the funds to expand their prevention work with additional strategies and events that will benefit Tabor College, the five school districts, and communities of Marion County in their efforts to prevent county-wide underage substance misuse.
More information about the DFC program can be found at https://www.cdc.gov/overdose-prevention/php/drug-free-communities/.
For inquiries, please contact Terry Bebermeyer, FACT, Inc. Executive Director at fact@usd410.net or at 620-947-3184, opt. 3.

title: New teachers on staff at Centre
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: There are two new teachers on staff this year at the USD 397 school district. Jessica Helmer is teaching 3rd grade. She recently received her teaching license through Wichita State University's…
content:
There are two new teachers on staff this year at the USD 397 school district.
Jessica Helmer is teaching 3rd grade.
She recently received her teaching license through Wichita State University's Teacher Apprentice Program which allowed her to work as a paraprofessional at the Centre School District and take classes online.
'I have worked as a paraprofessional at Centre for three years as well as substitute this past year. 2024 is my first year teaching,' said Helmer.
Born and raised in Marion, Helmer lives east of Marion in the country with her husband Paul and their four children, all of whom attend Centre.
'The Centre School district has been a wonderful place to work, with a positive atmosphere and great people to work with. I look forward to many more years at Centre, educating the minds of our youth,' said Helmer.
Taylor Minihan (Harms) is teaching English 9-12 and Yearbook.
She earned a Bachelor's Degree from Kansas State University in Family Studies and Human Services; Minors in Animal Sciences and Industry, as well as Leadership Studies in May 2016. She then earned a Master's Degree from Kansas State University in Counseling and Student Development in December 2019. Helmer is currently pursuing a Master's Degree in Teaching from Kansas State University.
Helmer served as a high school counselor for four years—one year at Marion High School and three years at Rock Creek High School.
Minihan grew up in Lincolnville.
'My parents are Mark and Kim Harms. I have two younger brothers: Cade and Payton. I met my husband, Chase (from Blaine, KS), while we were both attending Kansas State University,' said Minihan. 'My husband and I moved back to the area, where I worked part-time for my parents' ranch, as well as served as a substitute teacher prior to teaching English at Centre this year.'
Minihan said that Centre holds a special place in her heart for several reasons.
'My mom and youngest brother are both Centre graduates. My grandpa, Don Buethe, also served on the school board years ago. I grew up going to church with Centre families and had close friends through FFA and 4-H that attended Centre. It feels like home in many ways. I also sincerely appreciate the school culture and environment at Centre. It's one that feels warm, welcoming and supports student growth,' said Minihan.
The first-year teacher has several goals for the year.
'My goals begin with getting to know my students and their families. I really value clear and open communication, as well as building strong relationships. Another major goal of mine is to help make a strong connection for students between what they learn in my classroom and how they can use it after high school. Regardless of what they choose to do after high school, I want them to feel well-prepared to communicate effectively and professionally, construct a cover letter and resume, write professional thank you notes, compose workplace emails/documents and analyze various types of literature. My hope is to find creative ways to make ELA fun and useful through various instructional methods that work well for all learning styles,' said Minihan.

title: Family grateful for community support after accident
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Vinduska family's Christmas looks very different this year after Madison and her son Miller, 3, were in a car accident on Nov. 22 on US-50 and Northeast Lake Rd/Indigo Rd. (also known by locals as…
content:
Mark, Miles, Madison and Miller Vinduska of Marion in a Christmas photo last year. Their Christmas looks different this year as Madison recovers from a car accident she and Miller were in on Nov. 22.
The Vinduska family's Christmas looks very different this year after Madison and her son Miller, 3, were in a car accident on Nov. 22 on US-50 and Northeast Lake Rd/Indigo Rd. (also known by locals as the 13-mile road). While Miller was fine, Madison suffered serious injuries that resulted in several surgeries while hospitalized at Wesley Medical Center.
On Monday, Dec. 9 she was transferred to Madonna Rehabilitation Hospital in Lincoln, NE. The non-profit hospital provides health care services to patients faced with spinal cord injury, stroke, traumatic brain injury and other serious conditions. It also offers an intensive therapy program seven days a week and 24-hour rehabilitation nursing and physician supervision services.
'She's come quite a ways from when we first arrived here,' said her husband Mark. 'Wesley was fine, but they're geared towards medical needs. Madonna's a different atmosphere and it feels good. She usually does about five therapies a day. Some of it's occupational therapy, some of it's physical therapy, speech therapy, and they have another one called assistive tech, and that's basically technology geared towards people with disabilities.'
Mark explains that Madonna's motto is to start with what's necessary and then do what's possible and then do the impossible.
'They just see what she can do and build around that to see what abilities she'll gain back,' he said. 'They come in and work her arms, stretch her arms and work her legs over. They're always constantly feeling for changes or things that they can build on. She's usually got something going from about 5 in the morning until 2 o'clock or so, and then it's rest after that. She is making progress here, and it's good to see that in her.'
Madison's mom Robin and Mark are with her most of the time and other friends and family rotate in and out.
'I'm usually there to see all of her therapies. I spend the night there probably about half of the time. We're staying at a Madonna-owned house that's right across the street from Madonna so it's walking distance,' said Mark.
Mark's employer, Marion Die and Fixture, has been very understanding and worked with him during it all.
'They've set me up with a computer to work remotely when I get time to get back to that. I anticipate we're gonna be here for a while,' said Mark.
The medical professionals and staff at Madonna have not given the family any timeline of what to expect.
Madison's sister Olivia and her husband Douglas have been caring for Madison and Mark's two boys, Miller and Miles, 6.
'That's working out pretty well. I didn't want to try and transfer the kids' school system up here to Lincoln, but it's hard being away from them,' said Mark.
And people from all over have been reaching out to help.
'The support we've gotten from the community and everybody, it's outstanding. I would have never guessed there's just that much good out there,' said Mark. 'Everybody's been great about stepping in. My mom's been helping watch the kids when she can, and everybody wants to help.'
For now, the best way to help is through donations at an account set up at Central National Bank.
'People can come in and donate to that account. I've joked about paying child support to Olivia and Douglas now, but they gotta help pay for food and stuff, too. I try and make sure that they've got what they need to get the kids around so money to that account is helpful,' said Mark.
Madison can get cards and packages at the hospital if they are addressed to her. Send to Madison Vinduska, c/o Madonna Rehab Hospital, Room S05, 5401 South St., Lincoln, NE. 68506.

title: Area Sports Roundup 1.22.25
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Goessel Boy's basketball – The Bluebird boys competed against Little River on...
content:
Goessel
Boy's basketball – The Bluebird boys competed against Little River on Tuesday, Jan. 14. Little River won 56-24.
Coming- The Bluebirds will next compete in the Centre Tournament at Centre January 21-25.
Girl's basketball – The Bluebird girls competed against Little River on Tuesday, Jan. 14. Little River won 73-9.
The girls next played at Canton Galva on Friday, Jan. 17. The game was close with Canton Galva winning with a final score of 42-37.
Coming- The Bluebirds will next compete in the Centre Tournament at Centre January 21-25.
Hillsboro
Boys basketball – The Trojan boys played away against Haven on Tuesday, Jan. 14 where they fell a bit short of a victory.
'The Haven game was a defensive battle. It was a tight game right up to the end. The boys worked incredibly hard all night. We weren't able to capitalize on some opportunities late in the game. We were led in scoring by Lincoln Wichert and Easton Shahan with 12 and 10 points, respectively. Seth Driggers was able to create three steals. The boys continue to compete with some tough competition,' said Coach Kyle Kroeker.
The final score was 41-35.
The Trojans next played at Hesston on Friday, Jan. 17 where Hesston won with a final score of 40-32.
'Both teams hung their hats on the defensive side of the ball. Seth Driggers had a solid game with 10 points and three steals. He created havoc all over the court. Easton Shahan (6), Noah Beavers (5) and Lincoln Wichert (5) cleaned up the boards on both ends. Again we had some chances to tie the game but weren't able to make it happen. I was proud of the team's heart and willingness to battle. I feel we are right there against some very tough teams. It will be exciting to see what we can do as we clean some different things up,' said Kroeker.
Coming—The Trojans will host the Trojan classic Jan. 21-25.
Girls basketball -The Trojan girls played away against Haven on Tuesday, Jan. 14.
'Tuesday was a physical game and we had some tough match-ups against Haven. We got pushed around in the first quarter and struggled to score on offense. We changed some things up defensively with a soft press back into our zone and we were able to settle in and hit some shots on offense. In the second half our girls continued to battle and get the defensive stops that we needed along with making just enough plays on offense to squeeze out a tough win. Proud of the girls,' said Coach Micah Ratzlaff.
The girls won 49-43.
Next the Trojans played away against Hesston on Friday, Jan. 17.
'I felt like we played really hard and gave good effort. Hesston had too much fire power for us down the stretch. Defensively we kept them well below their average, but we couldn't put enough points on the scoreboard to get the win,' said Ratzlaff.
Hesston won 39-30.
Coming—The Trojans will host the Trojan classic Jan. 21-25.
Wrestling – The Hillsboro/Canton Galva Trojans competed in the Halstead Boys and Girls Invitational Tournament on Friday, Jan. 17 and Saturday, Jan. 18. The boys came in 13th out of 19 teams with 50.5 points.
'The Halstead Invitational took on a different look this year, as it has always been our first opportunity for a two-day, double elimination tournament, much like what regionals and state have traditionally been. However, the continued rapid increase in the number of girls wrestling and in an effort to showcase them, Halstead made the decision to split the tournaments, hosting the girls division on Friday and the boys division on Saturday,' said Coach Scott O'Hare.
With one out due to injury, the Trojans only had three girls compete on Friday.
Sophomore Aimee Kelley got out to a solid start in the opening round, jumping out to a 7-0 lead on the #3 seed, but was eventually pinned late in the first period. After picking up a solid win in the next round, Kelley suffered her second loss and was eliminated. Freshman Anna King and junior Claire Morey both went 0-2. Therefore, all three were eliminated early in the tournament and wereunable to earn a medal.
Once again, the Hillsboro/Canton-Galva boys went into the tournament short-handed, missing four wrestlers from the line-up due to injuries and other commitments. Four of the guys with a bit more experience managed to earn some solid wins to earn trips to the podium, highlighted by senior Logan Rogers, junior William Andreas and freshman Magnusson Cathey each earning their first high school varsity medals.
The team was led by the performance of sophomore Jaxon Chrislip. He had a nice day, going 3-1 to earn 3rd place in a tough 144 lb bracket.
'We have used the past week talking a lot about consistency, progress, and fundamentals. This theme will continue for our team the rest of the season. In order to get a few of our younger guys some competition at their level, we plan to take several of them to a JV tournament in Nickerson on Tuesday and hold them out of next Saturday's varsity tournament at Eureka. A few of them will attend both tournaments. Hopefully this will help them gain some confidence that what they are learning is working and help them to continue to trust the developmental process,' said O'Hare.
Coming—The Trojans will compete on Saturday, Jan. 25 at the Eureka Boys & Girls Invitational Tournament.

title: IdeaTek is bringing gigabit fiber internet to Marion
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: MARION, Kansas – Super-fast fiber internet service is now available to hundreds of Marion families and businesses, thanks to a $1.6 million investment from IdeaTek. The Buhler-based company will…
content:
MARION, Kansas – Super-fast fiber internet service is now available to hundreds of Marion families and businesses, thanks to a $1.6 million investment from IdeaTek.
The Buhler-based company will deliver unlimited, uncapped speeds of up to 2.5 gigabits per second citywide, giving nearly 1,100 homes and businesses access to future-proof, 100% fiber technology.
Marion City Councilman Tim Baxa emphasized the importance of dependable, high-speed internet in driving community growth and economic progress, opening doors to new opportunities.
'Bringing fiber internet to every home in the city of Marion isn't just about addressing current needs — it's also about preparing for the future,' he said. 'We're thrilled to work with IdeaTek to bring cutting-edge, reliable fiber internet to our community, ensuring homes and businesses stay connected and giving our city the tools to thrive.'
Investing in fiber is a scalable solution for Kansas' future growth. While some providers use terms like 'Fiber-Powered' to disguise outdated technology, IdeaTek invests in true 100% fiber connections, offering symmetrical speeds, better reliability and scalable capacity — all at more affordable pricing than many existing providers.
'At IdeaTek, we're committed to bringing our high-speed fiber internet to every corner of Kansas, and we're excited to make it a reality in Marion,' said Daniel Friesen, IdeaTek's co-founder and chief innovation officer. 'True fiber internet is the gold standard in internet connectivity. Some may think the average user doesn't need fiber, but we believe everyone deserves the best possible online experience. Whether you're casually browsing or online gaming, our fiber network delivers unparalleled reliability. IdeaTek's ultimate goal is to provide fiber to all Kansas residents because fiber is hands-down the best technology for high-speed broadband.'
Friesen added, 'We're so confident you will prefer our service over others that we don't require contacts. We'll provide you with the best service, so we're not worried about you leaving.'
Marion residents can soon enjoy: Symmetrical upload and download speeds of up to 2.5 gigabits per second, perfect for streaming, gaming and working from home.
Unlimited data with no throttling, interruptions or lag time— internet when you need it most.

title: Tabor College receives $1.3 million challenge grant
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: HILLSBORO, Kan.—Fundraising for the renovation of the former Mary J. Regier Building,...
content:
HILLSBORO, Kan.—Fundraising for the renovation of the former Mary J. Regier Building, the future home of business and entrepreneurship, reached a significant milestone with the announcement of a $1.3 million challenge grant from the Mabee Foundation. To receive the money, Tabor College must raise an additional $1,383,972 by Jan. 14, 2026.
Tabor seeks to raise $11 million for the Business & Entrepreneurship Center. With $6.7 million already given toward the renovation, the challenge grant aids momentum toward adding to and renovating one of Tabor's two most historic facilities. The building and the H.W. Lohrenz Administration Building both opened in April 1920. Details of the facility additions and renovations will be released at a later date.
'This challenge grant results from the incredible partnership of Tabor College and the Mabee Foundation,' said President David Janzen, Ph.D. 'We're deeply grateful for the donors who have already supported our vision and look forward to speaking with those who will help us reach this goal. We're thrilled to move closer to the construction of this project, eagerly anticipating what God will offer our campus with this space.'
The challenge grant now represents the eighth Tabor has received from the Mabee Foundation. Other projects include the Wohlgemuth Music Education Center (1989), Campus Recreation Center (1992), Solomon L. Loewen Natural Science Center (1997), Townhouse Residence Halls (2006), Shari Flaming Center for the Arts (2017), and Jost Hall (2023).
'In God's faithfulness, donors are showing tremendous support for what a facility like this can provide,' said Ron Braun, vice president of philanthropy. 'We look forward to meeting this grant and completing fundraising over the coming months.'
Gifts for the Business & Entrepreneurship Center can be made by check or by visiting www.tabor.edu/give. Contact Braun via email, at ronb@tabor.edu, or by phone, at 620-947-3121 (ext. 1710) to learn more and make a gift of appreciated assets, stocks, commodities, real estate, IRA, or estate.

Boys basketball – The Trojan boys played at home on Friday, Jan. 31 against Minneapolis. They won 51-36.
'Against Minneapolis, we were able to have a steady stream of scoring throughout the game. The boys worked to get easy looks inside either from the drive or passes into the paint. Girls basketball – The Trojan girls played at home on Friday, Jan. 31 against Minneapolis. They won 32-20.
'This was another tough opponent with a good record coming off a super-talented Trojan Classic. We did show up and battled all night. We were good enough defensively and executed well at times on offense. We go through stretches where we can get some rhythm and put the ball in the basket and also find ourselves not finishing or making bad decisions. Our goal is to find ways to score in all four quarters and if we can do that, we will be scary moving into the postseason which is right around the corner. We have and will continue to play the toughest schedule of any 2A team this year. We look forward to playing good competition. I am blessed to do this with a great group of girls and coaches,' said Coach Micah Ratzlaff.
Coming—The girls will play on Friday, Feb. 7 at home against Halstead.
Wrestling – The Hillsboro/Canton-Galva Trojan wrestlers competed in a dual at Council Grove (CG) on Thursday, Jan. 30. The results were as follows:
106: Jameson Fetters (CG) over William Andreas (Fall 3:40)
126: Bradley Doornbos (CG) over Seth Schafer (TF 19-4 1:3)
132: Leo DeDonder (CG) over Copeland Krause (Fall 1:24)
138: Tripp Darbro (CG) over Lucas Sorensen (Fall 2:49)
150: Hadley Smith (CG) over Phoenix Fickes (Fall 3:20)
157: Logan Schlimme (CG) over Lincoln Epp (TF 20-5 1:49)
175: Tripp Stormont (CG) over Magnusson Cathey (Fall 4:38)
190: Cameron Hageman (CG) over Jackson Kleiber (Fall 4:19)
Girls 125: Briley Cannon (CG) over Aimee Kelley (Fall 1:45)
'Unfortunately we continue to battle illness and injuries, but on the positive side, this week was a great opportunity for several of our younger and less experienced wrestlers to get a lot of mat time. We were extremely short-handed for the varsity dual on Thursday evening at Council Grove, only able to fill eight weight classes including five of them with freshman wrestlers. That was a challenge against a pretty talented Council Grove team,' said Coach Scott O'Hare.
The Trojans competed in the Hoisington Cardinal Classic on Friday, Jan. 31 and the Marion JV Tournament on Saturday, Feb.1.
The challenges faced on Friday were even greater as basically the same group went to compete at the tough Hoisington Cardinal Classic Tournament. According to O'Hare, the highlight of the day was having two freshmen, Fickes at 150 lbs and Cathey at 175 lbs pick up a couple of nice wins to finish in the top four in their brackets.
'Although a few others who were scheduled to compete were not able to go on Saturday, the Marion JV Tournament offered a great opportunity for some of our younger wrestlers to gain more valuable experience and find some success. Sophomore Aimee Kelley really bounced back nicely from losses on Thursday and Friday to finish as the 125 lb girls' runner-up. It was great to see her, as well as a few of our guys, earn medals,' said O'Hare.
He said that for some, this three-day stretch provides a great mental and physical challenge that kids need to experience to prove to themselves what they are capable of doing.
'It really is a test of grit, having to make weight three days in a row along with competing in as many as eleven matches in that time. I am super proud of those that competed all three days,' O'Hare said.
As a whole, this group continues to make progress.

Over the next three weeks, we will be participating in a two-day tournament in Circle this Friday and Saturday as well as attending the boys and girls league and regional tournaments. We are hopeful some of them can get healthy and be prepared to make a push to make the podium at league and regionals, as well as earn a trip to state,' said O'Hare.

title: PBHS cheerleaders hope to attend prep camp
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Peabody-Burns cheerleaders Keira Banks and Mia Webster have been cheering for two...
content:
Peabody-Burns cheerleaders Keira Banks and Mia Webster have been cheering for two years in high school and both love it.
'I like how we always get to hang out with the little kids. And I when we do little cheer and we get to teach the little kids cheers and dances,' said Banks. 'We also do a lot of stuff with the community.'
'I love the team. Having all my friends around me and doing something that brings us together is so fun,' said Webster. 'It's also so much fun because in a small town. You grow up with these people so we are cheering on childhood friends and sometimes even family.'
And now the two sophomores may get to go to Hawaii this summer to attend Cheer Hawaii.
'My cheer coach nominated us. All we had to do is fill out an application and register,' said Banks.
Webster added, 'Cheer Hawaii is a college prep camp that I get the opportunity to go to this year. My sister Chloe and one of my best friends Sarah went last year and really enjoyed the experience. You get to learn a lot about cheering and you get to experience Hawaii and the Hawaiian culture.'
According to PBHS Cheer Coach Danae Kyle, Cheer Hawaii is an invitational college prep camp that has a strong focus on higher skills, including stunting. The classes are taught by college cheerleading coaches.
'Cheerleaders must be nominated by their cheer coach who provides information about their work ethic, GPA, leadership skills, community service and extracurricular activities. Based on this information, the review board chooses their invitees. Approximately 200 girls are selected to attend.
They will stay at the University of Hawaii for seven days. They will have workout sessions each day, work with a coach and a team of about 12 other cheerleaders from all over the nation and prepare for a performance on the last day of camp,' said Kyle.
Kyle said that the girls will also get to experience a luau at the Polynesian Cultural Center, visit Pearl Harbor, learn how to Hula dance, attend a beach BBQ, experience Waikiki Beach and much more.
'I chose my nominations based on how I think the camp will benefit them. Both of these girls show willingness to try new things and adapt to changes well at practice, whether they are a flyer or a base for a stunt. I chose cheerleaders based on their practice attendance, the positivity they bring to the squad, their work ethic and the drive I see they have to become a better cheerleader,' said Kyle. 'I look for overall well-rounded individuals, not only as a cheerleader—but as a student as well. These two will make eleven cheerleaders that I have sent to this camp since 2019. The first year I sent cheerleaders, I was also chosen to be a coach at the camp. It was an experience I will never forget, and neither will any of these kids.'
The camp will be June 18-25, and the girls are working hard to raise the funds to be able to attend.
'Right now we're just fundraising and trying to raise enough money to pay for the camp and the plane tickets,' said Banks. 'The camp itself is $3,000 and that doesn't include the plane tickets and other costs like spending money.'
The girls have done raffles, bake sales and several fundraising campaigns. They have also done concessions stands at basketball games.
'One of my best-selling campaigns right now is Warrior Blankets. Me and my mom worked really hard to make blankets and the sale is going very well. They are available at basketball games or people can reach out to me on Facebook @ Mia Webster,' said Webster.
Banks said that people can donate by calling her grandpa Danny Peugh at 316-217-2279.
Something me and Keira are both doing right now is 'Pick a Space to Donate'. You can also do this at basketball games or through Facebook,' said Webster.

title: Hillsboro approves low-income benefit program
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Feb. 4 where they heard...
content:
The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Feb. 4 where they heard from Leslie Atherton of Kansas Power Pool (KPP) Energy about PACE Solar program needs.
Atherton said that KPP Energy continues to seek funding and tax credits for its solar project under the Powering Affordable Clean Energy (PACE) Act and presented two proposed resolutions for the council's consideration.
'The first resolution is to establish a qualified low-income economic benefit program, and that is related to a 20% tax credit. And the reason for the quick turnaround is the priority deadline for our application is February 15th,' said Atherton.
Atherton stated that things are somewhat up in the air with the new administration, but if the money is going to be there they want to be in line for it.
She explained that if the council adopted the resolution, KPP would apply for a 20% tax credit on the installed solar facility. If awarded the credit, KPP will calculate and allocate funds to the program annually for five years. The amount provided will be 50% of the cost difference between generating solar energy at the solar power facility and purchasing equivalent energy per kWh. These funds will be distributed by the city to program customers identified through the Low-Income Energy Assistance Program. The first credit distribution is expected in 2027, approximately one year after project completion.
The council and Atherton discussed different ways to distribute the funds but did not settle on exactly how they would do it.
'It's a really great benefit and kind of an unexpected benefit from this project. They can go back to low to moderate income. We see a fair amount of that within our customer base so anything we can do to help that out is really helpful,' said Hillsboro City Administrator Matt Stiles.
Stiles told the council that the city currently serves up to 50 accounts with the Low-Income Energy Assistance Program (LIEAP) which is administered through DCF.
The council approved the resolution which costs the city nothing.
The council also approved the second resolution to confirm no interconnection agreement is necessary for the solar facility.
The council also heard from Doug Teetzen of TCW regarding a security camera proposal and the Smart Town system.
'For the past few years, the city has considered implementing a security camera system at key facilities to mitigate liability and enhance security. Locations such as Memorial Park, the splash park and the rodeo arena have experienced vandalism and property damage. Installing security cameras may deter these activities and provide valuable evidence for prosecuting offenders,' said Stiles.
TCW will install new security camera using Hillsboro's fiber network and offered two pricing options under a three-year agreement—an outright purchase of $28,465 one-time, plus $549.86 monthly ($6,598.32 annually), totaling $48,259.96 over three years or a lease option of $11,345 upfront, with a $1,406.74 monthly recurring charge ($16,880.88 annually), totaling $61,987.64 over three years. The lease includes free replacement of any equipment under normal use. Funds for this project would come from the general fund and be allocated across the affected locations.
Stiles explained that the city also consulted with Gary McCloud from My Alarm Services who installed and maintains the existing cameras used by the Hillsboro Police Department, but the TCW proposal includes more locations than My Alarm Services.
Stiles told that council that based on technology, ease of use and cost, he recommended the TCW proposal.
'The ability to monitor the system from City Hall is a significant advantage that we currently lack. Additionally, expanding the TCW system in the future to locations like the bowling alley or Schaeffler House appears to be more accessible and quickly deployed,' said Stiles.
The council voted to approve TCW's proposal for the lease option.
In other business, the council:
*approved vouchers totaling $567,187.40.
*approved the purchase of activated carbon for the water treatment facility for $27,360.
*approved the purchase of 85 LED streetlights using grant funds totaling $36,428.87.
*approved a proposal to repair the foundation of the Delores Dalke Family Aquatic Center building for $22,900.
*agreed to hold a special meeting for strategic planning at 6 p.m. on Thursday, March 13.
*met in executive session for 10 minutes to discuss personnel matters for 10 minutes.
*learned that the memorial service for Carolyn Ray will be at 1 p.m. on Sunday, Feb. 16 at the Hillsboro American Legion.
*heard that the city is hosting a Love Hillsboro, Love Kansas event on Friday, Feb. 14 in the afternoon at City Hall. This is part of the Love Kansas grant program. See flyers and advertisements around town and online for more information.
*Learned that bowling alley naming public submissions closed on Jan. 31 with over 100 name suggestions received. The response from the community was excellent. A finalist list will be presented to the council on Feb 18 for selection.
*Heard that Saturday, Feb. 22 is a busy day in Hillsboro—Kiwanis Biscuit & Gravy Fundraiser at the Senior Center; Legislative Update with Rep. Mike King at 9 a.m. at City Hall; Youth Entrepreneurship Challenge at Tabor College starting in the morning.
*Learned that the latest episode of Coffee with the Mayor was released on Jan. 31 featuring a conversation with Clint Corby, Superintendent of USD 410.

title: Marion County celebrates National FFA Week
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: National FFA Week is Feb. 15-22. FFA chapters around the country are going all out to celebrate the annual event and Marion County's school district chapters are no exception. FFA, Future Farmers of…
content:
Centre FFA members Kaden Hutchison, Addison Bina and Kaitlynn Bina make sausage and serve pancakes on Saturday. In the back, Ryleigh Jones, Cheyenne Helmer and Brogan Plett make pancakes. The group kicked off National FFA week with a community breakfast in Burdick. They will have other activities throughout the week to celebrate FFA. Centre FFA members Ryeigh Jones, Cheyenne Helmer, Brogan Plett and Kaitlynn Bina make breakfast for the Burdick community at the Burdick United Methodist Church on Saturday, Feb. 15. The event kicked off National FFA Week for the group. The Hillsboro FFA Chapter kicked off National FFA Week with a community pancake feed on Saturday, Feb. 15 where FFA members made and served pancakes to those who attended. They will have other activities throughout the week to celebrate FFA.
National FFA Week is Feb. 15-22. FFA chapters around the country are going all out to celebrate the annual event and Marion County's school district chapters are no exception.
FFA, Future Farmers of America, is a youth organization whose mission is to help students develop their potential for leadership, personal growth and career success through agricultural education.
'FFA gives students the opportunity to grow and learn about and perform real-world job skills that will help them be successful post-high school. Plumbing, welding, and construction jobs are now paying very well. FFA students learn the skills needed to perform these and other jobs, giving them a head start in the labor force as they graduate,' said Goessel High School Ag Education teacher and FFA Sponsor Nathan Graber.
Centre High School Ag Education teacher and FFA Sponsor Emma Jacobson adds, 'FFA is valuable for our high school students to develop real-life skills they can use at home or in a career someday. Those skills may include welding, cooking, animal husbandry, record keeping or gardening. Beyond that, FFA exposes students to multi-faceted careers in Agriculture. Many people think FFA is just for kids raised on a farm, but we have students from all different backgrounds. FFA also provides scholarships to our graduating seniors so they can have financial aid to pursue education after high school.'
'FFA is a great organization, not just for the farm kids. FFA provides leadership opportunities and experiences for all students to grow themselves,' said Marion High School Ag teacher in charge of FFA Charlie Bestwick.
The FFA chapters are active all year long and often focus on the community.
'Being in FFA at Goessel includes judging contest opportunities and leadership development events. As a chapter, we also put on a community pancake feed, Kiddie Barnyard in the spring for the local elementary school, a coat drive and several other events. Our members take an agriculture class to be part of our FFA. Some of the classes are Ag Mechanics and Advanced Mechanics, Horticulture, Ag Explorer, Animal Science. In these classes members build projects, grow plants for the spring plant sale and oftentimes, projects are for outside community members,' said Graber.
'Hillsboro is a small but mighty chapter. Some of our members are rural and some live in town. We participate in a wide range of events —Ag Sales, Food Sci, Poultry Evaluation, Meats, Horse and Livestock Judging, Employability Skills, Ag Communications, Welding Competitions, etc. This past year we added Land Judging to our list of events. We are very involved in our school. We try to do things for the students and staff. At the beginning of the school year, the officers write each staff member a note welcoming them back to school. The second day of school we do a popsicle day to welcome back all the students,' said Roberts.
Jacobson, who advises the Centre FFA program with Jon Meyer, said 37 of the 47 high school students are FFA members enrolled in an Ag class.
'We offer Food Science, Animal Science, Exploratory Ag, Plant Science, Welding Shop and Wood Shop Ag classes. One aspect of the FFA is attending district contests that expose students to Ag careers such as Agronomy, Vet Science, Livestock Judging and many more. We also compete in leadership development contests such as speech, parliamentary procedure and Ag sales. On district competition days, typically Wednesdays, it's not uncommon for our school to take a busload of students to compete, which can be a high percentage of our high school. Our school administration and teachers are highly supportive of our FFA members in their competitions. On a given school year, our FFA members attend around 25 district and statewide contests,' said Jacobson. 'Over the past three years I have taught at Centre, our school has had a state-winning agronomy team that competed at Nationals and a state-placing nursery landscape team.'
For National FFA Week, the school chapters are amping up the activities. And all for a purpose.
'It is a great time to share what the students have been doing with our community. It also allows us to put FFA in front of future generation students and share with them about what they can look forward to in their future with FFA,' said Graber.
Goessel FFA sponsors a 'Drive your Tractor to School' day.
'And we celebrate by doing a spirit week by dressing up for school as farmers or your favorite animal to name a few,' said Graber.
'National FFA Week is celebrated during George Washington's birthday. The FFA center was built on land owned by George Washington,' said Roberts. 'It is our goal to do something each day of the week. We kicked off the week with our Annual Community Pancake Feed. The members were up bright and early on Saturday morning to prepare pancakes. On Monday, we hosted donut and juice day with sponsorship from the Jacob Yoder Agency – Marion County Farm Bureau. Tuesday we are doing an 8th-grade FFA Introduction Program and have them participate in a couple of FFA judging events. Wednesday is Implement Day and then at lunch we have invited two state FFA officers to visit with our members and have a taco bar. Thursday is our staff's favorite day—we will prepare breakfast for all USD 410 staff members. It will be held in the Ag Shop, and during Resource we will have our Ag Olympics. On Friday, our members will wear their chapter shirts and we will welcome the elementary students to school. It is a jam-packed week but a fun week. My favorite week of the year.'
Marion High School is celebrating FFA week by having multiple dress-up days planned, a teacher appreciation breakfast and a trip to the Western Farm Show at the end of the week.
Jacobson said that their week kicked off with a free community breakfast hosted at the Burdick United Methodist Church from 7-10 a.m. on Saturday, Feb. 15 where FFA members served pancakes, locally sourced Burdick sausage and coffee for the Centre community.
'On Tuesday we will host a school-wide Ag Olympics competition. Wednesday's activity is an Ag lesson with our 2nd-grade class where FFA members will teach where our food comes from and get to make personal pizzas. On Thursday, our FFA chapter hosts a Faculty and Staff Breakfast at our school, and Friday our FFA members will recruit future FFA members with a middle school recruitment activity in an Ag Explorations class,' said Jacobson.
Graber feels that FFA is important now more than ever.
'Agriculture is changing. We don't have large numbers of farms, we have small numbers of large farms. Most students don't know what agriculture is. Being in FFA gives them the opportunity to explore options and possibilities that they otherwise never get the chance to do. It also shows them that Agriculture isn't just farming. It's banking, grocery stores and sports equipment like footballs; it's makeup and beauty products. Agriculture is a part of everything. Each year I challenge students to find something that doesn't pertain to agriculture. No one has been able to find it yet,' said Graber.

Boys basketball – The Trojan boys traveled to Smoky Valley on Tuesday, Feb. 11 where they won 62-32.
'From start to finish, we were able to control the game against Smoky Valley. We were able to capitalize on their turnovers and shared the ball very well. Lincoln Wichert had 22 points and 10 rebounds to get a double-double. Nash Dickinson added 13 points. Seth Driggers flew around all night to record six steals and eight deflections. Owen Dalke led us in assists with four. It was a great team win,' said Coach Kyle Kroeker.
The boys played at home against Council Grove on Friday, Feb. 14 and won 46-40.
'It was a battle all night. Back and forth, down five in the fourth quarter. We were led in scoring by Lincoln Wichert with 24 and Nash Dickinson with nine. Noah was a beast on the boards with nine rebounds and Easton Shahan distributed the ball well with four assists. I was proud of the grit the boys showed. Girls basketball- The Trojan girls played away against Smoky Valley on Tuesday, Feb. 11. They won 52-42.
The girls played at home against Council Grove on Friday, Feb. 14 where they won 51-22.
Coming—The Trojans will play at Nickerson on Friday, Feb. 21.
Wrestling – The Hillsboro/Canton-Galva Trojans wrestling boys competed in the Central Kansas league 2025 Boys Championship on Thursday, Feb. 13.
'Our boys team wrapped up their regular season competing on Thursday at the tough CKL Tournament at Hesston. Although still very young, we finally returned to the mat with the majority of our remaining roster competing. Sophomore Jaxon Chrislip led the way with a solid Runner Up finish in the 144 lb bracket. He dominated his first three opponents before his next opponent was forced to medically forfeit, sending Jaxon into the championship match. He fell to the #1 seed, Beaver from Hoisington. Our other top four medalists included senior Logan Rogers who placed 3rd at 215 lbs and fourth place finishes by sophomore Lucas Sorenson at 138 lbs as well as freshman Phoenix Fickes at 150 lbs,' said Coach Scott O'Hare.
On Friday, Feb. 14, the girls made the trip northeast to Rossville for the 3-2-1A Girls Super Regional Tournament. KSHSAA restructured the girls postseason this year by separating the girls classifications to match the boys. In doing so, rather than hosting four regional tournaments where the top four finishers advance to state, they held two larger Super Regional tournaments with the top eight from each advancing to state. Therefore, this super regional hosted 42 teams with just under 200 wrestlers. Sophomore Aimee Kelley led the way, picking up two solid wins before getting eliminated in the consolation third round of a large bracket with 24 girls. title: Adventures through food
author: Shana Thornhill
description: I have always been adventurous. Sure, my family would probably use words like 'accident prone,' 'plum crazy' or 'precocious' (if they were feeling generous). Sure, I rode my tricycle down the stairs.…
content:
I have always been adventurous. Sure, my family would probably use words like 'accident prone,' 'plum crazy' or 'precocious' (if they were feeling generous). Sure, I rode my tricycle down the stairs. Twice. Yeah, I used to sled down our steep driveway face-first. Okay, so I rode my brother's ten-speed bicycle when I was too short to reach the ground (and had to aim for a tree or carport pillar to dismount). Like I said. Adventurous.
As a teenager, my heroes were naturally characters like Indiana Jones, Rambo and Crocodile Dundee. I developed an Australian accent and carried a bush knife. I persuaded my parents (somehow) to get me a compound bow and practiced with it in the backyard (while carrying the bush knife). A favorite high school teacher (who happened to be an archaeologist) gave me his old fedora and taught me how to
sharpen and throw a Marshalltown trowel.
Young adulthood brought its own adventures, like learning to ride a motorcycle and skiing (not at the same time, but there was a time I probably would have tried). Learning and trying new things is lots and lots of fun. Sometimes, though, it's not without consequences. Catching trees on a bicycle leaves marks. Overextending your elbow when practicing archery gets you a nasty smack with the bowstring. You get the picture.
One of my greatest adventures was becoming a mother, but it meant that I needed to scale the antics back a little bit if for no other reason than so my kids wouldn't try the same stuff I did. So the easiest way to have adventures was through food. There, too, I've always enjoyed new tastes and textures. Darling Hubby shares my love of all things delicious, so we started exploring new cuisines together.
Cajun, Indian, Lebanese, Greek, Thai, Japanese, Portugese and Brazilian were all delicious. Lately, the market has offered several varieties of Korean, so we were anxious to try. Korean fried chicken was a definite win. Next on the list was hot pot. Think of a simmering pot of flavored broth at your table that you can cook meat, veggies or noodles in, then eat as you go. Our first attempt was delicious but definitely pricy. Imagine our delight when we heard that a new place in Wichita offers all-you-can-eat hot pot for two hours for just $30 each, $35 if you also do barbecue (now think hot grill in
the middle of your table—cook and eat as you go).
The menu was truly staggering. Half a dozen different kinds of steak, ditto chicken, pork, seafood, veggies, mushrooms—choosing would have been impossible if we had to limit ourselves. But, we didn't! All they asked was that we try to keep waste to a minimum. So that first time, we ordered two or three items at a time, then ate before we ordered more. The new orders came out quickly so it wasn't an inconvenience to make many small orders. We didn't even use our full two hours, but we left full and happy, looking forward to our next visit.
So tonight, we took Darling Son, AKA the Bottomless Pit, AKA He Who Orders Meat With Extra Meat, With A Side Of Meat. It was quite a wait to get seated, but we knew it would be worth it. We made a bigger order to begin with since we knew how fast Darling Son can make food disappear into thin air. We headed up to the bar to choose from over a dozen different sauces, four kinds of kimchi and grab some fried gyozas (Dumplings. Potstickers. Japanese meat veranike). By the time we got back to the table, our food had arrived, the pots of broth were steaming and the grill was ready to go.
When I tell you we got our money's worth, I'm not exaggerating. Yes, we had veggies and mushrooms but mostly plate after plate of meat. My 'try something new' today was Lotus root. It's kind of like a non-spicy radish, pleasantly crunchy. Definitely tasty with the spiced pork belly freshly grilled at the table. We ate like fiends for an hour, barely able to cram a few sesame balls and cream cakes in before we called it quits. Our waiter told us we still had almost an hour left—but we looked at each other and agreed we couldn't eat another bite.
I sit here writing this doing a fair Santa Claus impression sans beard. It was time for the comfy sweatpants as soon as we got home. The jeans were too tight. Once again my sense of adventure has gotten me into trouble. Pretty sure this will pass though, haha.
If you're feeling adventurous yourself, check out K-Pot at Towne East in Wichita. Be sure to bring your appetite—you won't need a bush knife or Australian accent, I promise!

title: Commission takes major action on health department project
author: Adam Strunk
description: The project to build a new health department location in Marion County took a large leap forward at Monday's regular county commission meeting. The Commission approved a demo of the building on the…
content:
The project to build a new health department location in Marion County took a large leap forward at Monday's regular county commission meeting. The Commission approved a demo of the building on the department's future location at 1220 E. Main St. in Marion. It approved the ordering of a new prefab building to be placed on the property, and it voted on how to allocate the funding the project needed. The action happened following Commissioner Randy Dallke giving an update on an earlier meeting in the day aimed at cutting down costs for the project. 'I think we can get in and keep it under $1.5 (million),' Dallke said about the construction portion of the building. County Administrator Tina Spencer spoke on the overall project and said in total with furnishings and other soft costs it looked like it would come in at around $1.76 million. She said that funding for the project would come from a number of sources. She said previously the commission approved using $946,000 in remaining American Recovery Plan Act funds. Interest payments above budget projections would chip in another $258,000. There would be another $130,000 available through grant funds as well as from funding from the federal Local Assistance and Tribal Consistency program 'That leaves a balance to fund of about $422,000 for that whole project,' she said. She proposed that funding be used by funds generated for the county by the construction of the Diamond Vista Windfarm. Those funds amount to $1.1 million according to the discussion at the meeting. 'That's funding coming into the county and public health would be a good use for the county,' Commission Chair David Mueller said. The Commission approved that suggestion 4-1 with Kent Becker voting against it. The commission voted unanimously in favor of ordering a prebuilt metal building for the project. Finally, it approved paying $12,400 to Hett Construction to demolish the existing structure at the site with a 5-0 vote. 'The adventure moves to the next level,' Mueller said of the project. In other business, the board: The commission held an executive session to discuss contract negotiations as privileged matters under the attorney-client relationship.
Kevin Larson was appointed to the Marion County Advisory Committee for Prairie View
Marion County will be transitioning back to the EMS Charts program to help manage patient records. They voted to enter into a 5-year agreement with the company, to pay $3,016 annually, plus a $520 first-year fee.
The County supported two letters of support for a state grant to provide increased internet access in Marion County. On Feb. 28 Marion County Administrator Tina Spencer submitted a letter of support for a state grant to help extend IdeaTek internet service to parts of Marion County. The County would provide a $12,500 match for the state grant. On March 8 Spencer submitted a letter in support of the TCW Broadband's application to provide fiber access to parts of the county. That pledge included an allocation of $100 per fiber drop.

title: Wedel's Meats and Sweets offers many of Marion County's favorite treats
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Many in Marion County still talk about Wendell Wedel's cafe that he ran for years in Durham until the flood in 2019 caused him to shut down although new owners took over. The good news is that he now…
content: Wedel's Meats and Sweets makes peppernuts and has them available at his business in Durham or for sale at locations throughout the county. Wendell Wedel is known for his various cinnamon rolls. They can be purchased from his shop in Durham by calling him or messaging him through his Facebook page. Wedel's Meats and Sweets makes sausage and verenika as well as various sweets and has them available through his home-run business in Durham. You can call Wendell Wedel or message him through Facebook. Wendell Wedel makes and sells his pies or pie crusts through his business Wedel's Meats and Sweets located in Durham. Many in Marion County still talk about Wendell Wedel's cafe that he ran for years in Durham until the flood in 2019 caused him to shut down although new owners took over. The good news is that he now runs a shop out of his garage in Durham where people can still buy his homemade goodies. 'Our big thing is probably peppernuts. We're known for our peppernuts. We started with those and then we started adding things and kind of made it a retail business too,' said Wedel. Wedel makes peppernuts regularly—often as much as 60 pounds at a time— and has them available at his home location as well as sells them at locations all around Marion County including Carlson's Supermarket in Marion, Dale's Supermarket in Hillsboro, the Main Street Cafe & Bakery in Durham, Goessel Grocery & Deli in Goessel as well as at White's Foodliner in Lindsborg. He added his famous cinnamon rolls and then kept adding more as he felt like it. 'We just keep adding. I still make sausage, but I also have a company out of Wichita that makes our sausage, too,' said Wedel. 'But I'm back up and running.' Wedel makes lots of pies both for his home business customers and for a few grocery stores. He also does them for fundraisers if people need them. 'I did a fundraiser for Centre High School. That was a pretty good sized order about 175 pies,' he said. Wedel wants to do more with pies and crusts. 'I wouldn't mind doing a little more. We have a pie press so we can press a crust out. I would love to sell crusts to restaurants. I could definitely help restaurants out on their labor by making crust. I could sell them pies too, but it would probably be to where if they have their own signature pie recipe, I could do the crust for them and all they'd have to do is fill it,' said Wedel. 'And even those going to farmer's market, if they wanted to do little individual pie tarts, we can do that. It has to be the size that I have the dye for. I have a nine-inch dye and I have about a six-inch dye. Those are the two that I can press out.' He also does cream pies by special order. He makes his goodies for people to come and get from him as well as for grocery stores throughout Marion County and even beyond the county. 'As far as people wanting things, they call me, see if I'm home and then they tell me what they want and they come here and pick it up,' said Wedel. 'But as far as grocery stores, they usually call me when they're out. Sometimes I will check with them. I'll say, I'm coming that way, do you need anything?' Wedel also has a variety of fruit and cinnamon rolls. 'I usually try to keep the regular and a few fruit rolls on hand all the time. I try to keep pecan, too,' he said. Wedel doesn't have set hours as he is 'semi-retired', but he says he is there 98% of the time only leaving to run errands or go to doctor appointments. 'Just message or call me and let me know what you need,' said Wedel. 'I'm doing what I enjoy doing, and I will get you what you need.' Wedel Meat and Sweets is located at 828 Lawrence in Durham. You can call and order at 620-382-5840 or message on Facebook through Wedel Meat and Sweets or Wendell Wedel. Wedel posts throughout the week what he is making, but he will also take orders for other items.
