title: Brush up on your baseball lingo
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: While watching a Wichita Wind Surge baseball game this summer with family and a friend, a player hit a routine fly ball for an out. Instinctively, two of us said, 'can of corn,' a baseball idiom that…
content:
While watching a Wichita Wind Surge baseball game this summer with family and a friend, a player hit a routine fly ball for an out.
Instinctively, two of us said, 'can of corn,' a baseball idiom that simply means a lazy fly ball that is easy to catch.
Why is a routine fly ball called a can of corn? It's one of the more unusual baseball phrases, with numerous theories behind its origin.
One story on the Internet described the theory this way: 'One is that it comes from the action of grocery clerks using a stick to tip a can off a high shelf and then catch it (as to hand to a customer). In extended use, the phrase can refer to something easily accomplished.'
The can of corn reference during the game led to a brief discussion about other interesting baseball lingo.
Here are a few common baseball idioms. See how many you know and/or what the idiom refers to.
Worm killer – This actually can apply to baseball or golf. In baseball, it's a hard-hit ground ball that scorches through the grass.
Hot corner – Third base is known as the hot corner, because the third baseman is often the infielder who stands closest to the batter.
Ducks on the pond – That simply means there are one or more runners on the bases.
Foot in the bucket or stepping in the bucket – This refers to a batting stance where the stride foot moves toward the shortstop for a right-handed batter, or the second baseman for a left-handed batter, instead of directly toward the pitcher.
Charley horse – This is used both in and out of sports as well, but it's a common name for a muscle spasm or cramp. The spasms can occur in any muscle in the body, but often happen in the leg.
Came out of left field – This informal American idiom means something is unexpected, surprising, or unusual. For example, when I write a thought-provoking column, some would say that came out of left field.
Rhubarb – To most people, rhubarb is a kind of pie, but in baseball, rhubarb is a slang term that refers to a fight or argument. The term may have originated with New York sports reporter Garry Schumacher, who compared a messy tangle of cooked rhubarb fibers to on-field altercations. Another theory is that the term comes from a 1938 incident in which a Brooklyn Dodger fan shot and killed a New York Giant fan in a barroom argument over baseball. The term became popularized during World War II when it appeared in war communiques and dispatches.
Screwball – At first blush, you might think this refers to someone who acts a little unusual, but in baseball, it is a rare pitch that moves in the opposite direction of most breaking balls, like curveballs and sliders.
Took the collar – This is what you say when a player goes hitless in a game. It comes from a collar being shaped like a zero. A player does not want to wear the collar while wearing the golden sombrero, which is a batter who strikes out three times in a game.
Southpaw – A southpaw is any left-handed person, but in particular a left-handed pitcher in baseball.
Journeyman – This is an experienced and reliable player, as distinguished from a star player. Typically you need to sustain a long career in the pros to fall into this category.
Cup of coffee – This describes a very brief career in the major leagues, or a short time that a player spends in the majors before being sent back down. It comes from the beverage that one might consume during a short visit.
Moving on from baseball idioms, my dad, who drank an occasional cup of coffee, said the only thing coffee is good for is to wash down doughnuts.

title: Remembering "Doc" Kyle: 41 years at Tabor
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: HILLSBORO — Richard 'Doc' Kyle, Ph.D., was a celebrated professor, co-worker, advisor, and friend to many on the Tabor College campus. Over 41 years of teaching, Kyle bestowed knowledge upon his…
content:
Richard 'Doc' Kyle taught at Tabor College for 41 years. He died on July 15 at the age of 85.
HILLSBORO — Richard 'Doc' Kyle, Ph.D., was a celebrated professor, co-worker, advisor, and friend to many on the Tabor College campus.
Over 41 years of teaching, Kyle bestowed knowledge upon his students and colleagues, bringing his passion for his faith and Bible and history courses to thousands of students.
Kyle, 85, died on Monday, July 15. He first taught at Tabor College in fall 1972 and retired after the 2012-13 academic year.
'I have fond memories of my history course with Doc Kyle as an undergraduate in a Lohrenz classroom,' said Tabor President David Janzen, Ph.D. 'He spoke with authority and passion that combined with his memorable personality made him a legend in Tabor's history. We will miss Doc Kyle's presence on campus and in our community, but his legacy will live in a faculty lecture series named in his honor.'
'Doc Kyle was a quintessential professor: he would take his notes to class and then seldom use them, simply speaking from the wealth of wisdom he had collected over the years. He was tough yet fair to students; he also was quick to engage them in the hallway or at events. Doc Kyle helped influence two generations of students. The world is a better place for his work and service at Tabor College,' said Frank Johnson, PH.D, Tabor College Provost.
Kyle's passion for learning and educating came as a student and a professor.
He got a B.S. in Secondary Education from Kuztown University in Pennsylvania and then his M.A. in History from Temple University in 1965. In 1968, Kyle received his M.Div. in General Ministry from Denver Seminary followed by his Ph.D in History in 1972 from the University of New Mexico. He earned his Th.M. in History of Christianity and American Religion from Princeton Theological Seminary in 1980.
In 1999, Kyle was awarded the first of two recognitions as a Fulbright Scholar. He first taught American Studies at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academic in Kyiv, Ukraine, and then at Grodno State University in Grodno, Belarus in 2005-06.
The storied Tabor professor also published 12 books and penned pieces featured in more than 160 publications.
Kyle began a faculty lecture series in 1997 and it was later named in his honor in 2004. Dr. James Titah, assistant professor of chemistry, delivered the 26th lecture of the series in April 2023.
He led over 30 Interterm/study trips, including the first European tour in January 1981. Over 700 students took part in these trips, culminating with his final tour in his final year as a professor in 2013.
Kyle's time at Tabor included the classroom and the football field. He served as interim head coach in 1974 and defensive coordinator in 1973, 1975-76, and 1978-93.
A decorated playing career at Kutztown University (Pa.) culminated with multiple honors as the college's most valuable player (1957 and 1958) and later earning four professional contracts with the Baltimore Colts, Detroit Lions, Pittsburgh Steelers, and Los Angeles Rams. He was inducted into the Kutztown Athletic Hall of Fame in 1992.

title: Missing Peabody clerk found deceased
author: Jessie Wagoner
description: By Jessie Wagoner, Laura Fowler Paulus and Adam Strunk The Kansas Bureau...
content:
By Jessie Wagoner, Laura Fowler Paulus and Adam Strunk
The Kansas Bureau of Investigation has confirmed a body, believed to be Jonathan Clayton, Peabody interim city clerk, was located Sunday afternoon.
Christopher King, husband, called a reporter at Harvey County Now/Hillsboro Free Press to inform them of the development. He said he spoke with law enforcement Sunday evening, and they had communicated that his husband's body was located.
'I am sad to hear the news. I love Jonathan very much, and I was hopeful that he would be found alive,' King said.
Sheriff Chad Gay confirmed that the Harvey County Sheriff's Department investigated a report of a crashed vehicle shortly before 3 p.m. Sunday.
Gay said his office found a vehicle north of U.S. Highway 50, near the Old Trail Road junction, just east of Newton. According to a later release by the Kansas Bureau of Investigation, the vehicle was a red 2011 Chevrolet Silverado, registered to Clayton, 42, of Peabody.
Gay said deputies investigated the scene and believed the vehicle was heading westbound on U.S. Highway 50 toward Newton when it left the roadway and hit a tree. The release from the KBI stated the vehicle was driven off the roadway.
Gay said the location of the vehicle was difficult to see from the roadway. He said the body located was in a state of advanced decay. He said evidence found on the scene indicated the body belonged to Clayton.
Officially, the identity of the vehicle's occupant will be confirmed through medical autopsy.
Extensive searches
Law enforcement, friends and family have been searching for Clayton after he was last seen on Aug. 3. His cell phone was last pinged from a cell phone tower that morning at the Newton Holiday Inn Express, where those working reported Clayton had gone in to use the bathroom.
According to King, at the time of his disappearance, the Kansas Bureau of Investigation and the Kiowa County Sheriff's Department were investigating Clayton for potential financial crimes. While living in Mullinville, his hometown, Clayton assisted the Mullinville Community Foundation with applications for grant funding for community renovations. The Department of Commerce has terminated the grant to the Mullinville Community Foundation and is asking for $425,000 to be returned, however, the Mullinville Community Foundation says funds are missing and the Kiowa County Sheriff is investigating. King says the Mullinville Cemetery Board has also reported $70,000 in missing funds from when Clayton served as a board member. The KBI and Kiowa County Sheriff are also investigating those claims.
'I wasn't aware of any of this until after he disappeared,' King said. 'Each day I've found out a little more.'
In addition to his employment with the City of Peabody, Clayton also served as the unpaid grant administrator for the Peabody Main Street Association. PMSA received a $1.5 million BASE grant from the Department of Commerce, Clayton assisted the organization in obtaining the grant while he was employed at the Department of Commerce. After leaving that position he assisted them in filing the quarterly reports and necessary paperwork to maintain the grant. However, the Department of Commerce did not receive the necessary paperwork, notifying PMSA in July they would not be getting the second disbursement $750,000. The day of Clayton's disappearance he was scheduled to meet with the PMSA board to transfer files on his computer to one of their devices so they could attempt to save the grant.
When Clayton did not arrive at the meeting, PMSA attempted to contact the Department of Commerce but did not receive a call back. Rather they were served with a termination notice, demanding repayment of the first $750,000 disbursement of grant funds. The Depeartment of Commerce has since rescinded the termination and is now assisting PMSA in gathering all the necessary paperwork. PMSA board member Morgan Marler says the board has put in hundreds of hours going through all the documents and they are confident they have all the necessary documentation to submit to the Department of Commerce. PMSA has also verified no money is missing and Clayton had no access to PMSA funds.
No Crime in Peabody
Peabody Mayor Catherine Weems has stated multiple times there has been no criminal activity in Peabody. Clayton had no access to city funds.
'We do not have concerns about any criminal activity on the part of Jonathan Clayton during his city duties,' Weems said.
PMSA has also reviewed all of their financial records and all funds are accounted for. They have no concerns about criminal activity.
'Here in Peabody, all I'm working on is the missing persons case,' Peabody Police Chief Philip Crom said. 'There is no criminal investigation or allegations of criminal behavior in Peabody. I know the Kansas Highway Patrol has an investigation open, but I do not have details about that.'
Community connection
Clayton and King, a city council member in Peabody, operate CK Vintage an antiques and craft store in the city.
King says when the couple moved to Peabody they were warmly welcomed and both felt the friends they made in Peabody quickly became family. He and Clayton both became involved in community activities and organizations. He says Clayton was quick to connect with others and form relationships.
'There isn't a person who wouldn't describe him as nice and friendly,' King said. 'He is incredibly smart. I met him when he was 20 and even at 20 he was like a 40-year-old, a very old soul.'
Describing Clayton as his best friend of over 20 years, King recalled his last interaction with Clayton on the morning of Aug. 3.
'I had been sick the night before and he was going to Newton to pick up medication for me and some breakfast,' King said. 'The last thing he said to me before he left was, 'I love you very much'.'
The KBI continues to investigate the crash that claimed Clayton's life. At this time they have issued no further information.

title: Parkview Mennonite Brethren Church celebrates 150th anniversary
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Parkview Mennonite Brethren Church recently celebrated their 150th anniversary the weekend of Aug. 16-18. The celebration started on Friday with an evening program at the church where former pastors,…
content:
Parkview Mennonite Brethren Church heard stories of church patriarchs and held a cemetery dedication at Gnadenau Cemetery on Saturday, Aug. 17 during the church's 150th anniversary celebration. Photo by Michael Klaassen Parkview Mennonite Brethren Church celebrated its 150th anniversary with several events over the weekend of Aug. 16-18. On Sunday, Aug. 18 the church gathered together to focus on the future and take a group photo. Photo by Michael Klaassen
Parkview Mennonite Brethren Church recently celebrated their 150th anniversary the weekend of Aug. 16-18.
The celebration started on Friday with an evening program at the church where former pastors, Tim Sullivan and Steve Schroeder spoke on spiritual topics as well as shared some of the funniest things that happened during their pastorates. The program was followed by refreshments.
On Saturday, there was a historic tour.
'We had a historic tour that took the folks who wanted to go to the original Gnadenau Village site. We presented some historical facts there and had a talk for them,' said Betty Seibel, Chair of the 150th Anniversary Committee, who has been a part of the church for 85 years since she was born into it.
Siebel explained that the original Parkview MB Church started out as the Gnadenau Church when Jacob A. Wiebe immigrated here and began the church on Aug. 16, 1874, with settlers who arrived on the train in Peabody.
The original building was about two miles south and east of Hillsboro until a fire destroyed it in 1956. It was eventually decided to move the church to town at its current location on Main Street with the idea that it may encourage more people to join the Gnadenau members at the new location rather than driving into the country. The church changed its name to Parkview in 1963, because the city park could be seen from the church on Main Street. They also felt that Parkview was easier to pronounce than Gnadenua.
After the tour at the Gnadenau Village site, the tour headed to the Gnadenau Cemetery which is located two miles south of town on Indigo.
'At that place, we had what we called talking tombstones. We had several descendants of patriarchs of the church share a story in first person of that particular person. And we also had a brief dedication of our beautification of that cemetery, because it has gone from a field of tombstones to a garden of memory with the gazebo and all the trees we planted,' said Seibel.
In addition to the stories shared, they had about 15 other tombstones that the committee collected stories of the person's life and put them on QR codes.
'If a person wants to go out to the Gnadenau Cemetery and find those QR codes with your phone, you can read a little bit about each one. It's this new technology that Michael Klaassen did for us,' said Seibel.
After the tours, the group went to the MB Foundation in Hillsboro for a watermelon and bierock lunch. That afternoon participants enjoyed a small historical museum inside a room of the church.
'We had a 67-page timeline lining the walls of the room. Then we had sticky notes where they could pick one and if something significant happened in their life on that particular day—that they found the Lord as their savior or maybe the day that they were married in the church or whatever—they could write it on that sticky note and put it on the timeline at the appropriate place. They had a lot of fun doing that,' said Seibel.
The temporary museum also had some artifacts that people loaned the church to put on display.
'We had an old wooden chair that had been in the Gnadenau Church. The custodian at the time of the fire, for some reason, had had four of the chairs at his home that night. So they didn't burn. There was a communion set of communion trays that even had a lid on top. It was at the home of one of the deacons who had taken it home to wash all the communion cups the night of the fire, because back then, we washed them and put them back in. There was also a clock that belonged to the original pastor 150 years ago, Jacob A. Wiebe,' said Seibel. 'And they had some cute little replicas of farm equipment and a picture of one of the sod houses from when the settlers first came.'
Saturday evening, there was a banquet of traditional Mennonite food followed by a program with speaker Dwight Friesen who grew up in Parkview Church.
Sunday was a traditional Sunday school followed by the service.
'Our theme was 'Standing on the Promises'. Our focus on Friday and Saturday was the history of the church. On Sunday, our focus was looking forward. Where do we go from here,' said Seibel.
The committee has been working on the weekend celebration for some time.
'We began talking about it a couple of years ago that we knew 150 years was coming up. We looked at what we did for the 100th and the 125th and also just talked about how it gave us a chance to talk about who Parkview is and who we've been throughout history. We wanted to celebrate those things, so we chose the theme 'Standing on the Promises' largely just to reflect that it was a celebration of God's faithfulness. There's a lot we can celebrate about what we've done or what different leaders and different buildings that we've had and different programs that we've run,' said Parkview Lead Pastor Tom Byford. 'There's a lot of good things that have happened, but the heart of all of it is really God being good to his people and caring for his church. And so we wanted that to be the theme of the day. That it's not just about our specific church, but really about what God's done through people for generations.'
For more information on the celebration and to view the Talking Tombstones, go to https://parkviewmb.com/celebrate150/ and click on Our History.

title: HCF launches September match event
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Hillsboro Community Foundation (HCF) is holding a match event Sept. 1-30 called Dollars 4 Scholars in partnership with the Paterson Family Foundation. HCF, formed in 2004, serves to promote and…
content:
Hillsboro Community Foundation (HCF) is holding a match event Sept. 1-30 called Dollars 4 Scholars in partnership with the Paterson Family Foundation.
HCF, formed in 2004, serves to promote and facilitate charitable giving in support of projects and programs that enhance the quality of life in the City of Hillsboro and nearby surrounding areas.
They achieve this goal through close and coordinated ties with local city governments, the USD410 school district and area charitable organizations.
The foundation has four objectives which are to advise and assist donors who could benefit by using HCF to achieve their charitable objectives; to receive grants or bequests for the benefit of both specific and broad community charitable interests; to make grants from unrestricted community endowment funds to benefit worthy Hillsboro-area charitable, benevolent, cultural, religious, civic, health, scientific and educational purposes; and to encourage and assist qualified not-for-profit organizations in establishing their own endowments and restricted funds as part of HCF.
HCF is an affiliate of the Central Kansas Community Foundation which operates as a nonprofit, tax-exempt organization.
The HCF board consists of Chair Marisa Javier, Vice-Chair Daniel Moss, Secretary/Treasurer Kelly Groening, Clint Corby, Cord Cunningham, Michael Hagen, Chad Hughbanks, Ashley Kleiber, Jessie Nikkel, Eric Rector, Mark Rooker and Nicole Suderman.
For the Dollars 4 Scholars event, donors have the chance to double their impact on the future generation by donating to any of the 11 Scholarship Funds HCF currently administers, several of which award scholarships for academic excellence, leadership, and a commitment to community service. Other funds award scholarships for students with an interest in math, journalism, business, vocational or technical service careers.
'We are asking for donations to HCF scholarship funds so we may increase the number and size of scholarships awarded each year to graduating high school seniors,' said Groening.
Donations received during the month of September will be matched by a grant from the Patterson Family Foundation, doubling the impact of each donation.
The goal of the Match Event is to raise $70,000 in scholarship donations, which will be matched by the
grant. The 11 scholarship funds will each receive a $5,000 match from the grant with the remaining $15,000 match applied to the HCF operating fund.
HCF is holding the event because college and vocational school tuition costs continue to rise. HCF donors have committed to area high school seniors to assist them in furthering their education by establishing HCF Scholarship Funds over the years.

title: Marion County Scouting continues to thrive
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Many recently heard about the good that the Marion County Scouting America Pack 102 and Troop 102 have been doing. In August, the group, which is chartered under the Marion Kiwanis Club, participated…
content:
The Marion County Scouting America Pack 102 and Troop 102 had a summer campout. The final campfire was an awards ceremony that the families of the scouts were invited to join and celebrate with the group.
Many recently heard about the good that the Marion County Scouting America Pack 102 and Troop 102 have been doing. In August, the group, which is chartered under the Marion Kiwanis Club, participated in Scouting for Food and collected 470 pounds of food from the Hillsboro and Marion Communities for the Marion County Food Bank.
'We had 14 scouts, across the pack and troop, handing out fliers one weekend, and 14 scouts participate in picking up the food the next weekend. All of our scouts participated in at least one weekend, and we had 10 scouts who participated both weekends,' said Jess Snyder who serves as Troop Scoutmaster and Pack Cubmaster.
The program itself, originally called Boys Scouts of America, has been around in the U.S. since 1910.
Snyder isn't sure exactly when Marion County first had a troop, but she said they have had troops off and on since close to that time.
'I was given a uniform recently that dates back to World War 2 by the Marion VFW who was at some point our chartered organization,' said Snyder.
According to Scouting.org, the mission of the organization is to prepare young people to make ethical and moral choices over their lifetimes by instilling in them the values of the Scout Oath and Law which states that 'a scout is trustworthy, loyal, helpful, friendly, courteous, kind, obedient, cheerful, thrifty, brave, clean and reverent'.
The program focuses on character development, leadership and outdoor exploration to provide a lifetime of benefits. Marion County Scouting America Pack 102 and Troop 103 attended a Home Depot Workshop where the scouts learned how to handle tools safely as they built mini foosball tables. The older scouts helped the younger ones and taught them some of the safety rules they had already learned. Leader Jess Snyder said the workshops are free. 'A scout is thrifty so we use as many free activities as we can to earn ranks,' said Snyder.
'We focus a lot on outdoor skills and teaching kids to be good citizens. Our aims of scouting are what we use to help build young people of character, citizenship, leadership and physical and mental fitness. The aims are character development, citizenship training, leadership development and personal fitness,' said Snyder. 'There are seven methods of scouting that we use which are scouting ideals, patrol, outdoors, advancement, personal growth, adult association, leadership development, and the uniform.'
Snyder explains that the uniform gives the scouts a sense of belonging.
'It takes away the 'I'm better than you because I have name-brand and you shop at Walmart',' she said. 'The uniform helps level the playing field.'
The Marion County Pack consists of boys and girls from Kindergarten through 5th grade while the troop consists of boys from 6th through 12th grade. There is currently no girls' troop, but Snyder hopes one will soon start.
'I've got some people who are interested in leading if I can get some girls interested. We only need five girls to start a troop,' said Snyder.
Snyder took over leadership in Marion County when the former pack leader left in May. The troop leader left in January so she took over both groups.
'The program almost folded, because no one wanted to step up and take over. My nephews were in it, and I feel like scouting is very important so I decided to be the scoutmaster and cubmaster,' said Snyder. 'The pack is designed to be leader-led and the troop is designed to be student-led, but we have a young troop so a lot of my job will be teaching them how to lead until they are able to.'
Snyder said her main why for choosing to lead scouting again —she had led at various times in the past— was an experience a young scout had under her leadership.
'Her family had a fire that started in the oven. And no one noticed it because they weren't in the kitchen until she did. She knew how to get everybody out of the house, how to call 911 and where to go for the meeting place since that was part of our fire safety planning. The mom told me, 'You probably saved our whole family',' said Snyder.
The troop is just starting back up, but they have already been busy. In addition to Scouting for Food, they participated in the Florence Labor Day parade and hosted a recruiting event. They have also been doing fun activities.
'We do fishing. We do camping. We do crafts and snacks. The kids learn how to safely use fire, safely use knives, safely use saws and axes,' said Snyder. 'We show them what we're doing, and then we guide them. We let them try it, and then we enable them. We create a safe environment for them to fail because you learn a lot from a failure.'
The pack and troop meets from 6:30-8 p.m. every other Tuesday at the Marion County Lake Hall. Their next meeting will be Sept. 24.
The group is always looking for new scouts to join. If interested in signing up or for more information, go to beascout.com or call or text Snyder at 620-877-0235.

title: New teachers on staff in Goessel
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: There are two new teacher faces on the teaching staff this school year at the USD 411 district. Here is a little bit about them both. Luke Freeman will teach junior high science for grades 6-8. He is…
content:
There are two new teacher faces on the teaching staff this school year at the USD 411 district. Here is a little bit about them both.
Luke Freeman will teach junior high science for grades 6-8. He is also beginning his 5th year as a high school assistant football coach along with helping out with state powerlifting in the spring.
Freeman earned his Associate of Arts in General Studies from Hutchinson Community College and his Bachelor of Arts in Elementary Education from Wichita State University.
His goal for the school year is to build positive relationships with the students and staff.
'I had the privilege to grow up and go through the Goessel school district and was able to see the great staff that Goessel has and the great education that is provided at the Goessel school district,' said Freeman when asked about his decision to work at USD 411.
Elizabeth Alderfer will teach language arts, math, science and social studies for 5th grade.
Alderfer graduated from Goessel High School. She earned her Bachelor of Science in Elementary Education from Bethel College in 2023.
This is her first year teaching. She student taught 2nd grade last fall at Hesston Elementary School. In the spring she was a substitute teacher at Hesston and Goessel Elementary Schools.
Alderfer has a younger sister who is a sophomore at Goessel High School.
Her main goal for this year is to build and foster relationships with her students and coworkers.
'Growing up attending K-12th grades at Goessel I knew that the district valued quality education, relationships and community. I knew from subbing last spring that there are really great teachers at GES that I was eager to work with and learn from. My first few weeks here have been really great and I have seen firsthand all the hard work and dedication teachers put in to ensure students are learning and thriving at Goessel,' said Alderfer about what drew her to the USD 411 school district.

title: Football is America's favorite sport, but ...
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: A poll or survey is a snapshot of that moment of time. I wouldn't say, 'Take all survey results with a grain of salt,' but I would say, 'Don't make too much out of any particular outcome.' It's no…
content:
A poll or survey is a snapshot of that moment of time. I wouldn't say, 'Take all survey results with a grain of salt,' but I would say, 'Don't make too much out of any particular outcome.'
It's no surprise that a Pew Research Center survey of 12,000 adults found that 'America's pastime is no longer the sport played on a diamond, but rather a gridiron.
The survey asked, 'If you had to choose one sport as being 'America's sport,' even if you don't personally follow it, which sport would it be?'
Based on that question, we might assume that not all of the adults surveyed were sports fans. We can also assume that the results reflect the perception that people have regarding which sports are the most popular.
The survey question, found in a broader survey about sports fandom throughout the United States, revealed that 53% of Americans believe football is America's sport. Baseball came next on the list at 27%.
The rest of the list consisted of basketball (8%), soccer (3%), auto racing (3%), hockey (1%), and 'something else' (2%). In the something else section, the Pew Research Center invited respondents to write in another sport if need be. Golf, boxing, rodeo and more were suggested.
I'm surprised that basketball came in so low. Who exactly was surveyed? Obviously not the people in Lawrence, Kansas.
Advertisers likely found it interesting and helpful that football dominated in every major demographic in the country, whether it was men and women, older and younger adults, and ethnicities like white, Black, Hispanic, and Asian Americans. With such a broad audience, maybe that's why you see football star Patrick Mahomes in so many commercials.
But before jumping to obvious conclusions, you should know that while the survey said football is the national sport, it didn't mean the NFL was top-of-mind for the 12,000 Americans surveyed. Huh?
For example, the survey found that 62% of US adults say they did not follow pro or college sports closely, if at all. It also found that 63% of those adults talk sports with others 'just a few times a month or less often.'
While sports appear to dominate public interest in America (at least in non-presidential-election years), maybe they aren't as important as you'd think.
Only 7% of the adults considered themselves 'superfans' of sports, which is categorized as those who talk sports with others often and follow the most popular leagues. I would have thought that percentage would be higher, but that's not the case in this particular survey.
Politics may play a role in affecting the sporting world in presidential-election years. The 2016 election, the last presidential contest not impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic, is instructive. NFL ratings that season fell 8% from the prior year, with the decrease particularly concentrated in the first half of the regular season and before the election that year.
MLB's two League Championship Series that year were also down by double-digit percentages before the league ultimately hit the jackpot with a World Series win for the Cubs that was the team's first since 1908.
According to an opinion article by Joe Grigas in the Sports Business Journal, 'Despite a 7% viewership bump last year, largely due to Taylor Swift, the NFL should expect a drop in the 2024 season.
'With the NFL more popular than ever, many believe viewership will remain strong. However, the upcoming 2024 election, potentially the most volatile to date, will likely distract America,' said Grigas.
Now there's something I never expected to write in a sports column. Taylor Swift and her Swifties gave the NFL a viewership increase last year.
Suffice it to say, Americans are easily distracted. Maybe you or someone you know can identify with the following: 'If I had a dollar for every time I got distracted, I wish I had a puppy.'

title: Be aware: scams are on the rise
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: The City of Hillsboro recently sent out a warning to let people know they need to be aware of scams. 'We've had people get text messages regarding taking a survey for the city. They are taking…
content:
The City of Hillsboro recently sent out a warning to let people know they need to be aware of scams.
'We've had people get text messages regarding taking a survey for the city. They are taking advantage of our lead and copper survey that we've sent out to try and get residents to click on fraudulent links,' said Hillsboro City Administrator Matt Stiles.
In addition to texts, the scammers have been using emails and phone calls.
'We regularly have people contacted to pay utility bills over the phone, which is something we never do. Those calls typically target our senior citizens but sometimes others. There is so much increased activity happening right now it's a little overwhelming,' said Stiles. 'The city has taken a lot of proactive steps to prevent those types of things, but at the end of the day, people are human and people looking to take advantage can be persuasive.'
Marion Police Chief Zach Hudlin said that last week they had a resident tell them she received a call saying there was a tax warrant she needed to pay or the police would be there to arrest her.
'Thankfully she knew it was a scam and did not give them any information,' said Hudlin.
Hudlin said he received a text last week saying he had an overdue toll from the turnpike that was a scam.
The scammers aren't just attacking individuals. Stiles said there have also been attempts to spoof city staff emails internally, but those haven't affected the public.
He also said the CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) sent out a warning last week to public utilities about increased attacks on public infrastructure.
'Those attempts are mostly targeting control devices in systems, like valves or transformers, not customers. We don't have a lot of capabilities to remotely screw up operations and what we do have is secured and has alarms to notify us about changes. Still, you have to treat those threats as real and take steps to keep the bad guys out,' said Stiles.
The FBI has also warned against a jump in fraudulent online activity driven by the upcoming election and conflicts around the world.
'Do not click on suspicious links or provide any personal information. When in doubt, give us a call at City Hall at 620-947-3162,' said Stiles.
'If someone suspects that a call/text/email is a scam, they should call dispatch to report it to the police department,' said Hudlin.

title: Crofoot takes first in 100-mile race
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Kodi Crofoot, chiropractor and co-owner of Diamond C Fitness in Marion, has participated in numerous large races, including six 100-milers. However, completing the Hawk 100 in Lawrence at Clinton Lake…
content:
Kodi Crofoot competed in the Hawk 100, a 100-mile race, where she took first place for women and fifth overall. Photo by Rick & Kristi Mayo.
Kodi Crofoot, chiropractor and co-owner of Diamond C Fitness in Marion, has participated in numerous large races, including six 100-milers. However, completing the Hawk 100 in Lawrence at Clinton Lake last month may be her biggest accomplishment yet.
'I had attempted it back in 2015 and broke my toe all the way through and had to quit at mile 60. I never thought about doing it ever again because it's a tough course,' said Crofoot.
But then Crofoot joined a running group in Lawrence where she worked at a chiropractic practice to cover another doctor's maternity leave.
'I was having a great time with them. And I'm like, 'You know what? I'm gonna go back and finish this',' said Krofoot. 'Once I start something, I have to finish it.'
So on Sept. 7 and 8, she not only finished the race this time but she took 1st place for women and 5th place overall with 28 registered runners. The runners were allowed 32 hours to complete the race, but Crofoot finished at 27 hours and 47 minutes. Kodi Crofoot competed in the Hawk 100, a 100-mile race, where she took first place for women and fifth overall. Photo by Rick & Kristi Mayo.
The course for the race is a 25-mile loop which the runners complete four times. Parts of the course are back and forth switchbacks through trees and other parts are just rocks and roots making it easy for runners to trip.
'If you weren't picking your feet up, you were constantly hitting a toe on a rock or tripping on a roof. I went down twice. The first time, it had just turned dark and there were three little patches of mud. I just happened to slip and go forward onto my knees into the mud. And then the 2nd fall was in a creek bed and it was like a dip. I didn't lift my feet enough, caught a rock, went down on my right shoulder, hit my right hip and then my right knee which left a huge bruise on my hip that was there for weeks,' said Crofoot.
Her longest loop took eight hours and her shortest was six hours.
Crofoot said the first 50 miles were great. She completed it in 11 hours and 45 minutes, just 15 minutes short of her goal. From mile 50 on, she could have a pacer with her to help keep her going. For miles 50-75, Dave Box was her pacer and Dave Meeth served as pacer for the last 25 miles. She had previously served as pacer for both of them in their 100-mile races.
'The weather was perfect. It started in the 50s but then got up to 76 which caught up to me at mile 60. I didn't do enough salt or electrolytes so I did have some major stomach issues for probably three to four hours. I needed to eat, but I couldn't. I've never had that happen before so it wasn't pleasant. Once the nausea started kicking in, I would just walk it out, and then I could start running again. So that was kind of a back-and-forth for 12 miles. My stomach finally calmed down to where I could eat,' said Crofoot. 'It was the worst feeling, but I never thought once I was gonna quit.'
She said Box made sure she was doing salt and electrolytes about every five minutes.
'He got me back on to where I didn't think I was gonna fall over,' said Crofoot. Dave Meeth, Kodi Crofoot, Brian Crofoot, Dave Box. Kodi Crofoot took first place in the Hawk 100, a 100-mile race. Her husband Brian and pacers Meeth and Box were with her during the race supporting her and cheering her on to the finish line.
Another challenge in the race was getting off the trail and getting lost. While there were signs to mark the course, some of the signs curled up or turned during the race. One runner was ahead of Crofoot by a couple of hours, but she got lost and fell behind. Crofoot got lost a couple of times but didn't go too far in the wrong direction.
'I did miss a sign at one point. I saw a runner up ahead of me so I kept following that runner. Well, that runner wasn't a racer. It was just somebody out exercising. But luckily my mistake was maybe two miles. I learned not to do that again,' said Crofoot. 'I had to make sure to pay attention and try to remember what I did the last time I was here. Luckily I knew that from experience and getting lost myself. That was the big key for my win.'
Crofoot said that running a race that long is more of a mental challenge than a physical one.
'My mental state was 100%. I decided that even if I had to power-hike a lot of it, I was finishing it. I knew I could at least do the first 50 miles at a decent trek. I knew that would give me plenty of time to finish the last 50 even if I'm crawling,' said Crofoot.
At mile 88 she did have to sit down and change her drenched shoes and socks. Kodi Crofoot competed in the Hawk 100, a 100-mile race, where she took first place for women and fifth overall. Photo by Rick & Kristi Mayo.
'It got cool at night in the lower fifties, and I was just cold. I took off the wet shirt I had on all day and put a long sleeve on with a jacket over it so I wasn't cold and miserable,' said Crofoot.
Her favorite part of the race was being out on a trail with no cell service and no talking.
'Everything was just so smooth. So easy. It was just more of an easygoing race for me. Except for that stomach issue, I just felt good the whole time,' said Crofoot.
Crofoot said she is definitely not in the shape she was 10 years ago and is not bouncing back very quickly from the race, but it was all worth it.
She doesn't currently have another race planned, but she plans to do more even if she doesn't do another 100-miler race.
'I think I'm gonna drop back and just do some 50-milers. Just to get back into better shape. Those take me anywhere from seven to nine hours,' said Crofoot.

title: Young entrepreneur works to build a business
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Harper Stiles, an 11-year-old 6th grader who attends Hillsboro Middle School, has always been a natural artist who began drawing freehand from a young age. She even placed Overall Grand Champion for…
content:
Harper Stiles, 11, recently presented her new business, Harper Henna, at the Side Hustle Challenge put on by Central Kansas Entrepreneurship Center at Tabor College. She took second place in the competition.
Harper Stiles, an 11-year-old 6 th grader who attends Hillsboro Middle School, has always been a natural artist who began drawing freehand from a young age. She even placed Overall Grand Champion for Visual Arts out of all ages when competing in 4H at age nine and 10.
'My art is important to me. I improve not just by practicing and watching videos, but I have also taken lessons from a local artist,' said Stiles.
She recently added another artistic interest that fulfills her desire to create and allows her to start her own business.
'I became enthralled with henna during a recent visit to the Kansas City Renaissance Festival. So I decided to start a business giving temporary henna tattoos that last one to three weeks. Henna tattoos are for people who don't want a permanent tattoo. This might include people who like to change their mind, who don't like pain, who might scar from needles, who might want to test drive a real tattoo and for people who just want a fun, temporary experience, like kids,' said Stiles. 'I felt this was a business I could start now and grow as I get older and become more skilled.'
The young entrepreneur has been in business for about two months and has been practicing her art. She has already had her first paying gig.
'My mom agreed to book me for my brother's birthday party for $20,' said Stiles.
She has already set clear goals for how she will continue to grow her business.
'My goal is to start simple in what I offer and start with a simple target audience such as kids at a craft fair. I plan to practice throughout the year to become more skilled since I will be able to charge more if I can offer more detailed designs. I also need to practice with a steady hand and work on speed so I can do more in less time which increases my profits,' said Stiles. 'My long-term goal is to save money to go to college.'
In addition to doing parties, she plans to look into offering her services at farmer's markets and other carnivals in the area. Her main goal is to have her business ready for next year's Hillsboro Arts & Crafts Fair. She has already figured out what her expenses will be as well as the income she could make based on the amount of time and cost each tattoo takes. She plans to share a booth with her mom.
'My mom was a big part of this. She was very encouraging,' said Stiles.
'I'm so proud of the ideas that come out of her heart and the independent spirit she has. She just wants a way to express it. Finding those kind of avenues in a small town is a little bit harder,' said mom Rebecca Stiles.
Harper has scoped out the competition for her business.
'I looked up henna artists close to me and found two professionals who live in Wichita. They offer large body designs for events like weddings. I did not find anyone who offered what I'm doing and to the audience I'm looking at,' said Harper.
She took a big step in growing her business recently when she competed in the community division of the Side Hustle Challenge put on by Central Kansas Entrepreneurship Center at Tabor College. She wowed the judges and guests with her well-thought-out business plan and presentation in the Science-fair style event for small businesses. She was not phased by being the youngest one there, and she beat out adults by taking second place in the competition.
'This really provided an opportunity for her to be able to be creative and say, 'here's what I might be able to offer' and kind of start that journey at a young age,' said Rebecca. 'Seeing your kids do stuff is just fun.'
'Harper's got her mother's hustle, ambition and charm when it comes to these types of things. She gets to put her artistic skills to work doing something fun and enjoyable. We're very proud of her for stepping up, trying something new and putting herself out there. I definitely wasn't doing that when I was her age,' said dad Matt Stiles.
Those looking to schedule a henna tattoo or to hire Stiles for a birthday party or other event can email hennabyharperks@gmail.com.

title: USD 410 approves literacy program for elementary teachers
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The USD 410 Board of Education met for their monthly meeting on Monday, Nov. 1 where Superintendent Clint Corby explained to the board that beginning July 1, 2028, Kansas veteran educators serving in…
content:
The USD 410 Board of Education met for their monthly meeting on Monday, Nov. 1 where Superintendent Clint Corby explained to the board that beginning July 1, 2028, Kansas veteran educators serving in elementary school positions will be required to demonstrate knowledge of the science of reading to renew their professional licenses. This knowledge may be demonstrated by completing state-approved training or passing a state-approved literacy exam.
USD 410 will use Keys to Literacy to help HES teachers meet this requirement. Keys to Literacy provides a 36-hour program that can be completed with additional professional development days added to the 2025-2026 school calendar.
'It takes a significant amount of outside time. It's like getting a master's degree over the course of two years,' said Corby.
The board approved contracting with Keys to Literacy to provide training services for HES teachers to fulfill the KSDE 'seal of literacy' licensure requirement for $40,330.
The board also heard the Fiscal Year 2024 Financial Audit Report from Scot Loyd of Loyd Group, LLC. The report was positive and Loyd complimented Business Manager Jerry Hinerman for the preparation work that he did.
'Jerry did a great job always making sure that things are done right. That is not the case in every district or every city or county,' said Loyd.
The board approved the report.
The board made the following personnel changes:
* approved the resignation of Cheri Weinbrenner from her position as HES Preschool Family Advocate effective Nov. 1.
* approved the issuance of a contract to Mallory Ediger to serve as Hillsboro High School Forensics Sponsor for the 2024-2025 school year.
* approved the hiring of JoAnne Jorgensen as HES Preschool Instructional Aide for eight hours per day at the rate of $14 effective Oct. 21.
* approved the hiring of Krystal Paper to serve as Hillsboro Middle/High School Custodian for eight hours per day at a rate of $14 per hour effective Nov. 4.
In other business, the board:
*accepted an $85,050.00 donation from Enel Green Power NA, Inc. This wind farm donation occurs once a year.
* met in executive session for attorney consultation. No action was taken.

title: Buckle up, Marion County
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: This Thanksgiving Holiday, make sure to buckle up, Marion County. If you don't make occupant protection a habit now, start a new tradition. Beginning Nov. 21 through Dec 1, the Marion County Sheriff's…
content:
This Thanksgiving Holiday, make sure to buckle up, Marion County. If you don't make occupant protection a habit now, start a new tradition.
Beginning Nov. 21 through Dec 1, the Marion County Sheriff's Office will join many other law enforcement agencies across the state, including the Kansas Highway Patrol, in the Kansas Thanksgiving Safe Arrival traffic enforcement campaign funded by a grant from the Kansas Department of Transportation (KDOT). Although all Kansas traffic laws will be enforced, this extra provision will actively enforce occupant protection laws.
The Marion County Sheriff's Office will also provide education that serves as a reminder that buckling up saves lives.
Don't be a turkey, buckle up, every trip, every time. It's your best defense in case of a crash. Do it. If not for you, do it for them.

content:

title: Hillsboro's C.J. Hill named 2024 KCAC Bissell Division Assistant Coach of the Year
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: WICHITA, Kan.– The Kansas Collegiate Athletic Conference (KCAC) has announced that C.J. Hill has been named 2024 KCAC Bissell Division Assistant Coach of the Year. Hill led a Bluejay defense for Tabor…
content:
WICHITA, Kan.– The Kansas Collegiate Athletic Conference (KCAC) has announced that C.J. Hill has been named 2024 KCAC Bissell Division Assistant Coach of the Year.
Hill led a Bluejay defense for Tabor College that recorded 11 interceptions, seven fumble recoveries, 11 sacks, and 62.1 tackles per game. The Bluejay defense took four touchdowns back to the house, providing valuable scoring to aid the team in addition to their efforts on offense. The Bluejays held opponents to 25.8 points per game.
Hill's defense played vital roles in several key games throughout the season, most notably in the program's rivalry win over McPherson College in Week One, where two interceptions, one of which was a pick-six, helped Tabor cruise to a 20-10 victory over the Bulldogs.
Six of Hill's defensive players earned All-Bissell Division honors, including Brooks Gardner. Under Hill's leadership, Gardner became Tabor's career-leading tackler, finishing his career with 352 total tackles.
Hill was previously named KCAC Assistant Coach of the Year in 2018, making this the second of such awards.

title: Child care center hopeful for spring 2025 opening
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Progress has been moving forward on the Hillsboro Community Child Care Center (H4C), and the board hopes it will be ready this spring. 'It's coming to life. It's definitely been a long process, but…
content:
One of the classrooms of the Hillsboro Community Child Care Center scheduled to open in March of 2025. The center will hold 99 children. One of the classrooms of the Hillsboro Community Child Care Center scheduled to open in March of 2025. The center will hold 99 children. One of the classrooms of the Hillsboro Community Child Care Center scheduled to open in March of 2025. The center will hold 99 children.
Progress has been moving forward on the Hillsboro Community Child Care Center (H4C), and the board hopes it will be ready this spring.
'It's coming to life. It's definitely been a long process, but it's been exciting to see. We're hopeful for March that we're able to open,' said H4C Board Chair Tristen Cope.
The center, which will have five different classrooms—an infant classroom, a toddler classroom, an older toddler classroom, a young preschool classroom and an older preschool classroom—and a recreation room for school-aged children at some point for a summer care program, will fill a huge need for Hillsboro.
'This is a 3 million dollar project. This project is a $3,000,000 investment into our local community that has not used any tax dollars. It was built through private donations from our community and then also through funding that we received from grants. So that's a huge thing when you're looking at that investment that we're putting into the community,' said Cope.
Cope goes on to explain that the investment doesn't just stop there.
'It's not just the building and the $3,000,000 that's put back into the community. It'll be a business that we're running, and it's really not a small business when you're talking 99 children. That's a large business. We are hiring staff. I think we'll have close to 16 full-time staff members if we're at capacity,' said Cope. 'So we have that, and then we're also caringfor the children, which is a huge return on investment that's staying within the community as well. It's not just a childcare that we're opening. It's a huge investment.'
'And it boils over then into what comes back into the community because if you don't have childcare available in your community, people aren't gonna seek out jobs in your community. You can't grow your other local businesses if they do not have a place to take their children or they don't feel like your town or your community is a place they can grow or expand their family,' said Tiffany Miller who serves on the board as the H4C Child Care Representative.
'Which is really how H4C started. It started from a conversation between the Hillsboro Development Corporation and the Hillsboro businesses saying, 'We can't find workers. We can't find employees because there's no child care'. It's coming full circle again to allow us to help close that gap,' said Cope.
Kid's Connections, the current daycare center in Hillsboro located in the Hillsboro Mennonite Brethren Church, will be closing once H4C is ready to go.
'All of the Kids Connection kiddos would have the opportunity to come over to H4C. The hope would be that we'd have Kids Connection children there for a few weeks so they can get comfortable, and then we'd be able to bring on any new children that would want to start at H4C,' said Cope.
And Miller, who serves as the director at Kids Connection will be stepping down from the role.
'My plan was always to be done May of 2025. My board had known that for probably two years now. That was before all of this was even in the works, but it feels like a good time to be done now when H4C starts in March,' said Miller.
So as the construction continues, the board is working on hiring a new director.
'The application is live for a new director until the end of the year. The hope is that we can get somebody started in the new year,' said Cope. 'We want them to be involved in that initial planning process of the parent handbook and being able to be there to help hire our classroom teachers and additional staff that we would need.'
The new director would also work with Miller at Kids Connection to get to know the kids and families.
'The hope is to make that transition a little bit easier. So I'll take more and more of a step back and allow them to run the show,' said Miller.
Once the new director is hired, the plan is for the director to help conduct interviews and recruit additional staff members to give them a feel of what their team would feel like.
'We're planning on having Kids Connection staff apply for the new positions as well because they may want to switch. They may want to be an infant classroom teacher, which is not something that they have at Kids Connection. So everyone has to apply, which is part of the licensing requirements we'll have to go through. Then we would potentially take on however many from Kids Connection would want to join us,' said Cope. 'We will need lead teachers and some assistant teachers. We will also need those who may want to work part-time. So maybe they want to work before school or after school. We also need a cook.'
The center will hold up to 99 children. It will also be DCF contracted which means it will accept state payments for child care.
The board is excited to see the center becoming a reality and is thankful to all who have helped along the way.
'It's gone from this concept to something tangible. And this has been five years in the making, too. We started this in 2019,' said Cope. 'There's been a lot of passion, love and hard work that you put into this from not just the board but from the community and in-kind support such as the logo, the building, people sitting on our board and lots of blessings along the way.'
'We've been very fortunate in the community support that we've gotten financially and otherwise,' said H4C Board Secretary Erin Hein.
The board plans to have an open house for the community to see the center before it opens as well as a special event for all of the donors.
If interested in the director position, see the posting on Indeed or email hillsboro4c@gmail.com to request an application and job posting information. Applications for other staff will be available early next year. For general information and for upcoming announcements about open enrollment, follow along on the Hillsboro Community Child Care Center Facebook page.

title: Rising from the ashes
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: When a fire tore through The Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody early Sunday, Dec. 8, 2024, leaving the restaurant and bar charred and unusable, it felt like a total loss to owner Lindsey Marshall. And…
content:
Lindsey Marshall, owner of the Coneburg Grill and Pub which was recently destroyed in a fire, makes her famous 'smoked tequila' drinks at a Pop Up Brunch at Pop's Diner in Peabody on Dec. 29. There have been several fundraisers for the rebuilding of the Coneburg and opportunities for Marshall's food. Lindsey Marshall, owner of the Coneburg Grill and Pub which was recently destroyed in a fire, makes her famous 'smoked tequila' drinks at a Pop Up Brunch at Pop's Diner in Peabody on Dec. 29. There have been several fundraisers for the rebuilding of the Coneburg and opportunities for Marshall's food. Lindsey Marshall and some of her staff from the Coneburg Grill and Pub 'took over' Pop's Diner in Peabody on Sunday, Dec. 29 for a Pop Up where they provided some Coneburg menu favorites and live music. Marshall and friends are steadily working on rebuilding the beloved restaurant. Local musician Kyle Grigsby and Miranda Ainsworth helped clean out the fire debris from inside The Coneburg Grill and Pub. The two spent an entire day tearing out the bar, layer by layer, to see if it could be salvaged. Local musician Sam Schiltz and Miranda Ainsworth clean up debris at the Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody from the Dec. 8, 2024 fire. Many volunteers came in and helped clean up the inside of the building from the fire damage at the Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody. Many volunteers came in and helped clean up the inside of the building from the fire damage at the Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody. Many volunteers came in and helped clean up the inside of the building from the fire damage at the Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody. Mark Lyons and Doug Regier clean up debris at the Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody from the Dec. 8, 2024 fire. Matt Smith and Jayden Stinchcomg clean up debris at the Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody from the Dec. 8, 2024 fire. Devon and Jessica McGonigal help clean up debris at the Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody after the Dec. 8 fire. Jessica is a staff member at the Coneburg. Coneburg Grill and Pub staff members Miranda Ainsworth and Samantha Wilson jumped right in and started helping with cleaning up the debris after the Dec. 8 fire at the Peabody restaurant. Many 'relics' have been found during the clean-up after the fire at the Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody including these cans that were stashed in the concrete blocks behind the men's room. The rumors that original owner Shirley Strotkamp (who built the Coneburg in 1978) put concrete around the men's room to keep the rowdies from punching holes in the wall turned out to be true.
When a fire tore through The Coneburg Grill and Pub in Peabody early Sunday, Dec. 8, 2024, leaving the restaurant and bar charred and unusable, it felt like a total loss to owner Lindsey Marshall.
And it seemed like a total loss to the community who loved the popular spot as well. While the building was still standing, the amount of damage was vast. The kitchen was completely destroyed. The inside of the building was burned and blackened. Insulation and wires hung from the ceiling. The booths that often held hungry customers burned and melted.
But now, a month after the fire, Marshall and her many supporters are digging out from the ashes. They started with cleaning out the debris from the fire.
'We have made huge strides in the cleanup. We still have quite a bit to do before getting started on the next step —insulation, walls, new roof, etc— but are looking at getting back to work as soon as the snow clears. We have had many volunteers and hands when we needed them,' said Marshall.
While the focus right now has been clean up, the goal is to eventually rebuild. And Marshall has support for that, too.
'We do plan to rebuild. I have an excellent support group that has been backing us up with planning, building, ideas, and so on. Being in the service industry for so long has created some incredible networking. Most of us still keep in touch. As a matter of fact, my friend Matt Smith—with whom I worked 'behind the pine' 20+ years ago—has really taken the reigns on the project. His clarity and vision has kept me going literally since day one when I opened the Coneburg almost 14 years ago,' said Marshall. 'Matt and his Cool Guy HVAC Crew have put in many of their own hours to help us. They deserve the credit for getting us this far, this fast.
Marshall said that while she is anxious to be back in business, it will take some time.
'We will make this happen. We want to be up and going just as soon as possible. I'd love to have a more specific date, but we have to take it one step at a time. We want to make sure this is done right,' said Marshall.
And Marshall and her staff haven't just been cleaning up and focusing on rebuilding. They have still been able to get in the kitchen and cook through a few events.
On Dec. 14, The Brandin' Iron in Florence hosted Marshall and her staff for a lunch and then donated a portion of their sales to the crew and the clean-up process
'Sara Dawson and her crew were so awesome to work with. I loved seeing how other teams worked together, their flow for business, how they operated. It also allowed us to see many of our regulars for a bit. Sara was so very generous in offering us the chance to make some extra money, as well as raise more funds for The Burg,' said Marshall. 'That same day, Renee Fensky (owner of Bank Shots in Newton) offered staff members Miranda and Priscilla bartending shifts for an event she held. Talk about scratching each other's backs. If there's anything that this has taught me, it's to accept the help that is offered, and that we truly are all in this together.'
On Sunday, Dec. 29, Pop's Diner in Peabody allowed Marshall and her staff to host a Pop Up Brunch.
'The Pop Up Brunch at Pop's Diner was a great success. Our staff was so incredibly excited to get to work again, as well as seeing everyone's faces We were so happy to get cooking again. The amount of gratitude we feel towards Tim Peterson for allowing us the opportunity is unspeakable. He was so much help, and seemed happy to work with us,' she said.
Marshall is so thankful for all the good that has come out of such a traumatic event.
'Thank you. I've said it so many times over the past month. Thank you. It seems like such a simple couple of words. I don't know how to even start, or where to go with them anymore. Those two words are spoken, written and sincerely felt toward thousands of our friends and supporters far and wide. This has been a wild ride of emotion and humility. Be grateful for every little thing you have. It can be gone in the blink of an eye. We love you guys, and can't wait to get back at it,' said Marshall.
If interested in volunteering, keep an eye on Coneburg Grill and Pub Facebook. Marshall tries to keep that updated and plans on putting together a few lists of project needs for people to donate toward.
Monetary donations are still being accepted. A special account at Vintage Bank was opened for those who would like to donate, and they have the opportunity to use a 501c. Reference the Coneburg Inn in Peabody.
The Peabody Association of Churches has also set up a tax-exempt fund where people can donate larger amounts. All of these funds will first be used to assist employees with wage assistance until more permanent assistance can be set up. Whatever is remaining will be used to supplement what is not covered by insurance for the rebuilding of the Coneburg.
