title: Scamming methods grow increasingly sophisticated
author: Adam Strunk
description: By Adam Strunk and Laura Fowler Paulus Chad Flesher, a Mount Hope Police Officer, recently received an alert from what he believed was his bank. The alert arrived via phone text message. He checked…
content:
By Adam Strunk and Laura Fowler Paulus
Chad Flesher, a Mount Hope Police Officer, recently received an alert from what he believed was his bank.
The alert arrived via phone text message. He checked the number and found the alert used the same five-digit number the bank used to send alerts to him in the past.
The alert asked if he made a purchase at an Apple Store in Los Angeles California. He had not.
He texted 'No' as the supposed bank alert requested. He then received a message informing him a person from his bank's fraud department would give him a call.
'I answered it,' he said of the call, adding that the caller had a Kansas City phone number.
'The guy sounded so convincing,' he said.
He said the man asked if he had a fraud alert set on his phone and then asked if he wanted to add the additional security step to his account.
Flesher said he had such a service in the past but not since purchasing his new phone.
The person on the other line sent him a code to use and said they'd have to do a test transaction to make sure the service was set up.
He followed the directions and went through with the transaction, and eventually, the conversation ended.
He looked at his online banking statement and noticed a $500 withdrawal to a different banking service.
No money was ever returned to his account. He learned the person he spoke with didn't work for his bank. He'd been scammed.
Fraudulent scams like this are nothing new, but the mimicking of a bank's fraud protection service added an additional level of subterfuge to the act.
'This one was super sophisticated,' he said of the scam. 'They knew where I banked. They knew my phone number.'
Flesher said he previously thought he'd been doing everything right in avoiding scams. He shared his story in hopes of preventing others from falling victim to scammers.
He thought that his information may have been compromised during the Christmas shopping process after he ordered from an online website.
'I bought some stuff online for Christmas presents from Chinese websites,' he said, surmising that the website may have turned around and sold his information.
'What I should have done, if someone legitimately used my debit card, it would have popped on my online banking,' he said. 'A charge in an Apple Store never did show up. When I did call my bank, I got their third-party people, and all they could do was turn my card off. The best thing to do if you get one of these calls is hang up and actually call your bank and talk to someone local.'
Last week, the Better Business Bureau released a report of the most common scams reported to it in 2024.
Of the 510 contacts it received from Kansas, 28.4 involved fraudulent online purchases. Seventeen percent involved employment scams. Another 16.7 percent involved 'phishing' or false communications and interactions aimed at gaining a target's personal passwords or information. Debt collections and fake sweepstakes rounded out the top five most common scams reported in Kansas.
Members of area law enforcement state that digital scams are becoming increasingly common.
'As so many people do this online bill pay and stop doing normal banking transactions and have gone to an online method, it just seems like the amount of scams go up a bit,' Mount Hope Police Chief Bart Moore said.
Marion Police Chief Zach Hudlin reported having a text in October saying he had an overdue toll from the turnpike that was a scam.
Marion County Sheriff Jeff Soyez said, 'We have seen a lot of different scams in the last year. We are seeing a lot of Bitcoin scams. People need to be aware of these. If someone is blackmailing someone through social media telling you to deposit Bitcoin, don't. We are also seeing people using Google Earth to blackmail people to send them money.
Peabody Police Chief Phillip Crom has been reading about the Brushing scam going around communities lately.
'This scam sends gifts to random people without names or addresses from the sender. When residents open the gift, they will find a QR code in the box or package and some will scan this code thinking it will reveal the name of the sender. Unfortunately scanning this code unlocks all information stored in their phones. In many cases this is bank information and personal information. Then the scammer will drain bank accounts and use personal information. So the best thing to do is not to scan any unknown QR codes. People can either keep the gifts sent to them or throw them away. Just never scan the QR code. If you receive a package like this and want to report it, call the police. We can make others aware. If you get notification for your bank, you have been a victim of one of these scams or someone has your bank information, please call your bank and have them lock your account for safety. Always be suspicious, when it comes to your financial and personal information,' said Crom.
In September, the City of Hillsboro sent out a warning letting people know they needed to be aware of scams after reports of people receiving text messages regarding a survey for the city. Scammers used texts, emails and phone calls to get residents to click on fraudulent links. And the scammers didn't just attack individuals but also attempted to spoof city staff emails internally.
As far as avoiding scams, law enforcement and the Better Business Bureau (BBB) give a number of recommendations.
The BBB recommended people avoid unsolicited emails from unknown senders and not click links or open attachments.
It also suggested researching online retailers before making purchases, avoiding sending money to strangers and not sharing sensitive information online. It also points out that various social media quizzes open the door to scammers looking for information. It states people should monitor their financial statements regularly and stay informed about new arising scams.
Moore, Crom and Soyez all recommended calling law enforcement if a person suspects what they're dealing with might be a scam.
Moore also suggested reaching out to other resources along with law enforcement, such as family members or a person's bank.
It's important to learn more about scams going on. Hillsboro Police Chief Jessey Hiebert will be doing a presentation on the Top 12 Scams at LifeLong Learning at Parkside in February and there are often other seminars available to the public.
Law enforcement believes that the number of cases is higher than reported since many do not report cases.
'I believe I had two or three cases last year. I'm not sure if this is because there hasn't been much in the way of scams in Peabody or that people get embarrassed that they have fallen prey to these scams. I try to reassure citizens not to be embarrassed. It happens to all of us at one time or another,' said Crom.

title: Post office worker's granddaughter earns full-ride
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Ginger Bergamo-McCulley, who serves as Post Master Relief in the Durham, Lehigh and Roxbury post offices, has worked hard raising not only her children but two grandchildren. And her hard work has…
content:
Lehigh and Durham Post Master Relief Ginger Bergamo-McCulley and granddaughter Kallie. Kallie was recently awarded a full-ride scholarship to Boston University and credits her grandmother's support for helping to make it happen.
Ginger Bergamo-McCulley, who serves as Post Master Relief in the Durham, Lehigh and Roxbury post offices, has worked hard raising not only her children but two grandchildren. And her hard work has paid off in a big way.
'My granddaughter Kallie got a full ride to Boston University,' said Ginger. 'I am so proud of her.'
Kallie, who will graduate this spring and has held a 4.33 GPA all through school, has known that she wanted to go to a top school like Boston University since 5th grade, but she also knew she wouldn't be able to do it on her own.
'She researched on her own what it takes to get into college and got herself well-rounded, joined all the clubs, joined tennis, band, choir, StuCo, whatever would make her well-rounded. She took a foreign language, and then found out about QuestBridge,' said Ginger.
According to their website, QuestBridge 'connects high-achieving students from low-income backgrounds with a thriving community and transformative educational, career, and life opportunities that help propel them to lives of fulfillment, meaning, and purpose'. They seek to 'create a more equitable society where every student can dream big, reach their potential, contribute to the world, and build a life that they love'.
'I heard about it through another kid at my school who also got accepted when I was a sophomore. He was a senior. So then there was a year of just me preparing for it. And then senior year, I got into it. I got accepted into the junior prep scholars and then into the match for the seniors,' said Kallie.
There were several stages to the application process. In the first step, Kallie has to write an essay and have several teachers write recommendation letters. She made it through that stage which led to a trip to Chicago and a tour of QuestBridge.
Kallie said that trip was the farthest she had ever traveled and loved that she got to do it with her grandma.
For the next stage, Kallie did another essay which got her to the final level. The next level consisted of choosing up to 15 colleges to apply to with QuestBridge paying the application fees. Kallie chose eight and ranked them in order of preference with Boston University at the top of her list.
'QuestBridge sends the applications in and the colleges accept you. They send that back to QuestBridge. So they don't know where they rank on your list and you don't know how many chose you. She got lucky and her first choice picked her. So that might be the only one. She might have all 8. We don't know. We'll never know. But the first one she wanted is the one that wanted her. That's the one she got,' said Ginger.
Along with the full four-year ride of tuition and room and board, QuestBridge pays for Kallie's travel to and from school for Thanksgiving, Christmas and summer breaks. They also sent her $1,000 to get a computer.
'She does have to do work-study, but she gets to keep all the money she makes,' said Ginger. 'The only qualifications are you gotta carry a C average of full credit, which is 12 credits a semester, and she has to live on campus.'
Kallie says she has known for awhile that she wanted to go to Boston University.
'What drew me there? The scenery, the history of it. They have a lot with hockey, which I'm not into sports, but I thought it was really cool. Their pre-med program was interesting to me, and I love their bands,' said Kallie.
'I just wish she would've wanted a closer school,' said Ginger. 'She was so scared; so nervous she was gonna make it. I told her 'You know what? I know you're gonna make it because you worked too hard for it to not make it. And because I don't want you to go there, you're gonna go to Boston'. And she got it.'
Kallie plans to be a radiologist.
'I just enjoy the complexity of it—the MRI, the CAT scans. It's not just breaking bones. It's literally all of the scans in the brain, and I've always been very fascinated by that. And then I found I can make it a career,' said Kallie.
While it has been a few weeks since she found out about it all, Kallie is still a bit in shock.
'Honestly when I first heard it, it was more of just the am I having a dream kind of feeling? And it's just now starting to set in that I'm going. It's happening,' said Kallie.
And she can't thank Ginger enough.
'My grandma has raised me and been a big supporter of me. I actually wrote an essay about her and how she supported me. She's been a huge support just even from the beginning. I knew I had that support no matter what I did even if I didn't go to Boston. I knew that I could always call on her. I could always ask her questions. She would always help me in any way she could,' said Kallie.
Kallie wants those in similar situations to hers to know there is hope for them, too.
'You can do it, too. It wasn't an overnight process. I knew I wanted to go to medical school since I was in elementary school. I have been working towards this goal for a while. It wasn't until I discovered QuestBridge that it was like, 'Oh my gosh. This could actually happen'. I did plan and really look into what I needed to do. What do the colleges wanna see,' said Kallie. 'Dreams can come true.'

title: Adventures with coffee
author: Shana Thornhill
description: My earliest memory of coffee is my Grandma Martha drinking a cup...
content:
My earliest memory of coffee is my Grandma Martha drinking a cup of Sanka instant decaf with me at Faspa. She had a special electric hot pot that I only ever saw her use to make her Sanka. She always had her Sanka in an orange Fiestaware cup—I remember the distinct round handle.
When company came over she'd get out the coffee percolator (you know, the white one with the blue flowers that you heated on the stove) and let me help put the grounds in the little metal basket. I was fascinated watching the water splashing up in the little glass bubble on top, getting darker and darker, until Grandma said it was ready. And no, little me couldn't touch the basket. It was hot!! And we needed more cups, with saucers this time.
We had a coffee machine at home, a pristine white Mr. Coffee. As far as I can recall, we only used it for company. It certainly wasn't in daily operation. I know my mom had a Corningware percolator too, probably Mr. Coffee's predecessor. And no, I wasn't allowed to drink coffee, Sanka or otherwise. It would either stunt my growth or turn my knees black. I didn't care to find out which.
I grew up and moved out and still really didn't think much about coffee. Once, in a fit of nostalgia, I bought some Sanka. That day, I learned to admire my grandmother's grit. That stuff was awful. Maybe the limescale in her ancient hot pot made it taste better, but I doubt it. One day, I was introduced to espresso, and then cappuccino. Wow, this stuff was GOOD! The best part? I was full grown, so it couldn't stunt anything, and if my knees turned black, well…
It wasn't until I met Darling Hubby that my coffee appreciation really began. Not only did he have a Bunn at home (the hot water reservoir really brews a pot of coffee quickly!), but he was used to drinking 4-shot iced mochas at work. That man was caffeinated, I tell you. Most of our married life, we finished off at least a pot of coffee a day between us, usually two. He even gets different coffee varieties as a Christmas present, so we get to try new flavors.
We didn't slow down much, even when Hubs passed a kidney stone. Then came COVID-19 (which he tested negative for, twice), and his sense of smell went wonky. Coffee didn't smell good anymore to him, it smelled unpleasant. Top that off with thinking that maybe that reservoir was harboring something that made him feel sick, and we made the hard choice to get rid of the trusty Bunn.
I couldn't take it. I got a mini pot so I could still have my morning joe. As Hubby's sense of smell came back, he started using my mini pot too. Finally, I caved and bought a full-size coffee pot so we didn't have to fight over who brewed first.
Now mind you, we have well water, and water softeners are for the weak. That means we get almost as much lime scale as Grandma used to. Keeping the ice maker and dishwasher clear enough to continue functioning is a job all by itself.
The coffee pot isn't any different. This pot has been bravely soldiering on for about a year now, but it's been taking longer and longer to brew a single pot because the hard water is leaving deposits. This morning, it gurgled and wheezed for over an hour to make a little more than 2 cups. It was time to run the vinegar through and clear it out.
Darling Hubby poured the vinegar water into the pot. We got a bite to eat and settled in to watch a movie while the vinegar did its stuff. The machine gurgled and wheezed and puffed. Suddenly it went POP and fell silent. 'Well, that's it,' observed Darling Hubs. He got up to have a look, and from the kitchen, hollered, 'You want to come give me a hand?'
When you pour water into a coffee maker, the reservoir water must come into contact with the heating element. The hot water travels up a tube to the outlet which distributes the hot water over the coffee grounds. That then drips down into the carafe, producing the elixir of life. Our water had heated and traveled up the tube, but the tube was blocked with sediment. The pressure built up further and further, until POP. The chamber ruptured, leaking hot vinegar water all over the counter.
I ran for towels, as Hubs discovered just how far 12 cups of water could leak. The coffee machine was hastily, unceremoniously and probably unnecessarily deposited in the sink as we mopped up the spill. The counter top is nice and clean, and the kitchen smells like a salad. And we no longer have a coffee pot. I guess now I know why my mom and Grandma kept those old percolators. Wish I would have.
Fear not, dear readers, Hubs has a cold brew carafe that will hold us over until we can get a new coffee pot. And remember wives, the Bible itself says that your husband should make the coffee. Don't believe me? Check out 'HE brews!'

title: Severe weather increases need for blood donors
author: Bill Bush
description: Only 3 percent of the population donates blood, according to Logan Wright, regional communicator for the Red Cross of Kansas and Oklahoma. What's worse is that, so far, severe weather in 2025 has…
content:
Only 3 percent of the population donates blood, according to Logan Wright, regional communicator for the Red Cross of Kansas and Oklahoma. What's worse is that, so far, severe weather in 2025 has caused the cancellation of more than 200 blood drives, resulting in 5,500 donations going uncollected throughout the United States.
'We would really love to increase that number [percentage of donors] by spreading the word and getting people in to donate, because it really does change lives at a very personal level,' Wright said. 'We encourage people to give, especially in the height of the winter.'
Illnesses, traveling for the holidays, and general busyness already contribute to lower donation percentages in January, which fittingly, is Blood Donor Awareness Month.
'It [blood] can't be manufactured, and it can't be stored very long, so we depend on our donors to give generously,' Wright said. 'We need a constant, recurring appointment to make sure that everything stays steady.'
Donors are allowed to give whole blood every 56 days. Donating platelets takes longer but can be done more often, and Wright said there is a need for both.
Platelets can be donated every seven days, and many people have standing appointments, according to Wright. She said the process takes about three hours, and many donors say the process is their 'me time' to unwind from the daily stresses of life.
Donors can relax, watch a movie, or listen to music.
'In a few hours, you'll have donated enough platelets to help as many as three patients,' Wright said.
She said they have regular donors in the 40 to 60 gallon club.
'Yeah, it's crazy, super generous,' Wright said.
To donate, Wright said to sign up for a mobile blood drive or contact the Wichita location at 1-800-733-2767 (1-800-RED-CROSS). You don't even have to know your blood type to donate. They'll tell you afterward.
Wright said the donation takes about an hour to complete. She suggests drinking an extra bottle of water to make sure you're good and hydrated.
'People are afraid that it hurts or they're afraid of needles, and some of those fears, I think, can be assuaged by coming to an appointment,' Wright said. 'But if that's something that people don't want to do, there's so much more for the Red Cross that they can do to support the mission.'
The Red Cross has volunteer opportunities to drive blood to and from places to be tested, check people in at blood drives, and help with other logistics of putting on a blood drive.
Another way to help is to host a blood drive. Wright said they work with organizations—businesses, churches, schools and colleges—to host and promote blood drives to provide convenient opportunities for people to give.
Donating soon has the added bonus of automatically being entered into a drawing for a chance to win two tickets to this year's Super Bowl in Louisiana. The cutoff for eligibility is Sunday, Jan. 26.
Wright said she didn't have statistics specific for the Hillsboro Free Press coverage area, because they bring all mobile donations to one location to process. There are a few opportunities to donate in Marion County during the next few weeks:
Hillsboro: Friday, Jan. 31: 11 a.m. – 4 p.m., Wohlgemuth Building, Tabor College, 400 S. Jefferson
Goessel: Monday, Feb. 3: 1 – 6 p.m., Goessel Church, 109 S. Church
Hillsboro: Monday, Feb. 24: 9 a.m.-2 p.m., Hillsboro High School, 500 E. Grand Ave.

title: There's ‘snow' excuse for waiting to try this great soup
author: Lindsey Young
description: As soon as the weather forecast called for snow this past week, I immediately began reviewing soup recipes I saved over the past year. It was time. Joey and I prepared our 'get ready to be snowed in'…
content:
Creamy parmesan sausage ditalini soup is hearty and full of flavors that stick to your bones. From the sausage to the parmesan, this soup is sure to warm you up on a cold day.
As soon as the weather forecast called for snow this past week, I immediately began reviewing soup recipes I saved over the past year.
It was time.
Joey and I prepared our 'get ready to be snowed in' list for the grocery store, and I was thoroughly ready to make some awesome, hearty meals while we were stuck inside.
The soup I'm sharing with you this week absolutely fit the bill for a cold day.
This recipe comes from the website 'Belaya.' You can find the original post at https://belaya.info/creamy-parmesan-italian-sausage-ditalini-soup.html. I added extra garlic and pasta in my version below. It ended up creating a much thicker heartier soup/pasta dish, so if you like your soups a little looser, I'd recommend halving the amount of pasta or doubling the liquid listed below.
Creamy Parmesan Sausage Ditalini Soup
Ingredients
1 tablespoon olive oil
1 pound Italian sausage (I used hot Italian)
1 small onion, diced (I used yellow)
6 to 8 cloves garlic, minced
4 cups chicken broth
14.5 ounces diced tomatoes, drained
16 ounces ditalini (or other small) pasta
1 cup heavy cream
1/2 cup grated parmesan cheese, plus more for serving
2 cups fresh spinach, roughly chopped
1/4 teaspoon red chili flakes, optional
salt and pepper, to taste
Directions
Heat the olive oil over medium heat in a large pot or Dutch oven. When it's hot, add the sausage and onions, breaking the sausage apart as it sautes.
When the sausage is cooked through and the onions are soft, add the garlic, sauteing for another couple of minutes or until it is lightly browned and fragrant.
Pour in the chicken broth and drained tomatoes, and stir to combine. Raise the heat to bring the mixture to a low boil, and add the pasta, stirring regularly to keep it from sticking to the bottom. Boil the pasta for the amount of time recommended on the box or until it's cooked to your liking.
Turn the heat down to medium-low, and stir in the cream. Then stir in the parmesan. Once the soup thickens and returns to a simmer, stir in the spinach, letting it cook for a couple minutes until it's wilted. Finally, add red chili flakes (if desired) and salt and pepper, to taste.
Serve the soup with more parmesan cheese sprinkled on top.
For the leftovers, you may need to add more broth (or a little water) to get it back to the same consistency. It will likely thicken more in the refrigerator.
Ours was definitely thicker than the original recipe intended, but I just couldn't see having half a box of pasta sitting in my pantry for who knows how long, so I figured there was no reason to skimp on the carbs.
This was warm, creamy and tasty. I really liked the bit of heat from the hot Italian sausage and chili flakes, too, but I also love that you can leave all that spiciness out and still have an amazing meal.
And it gave us another meal of tasty leftovers for later in the week, once the daily grind resumed. Work day or not, soup days and snow days are best combined.
Spice Up Your Life is a weekly recipe column by Lindsey Young, who describes herself as an enthusiastic amateur cook and can be reached through her website at spiceupkitchen.net.

title: Winning doesn't guarantee good sportsmanship will result
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: Losing and poor sportsmanship often go hand-in-hand. Fans, coaches and athletes have been known to be bad losers at times. It's easy to excuse bad sportsmanship as being frustrated after an emotional…
content:
Losing and poor sportsmanship often go hand-in-hand. Fans, coaches and athletes have been known to be bad losers at times.
It's easy to excuse bad sportsmanship as being frustrated after an emotional and hard-fought game. When we invest in something that we care about so much, we can easily say or do something that we later regret.
I know I've not always been a shining example of great sportsmanship, but hey, who has, right? Yeah, that's lame.
What's interesting to me, and maybe more concerning, is how often the winning team exhibits poor sportsmanship.
Take the Michigan and Ohio State football game, for example. After Michigan upset heavily favored and highly ranked Ohio State in a rivalry football game this past season, someone on Michigan's team thought it would be a good idea to symbolically plant a Michigan flag in celebration in the middle of Ohio State's football field.
Sometimes, in hyperbole, you hear that two schools don't like each other. In this case, it appears to be true.
It should surprise no one that Ohio State's football team took exception to what transpired at the end of the game. But what ensued was more than a little pushing and shoving. Michigan's flag plant sparked a five-minute brawl that led to the use of pepper spray by police, left players and coaches from both sides bloodied and resulted in one police officer receiving medical attention.
The issue is pride — something that rears its ugly head in all of our lives to varying degrees. Pride leads to arrogance, which rarely ends well.
There's no good excuse for bad sportsmanship by the winners or losers, but it's especially sad when the winners can't be gracious in victory.
Fortunately, there are times when good sportsmanship prevails, even in rivalry games. Exhibit A is the way Missouri University handled its upset win over the Jayhawks in men's basketball last December.
Court-stormings have been an issue for years. Usually after a big win or upset, fans of the home team rush the floor to celebrate the victory with the players and coaches.
It's a wild scene as players from the losing team try to get off the floor and to their locker room while trying to avoid getting trampled during the on-court stampede.
KU coach Bill Self has witnessed and been a victim of more than a few court-stormings over the years because KU is consistently one of the more successful programs in the country.
On this occasion, Missouri coach Dennis Gates was annoyed when the public address announcer warned fans not to storm the court because he thought they should be allowed to celebrate. However, to his credit, Gates made sure KU got off the floor prior to the court-storming.
So Gates called a timeout with six seconds to play. The timeout allowed the Jayhawks to safely get off the court as the buzzer sounded on KU's 76-67 loss to Missouri.
'Sportsmanship, that's all it is,' Gates said. 'That's how I would want to be treated when I become a Hall of Fame coach and I'm the No. 1 team in the country. I would want my opponent to respectfully do the same. No matter what's going on, I'm always going to treat people how I want to be treated. I think player safety is important.'
During that timeout, the KU players went together to their sideline. The coaches shook hands and Self waved to the MU bench. KU was able to get to their locker room safely before the fans stormed the court.
'They (the fans) deserve that moment, but I didn't want it at the cost of a player getting hurt, getting ran over, getting trampled,' Gates said.
Self said, 'That was a classy move by Dennis. Let's just call it like it is. That was a class move. Somebody could have gotten hurt because that was real court-storming.'
There was one positive anecdote from the Ohio State and Michigan post-game fiasco. During the melee, two Buckeyes and a Wolverine were seen huddled together on their knees in prayer. Good for them for displaying uncommon wisdom and real leadership, while the world around them was going crazy.

title: Celebrating Dr. Crumbine for Kansas Day
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Hillsboro's Sally Andrews has been intrigued by Dr. Samuel Crumbine ever since seeing a play about him in the 90s, and she is sharing her knowledge about the famous Kansas doctor just in time for…
content:
Sally Andrews, who works in medical records at St. Luke Hospital and Living Center in Marion, stands by the display case she made for staff, patients and guests to enjoy. The case contains information about Dr. Crumbine who was a famous Kansas doctor and one of the nation's leaders in the field of public health.
Hillsboro's Sally Andrews has been intrigued by Dr. Samuel Crumbine ever since seeing a play about him in the 90s, and she is sharing her knowledge about the famous Kansas doctor just in time for Kansas Day on Jan. 29. Andrews, who works in medical records at St. Luke Hospital and Living Center, has put together a display case full of items and information about the famous doctor for staff, patients and guests to enjoy.
'I collect old medicine stuff and old nursing stuff. When I was the Director of Nursing at Parkside, we went to a leadership conference and they had a play about him commissioned by the Kansas Health Foundation as part of the entertainment. It was so interesting to see in real life this kind of thing portrayed about this guy,' said Andrews. 'I didn't even know about him until I saw that play.'
According to the Kansas Health Institute, Dr. Samuel Jay Crumbine was born in Pennsylvania on September 17, 1862. He attended the Cincinnati College of Medicine and Surgery in the 1880s and then moved to Kansas. He started working in Dodge City in the same era as Wyatt Earp and Bat Masterson.
In 1899, Crumbine was appointed to the Kansas State Board of Health. In 1904, he moved to Topeka to begin working as the Secretary and Executive Officer of the State Board of Health.
Andrews has a fly swatter in the display to represent the anti-fly campaign that Crumbne began in 1906 to combat the health hazards of the fly. He was involved in the creation of the modern flyswatter and was responsible for the 'Swat the Fly' campaign designed to stop the spread of disease from flies and other insects.
Crumbine began a public health campaign throughout the state of Kansas targeting communicable diseases such as tuberculosis in 1907.
Part of this involved abolishing the common drinking cup in public facilities.
'They just had a metal cup on the faucet or the well handle. And everybody just drank out of it. When people started getting sick, everybody got sick because they drank off the cup,' said Andrews.
In 1911, Dr. Crumbine helped outlaw the roller towel.
'I still remember a fabric roller towel in the bathroom in Minneapolis when I was a kid. I remember it was ancient and you just pulled down a new part of the towel so you could dry your hand on a fresh place at least,' said Andrews. 'It's interesting how far we've come.'
Andrews said they also started recording vital statistics in Kansas under Dr. Crumbine's guidance in 1911.
'He started doing that, and the first food and drug laws. So we have had the safety of all this stuff—clean environment and food laws and stuff like that since the early 1900s thanks to him,' said Andrews.
One of Crumbine's best-known slogans was 'Don't Spit on the Sidewalk' because of his concern that the habit spread disease. Brick manufacturers produced bricks with the slogan, and Andrews has one of the bricks in her display.
'I think I paid $20 for my brick at a fleak market in the 80s,' said Andrews. 'There used to be one in the sidewalk in front of the old lumberyard (in Hillsboro) entrance, but it disappeared.'
In 1916, the Pullman Company donated a rail car for exhibits on food, hygiene, sanitation, prenatal, infant and child care. Venereal disease, tuberculosis and other communicable diseases were also featured. The car was named Warren after Dr. Crumbine's son who died that year.
'The Warren Car—the traveling health department—was so cool because that was kind of a first in its era because they just didn't have health departments at all and for them to go town to town instead of them making people come to them was kind of a novel idea,' said Andrews.
And it seems that the Warren Car made it's way to Marion County.
'When I was showing my old medicine things to some nursing home residents in the 1990s, a man named John Jost said he remembered the Warren Car coming to Hillsboro.'
Another fun fact that Andrews includes in her display is that Doc Adams on the famous TV series Gunsmoke was based on the physician.

title: Josie's Closet serves the community with medical equipment
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Josie's Closet, in Goessel, serves the greater Goessel area by loaning used durable medical equipment at no cost to those who need it. 'Medical equipment can really add up when you need multiple…
content:
Josie's Closet in Goessel serves the greater Goessel area by loaning used durable medical equipment at no cost to those who need it. They also accept donations of equipment and monetary donations.
Josie's Closet, in Goessel, serves the greater Goessel area by loaning used durable medical equipment at no cost to those who need it.
'Medical equipment can really add up when you need multiple items,' said Nancy Stucky. 'We provide a place for people to donate gently used equipment so that it can be loaned to others in need.'
Stucky serves as the Director of Josie's Closet. She started it in 2020 along with her brother and sister after her mother died in 2019.
'Her name was Josephine. So we named it after her. Our family thought it would've been nice to have had access to borrow some things when she was declining. Since we had a number of things, we thought it would be nice to pay it forward,' said Stucky.
The siblings checked around in the area and found that there weren't any services available like they had in mind, so they decided to set their own up.
'Goessel Church was willing to let us use the Sunday school room for our inventory. Our family was responsible for setting up this ministry to honor my mother, her faith and her willingness. She would've appreciated us willing to share these kinds of things,' said Stucky. 'We do have a board with a few additional members on it, and we are under the umbrella of the Goessel Ministerial Alliance (GMA). So if people want to make monetary donations, they can do that through GMA and it'll be tax deductible.'
In addition to monetary donations, the organization accepts donations of new and used medical equipment in good working condition. These donations are also tax-deductible.
All donated equipment is inspected and sanitized before use.
Types of equipment that are accepted and loaned include bed-assist rails, shower chairs, commodes, stool risers, folding and wheeled walkers, wheelchairs and transport chairs, canes—including quad-based canes, knee walkers and crutches.
'At the moment, we could use more shower chairs and what they call tub transfer benches—that's a wider shower chair. We don't have good wheelchairs at this point to loan out. We just have a few and they're all checked out. So that would be good as well. Those are the main things right now, but we always welcome anything. Things come and go. And it's been interesting that our inventory has kind of matched our needs. So with the donations that we've had over time, they have been able to meet the needs for things checked out,' said Stucky.
She said the idea is to loan items at no charge for the time people need them.
'And then hopefully they will return them so we could pay it forward. We realize that some of our items are probably longer term for those who are elderly, but we still hope that someday we'll get them back. We realize that some things may never come back and that is offset with additional donations. So we are always welcoming new donations,' said Stucky.
While the organization is based in Goessel, they are open to helping anyone from anywhere.
We say it's for the greater Goessel area, but anyone can come and get help. There are no requirements. We do get referrals from Newton Medical Center from their case management and home health. And we have loaned things to people in area towns and communities. There are no requirements for being eligible to use this service,' said Stucky. 'We're just happy to provide this service and to do it as a ministry. It comes partly out of our faith as well. I am a member of Alexanderfeld Mennonite Church and so that is an important part of putting our faith in action.'
Stucky said the motto of Josie's Closet is 'serving the Lord by serving the community' and she finds joy in doing that.
'It is touching to meet people who are at a point where they really need help and are so grateful to have this kind of help in their time of need,' she said.
Josie's Closet is located at Goessel Church at 109 S. Church St. in Goessel. Donations and loans are by appointment only. Please contact Director Nancy Stucky at 620-747-9359 or josiesclosetmedequip@gmail.com for questions or to schedule an appointment.

title: Hillsboro teen killed in car accident
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: A Hillsboro High School student died in a car accident and another...
content:
A Hillsboro High School student died in a car accident and another was seriously injured around 5 p.m. on Saturday, Feb. 8. The Kansas Highway Patrol (KHP) reported a 1991 Chevy Silverado driven by Sutton M. Redger, was southbound on Jade Road north of 170th Street. After traveling through a low-water crossing, the pickup left the roadway to the east and entered a field. The vehicle became unstable and rolled three times before coming to rest.
Redger and passenger Sean D. Mader, 16, also of Hillsboro, were not wearing seat belts according to the KHP. Redger was pronounced dead at the scene and transported to Jost Funeral Home.
EMS transported Mader to Wesley Medical Center where he underwent surgery for injuries to his leg. It is uncertain at this time what other injuries Mader sustained but KHP reported that his injuries were serious.
Redger was a beloved member of the HHS football and former member of the wrestling team. An email has gone out to parents stating that there will be counselors and youth pastors available on Monday and throughout the week to help students as they begin to process the loss.
The community has also set up a meal train and donation support for the Redger/Duerksen family if anyone would like to contribute. Go to https://www.mealtrain.com/trains/y57vle?fbclid=IwY2xjawIV5NVleHRuA2FlbQIxMAABHd0G5vmuumoqAB4nwb4PfBVSvFkB5o79VYCXt3u30ZQfpuD5xEeOeKL6rA_aem_QhJygR4xnvu3pTDs_Cw6aQ.
The Free Press will continue to provide updates on Mader as well as service details for Redger as information becomes available.

title: MCL to hold de-clutter workshop on Feb. 22
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Create order from chaos, once and for all, by discovering speedy shortcuts to combat clutter, simple ways to make organization stick and how to free yourself from the things you no longer want and…
content:
Create order from chaos, once and for all, by discovering speedy shortcuts to combat clutter, simple ways to make organization stick and how to free yourself from the things you no longer want and need.
Do you struggle to clean up your act, reduce the amount of clutter you have in your life and keep it that way? If you're like most people, it's challenging to find the time, energy and motivation to get these dreary chores done, no matter how much we crave change. In this interactive workshop, you'll discover ways to get the organization to stick, fast and easy clutter shortcuts, what to do if you need help and how to make some changes and get rid of things.
Then you need to attend the De-Clutter Class Workshop from 10:30-noon on Saturday, Feb. 22 at the Marion City Library. The workshop will be presented by Jill Miller.
The cost to attend is $10.00 with light refreshments served.
Jill D. Miller is passionate about helping people grow – professionally and personally. Miller is an award-winning author, business development consultant and corporate trainer.
As Headmistress of the Finishing School for Modern Women, Miller has worked with thousands of women since 2015, inspiring them to overcome obstacles and move toward their goals.
She was inspired to compile her favorites into her first book, 'Never Finished: Practical Advice for Modern Women to Inspire Your Fierce, Authentic Self,' published in October 2022.
To make reservations call the Marion City Library at 620-382-2442.

title: HHS hosts district FFA event
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Adi Winter competes in the Food Science event where she determined aromas...
content:
Adi Winter competes in the Food Science event where she determined aromas at the district FFA poultry and food science judging events on Feb. 5 in Hillsboro. The event was hosted by the Lyons FFA Chapter. There were 143 SR contestants and 211 greenhand (freshman) contestants.
Claudia Soo Hoo completes the carcass parts grading of the Poultry Judging event hosted by the Hillsboro FFA at the district FFA poultry and food science judging events on Feb. 5 in Hillsboro. Little River, Chase, Centre, Hillsboro, Maize, Wichita SE, Garden Plain, Mulvane, Hutchinson CTE, Buhler, Central Plains, Lyons, McPherson, Andale and South Barber.

content:
Goessel

Coming—The Bluebirds will play at Herington on Friday, Feb. 14.
Hillsboro
Boys basketball – The Trojan boys played against Wichita Trinity on Monday, Feb. 3. They won 54-50.
'It was a tight and physical game all night. We were led by some balanced scoring by Noah Beavers (13), Lincoln Wichert (12), and Easton Shahan (12). Noah added 12 rebounds to finish the night with a double-double. Seth Driggers and Easton Shahan had five assists. The game was back and forth down the stretch and ended with us getting a defensive stop to seal the victory. I was so proud of the fight we had all night. It was great to win a tight game,' said Coach Kyle Kroeker.
The boys next played Larned on Tuesday, Feb. 4 and won 54-24.
'On Tuesday, we were able to play some great defense only giving up 24 points total. We were very balanced in scoring. Seth Driggers led us with 12 points followed by Easton Shahan with 11. Anders Weisbeck had six boards to lead the team. The team is buying into tough, hard-nosed defense. We were able to cruise to a relatively easy win,' said Kroeker.
The boys ended the week with a home game against Halstead. The Trojans won 61-45.
'On Friday, we took on a high-scoring Halstead team. We knew we were going to have to find a way to slow down their scoring by playing team defense. Again, I was very proud of our defensive effort. Lincoln Wichert had 22 points and Noah Beavers with 14. Noah also led the team with seven rebounds. We have 22 team assists and Easton Shahan had five. We started with a lead and held it the whole way. We hope to continue this momentum we have right now,' said Kroeker.
Coming—The Trojans will play at home against Council Grove on Friday, Feb. 14.
Girls basketball – The Trojan girls played against Wichita Trinity on Monday, Feb. 3 and won 43-37.
Next the girls played Larned on Tuesday, Feb. 4 and won 28-16.
The Trojan girls finished out the week against Halstead and fell just short of a win. Halstead won with a final score of 28-23.
'I couldn't be more proud of this team after tonight's effort. Halstead is really talented and was coming off their first loss of the season against Hesston on Tuesday. Our coaches put together a game plan to try to slow them down and hopefully put us in the game in the fourth quarter and the girls were locked in and executed that game plan. Defensively, our girls frustrated Halstead all night long keeping them well under their scoring average. Offensively, we just couldn't put enough points on the board even though we hit some big shots and free throws down the stretch to keep us in the game and give us a chance. Again, super proud of the effort and this group has been a joy to coach through one of the toughest schedules around. They just keep showing up and playing hard. I love it,' said Coach Micah Ratzlaff.
Coming—The Trojans will play at home against Council Grove on Friday, Feb. 14.
Wrestling – The Trojan girls competed in the Central Kansas League (CKL) Women's Championships on Thursday, Feb. 6. None of them placed.
Next they competed in the Circle Girls Invitational on Friday and Saturday, but they also failed to place.
'Tough outings this week for the girls at the CKL Tournament on Thursday and the Circle Girls Invitational on Friday and Saturday. Girls wrestling in our league has grown rapidly and improved tremendously since girls wrestling was sanctioned a few years ago. Our Girls CKL Tournament has become very competitive and our program has just not progressed at the same rate yet. The Circle Tournament is also a very large and competitive girls tournament. Our goal is to continue to recruit girls here in Hillsboro, hopefully increase numbers, and get them all to a point where they can begin to compete at a high level in tournaments like these,' said Coach Scott O'Hare.
The Hillsboro/Canton Trojan boys also competed in the Circle 34th Annual Invitational on Saturday and Sunday, Feb. 7-8.
'Our boys team was still competing short-handed with several still out due to illness and injury, although we do have a few slowing getting back. We also had to hold a few out due to KSHSAA's limitation on competition points. Therefore, we had a pretty young group competing this weekend at Circle. It was nice to see sophomore Jaxon Chrislip back in the lineup after missing the past two weeks. He returned in solid form, rattling off three straight wins on Friday to earn a spot in the semifinals. He fell to the number two seed but secured a spot on the medal stand. On Saturday he dropped a tough loss in the consolation semifinals before finishing the day with a solid 16-7 major decision to earn 5th place,' said O'Hare.
Coming—We have a busy week ahead with the boys CKL Tournament on Thursday at Hesston before heading to Rossville on Friday and Saturday for the Girls 3-2-1A Super Regional Tournament. Wrestling begins at 2 p.m. on Thursday at Hesston and 1 p.m. on Friday in Rossville.

title: Goessel School Board accepts two retirements
author: Cynthia Goerzen
description: The Goessel school board met on Feb. 10 and accepted the retirement of long-time band teacher Scott Taylor and superintendent Mark Crawford. Both plan to retire at the end of the current school year.…
content:
The Goessel school board met on Feb. 10 and accepted the retirement of long-time band teacher Scott Taylor and superintendent Mark Crawford. Both plan to retire at the end of the current school year.
Taylor is completing 12 years of teaching band at Goessel, beginning in the fall of 2013. He teaches band students beginning in 5th grade and through high school. In a statement from board chair Kelly Booton: 'The Board of Education would like to congratulate Mr. Taylor on his retirement. We appreciate the level of excellence and his passion he has shared for our band program.' Junior high/high school principal Scott Boden offered thanks to Taylor 'for his years of service teaching at Goessel and the impact he has made on numerous students through the band program. We wish him the best on his retirement.'
Crawford is completing four years as superintendent, beginning in the fall of 2021. He was also the K-5 principal for the first three of those years. In a statement from Booton: 'The Board of Education would also like to congratulate Mr. Crawford on his retirement. We appreciate his guidance and leadership the past four years. Mr. Crawford is leaving USD 411 in a great position as we move forward.'
Turning their attention to another matter, the board reviewed current enrollment numbers. Crawford shared a list of statistics: five students in the pre-K three-year-old class, 11 in the pre-K four-year-old class, 18 in kindergarten, 18 first graders, 13 second graders, 19 third graders, 15 fourth graders, 20 fifth graders, 19 sixth graders, 20 seventh graders, 24 eighth graders, 20 freshmen, 25 sophomores, 21 juniors, and 21 seniors. Pre-K through 5th grade enrollment is 119 and 150 students at the junior high/high school building. The total USD 411 student enrollment for the current school year is 269.
Schools are now required to specify capacity limits for every grade level. Crawford shared a graph that shows how many more students each class could have. Some grades are already near their capacity, while others can have as many as six or seven more students.
Crawford is anticipating three exchange students next school year. One would be a sophomore, and two would be juniors.
In other business, the board:
* heard from Crawford that Bethel, Tabor, McPherson and Bethany College students had participated in an 'aspiring teacher career fair.' The students interviewed for teacher openings at area schools. Boden commented about the shortage of substitute teachers.
* listened to Boden's report about the recent STEMM (science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and medical) career presentations. He said agronomists had come to make presentations, as well as a sports medicine orthopedic surgeon, a civil engineer, a veterinarian, a leader from Washburn University's allied health programs and a quality assurance leader for Textron Aviation.
* heard from K-5 principal Jody Schmidt that Jill Martenson of the Chisholm Trail Extension had come to the school on Feb. 4 to make bread with 3rd, 4th and 5th-grade students.
* heard from Schmidt about activities that marked the 100th day of school on Feb. 7.
* heard from Schmidt that school counselor Janna Duerksen had talked to the K-5 students about honesty the 'character trait' for February.
* approved the purchase of Cengage Learning math curriculum, which renews the Big Ideas math curriculum currently used for grades 6-11. The current purchase is for the online textbook and teacher resources. The current textbooks can still be used. High school math teacher Brian Lightner explained the purchase.
* reviewed a letter from the City of Goessel regarding the portion of North Church Street on the west side of the junior high building. The city asked the board to consider 'granting the City an easement over the portion of the private road' on school property. The school board discussed the matter but took no action on the request.
* discussed the school's electronic device policy.

title: Tabor student's directorial debut leaves an emotional mark on audience
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Over the weekend, Tabor Music and Theatre presented Bright Star, a...
content:
Over the weekend, Tabor Music and Theatre presented Bright Star, a musical written and composed by Steve Martin and Edie Brickell.
'It takes place between two different time periods. It goes back and forth between 1923 and then 1946 after the war. It's set in North Carolina, in the Blue Ridge Mountain,' said Director London Eichelberger, a Tabor Student with an individualized theater major and a psychology minor. 'It goes through the story of a girl named Alice and her experience growing up. The plot goes back and forth between that storyline and her adult life. There is also the story of this kid named Billy Kane who just got back from war and wants to be a writer. It goes back and forth between those storylines and they're interweaved together without really knowing it.'
Hillsboro local Rylie Driggers starred as Alice and delivered an amazing performance that had many in tears.
In addition to an incredible cast of singers, the musical featured a live bluegrass band.
Eichelberger chose the show because of the music.
'I loved the music a lot. I knew that when we did the Bluegrass Mass a year ago here at Tabor, the students loved doing it and loved the music. And I thought if they love that kind of music, we should bring it back and try to do it for a show,' she said.
The musical was Eichelberger's directorial debut.
'It was for my senior capstone project. It's been super great and fun. It's had some challenges, of course, like directing my own peers has definitely been kind of a learning curve, but the cast has just been great. I've loved working closely with my peers and getting to take more of a leadership role,' said Eichelberger.
The show completely sold out for all four performances. It was performed in the Prieb Harder Theatre at Tabor, also known as the Black Box, which is a very small space.
'It has been quite the challenge of working in this much smaller space, learning how to navigate the backstage area and how that was gonna work. And I was pretty ambitious with what I wanted for certain set things. And so it's been quite the process, but I think we were pretty successful in that endeavor,' said Eichelberger.
She took advantage of the intimate space and had the audience surround the stage on three sides.
'I was thinking about the perspective of life and how we see it. Since the staging is kind of a 270 perspective—so not like a full 360, but just like three sides—it allowed the actors more range of motion. But also it prohibited the audience from seeing certain perspectives which is kind of how we view life. We don't get to see every perspective of everybody's life. Due to the show having such intense themes of loss, love, betrayal, hope, and more, I wanted the audience to see the show from different perspectives. In life, we are surrounded by people with deep-rooted lives and experiences. We will never be able to truly see every aspect of others' lives. And so I kind of wanted that to reflect in the show as well,' said Eichelberger.
The Tabor senior didn't just direct the musical but she had her hands in all aspects of the show.
'We had people build the set, but for the most part it was based off of drawings that I did. The set pieces were what I had in my brain. We had a prop master, but she and I worked closely together to get a good overall design for the show. And then I did all the costumes,' she said. 'My hands have been full, but that's okay. I enjoy the chaotic nature of shows, so it's been good for me. I wanted to tell a story in a certain way.'
Eichelberger wanted the show to have a rustic atmosphere to reflect the rawness of the human experience.
'Aged barn wood represented how the show and the characters grow and age through the show. The set pieces were minimal and created only a sense of what they are rather than just a complete picture. This allowed the audience to fill in what they observed in the show. I chose this because we all have our views of what others' lives look like,' she said.
Now that the show is over, Eichelberger is planning to finish up her semester and graduate in May and then move on to her future.
'I have a couple of shows in Wichita that I have been auditioning for and working with. I am also going to be the artistic director for the summer camp that they have here at Tabor,' she said.
But first she is going to enjoy the success of the musical. She is very pleased with it and how the performances turned out.
'The message and themes the show conveys definitely were evident to audiences and left an emotional impact that carried long after the show. I am so thrilled with the positive feedback. I know it means so much to not just me but to the cast as well. We have worked so hard and for it all to come to such an impactful end gives me such a drive to continue to create more. Big thanks to the community for the support and selling out my directorial debut,' said Eichelberger.

title: Marion County Health Department settles into new building
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Marion County Board of Commissioners met on Monday, March 3 where they learned from Marion County Administrator Tina Spencer that the Marion County Health Department is open in their new building…
content:
The Marion County Board of Commissioners met on Monday, March 3 where they learned from Marion County Administrator Tina Spencer that the Marion County Health Department is open in their new building at 1220 E. Main St. in Marion.
'They served their first client over there this morning,' said Spencer.
Spencer said that there were still a few pieces of furniture at the old location that the county needs to get rid of. The board agreed to post it for anyone who might be interested in it.
The board heard road updates from Road & Bridge Superintendent Steve Hudson.
Hudson explained that there are three main projects—the Nighthawk Project (at Canada between old 56 and new 56), the Limestone Road Project and 140th between Pawnee and Sunflower/Aulne Rd.—and one cost share application to apply for to help pay for the projects.
'And from what I understand, there's only a certain amount of money that's allowed in that pot and I think it's a maximum of $1 million. That's it,' said Hudson. 'We need to find out what kind of direction you guys would like to direct us. But I would like to recommend, with the new asphalt plant coming in in the county, we could certainly take advantage of it. And I would recommend doing an asphalt overlay on the Aulne road, the 140th between Pawnee and Sunflower. Just flat out pay for that. Just a three inch overlay. That would be three miles.'
'So were you not recommending doing the pace work, Steve, on that,' asked Spencer.
'There's only like two spots that were ever giving us any troubles at this point in time. They've healed up. I think it's finally dried out enough that it's not showing any weakness there. The rest of the road's solid. The only thing we'd have to do for that would be remove the sand that we put on it now in order for the oils and the surface to adhere better to the base. Because right now we've got a layer of sand on there to keep the dust down with the traffic and fill in the potholes.'
Spencer pointed out that the projects can cost more than the cost share application amount.
'So in the past we have like tried to combine, apply for the whole thing and then put our match up there to where we're putting in more than one project. Because the maximum award that we can receive is a million dollars. That doesn't mean that's the maximum the project can cost. So the county would have to put in the balance, you know, so if you put them together and put in like your 40% or whatever the board decides, you might be able to do it combined,' said Spencer. 'The last one I think we put 40. We've done up as high as 30/40% of the county putting in.'
After more discussion, the board agreed to combine the projects and move forward to see if the county can get cost share approval.
The board also discussed a project on 330th that is waiting on approval for an economic development grant.
Next the board, Hudson and Shop Supervisor Tom Holub discussed equipment. The board told them to move forward with getting a used belly dump truck with a new trailer for $85,000. The board also approved Road & Bridge to get quotes on a new dump truck.
Road & Bridge will look into selling a dozer and several other items.
In other business, the board:
*reversed encumbrances for three invoices—two for ambulance, one for road & bridge—for 2024.
*approved the 2024 county inventory. Dirks asked if the items could be listed differently in the future based on cost. Spencer stated that the process is not very good and needs to be revamped. She is looking at coming up with something better.
*learned that a representative from Sunflower Wind will be coming to next week's commission meeting.
*agreed to have Enterprise Fleet Management come present information to the board in a future meeting.

title: Hillsboro working with Mennonite Housing on housing project
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Hillsboro, KS - The City of Hillsboro and Mennonite Housing, a non-profit organization located in Wichita, are proposing to develop a new 24-unit affordable housing project just south of Dollar…
content: Hillsboro, KS – The City of Hillsboro and Mennonite Housing, a non-profit organization located in Wichita, are proposing to develop a new 24-unit affordable housing project just south of Dollar General. A meeting has been scheduled at 6:30 p.m. on March 21 at Hillsboro City Hall to provide information about the proposed project and obtain input from the community regarding the project design and management. 'We are excited to be able to help address the need for affordable housing in the Hillsboro community,' said Bryon Adrian, Mennonite Housing President and CEO. 'We look forward to developing a partnership with the community and to better understand how we can help out in the future.' The project, called Orchard Ridge, would be comprised of 12 duplex buildings, a clubhouse and a maintenance garage. The duplexes would be two- and three-bedroom units, each with a garage, constructed in an energy-efficient manner and include all appliances. A proposed clubhouse would offer a community room with a kitchen, a technology room and outdoor amenities including a covered patio, playground and basketball court. 'What an awesome opportunity,' said Mayor Lou Thurston. 'It feels great to be able to address housing needs within our community, and to do so, in partnership with an experienced and proven organization like Mennonite Housing makes the prospective outcomes that much stronger.' The proposed Orchard Ridge project is considered workforce housing, for individuals and families with an annual gross household income below 80% of area median income (AMI). Some units will have rent amounts tied to gross household income compared to AMI levels. The goal is to provide affordable housing options for a range of individuals and families. If you wish to learn more about the project and/or provide input to Mennonite Housing, please plan to attend the meeting.

title: County approves Health Department Building Project revisions
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Marion County Board of Commissioners met earlier than their regular time on Monday, March 25 to discuss the Health Department Building Project with Cody Nelson of NF Construction. Marion County…
content: The Marion County Board of Commissioners met earlier than their regular time on Monday, March 25 to discuss the Health Department Building Project with Cody Nelson of NF Construction. Marion County Administrator Tina Spencer mentioned that she felt the meeting was important to make sure the decisions being made are better for the project long-term. 'I just feel like part of my job is to just make sure that everybody's on the same page and that we're focusing on the needs and the project, not necessarily the dollar amount although the dollar is important too. Absolutely. But it's to come back around and make sure that we're kind of on the same page,' said Spencer. 'More information is always good. So the more information we can get, the better,' said Chairman Dave Mueller. Nelson explained that while it would cost a bit more, he and the architects would like to see the masonry stay in place on the exterior of the building. The decision had recently been made to go with a synthetic stone but Nelson wanted the board to rethink it. He explained that the way the synthetic stone has to be applied at the door and windows takes away from the appearance. 'I don't really like that detail because I think that's where it's gonna make it look bad just because of what we have to do with the product to make those returns. We have to miter the ends of those panels, and then they get caulked and glued together,' said Nelson. Another recommendation that Nelson and Spencer made to the board was to change from metal wall panels to a high-end aluminum product that is a similar product but with pre-finished metal that will give a wood grain appearance. 'It would look nice but not add a whole bunch of money,' said Nelson. The final changes recommended were to take the walls up to the ceiling for more privacy. The board approved the three recommendations of Nelson and Spencer to reinstate the masonry, metal reduction and higher walls for privacy for an approximate cost of $63,800 with Commissioner Becker voting against it. The funds for the changes will come from money from the wind farm that was given to the county. Spencer stated that she and Marion County Health Department Director Krista Schneider will be applying for a grant to help with the overall cost of the building and that she had heard that there could potentially be donations that could help that would come through the Marion Advancement Campaign. Commissioner Jonah Gehring said that many residents have been making comments about alternative fixes and other ways the county could go about getting a new Health Department building. 'I just wanted to take the time to let people know that a lot of this project is being paid by federal money. Yeah, it's still your taxes, but it's a chance to take some of that money from Washington and bring it back to Marion County, which would be around $200,000,' said Gehring. 'So take that into consideration. If we were to go out and buy a building or remodel a building, the county would be in for 800 plus. Right now we're in 200. So even though they're great ideas, they're not cost effective in this application—not to our local taxpayers, they're not cost effective.'

Family and friends gathered to support the Seth Mader Memorial Fishing Derby on Saturday at the Marion County Lake. Mader was killed in an ATV accident at the lake in 2022. All proceeds from the timed derby will go toward a memorial bench at the lake to honor Mader who died in an ATV accident on 2022. Seth Mader would have been 18 on Sunday, but his young life was cut tragically short in November of 2022 when he was killed riding his ATV at the Marion County Lake.
Mader was known for his love of the lake in general and fishing specifically so his family decided to honor him and his upcoming birthday by holding the 1 st Annual Seth Mader Memorial Fishing Derby on Saturday, April 6.
st Annual Seth Mader Memorial Fishing Derby on Saturday, April 6. 'We just wanted to memorialize and honor him in some way. We thought this would be a great way that people could fish, have fun and remember Seth,' said mom Erin Mader. 'His 18 th birthday would have been the 7 th . We don't get to do graduation or any of those things, but we can do this.'
th birthday would have been the 7th. We don't get to do graduation or any of those things, but we can do this.' The entry fee was by donation to help raise money for a memorial bench to be placed out at the lake. 50 participants officially registered—others came out to fish for fun—and over $1,000 was raised for the bench.
The event was about three hours long with awards presented after the fish were weighed and measured.
'We had places donate for the prizes such as Bomgaars, CSI, Vondy's Liquor, Last Change Bait Shop and several individuals,' said Mader. 'We ended up having eight winners total since we had four categories but then there were so many kids. We decided we would do a youth and adult for each category.'
The winning categories were largest fish by weight, longest fish by inches, smallest fish by weight and shortest fish by inches.
'We had a great turnout. And despite the wind, they caught quite a few fish. The event was a success,' said Marion County Lake Superintendent Isaac Hett.
Hett worked with the family to plan and host the event and offered to handle all of the registrations.
'All I did was kind of help them how we ran tournaments in the past. They'd never done it before so I told them what we've done and different ideas for prizes and things like that. And I told them that I would take care of all the registration so they didn't have to mess with it. That way, if people wanted to sign up, they didn't have to go find Erin or Mike [Mader]—they could just come here to a central spot,' said Hett.
Not only did people from all over the county come to support the event and family, but the Mader family had friends and family come from outside the county both show up in person and send financial support in the mail.
Christine Ayers and her son 16-year-old son Cody drove from Texas to attend the derby and remember Seth.
'I have known Erin since my son was four. Her mom sold us our house our at Willow Glen when we had just moved to Hillsboro and she told me she had a daughter my age and thought we would be really good friends. We met and we've been friends ever since,' said Ayers.
Ayers had moved away to Texas but visited often and was here the night that Seth died. She knew she had to come and be at the derby to celebrate Seth and his 18 th birthday.
th birthday. 'I just love Erin. I love her family. She's just got a special place in my heart,' said Ayers.
People not only fished but hung out and visited sharing memories and stories about Seth and enjoying time together.
'We want to give a huge thank you to everyone who came out and fished, donated and supported us in any way,' said Mader.
The family is not yet sure if they will make this an annual event, but it is definitely a possibility.
'If we decide to make it an annual derby, we will use the future proceeds toward other charities and benefits,' said Mader.
To give to the memorial bench, you can donate to the Seth Mader Memorial account at Emprise Bank in Hillsboro.

title: County progresses on projects
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Marion County Board of Commissioners met on Monday, April 15 where they heard updates from County Administrator Tina Spencer. Spencer gave several project updates beginning with the 1240…
content:
The Marion County Board of Commissioners met on Monday, April 15 where they heard updates from County Administrator Tina Spencer. Spencer gave several project updates beginning with the 1240 Commercial Drive remodel which now houses Road & Bridge, Planning & Zoning and Emergency Management..
'All the departments have moved in there. The phone system is not in place yet, but the calls are being forwarded to cell phones for now. So we should have those hopefully within a few weeks,' said Spencer.
She said there is a broken-down wooden fence around the property but Road & Bridge will remove it. A sign will be completed and installed in a few weeks.
'On the Health Department Project, the architect is helping us with the contract for NF Construction so we're waiting on some details for that. But that should be ready for approval soon. And the demolition contract has been fully executed, so they'll coordinate the beginning of the demolition since it's the same contractor who is also doing the prep work of the site. They want to not mobilize twice,' said Spencer.
Electrical work has begun on the County Administrator's office space.
Spencer reminded the commissioners that all county offices will be closed on Friday for active shooter training for all county employees.
Spencer has been meeting with department heads on a regular basis and will continue to in her role as County dministrator.
'When I had the department head meeting, I asked the department heads if they might be interested in having some budget training because that's not something we've ever really done,' said Spencer.
Spencer said that is something that the Lloyd Group does with other counties and could do with Marion County.
'They were all very interested in that. If we're gonna go ahead and use him for his full contract, what I would like to do would be to shift that process and have him do a session with the department heads. That's a training session on the budget and on their particular funds and how they work,' said Spencer.
Spencer said he would come on a day that the department heads present to the board so he gets in on those conversations and then shift the rest of his time to help with discussions about how they want things set up moving forward in the future for capital projects and those kind of matters.
The board liked the idea and approved a letter of engagement with the Lloyd group. The meeting with Lloyd will be in May.
In other business, the board:
*met in executive session for personnel matters of non-elected personnel.
The board will meet next on Monday, April 22.
