title: USD 410 approves increased budget
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The USD 410 School Board met on Monday, Sept 9 where they opened with an Exceeding the Revenue Neutral Tax Rate Hearing as required by Kansas statutes. They also held a 2024-2025 budget hearing. The…
content:
The USD 410 School Board met on Monday, Sept 9 where they opened with an Exceeding the Revenue Neutral Tax Rate Hearing as required by Kansas statutes. They also held a 2024-2025 budget hearing. The hearings provided an opportunity for the board to hear public comments concerning the 2024-2025 proposed use of all funds and the amount of tax to be levied. No members of the public attended.
Jerry Hinerman, Business Manager for USD 410, explained that remaining revenue neutral would mean a loss.
'If we were to remain revenue neutral across all funds, we would have $88,500 less in local taxes and $53,000 less in state. We have about a $141,000 less to work with,' said Hinerman.
The board voted to approve exceeding the revenue neutral tax rate. They also approved a resolution to authorize a Local Option Budget Percentage in an amount of 33% for the 2024-2025 school year and approved the 2024-2025 budget as published in the Hillsboro Star-Journal on Aug. 28.
Superintendent Clint Corby gave bond project updates.
He explained that 10 of the projects have come in around $411,000 under budget while four projects have come in around $179,000 over budget.
'That still gives us $232,000 less than we thought we were going to spend. I'm happy about where we've been and how that's going,' said Corby.
The board also made the following personnel changes:
*approved the resignation of Jayne Smalley from her position as Hillsboro Elementary School Custodian effective Sept. 1.
*approved a salary increase of 5.87% for FACT Director Terry Bebermeyer along with a health insurance contribution equal to a $1,600 deductible single coverage health insurance premium for the 2024 – 2025 school year.
*approved the issuance of a contract to Dan King to serve as Hillsboro Middle School Assistant Wrestling Coach for the 2024-2025 school year.
*approve the issuance of a contract to Mallory Shewey to serve as Hillsboro High School Girls' Assistant Basketball Coach for the 2024-2025 school year.
*approved a contract to Esther Richert as .5 Junior Class Sponsor for the 24-25 school year.
*approved the hiring of Laura Schmidt to serve as OASIS Van Driver at a rate of $16.10 per hour for 4.5 hours per day effective Aug. 22.
In other business, the board:
*approved the cost of an upgrade for the fire alarm system at HMHS in the amount of $285,931.14. The original estimate was $150,000. The upgrades will include new control panels, new wiring, new sensors, pull stations and a new speaker system.
'This really makes it a lot safer situation. When firemen go down and they can see exactly where it is, it helps response time significantly. The other piece that this does is it ties a speaker system into it to give directions,' said Corby.
*heard a report from board member Jessey Hiebert that the Technology Excellence in Education Network (TEEN) now has 54 virtual students aged 19 and under and 5 adults. They have 80 students enrolled in TEEN online campus classes.

title: Goessel School needs custodian and substitute teachers
author: Cynthia Goerzen
description: Goessel school board met on Sept. 9 and heard from superintendent Mark Crawford that the junior high/high school building needs a full-time custodian, also janitors to help with events. He said the…
content:
Goessel school board met on Sept. 9 and heard from superintendent Mark Crawford that the junior high/high school building needs a full-time custodian, also janitors to help with events. He said the school hosts a lot of evening and weekend events, and it is hard to keep up. Board members Ben Schrag and Patrick Flaming mentioned other schools that hire a business for janitorial work.
Crawford said the school also needs two more substitute teachers.
Turning their attention to another matter, the board heard from junior high/high school principal Scott Boden about a new after-school activity that high school students can choose if they are not involved in fall sports, since practices and competition times would conflict. High school social science teacher, Gerard Dunne, plans to lead an esports club.
Boden said the school plans to sign up for PlayVS, which is affiliated with NFHS. Madden was mentioned as a possible game. The school will try esports in the fall and might consider participating again in the spring season.
According to Boden, Goessel would expect to compete against other schools. Spectators would be welcome. Watching online might also be an option.
Students will bring their own gaming devices to begin the program. The school might purchase equipment in the future. Boden expected an esports option would increase involvement in school; a lot of students are not involved in other sports. He said there are some attendance issues and had wondered, 'What can we do that connects kids?' He knew of a Goessel graduate who is playing esports in college. Some other schools in the Wheat State League are looking at it but don't have it yet.
Standard eligibility rules will apply for participation, like all other activities. Students have to be 'in good standing,' pass all their classes and not have excessive absences.
In other business, the board:
* heard a report from new elementary school principal Jody Schmidt. She said most of the kindergarten parents attended the Kindergarten Koffee. She said the Olympic-themed Family Reading Night was a success.
* heard from Schmidt that the 5th graders would be participating in Starbase at Salina again this year. The program provides experiential learning experiences for science, technology, engineering and math.
* heard from Schmidt that the 10 new elementary school students seem to be adjusting well.
* heard from Boden that 20 high school students and 13 junior high students are participating in football. 16 high school students and 26 junior high students are playing volleyball. Five high school students are participating in cross country. Nine high school students are cheerleaders.
* heard from Boden that the high school is using a temporary portable air conditioning unit until the rooftop unit is replaced.
* accepted a $5,000 Farm Credit Services grant for a livestock facility that would be used to educate students about proper handling and care of animals.
* heard from Schmidt about a large hole in the grade school playground. She expressed gratitude to Ben Schmidt and Donna Washmon for filling it in.
* heard about professional development opportunities for teachers. Schmidt mentioned Wheat State League Professional Development Days at Canton-Galva and Solomon.
* heard that 47 students are participating in the high school musical, Little Mermaid.
* heard that Sept. 25 will be an early release day for teacher in-service in the afternoon.
* approved the month's expenses of $149,663.93.
* held a budget hearing prior to the regular meeting and adopted a revenue-neutral budget for the new school year as published previously in the Hillsboro Star Journal. Crawford emphasized that the budget will not exceed last year's taxation rate. He said property taxes should remain 'about the same' or drop slightly.

title: Area Sports Roundup 9-18-24
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Goessel Volleyball – The Bluebirds went 2-0 to open league play on Tuesday, Sept. 10. The scores were as follows: Goessel defeated Herington 25-8, 22-25, 25-23. Goessel defeated Solomon 25-15, 25-16.…
content:
Goessel
Volleyball – The Bluebirds went 2-0 to open league play on Tuesday, Sept. 10. The scores were as follows: Goessel defeated Herington 25-8, 22-25, 25-23. Goessel defeated Solomon 25-15, 25-16.
The Bluebirds went 5-0 on Saturday after winning the Bluebird Invitational Volleyball Tournament that they hosted at home. This is the first time they have won the tournament since 2017.
The scores were: Goessel defeated Central Christian 25-14, 25-14. Goessel defeated Southeast 25-10, 25-15. Goessel defeated Sedgwick 25-21, 25-17.
Goessel is now 9-1 on the season.
Coming—The Bluebirds will play at home on Thursday, Sept. 19.
Football – The Bluebirds played Centre at home on Friday, Sept. 13 and won with a final score of 56-8.
Coming—The Bluebirds will play at home against Rural Vista at 7 p.m. on Friday, Sept. 20.
Hillsboro
Volleyball – On Tuesday, Sept. 10, the Trojan volleyball team hosted another home night, once again competing against two state ranked teams. The Cheney Cardinals and Hesston Swathers both entered the night ranked in the top 10 in 3A. Both matches were epic battles from the start for the Trojans. Both matches went three sets; both matches required extra points to win; and in both matches the scores were very close.
The Trojans battled their way to an early lead against the Cardinals in the first set only to see the Cardinals claw their way back into it. After a seven-point run by Cheney pushed them ahead, Hillsboro never gave up and behind the serving of senior, Skylar Voran, went on a five-point run of their own to take back the lead. It was point for point from there on out until Cheney finished the game at 25-23. The second set was another battle as both teams traded leads until Hillsboro closed the door with a 27-25 win. Going into the final set, Hillsboro found themselves down early but clawed their way back to within 1 at 17-18. The battle continued but Cheney pushed the lead to 24-20. The Trojans, however, did not give up and fought for a couple more points before Cheney finished the game.
Lauryn Vogt and Kingzley Ratzlaff combined for 35 kills in the match, while Talia Jost
added 5 of her own. Ella Potucek and Ratzlaff had 23 and 10 assists respectively. Amyah
Werth, Ratzlaff, and Vogt combined for 56 of the team's 82 digs.
In the nightcap, Hillsboro faced league foe, the Hesston Swathers. Throughout the first game the Trojans held a four-point lead which grew behind the serving of Ella Potucek. They were able to maintain this margin throughout the set. Hesston's big hitter, Kendall Breugem, caught fire in the second game and they won with the same score as the first game. The tie-breaking game was a battle. The Trojans found themselves down 12-17 at one point but chipped away at the lead. With the score at 16-20 Hillsboro went on a 6 point run behind the serving of sophomore, Daisy Klein. At that point the game seesawed back and forth until the Trojans were able to tie it up at 28 and win the last two points, once again with Klein at the serving line. The final game ended 30-28. The girls had nine aces in the match and improved blocking to help slow down the Hesston offense. Ratzlaff had a season-high 20 kills and Vogt added 14. Amyah Werth kept the ball off the floor with a season-high 31 digs.
'What an incredible night of volleyball. We matched up with two very talented and well-coached volleyball teams, and it proved to be an entertaining and competitive night in the gym. I am proud of the girls and the way they battled both teams,' said Coach Sandy Arnold.
The final scores were: Cheney defeated Hillsboro 25-23, 25-27, 25-22. Hillsboro defeated Hesston 25-20, 20-25, 30-28.
The Trojans headed to their second tournament of the season as they traveled to Southeast of Saline on Saturday, Sept. 14. The girls started pool play with the home team SES Trojans. The girls played consistent offensive volleyball and steadily increased their lead each game.
In the second contest of pool play, Hillsboro faced Circle. Circle held a three-point lead at 13-10 when Lauryn Vogt took over at the serving line and helped the Trojans to an eight-point run which they held the rest of game one. In the second set Hillsboro held a small advantage, but Circle chipped away at the lead, tying it up. The battle then ensued as both teams traded points until Circle put the game away at 30-28. The Trojans came out strong in the 3rd and final set and took another larger lead. With the score at 21-17, Daisy Klein went to the serving line and rattled off the last four points of the game for Hillsboro.
In the final match of pool play, Hillsboro faced 4A's Concordia. The Trojans were able to hold their early lead and defeat Concordia in game one 25-18. In the second game Hillsboro found themselves in a little hole but continued to be aggressive and creative in their attack. Serving runs by Vogt and Skylar Voran helped the Trojans secure the win 25-23 despite the efforts of the Panthers to continue the game.
With a first-place finish in their pool, Hillsboro would face the second-place finisher in Pool B, Salina South, in the semifinals. Despite a big early lead for the Trojans, the Cougars did not go away and clawed their way back into the lead. The Trojans kept their composure and steadily fought their way back in front and kept the lead to win game one, 25-22. Game two went back and forth with Salina South grabbing an early lead. The Trojans, however, kept attacking from the front row and serving line and came out on top 25-19. In both games, Voran had key terms of service that ignited runs for the Trojans.
This win boosted the Trojans into the championship against the number one team in 3A, the Beloit Trojans. Beloit gave Hillsboro its toughest competition of the day. Their tough serving, big block and balanced attack proved to be too much for the Trojans. The girls kept attacking and worked on finding ways to score throughout the match and never gave up.
'Saturday was a positive day for us. We played confidently and more consistently. We also found places we can continue to strive for improvement. We have made some strides in areas where we needed work and it showed in our performance,' said Arnold.
Coming—The Trojans will plays at Halstead on Tuesday, Sept. 24.
Tennis – The Trojans competed in the Smoky Valley Viking Classic on Thursday, Sept. 12. Cassidy Bernhardt played #1 Singles. The final scores were: lost to Karli Haase, Ellsworth, 0-8; lost to Josie Baer, Chapman, 4-8; lost to Tessa Herrman, Abilene, 1-8.
'Cassidy ran into some really good, experienced singles players today. She was right in both of her last two matches, leading Baer for a while and taking a lead in the first three games against Herrman in her final match. She really is improving in her singles play and gets better each tournament. Staying consistent and true to her game, while making some needed adjustments along the way, will help her down the road,' said Coach David Ediger.
Claire Morey and Maylee Hardey played #1 Doubles. The final scores were: lost to Molly Martin and Elyse Griffin, Hesston, 1-8; lost to Jill Hett and Madelyn Mauk, Smoky Valley, 4-8; lost to Zora Carver and Lillie Fulton, Smoky Valley, 3-8.
'I saw some good things out of our doubles play today. Claire is being aggressive at the net, getting to a lot of volleys and putting them away. Maylee continues to be consistent in getting balls back. It was a tough day as far as finding a win, but overall I am pleased with the direction they are moving,' said Ediger.
Coming—The Trojans will compete at Lyons on Monday, Sept. 23.
Cross Country – The Trojans competed at Wamego on Sept. 14.
'The Trojans had a great day at Wamego this past Saturday,' said Coach Brielle Loewen.
On the girl's side, Quinlyn Funk (20:48.61) and Riley Richert (20:53.69) placed in the top 15. Jaidyn Frantz (22:23.88 PR) received a medal placing in the top 40, and Nora Hein had a strong finish at 27:25.68.
Leading the Trojans on the boy's side was Wyatt Dies with a PR of 21:33.39, Casen Steinert at 21:58.39, Ben Werner at 24:11.42 and Elijah Holmes with a time of 25:15.36 PR.
Coming—The Trojans will next compete at Herington on Thursday, Sept. 19.
Marion
Cross Country – Marion Cross County competed at Wamego on Saturday, Sept. 14.

title: Still time to register to vote in general election
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Even if you didn't vote in the recent August primary or are not registered to vote, you still have time to register to vote in the Nov. 5 general election. To check your voter registration, visit…
content:
Even if you didn't vote in the recent August primary or are not registered to vote, you still have time to register to vote in the Nov. 5 general election.
To check your voter registration, visit myvoteinfo.voteks.org or inquire at the Marion County Clerk's Office. It takes less than 30 seconds to check your voter registration online. You can also find your polling place location on the site.
Who can vote
To vote in Kansas, you must be eligible and registered. Every resident of Kansas who is a U.S. citizen and is 18 years of age (or will be by Nov. 5) or older is eligible to register.
'Even if someone won't be 18 before Oct. 15 but will be by the election, they need to register to vote before Oct. 15. Once they have had their birthday, then they will be registered to vote,' said Marion County Clerk Ashley Herpich.
How to register to vote
Individuals registering for the first time in Kansas are required to submit a document to prove their U.S. citizenship. A list of valid citizenship documents can be found online at voteks.org.
First, obtain a Kansas voter registration application from the county election office or at voterks.org. You can also register online but must have a valid Kansas driver's license or nondriver's identification card.
'You can register online at kdor.ks.gov/Apps/VoterReg, through DMV when getting your driver's license or you can come to the Clerk's Office to fill out a voter registration form,' said Herpich.
If not applying online, return the fully completed application to your county election office by mail, fax or in person. County addresses are listed on the back of the application. The Marion County address is 200 S. Third, Suite 104, Marion, KS. 66861.
The deadline to register to vote in the general election is Oct. 15 by 5 p.m.; applications postmarked by that day will be accepted and processed for that election.
If the postmark is missing or illegible, the application will be accepted only if received in the election office by the ninth day before the election.
Applications received during the 20-day period when registration is closed will not be valid for that election. These applications will be processed beginning the day after the election.
How to vote
Once you are registered, Kansas allows voters to cast their ballots in several ways including advance voting. This can be done two ways—advance mail ballot and early in-person voting.
The advance mail ballot allows a registered voter to vote in advance by mail. The voter must complete an application for an advance ballot and include their driver's license number or a copy of their photo identification. The advance voting application can be found at sos.ks.gov/forms//elections/AV1.pdf.
'The deadline to apply for a mail ballot is Oct. 29,' said Herpich.
Early in-person voting begins up to 20 days before an election at county election offices. The dates and times for early voting in Marion County are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Oct. 21-25, 1-3 p.m. on Sunday, Oct. 27, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Oct. 28-Nov. 1 and 8:30 a.m. to noon on Monday, Nov. 4. Early voting takes place at the Marion County Courthouse at 200 S. Third in Marion.
Absentee voting is another option for voters to cast their votes. This is an option for voters who cannot or do not want to vote in person to cast mail-in or drop-off ballots through absentee voting or vote-by-mail programs. This is also an option for college students who can't make it home to their county to vote. To apply online, go to vote.org/absentee-ballot/Kansas or go to the County Clerk's office. The deadline to apply for an absentee ballot is Oct. 29.
Mail-in ballots must be postmarked by Election Day and received three days after the election which is Nov. 8.
You can also vote at your polling place on Election Day (Nov.5) from 7 a.m.-7 p.m. Check myvoteinfo.voteks.org if you are unsure of your polling place location.
Whether you are doing advance in-person voting or voting on Election Day on Nov. 5, state law requires Kansas voters to show photographic identification when voting in person. The following documents may be used to meet photo ID requirements for voting: driver's license or ID card issued by Kansas or another state; U.S. Passport; U.S. Military ID; ID card issued by a Native American tribe; employee badge or ID issued by a government office; student ID card from an accredited postsecondary education institution in Kansas; concealed carry license issued by Kansas or another state; public assistance ID card issued by a government office.
Exemptions from photo ID requirements exist for permanent advance voters (voters with illness or disabilities); military and overseas voters and their spouses and dependents; and voters with a religious objection who sign a Declaration of Religious Objection. Voters age 65 or older may use an expired photo ID.
If you have questions, call the Marion County election office at 620-382-2185. You can also find election information on their website at marionccoks.net.

Goessel Volleyball – The Bluebirds went 2-0 in league play on Tuesday, Oct. 1 at Canton-Galva. Football – The Bluebirds played Central Plains on Friday, Oct. 4. Central Plains won with a final score of 50-0.
Hillsboro Cross-country – The Trojans competed at the Berean meet on Thursday, Oct. 3. Leading the Trojan girls was Riley Richert with a 4th-place finish in a time of 21:26.29, Quinlyn Funk had a 7th-place finish with a time of 22:07.61, Jaidyn Frantz 15th place at 23:41.51, Nora Hein in 28:30.64, Anna King in 31:13.00 and Gabi Sibayan in 41:34.00. Leading the Trojan boys was Wyatt Dies in a time of 22:16.38, then Ben Werner at 24:01.94, Casen Steinert at 24:34.69 and Elijah Holmes in a time of 27:28.52. Coming—The Trojans will next compete on Thursday, Oct. 10 at Sterling. Girls Tennis – The Trojans played Tuesday, Oct. 1 at Ellsworth. For the #1 Singles, Cassidy Bernhardt lost to Adalyn Pfizenmaier (Clay Center) 0-8 and defeated Heather Ward (Hoisington) 8-4. In the 3rd place match, she lost to Grace William (Osborne) 1-8 and finished 4th. 'Cassidy was in all of her matches despite what the final score indicated. Most of her games went to several deuce points. After having a big lead against Ward, she let Ward back in the match a bit, but then refocused and closed it out strong,' said Coach David Ediger. For the #1 Doubles, Claire Morey and Maylee Hardey lost to Annalea Hendrickson and Ella Kramer (Clay Center) 0-8 and lost to Claire Crutcher and Reese Merlau (Hoisington) 0-8. In the 5th place match, they lost to Finley Edwards and Kaylee Felker (Scott Community) 4-8 and finished 6th. 'It was a rough day for Claire and Maylee. The first two matches they couldn't get on track. They played much better in the match against Scott. They had a chance to pull within a game in the match at 4-5 but couldn't get it done,' said Ediger. The Trojans next competed on Saturday, Oct. 5 at the league meet in Hillsboro. For the #1 Singles, Bernhardt lost to Reese Merlau (Hoisington) 0-6, 0-6 and defeated Madison Richey (Haven) 9-3. In the 5th place match, she lost to Katelyn Leis (Smoky Valley) 2-9 and finished 6th. 'Cassidy played really good tennis all day. Her match against Merlau, who ended up being the league champion, was a good match. She played much better than the score shows. After a convincing win against Richey, she played a very good player in Leis. She battled the entire match and had Leis on the defense for several games. Cassidy has really improved as a singles player this year,' said Ediger. For the #1 Doubles, Claire Morey and Maylee Hardey lost to Heline and Carver (Smoky Valley) 3-6, 1-6 and lost to Popp and Rose (Haven) 4-9. In the 7th place match, they defeated Kinast and Hathaway (Nickerson) 9-1 and finished 7th. 'Our doubles team played pretty well all day. They were right in the first two matches against two really good teams. After dropping the first game of the final match, they rattled off nine straight games for the win,' said Ediger. Coming—The Trojans will next compete at Regionals on Oct. 11-12 in Conway Springs. Volleyball -The Trojand hosted their last regular season triangular on Tuesday, Oct. 1. The competition for the evening were the Pratt Greenbacks and Hesston Swathers, both teams from the Central Kansas League. On the special 'dig pink' night, all three teams wore pink in honor of breast cancer awareness month. For the first matchup, the Trojans met up with Pratt. In the first game, Hillsboro went on a 10-point run behind the serving of Kingzley Ratzlaff to take a 13-7 lead. Daisy Klein and Lauryn Vogt added four-point serving runs of their own to add to the lead. Hillsboro went on to win the game 25-12. The second game was a different story as Pratt kept the game close coming back from a deficit to pull within one of the Trojans at 16-17. Fortunately, after a timeout, the Trojans got a side out and were able to increase the lead and hold onto it for a 25-22 win. In the final match of the night, Hillsboro faced the Swathers from Hesston. This would be the second meeting between the two teams this season. In the first meeting the Trojans escaped with a win in a three game thriller. This match proved to be just as exciting. In the first game, the Trojans fought back from being behind 18-23 to tie the game at 23. The teams also tied at 24. Hesston was able to put up the final two points to win the first game 26-24. Hillsboro took the lead early in the second game, but Hesston would not go away and erased a 20-24 deficit to take the lead 25-24. The Trojans did not give up. When Hesston missed their serve at match point after a timeout, Hillsboro scored the next two points to preserve the win at 27-25 and force a game three. The last game of the match seesawed back and forth until Hesston was able to pull away for a 25-21 victory. The final scores were: Hillsboro over Pratt 25-12, 25-22; Pratt over Hesston 25-23, 27-25; Hesston over Hillsboro 26-24, 25-27, 25-21. 'As expected it was another tough league night for us. All three teams went home with a split on the night. Pratt is much improved and very scrappy. Our girls served well to keep them out of system in the first game but then missed too many serves in the second. Hesston served well against us and that did not allow us to attack as well as we would have liked,' said Coach Sandy Arnold. 'It was a competitive night of volleyball and we competed against two tough teams. The girls showed grit and never gave up— even at the toughest moments. The best part is we learned more about areas that need to be strengthened and we can go to work on those areas in our practices.'
Coming—On Thursday, Oct. 10, the team will head to Great Bend for a triangular with the Panthers and Emporia. The Trojans will end their week on Saturday, Oct. 12, when they host the Trojan Invitational.
Marion Cross-country – Marion competed at the Halstead meet on Thursday, Oct. 3. 'The Halstead meet is always a tough meet with great competition. Today was no different,' said Coach Jason Hett. Brooklyn Beery led the varsity girls in a 25th-place finish in a very fast field. 'Brooklyn competes well and will be in the mix later this season,' said Hett. Izy Branson placed 46th and has continued to get stronger each week. 'We look for her to make a push these next few weeks,' said Hett. On the varsity boys' side, times were a little off for their normal pace. 'Eli (Klenda) ran a gutsy race placing 10th in a very fast field. Luke (Wessel) has been battling some shin splits, and it impacted him a little today. He will bounce back and be ready to make the final push,' said Hett. 'Zayden (Janzen) continues to compete for this group and has made great strides this season. Harrison (Beery) and Owen (White) battled the heat today, but those two will need to move up these next few weeks to get some big team points that we need. I believe they are up for the challenge.' Keenan Lange and Jaxon Salsbury rounded out the varsity group. 'They know where they need to be and will continue to push these next few weeks to get there. The boys finished in 6th place as a team out of 14 schools. The work continues this next week as we make the final push to get back to Wamego as a team. I believe this group has what it takes to get back and they are ready and committed to do the work it takes,' said Hett.
Coming—Marion will next compete on Thursday, Oct. 10 at North Newton.

title: PMSA funding remains in limbo as Department of Commerce continues to delay payment
author: Jessie Wagoner
description: In July, when the Peabody Main Street Association (PMSA) was notified by the Department of Commerce that there were concerns regarding a $15 million Base Grant Award and the second disbursement of…
content:
In July, when the Peabody Main Street Association (PMSA) was notified by the Department of Commerce that there were concerns regarding a $15 million Base Grant Award and the second disbursement of funding, $750,000, would not be issued, the association believed the issues would be resolved quickly with the money arriving soon. Now, three months later, despite providing the Department of Commerce with all the information requested, the funding remains in limbo.
PMSA was initially awarded the $1.5 million BASE Grant from the Department of Commerce in May 2023. The group used the first $750,000 to complete numerous projects in the historic downtown business district of Peabody. However, when it came time for the second disbursement of funds to be issued in late January, the funds did not arrive. The group was notified in late July by the Department of Commerce they had not received all the documentation required. At the time, Jonathan Clayton was serving as the unpaid grant administrator for PMSA and was responsible for submitting all the documentation for the grant. Clayton was missing at the time. He was located three weeks later, deceased in his truck, the victim of an apparent motor vehicle wreck.
According to Morgan Marler, PMSA Board Member, from the moment PMSA was notified by the Department of Commerce of the problem, they jumped into action. The volunteer board dedicated hundreds of hours to attempting to locate all the documentation requested by Commerce. They provided the Department of Commerce with financial documents showing grant funds had been spent appropriately. They closed their previous bank accounts and opened new ones in an effort to prove to Commerce that no one would be able to access the funds. Despite those efforts, the second disbursement of money has not been issued and one contractor has yet to be paid for work performed.
'There is still one project that has a remaining invoice to be paid,' Marler said. 'It was due to be paid with the second disbursement of BASE grant funds which we were expecting in late January 2024.'
The Hillsboro Free Press has reached out to the Department of Commerce multiple times to find out when the second round of money will be disbursed to PMSA. No date was given.
'A site visit was conducted at the end of September, and the Department of Commerce continues working closely with Peabody Main Street to bring the grant back into compliance,' Patrick Lowry with the Department of Commerce said.
Marler says PMSA has received no clear indication from the Department of Commerce on when or if the second round of funding will be issued. While the Department of Commerce seems in no rush to make a decision, PMSA is concerned time is running out as all grant projects are supposed to be completed by the end of April 2025.
In early 2023, the Department of Commerce approved the projects to be funded with the grant funds. A large portion of the remaining $750,000 was to be spent replacing all of the sidewalks in the Historic Downtown Business District—improvements that are desperately needed. The sidewalk replacement is being completed in conjunction with an imminent downtown waterline replacement project being completed by the City of Peabody.
'We've already missed out on ten months of time we could have been working on second-phase projects, due to the repeated requests by Commerce to resubmit documentation,' Marler said. 'We only have six months remaining to complete all those projects. That's very, very frustrating for us. And for our community.'
Marler says this ordeal has been challenging for PMSA and believes it is a problem many small, rural towns could encounter if they accept grant funding through the state. In small, rural communities it isn't uncommon for these types of projects to be taken on by volunteers, as the communities don't have the funds to hire grant administrators or city administrators. This is a luxury Marler says small towns, like Peabody, cannot afford.
'Small communities are the ones that most benefit from these types of programs, yet have the least capacity to manage the increasing bureaucracy that comes with accepting that financial assistance,' Marler said.
PMSA encourages Marion County constituents to contact their legislators and encourage them to support the second half of the BASE grant funding for Peabody. They also feel it is important for the state to develop methods to ensure small rural Kansas communities can remain competitive in the grant process.
'It may mean that the State of Kansas develops a system that provides professional assistance to those small towns to help manage the increasingly burdensome reporting requirements they are placing on us,' Marler said.

title: Marion County Food Bank celebrates three years at new location
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: The Marion County Food Bank, which serves anywhere between 500-700 every month, moved into a new building at its current location in Marion three years ago this week. It was established through the…
content:
Marion County Food Bank Volunteers Margaret Tice, Elven Marshall, Jane O' Connor and Manager Cathy Henderson ready bags of food for those in need. The organization is celebrating three years at its new location.
The Marion County Food Bank, which serves anywhere between 500-700 every month, moved into a new building at its current location in Marion three years ago this week. It was established through the generosity of donors and the assistance of four grants totaling $174,000.
'The Marion County Food Bank's upcoming third anniversary is a testament to the community's dedication and support. The food bank stands as a beacon of community spirit, unaided by federal or state funds. Its mission aligns with the biblical call to 'feed my sheep', a principle that has guided its operations. With divine inspiration and the tireless efforts of volunteers, the food bank has been a pillar for the residents of Marion County, offering sustenance and hope. This milestone reflects the strength and efficiency of a united community working towards the common good,' said Gene Winkler, Marion County Food Bank Treasurer.
The food bank has been serving hungry people for over 50 years. It started in a small, 150-square-foot room on the alley behind Valley United Methodist Church and was known as the food pantry. It eventually moved to an abandoned gas station at 1220 East Main owned by the Marion Advancement Campaign (MAC).
'Back in 2015, we had a dream to start a food bank in Marion—even if it was in an old filling station—to be able to provide food for our neighbors who just need a little help. The MAC Foundation, along with the Kansas Food Bank in Wichita, stepped up to fulfill our dream. I can tell you that if it was not for the MAC Foundation, we would not have the Marion County Food Bank in Marion,' said Winkler.
Since its opening at the 1220 East Main building, the operation has been conducted entirely by volunteers including Cathy Henderson who has volunteered since the food bank was located at the Valley United Methodist Church Food Pantry. She now serves as manager and is responsible for recruiting, training and managing volunteers plus ordering and managing food inventory from the Kansas Food Bank and Carlson's Grocery.
In 2021, the food bank moved to its current location at 906 East Main.
The Marion County Food Bank has faced significant challenges over the past three years, navigating through the impacts of COVID-19 and grappling with the surge in food costs due to high inflation. There continues to be a need for financial donations. For example, this past summer, the food bank's income was $7,485 while the expenses were $30,524.43.
Despite these hurdles, the food bank remains steadfast in its mission to support food-insecure neighbors.
'This includes senior citizens often caught in the difficult position of choosing between food and medicine. The organization extends its support to families, understanding that even the basic act of enrolling children in school can strain a household's food budget. While the food bank may not be able to meet all food needs entirely, it plays a crucial role in supplementing food purchases for those in need. Last year alone, the Marion County Food Bank provided over 141,700 meals,' said Winkler. Marion County Food Bank Volunteer Kay Steel gets fresh produce ready for the bags of food for those in need.
According to Winkler, the community's spirit of volunteerism and generosity shines through in the gratitude of those who benefit from the food bank's services.
'Acknowledgments are due to individuals like Pam, who contributes fresh vegetables from the community garden, and the churches of Marion County whose collective efforts on Shared Sundays result in substantial food donations. The heartfelt contributions from community members who donate monthly are the backbone that allows the food bank to continue providing for those in need,' said Winkler.
So far this year, the food bank has served 8008 people. Of that number, 1695(21%) are seniors, 4251 (53%) are adults and 2062 (26%) are children. 115,211 pounds of food have been donated or purchased.
The Marion County Food Bank is open for those in need on Mondays 9 a.m.-12 p.m. and Thursdays 4:30-6:30 p.m. Financial donations can be taken to the food bank during operating hours, to Gene Winkler at his shop, to any pastor in town or mailed to the Marion County Food Bank at PO Box 3, Marion, KS 66861. Make checks out to Marion Advancement Campaign and write food bank in the memo line. Food donations can be taken directly to the food bank during operating hours or placed in designated bins around town.
For more information, visit marioncountyfoodbank.org.

title: GHS Volleyball raises money for the National Kidney Foundation
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Goessel High School (GHS) volleyball team did some fundraising over the summer and not only raised money for their volleyball program but also raised a substantial amount for the National Kidney…
content:
The Goessel High School volleyball team recently donated money to the National Kidney Foundation from the proceeds of their fundraiser this past summer.
The Goessel High School (GHS) volleyball team did some fundraising over the summer and not only raised money for their volleyball program but also raised a substantial amount for the National Kidney Foundation.
'We simply needed to do some fundraising for our volleyball program, but I decided to turn it into something bigger by having our five seniors all choose a local organization they felt worthy to donate 50% of the proceeds to,' said Coach Crysta Guhr. 'They all came up with great choices. But the National Kidney Foundation was the clear winner because the senior who proposed that has a dad who battles kidney disease. We voted unanimously for that to be our organization.'
The Bluebirds raised the money by doing a serve-a-thon.
'Each player served 100 serves, and we kept track of each girl's success. We met as a team and everyone contacted potential sponsors. They had a choice to give a flat donation or sponsor a player by serves made. We had a lot of flat donations and some who chose to give per serve made,' said Guhr.
The girls served in their practices throughout June, came up with the totals and met again to contact each sponsor.
'It was clear from early June that this fundraiser was going to far exceed expectations,' said Guhr.
In July, when all the donations came in, the team met again to write thank-you notes to everyone who gave.
'I don't know how many we sent out, but it was hundreds. The generosity of our community was amazing. But we also had a lot of people from around the country and even a couple from overseas give to our team. It was humbling, to say the least,' said Guhr.
The team raised $8,300 and donated $4,150 to the National Kidney Foundation.
'I reached out to the National Kidney Foundation to see if there was a person or persons who could come receive our gift. That's how I got in touch with Gary and Loretta Hoffsetz. Loretta is a donor recipient and both she and Gary do a lot of work within the organization,' said Guhr. 'They were so gracious and came to our matches on Sept. 19 to receive the check.'
The team also had Mike Jantz, one of the most successful volleyball coaches in Kansas—now turned official—come out to officiate the matches.
'Mike also has kidney disease and he is awaiting a transplant. He is at the top of the list. Mr. Lightner (athletic director for GHS) worked to get him here that night, and it was really, really special. I think more than anything, our girls have been able to advocate for something bigger than themselves, and also play for something bigger than themselves this year,' said Guhr.
'I am very proud of the volleyball team and their coaches for their efforts to raise this significant amount of funds. The evening of volleyball was organized completely by the coaches and exceeded our expectations. Our league commissioner was able to bring Mike to work these matches for us, and we are thankful to him for that effort,' said Lightner.

title: Food banks offer practical tips for holiday donations
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Approximately 49 million people—one in six people in the U.S.—rely on food assistance according to Feeding America. 100% of U.S. Counties, including Marion County, have food insecurity. And this…
content:
Approximately 49 million people—one in six people in the U.S.—rely on food assistance according to Feeding America. 100% of U.S. Counties, including Marion County, have food insecurity. And this holiday season, more families face hunger than at any point in the past 10 years.
While food banks and pantries receive donations throughout the year, a majority of donations come in during the holiday season. And while all donations are welcome, some items are more helpful than others.
'Holidays are upon us, which means it's the 'giving' season. As you clean, declutter, and empty out your cabinets, there are a few helpful reminders when considering donating,' said Main Street Ministries Food Bank Manager Ciara Cox. 'Any opened items must be discarded as they will fail inspection. Expired goods may or may not pass inspection—various factors are considered. To be responsible stewards of our resources, it's better to provide non-expired items.'
According to Cox, dairy products and baby food must be within the expiration date. And all food items must have a nutritional label.
'Any unreadable expiration dates will result in the item being discarded,' said Cox.
Cox says to keep in mind that not everyone has the means to purchase 'extra' ingredients. So choose pouches and pull-tabs over canned goods that require a can opener for items such as tuna and soups. She also suggests food labeled 'just add water' with items such as muffin mix, mashed potatoes, pancake mix and Velveeta Shells instead of Kraft Mac & Cheese.
'Whatever makes it simple for our neighbors to use is best,' said Marion County Food Bank Treasurer Gene Winkler.
Refrigerated and fresh foods are accepted on a limited basis at both food banks. These include eggs, produce, milk, juices and beef.
'Hamburger along with hamburger helper is always appreciated,' said Winkler. 'Peanut butter and jelly. Ketchup is always good.
Other good ideas are apple sauce, mixed veggies, cream corn, pork and beans, any canned beans, chili, tuna, canned meat, baking supplies, condiments, spaghetti sauces, Chef Boyardee, ramen, cereal and pancake mix.
'We encourage boxed meals, pasta and pasta sauce, condiments, kid-friendly cereal, all vegetables, all fruits, all grains, peanut butter and jelly, soups, saltines, shelf-stable dairy products, canned meats and bagged beans. These items help us ensure a balanced plate year-round as we operate on a 'food group' method,' said Cox.
Items that are in season are also appreciated especially for Thanksgiving.
The Marion County Food Bank in Marion has turkeys coming this year from the Kansas Food Bank in Wichita, but they need boxes of dressing, corn, green beans and other traditional Thanksgiving food items.
For the Main Street Ministries Food Bank in Hillsboro, it is better to provide meat vouchers instead of actual turkeys for Thanksgiving. Financial donations can help with the meat vouchers, and items to go along with the turkey are helpful.
'Not everyone knows 'how' to cook a turkey nor do they always have the means to do so. Storing a turkey requires freezer space that may not be available,' said Cox.
Non-food items are also highly requested and appreciated, including toilet paper, shampoo and conditioner, laundry detergent, dish detergent, baby diapers and wipes and feminine hygiene products.
Whatever is donated is very much appreciated by both food banks.
'At Main Street Ministries, we strive and are committed to being good stewards of resources. Food insecurity and food waste is a real thing. Significant issues. If the goal is to combat hunger, then we must restore hope by providing quality foods that individuals like, need and want. These reminders and alternatives can help make meal preparation easier for everyone. Happy hearts. Full tummies,' said Cox.
This time of year is also good for financial donations.
'If the donations are six hundred dollars or less, donors can automatically deduct if they itemize their taxes. If the donation is more, say $1,000, we will send them a paper they can use for the donation,' said Winkler.
The Marion County Food Bank is open from 9 a.m.-12 p.m. on Mondays and 3-6 p.m. on Thursdays and is located at 906 E. Main St. in Marion. Donations can be taken to the food bank or placed in the bin at Carlson's Supermarket in Marion. In addition to food donations, they accept checks and cash. Checks should be made to the Marion Advancement Campaign which oversees the Marion County Food Bank. Anyone is welcome who needs food assistance.
The Main Street Ministries Food Bank is open from 9 a.m.-12 p.m. on Saturdays and is located at 415 S. Main in Hillsboro. In addition to food donations, they accept checks and cash. Donations are accepted at any time and can be left on the white table at the bottom of the ramp at the food bank or in the bin at Dales Supermarket in Hillsboro. If you have perishables, call ahead of time to meet at 620-947-3393 (Main Street Ministries) or 407-668-1383 (Cox). Anyone is welcome who needs food assistance.

title: Johnson named VP of Advancement of Tabor College
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: HILLSBORO, Kan. — Tabor College has named Frank Johnson, Ph.D., as its new vice president for advancement. Johnson was first named vice president of academic affairs and Title IX coordinator in 2010…
content:
Frank Johnson
HILLSBORO, Kan. — Tabor College has named Frank Johnson, Ph.D., as its new vice president for advancement.
Johnson was first named vice president of academic affairs and Title IX coordinator in 2010 and was then promoted to provost in fall 2023. He is currently in his 15th year as a member of the college leadership team. He will continue to provide leadership to Tabor's academic office through the 2025 spring semester. The position change will begin after hiring a new vice president of academic affairs.
'Thank you to President David Janzen for granting me the privilege of stewarding Tabor's advancement efforts,' Johnson said. 'The past 10-plus years have prepared me to step into a new venture, and I am humbled that God would entrust this integral position to me.'
Johnson will work closely with the president's office, including Ron Braun, vice president of philanthropy. Johnson, Tabor's longest-tenured vice president/dean of academics, has provided invaluable leadership to the college's academic programming. Tabor now boasts over 30 degrees on campus, including in-person undergraduate classes and two master programs that meet online and in-person. 'Dr. Johnson has been a tremendous support to me and played a vital role in bettering Tabor's future and fulfilling our mission as a college,' Janzen said. 'He demonstrates a passion for what God is doing at Tabor and will be a wonderful leader in growing Tabor's endowment, raising annual scholarship funds and leading capital campaigns. We're thrilled that our advancement efforts will be under his leadership.' Over the past two years, Tabor has raised nearly $4 million for its Annual Fund, setting its two highest marks in its 100-plus-year history. During the same time, Tabor received an additional $16 million in restricted giving toward key projects, positions, and scholarships, growing its endowment by 25%. Johnson said he looks forward to partnering in the college's fundraising, including raising its endowment. Johnson will oversee Tabor's alumni, public relations, marketing and communications staff. He will also work with district and national leadership of the U.S. Conference of Mennonite Brethren Churches. 'Having recently celebrated Homecoming and hired several recent graduates, I am reminded yet again of the depth of relationships through the greater Tabor community,' Johnson said. 'We look forward to enhancing and adding to how our current students and alumni can connect on and off-campus.' Before coming to Tabor, Johnson served as special assistant to the president for institutional planning, strategy, and research at Goshen College (IN). He taught history at MidAmerica Nazarene University (KS) and had brief stints in administration at Mount Vernon Nazarene University (OH) and Sterling College (KS). Johnson earned his B.A. in history education at Olivet Nazarene University in 1986. He completed his M.A. in U.S. history in 1991 and earned his Ph.D. at Michigan State University in 1996.
'Having served in Tabor leadership for over a decade, I wholeheartedly believe the Lord has been preparing me for this role,' Johnson said. 'My family and I are committed to the work being done at Tabor, and I am grateful that I can play a part in what's to come.'

title: Wendy's to close
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: While many in Marion County already complain about insufficient dining options, there will soon be even fewer options. Hillsboro Wendy's, owned and operated by Wenspok, will close next week. The…
content:
Wendy's will close permanently on Nov. 27.
While many in Marion County already complain about insufficient dining options, there will soon be even fewer options.
Hillsboro Wendy's, owned and operated by Wenspok, will close next week.
The Hillsboro Free Press received the following statement from mediarelations@wendys.com, 'Wendy's of Hillsboro will be closing on November 27. We are grateful to the community for their support over the years, and we hope they will continue to visit us at our nearby locations in Newton and McPherson. We greatly value the contributions of our Hillsboro team members, and we are currently assessing transfer opportunities.'
The news has come as a shock and disappointment to both city officials and the frequent customers who gather there.
'It's disappointing to hear that Wendy's will be leaving Hillsboro, especially with such short notice,' said Hillsboro City Administrator Matt Stiles.
'I am sad to hear about the closure. Wendy's has been a part of our community for many years, serving not only as a place to get something to eat but also as a local employer and a community gathering place,' said Hillsboro Mayor Lou Thurston.
'We hate to see it closed. We don't know where we are going to meet now. We've been meeting here for 16 years,' said Jim Boese, who regularly meets there with other retired farmers and men to visit over coffee in the mornings.
'Yeah, it's too bad. We need a family restaurant in this town real bad,' added Wendy's regular Dennis Penner.
'I hate that they are closing. I don't know where we'll go. It's terrible. I don't know what the real reason is that they wanna close, but I heard they're closing over 100 stores. I guess they aren't making enough money,' said Bob Delk, who also shows up almost every morning for Wendy's coffee. 'We're wondering about meeting at the senior center. Some guys there on Friday so maybe she would let us come in and drink some coffee there. We just don't know what to do. We talked about Starbucks (at Tabor), but they don't wanna go there. They said that's all too expensive.'
It is unclear what will happen to the Wendy's building which is locally owned.
'We are in contact with the building ownership and will be working to fill the space. We're not sure what that will be at this point, but there are several options we are looking at,' said Stiles.
'While this is a loss for our city, I remain optimistic about the resilience and entrepreneurial spirit of our community. Hillsboro is known for its strong local businesses, and we will continue working together to support opportunities for growth and development in our town,' said Thurston.

title: Hillsboro women team up to bring color to Parkside
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Up until a month ago, the biggest painting project that Kayla Gallaway had ever completed was an 18 x 24-inch canvas. But then Betty Seibel asked her to paint a 6 x 25-feet mural on her cinder block…
content:
The mural that Hillsboro's Kayla Gallaway completed for Parkside Homes resident Betty Seibel.
Up until a month ago, the biggest painting project that Kayla Gallaway had ever completed was an 18 x 24-inch canvas.
But then Betty Seibel asked her to paint a 6 x 25-feet mural on her cinder block wall outside her Parkside Homes apartment.
'Betty sent several pictures. I was like 'Yeah, I can do that.' So then I kind of found one I liked and pieced in other pieces to make it bigger and the right length I needed. And then I primed, sketched and painted,' said Gallaway.
Seibel said she was tired of looking out her window at all the dead vines on the wall so she knew she needed something else to look at.
'When I first thought to do this, I talked with my kids. I guess I'm a spoiled mama because my husband Bob always had our landscaping so perfect. And then I move here and there's a strip of grass that only gets watered when God waters it so it looks bad. And then there's all these dead vines on the wall. It's the only part about moving here that's depressing to me. And my son told me, 'Then you need to change it, whatever it takes'. And I said, 'Well, I'm thinking about having the wall painted even though it will cost me',' said Seibel.
Her kids told her to do it. So she got permission, had maintenance take all the vines off and had someone pressure wash the wall. Next she called up Gallaway after someone suggested her for painting the mural. And now she has a beautiful mural that she enjoys.
'I am more than pleased,' said Seibel.
The mural is a mountain scene full of trees and a river. There are also moose that were added toward the end.
'A picture came up on Facebook of the Grand Tetons, and there was this moose and calf in front. And so I texted her the picture, and I said, 'These mountains look a lot like what you're doing, but I don't see any moose'. She texts me back, 'You want moose? I'll give them to you.' So she added those. And that was just the cow and the calf. And then about 2 days later, here comes a Grand Tetons on Facebook with the bull moose. And so I text that to her and I say, 'I want a bull too'. And she said, 'Why not?',' said Seibel. Kayla Gallaway paints a 6 x 25-feet mural at Parkside for Betty Seibel who was tired of looking at dead vines from the window of her apartment at Parkside Homes.
Gallaway said since it was outside she had to use exterior wall paint which she had never used before but she found it to be very similar to interior paint.
She found the project interesting and rewarding in that she only used six colors for the entire detailed mural.
'Some you have to mix together to get the shades you want. So there's color theory and it's fun,' said Gallaway.
It only took Gallaway a few weeks to complete the large piece.
'I really wanted to be done earlier, but I missed a couple days because of weather. It has to be over 50 to paint. And it can't be raining. And the wind is a pain,' said Gallaway. 'But I'm gonna miss painting it. It was such a fun project.'
And Seibel couldn't be happier.
'I sit in my recliner and I look right out at that, and it just puts a smile on my face. I'm loving it,' said Seibel.

title: Hillsboro artisan sells creations
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Michelle O'Hare, who lives in Hillsboro, has always enjoyed creating both for herself and for others. 'I always like making things, and I like making my own gifts for people,' said O'Hare. The last…
content:
Michelle O'Hare started making wooden creations a few years ago. She began selling them this weekend at Hillsboro's Down Home Christmas. Michelle O'Hare makes cutting boards of all shapes and designs. She also makes other Christmas wood items, sketchbooks, notebooks and more. Michelle O'Hare has been using a diode laser to cut, engrave and etch sketchbooks, and then stains and paints the designs.
Michelle O'Hare makes Christmas trees and other wood creations that she sells and gifts to loved ones.
Michelle O'Hare, who lives in Hillsboro, has always enjoyed creating both for herself and for others.
'I always like making things, and I like making my own gifts for people,' said O'Hare.
The last few years she has been making wood creations using a diode laser.
'I talked to my husband about it several times, and he decided to buy it for me for Christmas like two years ago. It's just so cool looking and so precise,' said O'Hare.
She had been playing around with it and using it for her son Kyson's projects.
'We've designed some files and gone and looked for files. There's a lot of files online that you can get. I saw some notebooks when I was just looking for files one day and thought, 'Well, that would be fun'. So I bought the little binding machine and things I needed, and I started making some of those. I gave some away last year for Christmas for coworker gifts and things like that. It just kinda took off,' said O'Hare.
She started with notebooks and then started making sketchbooks about a year ago.
'I cut them out and then I engrave them or etch them and then some of them I stain and some of them I paint the engraving to put color to it,' said O'Hare.
She also made some ornaments and other Christmas items.
'I've been doing cutting boards. So probably everybody I know who had a wedding in the last two years has gotten a cutting board or something with their name or something on it. So I've been doing some gifts like that. I made a couple of things for some baby shower type stuff,' said O'Hare.
And in addition to giving her creations as gifts, she has begun to sell them. She had a vendor table this past weekend at Hillsboro's Down Home Christmas.
'This is the first day I've sold anything to the public. It was kind of overwhelming preparing for it. I signed up to do this maybe three weeks ago so I haven't slept a lot. It takes awhile for the engravings to get done and then I gotta paint them. And, of course, I work full time,' said O'Hare.
Her table did well and she had many customers purchase her items.
'You don't ever know if you're the only person who likes your own stuff. Everybody was very complimentary and that really boosted my confidence a little bit. I was really glad that I did it because everybody was very positive and complimentary, and that made me feel really well. Whether they bought anything or not, it was nice,' said O'Hare.
O'Hare does plans on participating in some craft shows in the spring and plans to do more sales between now and then.
'I took a couple of orders today for a couple of different signs. Some of the people saw some stuff I had on the cutting boards and wanted signs, and so I have orders for those. And then somebody else asked me about a cutting board,' said O'Hare. 'I also intend to do some more sales and possibly do some online or Facebook sales and stuff like that. If someone knows me personally, they can just ask. I'm not opposed to making things. I'm just not ready for too many orders quite yet.'
O'Hare does not have a business Facebook page set up yet but she plans to in the near future so be on the look out for it.

title: Writer's family enjoy Christmas tree shenanigans
author: Shana Thornhill
description: 'You know,' I mused, glancing at Darling Hubby, 'part of me thinks it might be a good idea to get a fake tree this year.' As I spoke, images of dry needles all over the floor, sawdust all over the…
content:
'You know,' I mused, glancing at Darling Hubby, 'part of me thinks it might be a good idea to get a fake tree this year.'
As I spoke, images of dry needles all over the floor, sawdust all over the patio, and the absolute itchiness of cleaning up after Christmas flashed before my eyes. Heck, if we'd get one of those fancy pre-lit trees, we wouldn't ever have to worry about wrapping strings of lights anymore either. Sheer bliss, certainly.
'You tell that part of you to shut up,' he replied bluntly. The children, when their opinions were solicited, agreed with their father. Apparently it just isn't Christmas without a fresh-cut tree. Not, mind you, a pine, or a spruce. Unfortunately not a beautifully scented, soft-needled balsam fir. No, our Christmas trees for the last ten years or so have been Eastern Red Cedars, AKA junipers, AKA the Scourge of the Prairie. We figured we were doing our part for conservation by cutting the darn things down and putting them to use. Plus, we have the added bonus that, once we get the tree inside to decorate it, it's so sparse that you can see all of the lights through the tree, so we get double the bang for our decorating buck, so to speak. They even smell kinda good, so there's that. And the best part? They're FREE.
At first, Darling Hubby took the kiddos out to select our tree every year. The last few, however, the kids have ventured out on their own, armed with a chainsaw, to select this year's Christmas weed. This year, seemingly seconds after they trooped out the door, I heard them carrying on on the front patio. Sure enough, they'd carried back a tree already and were discussing where to cut the trunk, and doing so in atrocious Scottish accents.
Chuckling a bit, I looked out to see the tree, which looked suspiciously full and luxuriant. Nah, can't be. Junipers just don't grow like that. Getting involved with the ongoing loud Scottish debate (or was that Irish? Welsh? COCKNEY?), I asked to see the tree standing up for reference. Darling Son reached deep into the greenery, seized the trunk, and, after a few attempts, hauled the thing upright.
Those of you who know my darling son know two things: he is not a small person, and he is serious about weightlifting. His struggle with the tree spoke volumes. When fully upright, that thing was taller than he was; indeed, it was taller than his sister would have been had she been standing on his shoulders. We're talking halfway up the second story of the house here. Impressive, to say the least.
After cutting three feet off the bottom and two feet off of the top, it was deemed the right height, at least by the people still conversing loudly in some sort of attempt at Gaelic. After some difficulty in locating the base, the tree was mounted, more or less straight, depending on who was yelling at the time. Darling Daughter began attacking the branches with a lopper, hacking at the five-foot-long lower branches in an attempt to force it into the same shape as a domesticated pine.
Then came the special moment where the tree was stuffed, bottom first, through the front door and muscled into the corner by the window. Much discussion ensued about which side was meant to face the wall, with a compromise eventually being reached amidst flurries of brogue. About a foot and a half of the top of the tree was removed where it bent at the ceiling, almost taking out a light fixture in the process. More Scottish hollering ensued as the peppery green smell began to permeate the room. The decorations were brought down from the attic, and with Darling Daughter belting out directions like William Wallace himself, the lights were soon applied in a mutually satisfactory manner.
I, of course, contributed by carefully approaching the Highland melee with jugs of hot water. The theory is that it keeps the tree green longer, but if the number of needles already on the floor was any indication, the thing was dead on arrival. After a few silver ornaments and Auntie Darlene's hand-crocheted snowflakes were applied, we all admired this year's version of a Christmas tree. Verra bonny indeed, bless the wee kiddies (who aren't so wee anymore).
And now as I sit, admiring ALL of the lights on the tree, basking in the joy of the memories this year brought, I feel so blessed. It hasn't all been rosy, but we have each other. I hope that all of your blessings outweigh your hardships and that your blessings only increase. Merry Christmas and Happy New Year to all of you!

title: Series on farm succession planning available in Marion
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Registration is now available for a four-part workshop series aimed at helping Midwest farm families develop succession plans for passing on or leaving the business. The series, Leaving a Lasting…
content:
Registration is now available for a four-part workshop series aimed at helping Midwest farm families develop succession plans for passing on or leaving the business.
The series, Leaving a Lasting Legacy for Midwestern Farm Women, will be available at the Marion Extension office at 1116 E. Main St. in Marion as well as other location and online. It is being produced through a partnership between extension professionals at Kansas State University, University of Nebraska-Lincoln and Purdue University.
Registration is available online for those wishing to attend in person and costs $60 through Jan. 12, which includes meals and educational materials. The fee increases to $75 after Jan. 12. Organizers say there is an online option available for $75, but 'highly encourage' participants to attend in-person due to the value of group discussions with other participants.
The workshops will be held on successive Tuesdays, beginning Jan. 21 and 28 and continuing on Feb. 4 and 11.
'The focus of the workshops is to help people figure out how to set up their succession plan and find the resources they need to implement it on their farm,' said LaVell Winsor, a K-State farm analyst.
This year's workshops continue a tradition of educational classes for women in agriculture from K-State's Department of Agricultural Economics, which hosted a series on farm finances in 2020, risk management on the farm in 2022 and land leasing in 2023.
'Succession planning has become a hot button topic, though it should have been that way forever,' said Ashlee Westerhold, director of K-State's Office of Farm and Ranch Transition. 'In agriculture, we're always in a state of transition. So there are a lot of questions, whether you're age 45 and thinking that (the family's) farm will some day be yours, or you're age 75 and wondering how you're going to pass that to the next generation.'
According to data from the U.S. Census, 70% of U.S. farmland will transfer to the next generation within 20 years.
'There are farms and businesses locally that didn't transition to the next generation due to a lack of planning. These folks had worked their whole life, hoping to build a legacy only to have it taken away from their heirs upon their passing. This can be avoided with proper planning,' said Ag & Natural Resources Agent Bret Toews who works in the Marion office.
The topics that will be covered in the four-part workshop series include: Motivation for succession planning.
Family communication around estate and transition planning.
Financial aspects of estate and transition plans.
Legal aspects of putting your plan into place.
'We'll also talk about how to pick a provider for all of those pieces,' Winsor said. 'The goal is to give people the tools they need to succeed. They can take them home, work on the plan with their families and start to put their succession plan together.'
'Estate Planning is not a one size fits all type of thing, especially in our family farm businesses as there are so many variables. It takes a team of professionals that can help you navigate them. We hope that this workshop series gets those conversations started and it can secure the future of our residents, farms and businesses,' said Toews.
The workshop is part of K-State's Women in Ag series, though all sessions are available to all people.
Officials urge those interested to register by Jan. 12

title: Mennonites have delicious history of New Year's Cookies
author: Wendy Nugent
description: Kris Schmucker recalled that when she was growing up, New Year's Day wasn't a big deal in the Mennonite community where she grew up. 'We'd go to church in the evening, and we'd have a slideshow…
content:
Harvey County Historical Museum & Archives Curator and Archivist Kris Schmucker looks over a book about Mennonite cooking. Photo by Wendy Nugent
Kris Schmucker recalled that when she was growing up, New Year's Day wasn't a big deal in the Mennonite community where she grew up. 'We'd go to church in the evening, and we'd have a slideshow reviewing the year, and we ate New Year's Cookies,' Schmucker said about people who attended Alexanderwohl Church in rural Goessel. 'They have stopped doing that in the last 10 years. Everything was very church-related.' Schmucker is the archivist and curator at the Harvey County Historical Museum & Archives in Newton. Mennonites who attended that church came to Goessel from Russia in 1874. Christmas was a little different with those Mennonites than it is today, Schmucker said. First, they had Christmas Eve. 'That was usually a children's program,' she said, adding then they had First Christmas, which was on Christmas Day, and then Second Christmas on Dec. 26. 'The idea was on Christmas Day, you'd go to one set of grandparents, and on Second Christmas, you would go to the other grandparents.' Schmucker's grandma called the days First Christmas and Second Christmas, she said. It wasn't Schmucker's experience, but it was her grandma's. 'We probably would've had another gathering on New Year's Day with my other grandma,' Schmucker said. They made New Year's Cookies, which are more of a fritter than a cookie, the day before New Year's Day. 'They were served for faspa on New Year's Eve, and then they would eat them throughout the day on New Year's Eve,' Schmucker said. Another treat that's associated with Mennonites is peppernuts. 'Peppernuts probably is a tradition that goes back to Holland in the West Prussian time period,' Schmucker said. That timeframe is in the 1500s to 1700s, she said, and peppernuts are unique to the Low German Mennonites—the people who came from Russia. It's a Christmas food, and they eat it all through the holidays, but it's not just eaten at Christmas. 'It's just a holiday treat,' Schmucker said. In the 1500s, spices were the most expensive things people had in their homes. 'A pound of ginger would buy a sheep,' Schmucker said. 'Just plain black pepper was the most coveted of spices. It was rare and expensive. These cookies are made in Scandinavian countries, too, and Dutch countries.' Sugar nuts might be the oldest version of peppernuts. They are the same size as peppernuts but have no peppernut flavoring or spices in them. They were made from baking ammonia and were white and sprinkled with sugar. Some recipes include cornstarch, which gives them a lighter feel. As Schmucker grew up, New Year's was a secular holiday. 'I've grown up in Alexanderwohl,' she said. New Year's Cookies in Low German are called Portzelkje. In the Mennonite community, Schmucker expects there was a lot of visiting since people had time off. 'Apple fritters would've been another thing they would've made,' she said. 'I never picked up [New Year's Day] was that important. It was a quiet day.' When Schmucker was growing up, she said most people going to Alexanderwohl, Tabor Mennonite Church or Goessel Mennonite Church were from the 1874 migration from south Russia, now Ukraine. It's still Christmas until Epiphany in the Mennonite Church, she said.
'Epiphany is still part of our Christmas season,' Schmucker said, adding it's on Jan. 6, when the three wise men visited baby Jesus. 'We don't really sing Christmas hymns until Christmas and after.'

title: Area sports roundup 1.15.25
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Goessel Boys basketball – The Bluebirds were finally able to start their semester basketball play on Friday, Jan. 10 at a home game against Solomon. Solomon beat Goessel with a final score of 51-13.…
content:
The Hillsboro/CantonGalva wrestlers were a bit shorthanded at their tournament in Herrington on Saturday, Jan. 11, but they didn't let that stop them from showing up and competing well. 'We saw some marked improvements in areas we had struggled with prior to break and a few kids really stepped up, showing that things are beginning to click,' said Coach Scott O'Hare.
Goessel
Boys basketball – The Bluebirds were finally able to start their semester basketball play on Friday, Jan. 10 at a home game against Solomon. Solomon beat Goessel with a final score of 51-13.
Coming—The Bluebirds will play at Canton Galva on Friday, Jan. 17.
Girls basketball – The bluebirds played at home against Solomon on Friday, Jan. 10. The girls won 52-34.
Coming—The Bluebirds will play at Canton Galva on Friday, Jan. 17.
Hillsboro
There were no basketball games due to the weather.
Wrestling – The Hillsboro/Canton Galva wrestlers competed in the Charles McMillim Invitational at Herrington on Saturday, Jan. 11. It was scheduled for the Girls Division to be on Friday with JV and Varsity Boys on Saturday, however, due to inclement weather on Friday, everything was wrestled on Saturday.
For the girls tournament, Hillsboro came in at 14th place out of 16 with 11 points scored by Khloe Willis-Dirks (4-7).
For the varsity boys, Hillsboro placed 9th out of 12 teams with 46.5 points.
Jaxon Chrislip (7-6) scored 14.5 team points.
Phoenix Fickes (9-7) placed 5th and scored 13.0 team points.
The highlights of the day included the 4th place finish by Willis-Dirks in the 120 lb weight class in the Girls Division, three freshmen (Seth Schafer, Copeland Krause, and Magnusson Cathey) all earning runner-up finishes in the JV division and sophomore Chrislip earning a third-place finish in a tough 144 lb varsity bracket. In doing so, Chrislip picked up two pins, a tech fall, and outscored his opponents 27-4 with all four points coming in a 4-1 loss to Griffiths from Herington, the #2 ranked wrestler in Class 3-2-1A. Freshman Fickes also wrestled a solid tournament, going 3-2 in the 150 lb varsity division.
'It was great to get the majority of the team back on the mat after Christmas Break to see what kind of progress we made with practices since late December. All four of our girls competed, but teamwise, we were a bit short-handed in the boys varsity tournament, as a couple of our upperclassmen were unable to compete and we made the decision to have a few of our freshmen and less experienced wrestlers compete in the JV division. Therefore, just due to the number of competitors alone, the team results were not impressive for us. With this young team, we tried to put our focus more on improvement and development. Overall, we saw some positive things to continue to build on. It may not show up entirely in the wins and losses, but they battled hard showing improvements in positions and techniques, competed with a good attitude, and showed a lot of effort. If we can continue to get that from them, we can continue to fix technical mistakes,' said Coach Scott O'Hare.
Coming—The Trojans compete next at Halstead on Saturday, Jan. 18.
'The boys and girls varsity teams will be back in action this week at the Halstead Invitational. The girls will compete starting at 2 p.m. on Friday and the boys will be at 9 a.m. on Saturday. We will use this week of practice to continue cleaning up some technical aspects as well as keep developing mental and physical toughness to help our wrestlers compete in tough matches,' said O'Hare.
