title: Kansas Functional Medicine offers personalized approach to health
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Heather and Paul Fay have owned and operated Fay Family Chiropractic and Nutrition in Marion for several years, and they have recently launched a new addition called Kansas Functional Medicine where…
content:
Heather and Paul Fay run Fay Family Chiropractic in Marion. They also recently started Kansas Functional Medicine which serves to help others feel their best through a holistic, personalized approach to health.
Heather and Paul Fay have owned and operated Fay Family Chiropractic and Nutrition in Marion for several years, and they have recently launched a new addition called Kansas Functional Medicine where Heather helps people overcome chronic health challenges and achieve lasting wellness.
'We've always done some type of nutrition with the clinic. We've just noticed more people come in with physical complaints to the chiropractor. A lot of them were also struggling with gut issues and everything's interconnected. So we decided to drop more heavily into the functional which is what I do while my husband does straight chiropractic,' said Heather. 'But they both work together.'
Heather said they use chiropractic care to ensure the body is aligned so the nervous system can communicate to itself.
'Our main focus is honestly on gut health. We see people that have weight that's just not budging. They've got low energy. Brain fog is a big thing. Mood swings, skin issues, regular digestive complaints. The gut is really just the center of all of it,' said Heather.
Heather explains that 90% of serotonin, the feel-good neurotransmitter, is produced by the gut. So if the gut isn't working correctly, there can be mental health issues as well as digestive issues.
'So we start with the gut and then it can have this ripple effect through the whole body, and suddenly they start feeling better all over the place. It just creates a positive change everywhere,' said Heather.
Heather says the typical patient she sees is exhausted and has almost given up hope.
'They feel stuck. They feel like maybe they're never gonna feel better. They're going to the doctor, they're having labs drawn, the doctor's saying everything's normal. And they're like, 'I'm not normal. This is not normal. Is this gonna be my normal?' They're frustrated and that's exactly where I step in,' said Heather. 'So I take the labs but don't look at them under normal values. I look at them under optimal values. We can take lab work that they might see as normal and identify underlying infections or different things because we're looking at them having optimal health and feeling good instead of just being alive and surviving. So the big thing is helping them to take back control of their health.'
Heather says she then works hand in hand with them looking at the whole body— nutrition, sleep habits, stress level, all the different things that could be happening that could be impacting health.
'It's very customized, it's very individualized for each person. And carry that through so that at the end they have this nice, big toolbox of things they can lean into to take their health and continue to take it to the next level,' said Heather.
Heather explains that to get started, a person can call or go online and initiate a discovery call with her.
'We would start with that call where we're just chatting to see if it's a fit. It does not cost anything. It doesn't commit them to anything. It's just a phone call with me. They can talk about where they're at. I can talk about what we have to offer and see if we're even a good fit for each other. And if we say we'd like to go ahead with that, then we go through a really comprehensive health history,' said Heather.
Heather said they will get a thorough understanding of the health history as well as labs and images to have a big picture of what's going on. They will then recommend more labs as needed and create a personalized plan.
In addition to personalized plans, Heather offers one-on-one support and educational resources.
'They get access to tools that just help keep them on track. The whole thing is very collaborative. We're very much working together. Not everybody needs handholding, but some people do. And so we just meet them where they're at and help empower them so that we can move through the steps together,' said Heather.
Heather makes sure she carves out time for her patients.
'We want to make sure that they're feeling heard. It's really important to us to connect. And once somebody is our patient in either capacity, if it's in functional medicine or if it's chiropractic, it's really like your family now and we're gonna treat you that way. We really want to offer people the best,' said Heather.
Heather enjoys seeing when changes start to happen.
'One of the most beautiful things is to see somebody, and you can see it in their face when they come in, and they're excited and you see that their work is sparking hope in their life. They're taking back their control. The joy is coming back in them. It is just really great,' said Heather.
According to Heather, they are outside of the insurance model so they do not work with insurance.
'The best way for people to connect with us is a self-referral. They can go to our website or they can give us a call,' said Heather.
While Heather can meet in person with her patients for functional medicine, she does many of her appointments by Zoom. And she is frequently available by text between sessions for her patients.
She typically treats chiropractic patients on Mondays and Wednesdays and does functional medicine the other days while Paul does chiropractic care five days a week.
For more information, go to www.kansasfunctionalmedicine.com or call the clinic at 620-381-2142. Fay Family Chiropractic and Kansas Functional Medicine is located at 410 E. Main St. in Marion. The hours are 9 a.m.-1 p.m. and 3-6 p.m. on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday, and 7 a.m.-12 p.m. on Tuesday and Friday.

title: Goessel mayor welcomes new public works director
author: Cynthia Goerzen
description: The Goessel city council met on Jan. 13, a week earlier than the regularly scheduled meeting date, due to a national holiday, Martin Luther King Jr. Day. The new public works director, Alex Goossen,…
content:
The Goessel city council met on Jan. 13, a week earlier than the regularly scheduled meeting date, due to a national holiday, Martin Luther King Jr. Day. The new public works director, Alex Goossen, attended the meeting. He began his work for the city on Dec. 9. According to a statement from mayor Evan Esau, Goossen is a 'Goessel High School graduate. Alex brings a wealth of experience to his new role, most recently serving as Park Manager at Meade State Park' and wanted to move back to this area. 'His dedication and expertise are already making a positive impact, and the city looks forward to the contributions he will bring in enhancing the town's infrastructure and services.' Esau stated, 'The City of Goessel warmly welcomes Alex back to the community and looks forward to working with him to continue improving our great town.'
The council thanked Goossen for his work with snow removal and commended him for getting his water operator license. He will enroll in the KRWA (Kansas Rural Water Association) 18-month training program for wastewater to obtain that license.
Turning their attention to another matter, the council again discussed cats. Rabies vaccination is required for cats, according to Ordinance 2-208. The council considered options for dealing with stray cats in town. They ask that residents not feed cats that do not belong to them; the suggestion was made that the cats can eat rats. Council members mentioned that Buller Street is one specific area in town that seems to have an issue with stray cats, although other areas do too. James Kraus, volunteer animal control officer, is willing to come and take care of the problem. The number to call is 620-392-3250; residents are encouraged to call that number for help with strays.
In other business, the council:
* established June 21 as the city-wide garage sale date and June 28 as the city-wide clean-up date.
* thanked Funk Electric for taking down the Christmas lights.
* wished to thank those who helped with snow removal.
* heard the police report. One burglary case was sent to the county attorney for prosecution. One case of suspicious activity was reported. A new body camera was purchased for the police department. The council estimated a cost of $525 at last month's meeting.
* talked with Tim Wiebe about the lots he purchased at Buller and Kansas, in the northwest part of town, west of the baseball diamonds. His son Colton is planning to build a house on one of the lots. Plans are to eventually build rental houses on the other lots. Council member Amanda Voth told him that Goessel needs houses big enough for families and no trailers or mobile homes.
* discussed campers/RVs, noting that they should not be parked on a street. The council discussed various options for requirements.
* discussed private streets in town. The council plans to send a letter to owners of those streets describing their options, whether to continue maintaining their own street, or grant an easement to the city so the city would maintain the street. The owner would pay surveying costs.
* discussed the municipal judge position. Greg Nickel is currently the municipal judge, at a cost of $600 a year.
* discussed pay for council members. They receive $75 for each regular monthly council meeting and $50 for additional special meetings or workshops. The mayor receives $120 for any meeting.
* approved the month's expenses of $28,947.62.
* changed the date of the February meeting to Tuesday, Feb.18, due to a legal holiday on the regular meeting day.
* held a special meeting on Jan. 2 to talk about the USDA Rural Development sump pump program regarding the matter of illegally dumping sump pumps, drains, and gutter systems into the public sewer system. A survey will be sent to residents.
* mentioned that the council will have a work session to discuss housing needs in Goessel.
* briefly discussed fire hydrants.
* noted that someone saw a fox in town.
* talked about nuisance properties.

title: Hillsboro Rec launches corporate challenge
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro Recreation Department is offering an exciting new opportunity for local...
content:
The Hillsboro Recreation Department is offering an exciting new opportunity for local businesses in Hillsboro called the Hillsboro Corporate Challenge Cup. It is a friendly competition between
local businesses through competitions from February through August.
'It's just an idea that I've had trying to get businesses to interact with each other and have a friendly competition. I know Hutchinson did this years ago and their format was a little different than what we're looking at,' said Director David Ediger. 'It's just a way to get businesses to compete against each other, have a good time and have something for our adults in our community. That's kind of the thought behind it.'
While Ediger wants to keep a lot of the challenges a surprise, he promises a wide variety of activities.
'We've got sports in there. We've got trivia. We'll have a skills competition,' said Ediger. 'We're looking at probably starting with bowling or a pool tournament or maybe both on the same day. We're still trying to figure that all out. It depends on how many teams we get, but we want to start indoors while it's cold and then do some outdoor stuff once it warms up.'
As far as the number of teams, Ediger would like every business to have one.
'We probably won't get that many. I'd like to at least have 10 or 12 teams. But we'll go with as many as we get. We've tried to allow for small businesses. We've tried to think of everything like small businesses that only have five or fewer people can go with another business. Even retired people can join. Ministerial Alliance and school people. We have tried to think of everyone. We are trying to get everyone involved,' said Ediger.
Ediger and his team know that this first year will be a lot of trial and error. They plan to learn a lot this year and make the following years even better.
'We'd like to do it every year,' he said.
Part of the fun of having it year after year will be to have a traveling trophy.
'We want to have a traveling trophy that we will give out that last day in August. We're having a big day out at the sports complex. We'll do some skill challenges, maybe an obstacle course, some different things, corn hole, things like that. And then have a cookout and crown the champion that night,' said Ediger. 'We want that last day to be a summer games day and have a day where we do a lot of different contests and hopefully have everybody together at one time. And end the season with that and take a break for a few months and then start up again.'
Teams have until Saturday to get enrolled.
'It's only a hundred dollars per business/team to get in it. So if two businesses go together, they can split that however they want and we can send an invoice for payment. The fee will cover the competitions, awards, cookout and everything,' said Ediger. 'If they're hesitant about the competition, just remember it's for fun. You have some bragging rights, but it's mainly for fun. It's just to get people out to do something. We have so many activities for our kids, but we don't have a lot for adults. We thought this might be a fun engaging way to get them going.'
Ediger encourages people to call if there are any questions or ideas about teams. He and his staff are also more than willing to help people sign up if needed.
For more information, go to https://hillsboroks.recdesk.com/Community/Program/Detail?programId=1516 or contact Ediger at dediger@cityofhillsboro.net or at 620-947-3490. To register, go to hillsboroks.recdesk.com. The deadline to register is Saturday, Feb. 1.

title: Tabor College achieves second-best undergraduate retention, record graduate enrollment in spring 2025 semester
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: HILLSBORO, Kan.— Tabor College's 2025 spring retention is its second-best on record, reaching 93 percent and having all four classes retain 90 percent or more of their students. The achievement also…
content:
HILLSBORO, Kan.— Tabor College's 2025 spring retention is its second-best on record, reaching 93 percent and having all four classes retain 90 percent or more of their students. The achievement also brings the college's 10-year average to 89 percent.
'These outstanding retention and graduate numbers confirm that students are thriving at Tabor College,' President David Janzen, Ph.D., said. 'I am so proud of our faculty, coaches and staff who serve students very well and the students who engage with our campus culture and decidedly Christian mission.'
The total SP25 enrollment for Tabor is 635. That includes 465 undergraduate students on campus, 61 in dual-credit classes and 109 in the college's graduate programs. With the addition of the healthcare leadership concentration to its M.B.A., the college's diverse graduate portfolio continues to blossom with a second-straight spring of record enrollment.
'I'm very grateful for our faculty and staff's dedication to the lives of our students,' Provost Frank Johnson, Ph.D., said. 'Retention of this magnitude is a massive achievement, and I'm humbled to serve alongside them as we fulfill our calling in leading our students.'

title: Area Sports Roundup 2.26.25
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Goessel Boys basketball – The Bluebird boys played against Rural Vista on Thursday, Feb. 20. Rural Vista won 61-28. Next the boys played at home against Hartford on Friday, Feb. 21. The boys closed…
content:
Goessel
Boys basketball – The Bluebird boys played against Rural Vista on Thursday, Feb. 20. Rural Vista won 61-28.
Next the boys played at home against Hartford on Friday, Feb. 21. The boys closed out senior night with a 51-47 victory over Hartford in a close back-and-forth game.
Coming—The Bluebirds have postseason play this week. State will be March 12-15.
Girls basketball- The Bluebird girls beat Rural Vista 40-30 at home on Thursday, Feb. 20.
The girls next played at home against Hartford on Friday, Feb. 21. They fell behind big early but made a great comeback to win 41-35.
Coming—The Bluebirds have postseason play this week. State will be March 12-15.
Hillsboro
Boys basketball – The Trojan boys played against Hoisington on Monday, Feb. 17 and won 57-40.
'We had a solid offensive night against Hoisington. We were very efficient in all phases. The team continues to play very tough defensively. We led in scoring by Lincoln Wichert with 26 and Easton Shahan with 11. Lincoln led in rebounds with seven and Easton in assists with eight. The team is buying into tough, hard-nosed defense night in and night out. When we can hold a team under 30% from the field, we have a great chance to win,' said Coach Kyle Kroeker.
The Trojans played away at Nickerson on Friday, Feb. 21 and won with a final score of 47-33.
On Friday against Nickerson, we struggled a little offensively, but our defense only allowed 33 points overall. Noah Beavers was a rebound shy of a double-double with 13 points and nine rebounds. Nash Dickinson followed with 12 points going 3/5 from the three-point line. Easton Shahan had nine assists on the night. For the second straight game, we held them to under 30% shooting,' said Kroeker.
Coming—'As we enter into postseason play this week, our defense will be a huge strength of this team. We play great team defense and they are doing the things that don't always make the box score. I am excited to see what we can do going forward. We start with Marion on Thursday and we look forward to the Marion County rivalry. Many of the boys grew up playing one another and know each other well. It should be a fun competition,' said Kroeker.
Girls basketball – The Trojan girls played against Hoisington on Monday, Feb. 17, and won 43-28.
The Trojans played away at Nickerson on Friday, Feb. 21, and won with a final score of 69-12.
'The Lady Trojans had another good week with wins over Hoisington and Nickerson. Our defense showed up both nights which set the tempo. On offense, we were able to capitalize off of steals creating fast break points. We also shared the basketball really well and were able to hit shots,' said Coach Micah Ratzlaff.
Coming—'We are looking forward to the first round of regionals on Friday against Sacred Heart. This is a tough matchup for us against a good team. We look forward to the challenge and competing at a high level,' said Ratzlaff.
Wrestling – The Hillsboro/Canton-Galva Trojan wrestlers competed at the KSHSAA 3-2-1A Regional Tournament at Fredonia on Saturday, Feb. 22.
For Hillsboro, Jackson Kleiber (6-26) scored 2 team points when he won over Jaxon Swafford of Rosallia-Flinthills HS in consolidation round 2.
For Canton-Galva, William Andreas (11-24) placed 4th and scored 8 team points when he won by fall over Joshua Cumpton of Cherryvale HS in consolidation round 1 and then won in sudden victory in consolidation semifinals over Owen Coover of Erie HS.
Jaxon Chrislip (20-12), also of Canton-Galva, placed 4th and scored 11 team points when he received a bye in championship round 1, won by major decision over Broc Ivy of Humbolt HS in the quarterfinal and won by major decision over Haiden Edens of Caney Valley HS in the consolidation semifinals.
'The Regional Tournament really became a mirror image of this season, particularly the second half of the season. Although our expectations remained the same, the reality was that this team was very young and inexperienced as a whole, with the exception of our only senior, Logan Rogers, along with Jaxon Chrislip, who is only a sophomore but has several years of wrestling experience at the youth and middle school levels. The rest of the regional roster included one junior second-year wrestler, two additional sophomores and three freshmen. Most of this group just started wrestling within the last one to three years. It is a lot to ask of them to be prepared to compete for placing at a large high school regional tournament, but they have worked hard, battled, and improved to at least allow themselves to be competitive at this level,' said Coach Scott O'Hare.
Andreas and Chrislip will be heading to state next.
'Obviously we are very proud of William and Jaxon for placing in the top four and earning the right to represent Canton-Galva at the 3-2-1A State Wrestling Tournament next weekend in Hays. In only his second year wrestling, Andreas will be making his first trip to state. Chrislip will be returning for his second trip to the state tournament after qualifying last season as a freshman,' said O'Hare. 'The regional tournament is always very emotional, with a roller coaster of highs and lows. With each win, wrestlers advance one step closer to qualifying for state. However, as the tournament progresses, with each loss, the season comes to an end for some. We had a handful of wrestlers get to within one or two matches, but the most heartbreaking elimination is for any of the seniors. Our lone senior, Logan Rogers, has been in our program for several years and came up short this weekend of making it to state. His work ethic, grit and fun personality will be missed in the program next year. We wish him the best.'
Coming—As we prepare for the state tournament this week, we also have a lot to look forward to for Hillsboro/Canton-Galva wrestling in the future. We had a lot of young guys gain some great experience this season and are excited to see how they continue to progress and develop,' said O'Hare.

title: Good oral health should start early
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: February is National Children's Dental Health Month. According to the American Dental Health Association, good oral health is important because children and adolescents with poor oral health are more…
content:
February is National Children's Dental Health Month.
According to the American Dental Health Association, good oral health is important because children and adolescents with poor oral health are more likely to have oral pain, miss school and perform poorly in school than their peers with better oral health.
Oral health impacts a person's overall health and well-being throughout life, so early prevention and intervention in childhood and adolescence are important.
This means that dental visits for children and adolescents are important. During visits, children, adolescents and parents can learn about oral hygiene, fluoride, injury prevention and nutrition.
But when should children start these visits?
'The American Dental Association recommends children visit the dentist when they get their first tooth, or when they turn one year old, whichever comes first. We don't always have a lot to do in this first visit, but it allows for establishing care at a dental practice and providing education for the parents on how to best help take care of the child's oral health,' said Dr. Adam Richards, DMD, of Marion Family Smiles.
Dr. Richards says that good oral habits begin at home.
'Children can brush and floss on their own to start building the necessary dexterity, but we recommend having a parent or guardian brush and floss for them until about the age of eight,' said Dr. Richards.
Establishing a habit of brushing twice a day and flossing once contact is made between two or more teeth must start early and be consistent.
'It can be difficult for a parent or guardian to make this happen and it may seem like a battle some days, but the important thing to remember is that it is a battle worth fighting,' said Dr. Richards.
Many parents wonder about whether or not to use fluoride toothpaste.
'I do recommend the use of fluoride toothpaste. Fluoride has been proven to strengthen enamel and repair minor defects in it. However, it is important to note that we don't need more than a rice grain-sized amount on the toothbrush for children under the age of three and a pea-sized amount for children over three. When children learn how to swish and spit, they may also add fluoride mouthwash to further aid in cavity prevention, but not until they are at low risk of swallowing it,' said Dr. Richards.
While many fear dentists, it's important to remember that dentists are there to help. Starting that relationship early is key to strong oral health.
'The most important thing to remember is that dentists are here to help improve the oral health of all of our patients. Please come and see us. We are not going to judge you on how your mouth is, but we would love to help you improve your overall health,' said Dr. Richards.

title: Tabor offers dining options for the community
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Even though Marion County recently lost a favorite local eatery spot when Wendy's closed in November, the county has many dining options. And there are two great options in Hillsboro that many do not…
content:
A Tabor student takes the orders of community members at Tabor's Courtside Grill. The Courtside Grill and the cafeteria are two great dining options at Tabor College for both students and the public to enjoy.
Even though Marion County recently lost a favorite local eatery spot when Wendy's closed in November, the county has many dining options. And there are two great options in Hillsboro that many do not even think about when choosing a spot to grab a bite.
'For the most part two, we have two places for the community to eat— our Courtside Grill and the cafeteria,' said Tabor College Director of Food Service Dino Diaz.
The Courtside Grill, located next to the Jay Shop and across from the gym in the Student Center, is open from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. Monday through Friday and then during games.
'That serves your standard grill fair—grilled burgers, french fries, chicken sandwiches, spicy chicken. On Wednesdays, we do boneless wings. We sell them by eight or six and those are all combos. We do Philly steak sandwiches, chicken Philly's, quesadillas, etc. On Fridays, we do certain wraps. I think it's Buffalo chicken right now,' said Diaz. 'I will say that, in general, this time of year with the basketball games, it is a massive crowd out there, so get here early if that's what you want.'
Not only is the food appetizing, but it is very affordable. Most combos, including a soda, are available for well under $10. It is the only place in Hillsboro to grab a burger and fries in a short amount of time.
The Tabor College cafeteria is probably better known to the public than the Courtside Grill is.
'We average about 20 to 30 community members on Sunday. The rest of the week it's a trickle-in kind of a scenario,' said Diaz.
The cafeteria menus are all posted online on the Tabor website at Tabor.edu.
It is open Monday through Friday from 7 a.m.-7 p.m. for continuous service, but there is not hot food out the entire time.
'The kids can come in and get a bowl of cereal or they could come and get a snack or soda. But the meal times are when the public will most likely want to be here. We do breakfast from 7-9 a.m., lunch from 11 a.m.-1:30 p.m., and dinner from 5-7 p.m.,' said Diaz.
Diaz said that the food is a buffet so they do not allow people to take food out.
For lunch from Monday through Thursday, they also offer fresh, toasted subs, made to order.
'In general, our big rush comes at 10 minutes to 12. And that is a pack-the-house moment most days of the week. So it's advisable to come right around 11 or after 12:30,' said Diaz.
They are open on the weekends, but not for breakfast. It's just lunch and dinner. Saturday lunch is 12 to 12:45 p.m. and dinner is 5 to 5:45 p.m. Sunday dinner is 5-5:45 p.m.
'We generally charge $7.50 for breakfast, $8.50 for lunch, $9 for dinner. And then we do Sunday lunch, and at certain times throughout the year, we do specials. And that is $13.50. Sunday lunch is 11:30 a.m.-1 p.m.,' said Diaz.
'For Sunday lunch, there's gonna be fresh bread. We do fresh fried chicken, mashed potatoes and gravy. It's just a comfort food meal. There's a rotisserie chicken and a freshly roasted whole meat of some kind—good ham or something like that. So it's a good deal,' said Diaz.
Diaz said they offer a senior discount for 65 and over at Sunday lunch.
'And a church bulletin discount if someone brings in their church bulletin. Both of those work out to be $10.75. So that's a steal,' said Diaz.
Both dining options are only open to the public whenever the college is in session.
'So, for example, if the students go on spring break, we are not open to the public,' said Diaz.
Diaz recommends checking the website to see if Tabor is in session or calling the Tabor switchboard at 620-947-3121 and asking if school is in session if you aren't sure.
'Our primary focus is serving students, but we will always try to accommodate anybody that comes in the door. We have stuff available for community members, and I think they will be happy with what they find here if they haven't been here before. People that come on Sundays is a pretty wide group of people,' said Diaz.

title: St. Luke's adopts new mission statement
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: St. Luke Hospital and Living Center in Marion recently changed their mission...
content:
St. Luke Hospital and Living Center in Marion recently changed their mission statement after months of working through what they wanted the statement to say.
The new statement is 'Our mission is to serve our communities by providing excellent healthcare with compassion'.
CEO Alex Haines said the decision to change the statement came from the board's strategic retreat this past summer.
'The question was is our mission statement still valid? Are we happy with it? Does this still meet what we're trying to do? We didn't want to completely scrap everything, but refresh and re-look at it,' said Haines. 'The board put together a committee with representation from different departments such as nursing, radiology, the living center, the business office and asked 'What do we want the mission of our organization to look like'?'
The previous mission statement was 'Our family will take care of your family for a lifetime as we compassionately serve you beyond your expectations'.
'We wanted something a little more short and concise,' said Haines.
Haines told the committee that a mission statement is important both for the community and for the organization.
'I think for us it's a guiding internal statement. From a board and an administrative standpoint, when we are faced with difficult decisions or things that aren't as clear, when we're not exactly sure what the right thing to do is, we reflect back on our mission statement to help guide us to make that decision. We wanted it to be something to revert back to and say, 'Is our decision meeting our mission?' The industry and entity can get stuck in the weeds. We need to remove ourselves sometimes and make sure that we are doing what we're saying that we're here to do,' said Haines.
It was important to the committee to not use the word Marion since St. Luke is a district hospital.
'Our job is to serve the district which has a lot more communities than just Marion—we have Burns and Lincolnville and lots of different towns that are not Marion. We want everyone outside to feel like this is their hospital, too, not just Marion. We really intentionally came up with the word communities, plural,' said Haines.
The committee also spent time evaluating what the organization's role is in the community.
'I keep hearing people say the hospital is so important to the town from an employer standpoint and people feeling safe to live this far away from a big town because they have a hospital. And if they didn't have one, people would choose not to live here because they didn't feel safe,' said Haines. 'There's lots of industries in these towns that have a role to play. We can't survive without the grocery store. When our heat or air conditioning goes out, we want someone to come fix it. When the power is out in the middle of the storm, we want someone to come fix it in the middle of the storm. And we need all of those people doing their roles in order for the community to work, because if one of them doesn't, it makes it more challenging. The hospital's job is to be here 24/7 in the event someone needs something. That doesn't stop at night or on the weekends. It doesn't stop when there's bad weather. People actually need us to be here to do what we do so that the community can function so everyone else can do their role. We all need each other. And I think it's important for us to remember what our role is. Anyone who enters our door, we're here to serve them.'
Haines said the word compassion came up often as well so the committee made sure to include it in the statement.
'I think it's something that sets us apart from the larger organizations because we know our patients. We know that they have some needs that are outside of directly what we're caring for them. I've heard story after story after story of the things that our staff have done for our patients that have nothing to do with their healthcare. We've had people traveling through town that we've helped out with rides. We've helped them get their animals to the vet. We've helped them coordinate lots of different things. And that's the compassion part of saying, 'Hey, you come here and you're gonna get excellent healthcare, but we're also going to go a little bit above because that's what we do.' And it was very important to me that we have excellent healthcare there, because that's what we do. If we're not providing excellent healthcare, people will go somewhere else,' said Haines.
Haines is pleased with the new mission statement and the organization has now fully adopted it and is implementing it into all areas.
'We will fall short of this from time to time. There'll be instances where we don't provide excellent healthcare, and we miss the mark on our compassion. But the point is to remind us, that's what we're striving for. Our goal is to do that, and it's work to do that. It's not easy. That's why it's there. I tell the staff that even though we fall short sometimes, we got to remind ourselves that we got to keep working to strive to do this every day,' said Haines.

title: ‘Orange' you glad these weird cookies made an appearance?
author: Lindsey Young
description: Joey puts up with a lot of weird stuff when it comes to this column. The poor guy watches me put random ingredients in our shopping cart all the time and never knows what I'm going to come up with…
content:
Cheetos cookies are a novelty that brings lots of conversation to a get-together. With cheesy dust both in the dough and on the outside, these are an interesting take on a sugar cookie with a savory twist.
Joey puts up with a lot of weird stuff when it comes to this column.
The poor guy watches me put random ingredients in our shopping cart all the time and never knows what I'm going to come up with next.
With that said, he's a terrific sport. He tries all my experiments and gives his honest opinion—sometimes helping me raid the spice cabinet to try to improve upon a first attempt.
That was not the case with this week's recipe.
In this case, he refused—point blank—to try it.
In Joey's defense, I probably went off the deep end a bit with this one: Cheetos cookies.
This comes from the blog 'The Spiffy Cookie.' You can find the original post at https://www.thespiffycookie.com/2018/03/05/cheetos-cookies/. I didn't change the recipe because, honestly, I had no idea how this was going to turn out.
Cheetos Cookies
Ingredients
4 cups Cheetos puffs, divided (I used a 7-ounce bag)
1/4 cup butter, softened
1/4 cup shortening
1/2 cup sugar
1 egg
a few dashes of orange food coloring
1 1/4 cup flour
1 tablespoon cream of tartar
1/2 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
Directions
Crush all of the Cheetos until they are fine by either smashing them in a Ziploc bag or by running them through a food processor.
In a mixing bowl, beat the butter, shortening and sugar for a couple of minutes until it is a light yellow.
Beat in the egg and food coloring. (You don't have to use the food coloring, but it does make for a striking vision to have these a super bright orange.)
Beat in half of the crushed Cheetos, the flour, cream of tartar, baking soda and salt. Once everything is well combined, scoop the dough out in about one-inch balls.
Put the rest of the Cheetos dust into a bowl and roll the balls in the crumbs to coat them. Put the balls on a plate, cover them and refrigerate for at least one hour.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Prepare your baking sheets by lining them with parchment paper, and place the chilled dough about two inches apart on the sheets.
Bake for eight to 10 minutes or until the cookies are set up and just starting to brown on the sides.
Let them cool, and then transfer them into an airtight container.
These smelled really nice while they baked. It reminded me of warm, cheesy popcorn. For the flavor, they weren't as cheesy as I thought. They were more of a corn-chip forward sugar cookie.
I actually made these a few weeks ago, and several readers helped sample them in Joey's stead. The reaction was mixed, but most thought they were an OK little cookie. Really, these are more about what they are than how they taste. They are definitely a conversation starter.
That being said, this is probably a one-and-done recipe for me, and not just because I would have to eat another batch totally by myself. Joey can only take so much.
Spice Up Your Life is a weekly recipe column by Lindsey Young, who describes herself as an enthusiastic amateur cook and can be reached through her website at spiceupkitchen.net.

title: Marion man makes lures for fun and ministry
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: by Alece Lehrman and Laura Fowler Paulus After Marion couple Scott and Yvonne Powell retired several years ago, they decided to pick up some hobbies. He began making handmade fishing lures and she…
content: Scott Powell with a fish he caught using a lure he made. He makes lures and gives them away to anyone who wants them. He includes a tract with the lure called 'Get Hook'd On Jesus' that shares the gospel. The lures are made out of corks that would otherwise just go to landfills. Yvonne Powell holds up the lure she used and the fish she caught on it. Her husband made and signed the lure. He makes them and gives them away. Scott Powell of Marion makes lures and gives them away to anyone who wants them. He includes a tract with the lure called 'Get Hook'd On Jesus' that shares the gospel. The lures are made out of corks that would otherwise go into landfills. Scott Powell, of Marion, make lures and gives them away to anyone who wants them. He bevels them, paints them and assembles them about 20 at a time. He signs them on one side and puts Matthew 4:19 on the other. by Alece Lehrman and Laura Fowler Paulus After Marion couple Scott and Yvonne Powell retired several years ago, they decided to pick up some hobbies. He began making handmade fishing lures and she found different projects to keep her busy from crafting to selling antique jewelry on eBay. The couple was fishing in Texas when he found a small piece of wood and started whittling it. Then he got the idea to whittle the piece of wood into a lure. 'Yeah, good luck with that,' Yvonne said. Since then he has switched to using corks. He found that they worked better and they moved through the water more smoothly. 'I just got tired of paying six to eight bucks every time I lost a lure so I whittled a bunch of them. The first step is I bevel them, so it takes a diving motion,' said Scott. Beveling is when a square object is changed into a sloped shape. After this step, Powell adds white gills and paints the front and back of the cork red. 'At first I would paint them green like frogs, but I did some research and found that bass are more attracted to the color red. From what I've read, the bass will hit 3:1 red and white to any other color,' said Scott. 'So I decided to go with red and white and it has been extremely successful. I've caught over 400 largemouth bass using these things.' He also takes the time to sign them with his name on one side. On the other side, Powell started adding the Bible verse Matthew 4:19 which says, 'And he saith unto them, follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.' The next step is to paint the corks in polyurethane. Then he drills a hole, places a paperclip through them and attaches a hook. 'Then I put a split ring on the front and turn it and put it on there. And then I'll put a little red feather. Just drill a hole, put a feather in there, put some crazy glue and it'll stay there forever,' said Scott. He makes them 20 at a time because the hooks come in a pack of 20. Scott makes an assembly line to mass produce them and make it easier on him. 'It doesn't make any sense to paint one of 'em so I paint 20 of 'em,' he said. Originally Scott just made these for himself until a man at his church asked him to make some for his son-in-law as a Christmas present. The man asked him to sign it and that is when Scott got the idea to sign each lure. 'That's when I started signing them all and putting the scripture on them,' said Scott. Now Scott hands the lures out to people. He also developed a gospel tract to go with the lures named 'Get Hook'd on Jesus'. Whenever he is asked about his fishing, he will hand out a lure and ask if they would like to join his wife and him at church. Scott said, 'It's fun. I enjoy doing it.' These lures are also given to friends and make great presents for fishermen. Yvonne said, 'Fishermen need God, too!' The couple enjoys going to church services, renovating the house next to theirs that they recently bought, and fishing. They met 13 years ago on a dating app when they found out that they both loved to fish. Once the house that they are renovating is finished, it will be used to house missionaries and family when they are visiting. Scott likes to fish at Marion County Park and Lake. While fishing, Yvonne and Scott do CPR—Catch, Picture, Release. He also likes to show family and friends how to make handmade lures. The corks used for the lures are donated as the couple do not drink. To donate corks or to get a lure, email Scott at lscottpowekk@gmail.com or message him on Facebook at https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?id=100011693052812.

title: Central Kansas Counseling Center opens Hillsboro office
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Hillsboro recently had a ribbon-cutting for a new, much-needed business in town—Central Kansas Counseling (CKC), a counseling center whose mission is 'partnering with people as they pursue living…
content: Hillsboro Chamber of Commerce Director Lisa Donahue, CKC therapist Heidi Goerzen, CKC therapist Jim Paulus, CKC Intern Bailey Penner, CKC therapist Erica Haude, CKC therapist Leah Fish, CKC founder and therapist Blake Buhrman, CKC founder and therapist Carlin Buhrman, Hillsboro Chamber of Commerce board member Mark Rooker and Hillsboro Chamber of Commerce board member Amy Bauer. Central Kansas Counseling Center (CKC) and the Hillsboro Chamber of Commerce held a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the center located at 315 N. Lincoln on Wednesday, March 20. The center has openings, and the staff are available to help clients pursue more healthy, courageous and authentic lives. Central Kansas Counseling Founders Blake and Carlin Buhrman, Licensed Clinical Professional Counselor Erica Haude, Licensed Professional Counselor Leah Fish and Intern Bailey Penner. Not pictured is Temporarily Licensed Marriage and Family Therapist Jim Paulus. The staff at the Hillsboro branch of Central Kansas Counseling are available to see those needing counseling services in Marion County and surrounding areas. Hillsboro recently had a ribbon-cutting for a new, much-needed business in town—Central Kansas Counseling (CKC), a counseling center whose mission is 'partnering with people as they pursue living healthy, courageous, and authentic lives so that our communities are changed now and for future generations.' They are here to help those in Marion County in any way they can. CKC began in 2014 in Hesston at Hesston Mennonite Church when co-founder and therapist Carlin Buhrman began seeing clients. She and husband Blake started the practice. While Blake handled more of the business side of the center, Carlin Buhrman continued to work a full-time job while seeing clients on top of it until she felt she needed to quit her job to do what she could with seeing clients at the new counseling center. She continued to see clients full-time as the only counselor for a few more years. In 2018, two more counselors joined, and the center moved to a new facility at the beginning of 2019. They had a great relationship with the church but had outgrown the space. 'One of the questions our landlords had for us at the beginning was how many therapists do you think this space, this town, this rural area can handle? And we really had no idea. We really thought maybe we would reach a limit at some point, but the response of the community has been so welcoming, and they're interested in mental health. They're open to moving toward health in lots of different ways. And so we've been able to just continue to add people to expand the services we provide and see more and more people,' said Buhrman. Erica Haude, of Hillsboro, joined the practice in the fall of 2020 and commuted to Hesston to see clients. 'I was just working two days a week and seeing clients. And then I was considering what it would look like to add a third day. And our offices were full,' said Haude. CKC added more offices and more therapists. 'The Hesston space was full. And I think at that point, I mentioned to Blake ‘I wonder what it would look like to do another location in Hillsboro'?' said Haude. Haude and the Buhrmans sat down and dreamed what it would look like to open a location in Hillsboro. Haude already had a large Marion County client load so they felt there was a need in Marion County. 'We talked about it knowing that at any point if it felt like it wasn't viable or it didn't make sense for either the community or for us, we could always pull the plug. And I would just stay at Hesston because I was really happy there and even now I go there once a week,' said Haude. 'We saw more and more Marion County people coming to Heston. And even on my caseload, I was seeing people as far as Lindsborg or Salina. I just kept seeing people from up North and thought maybe this is an underserved community—there are providers in this area, but there just aren't many.' Haude said it all happened organically. She met another counselor, Leah Fish, at the Hillsboro swimming pool and convinced her to join the practice in Hillsboro. The Burhmans decided to go for it and opened the Hillsboro office in August of 2023 with Haude and Fish. They added therapist Jim Paulus in January. They also added an intern, Bailey Penner. And the decision was clearly the right one as clients have been filling the open slots. Part of the benefit of having so many therapists between the two offices is that there is a good chance of finding a good match between client and counselor. 'I always tell people that finding a therapist is a lot like finding a doctor that you really like and you connect with. One of the great things about our office is that we have three providers plus an intern in Hillsboro. We have another eight in Hesston. Find someone that you connect with that you feel comfortable with. We want it to be that. I always want people to feel empowered,' said Haude. For those worried that maybe they don't need counseling for their issues, Buhrman offers encouragement. 'I just want to normalize the need for therapy in people's lives. There's not a person on this planet who goes through their whole life without circumstances that affect them. And that affects their mental health. That looks very different from one person to another, but mental health support is just another resource to access,' said Buhrman. 'And some people do it once. Some people may do it on and off throughout their whole lifetime. But to know it's there, it's really important and it's really normal to use the resources around you to get through things.' Buhrman had one more thought to add to reassure people about counseling. 'A therapist in Hesston once said, ‘No problem is too small for counseling' and that just feels inviting and inclusive. A lot of people show up feeling like they don't have big enough problems. If we're all working on even our smallest problems, we're making the world a healthier place which I think is important,' said Buhrman. CKC is located at 315 N. Lincoln in Hillsboro. They will also see Marion County clients at their Hesston location if preferred. To schedule an appointment, call 620-869-9986 or go online to centralkansascounseling.com.

title: Trojan golf works to build experience in players
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: The Hillsboro High School Golf team returns with a large but inexperienced roster. But they bring back top-returning golfers junior Lincoln Wichert and senior Annaliese Jorgenson. 'Lincoln earned a…
content: The Hillsboro High School Golf team returns with a large but inexperienced roster. But they bring back top-returning golfers junior Lincoln Wichert and senior Annaliese Jorgenson. 'Lincoln earned a varsity spot in the line-up part way through his freshman year and was part of the team that qualified for the the 2A State Tournament in Emporia that season. He was our top varsity golfer last season, earning top 10 finishes in a few regular season tournaments and he qualified for the 2A State Tournament in Hesston as an individual player,' said Coach Scott O'Hare who begins his 26th year as Hillsboro High School head golf coach. He is joined by Assistant Coach Phillip Thiessen who is starting his 1st year coaching. 'Annaliese Jorgenson is our only other returning varsity team member. She played in all varsity tournaments last season and earned a couple of top 10 finishes during the regular season,' said O'Hare. The coaches are uncertain who the other key players are at this time since aside from Jorgenson the senior class players consist of three other girls who have primarily played in JV events up to this point and Wichert is the only other upperclassman on the roster. The rest of the roster consists of three sophomores who all played JV events last season and eight freshmen. 'We will be very young and inexperienced. Due to the time they have spent improving during the off-season, I believe Lincoln and Annaliese are set up to have a solid season and lead the team. Beyond that, we will have to see how some of the returning golfers and freshmen progress as the season gets underway,' said O'Hare. 'I am hopeful that a few of them will be able to contribute and allow us to field a competitive varsity group with at least four to six golfers, as four are required to compete for team scores in tournaments. We will do our best to get our golfers as many competitions, varsity and JV, as possible to help them gain more experience.' O'hare feels his biggest obstacle this season will be working with a large group of golfers with a wide range of experience and ability levels. 'We will need to find the most efficient and effective ways to help our more experienced golfers progress while getting our less experienced golfers the basics and skills they need to get them started in the game,' said O'Hare. The team is already hard at work on their goals for the season. 'I think our primary goal will be to get to a point where we have two to four more golfers prepared to join in with Lincoln and Annaliese who have the skills and confidence to participate in 18-hole varsity tournaments. That will also give us the ability to get other golfers additional experience in our JV schedule of tournaments. Obviously, beyond that, we hope to see all of our golfers learn the basics of the game, become more familiar with the competition rules, and continue to improve throughout the season,' said O'Hare. Coming—The Trojans get started at 1 p.m. on Tuesday, April 2 at the Herington Invitational.

title: Goessel City Council works on flooding issue
author: Cynthia Goerzen
description: The Goessel city council met on March 25 and discussed the flood control project. Mayor Evan Esau talked about concrete and debris that need to be removed from the creek that runs through town. Some…
content: The Goessel city council met on March 25 and discussed the flood control project. Mayor Evan Esau talked about concrete and debris that need to be removed from the creek that runs through town. Some trees also need to be removed, as well as a dam on private property. It was noted that some property owners in that area have already removed the trees on their property pointed out by Darin Neufeld of EBH Engineering. He had walked through the creek area with members of the council to show them specifically what needed to be removed for the water to flow through town to avoid flooding. The council noted that it is the responsibility of homeowners to clean out their culverts. Turning their attention to another matter, the council spent some time discussing equipment. The tractor that had been repaired does not work; it still has the same problem. The city will pay for the parts that had been billed, but will not pay for the labor yet. The city's road grader does not work either, and parts are no longer available to fix it since it is old. The council has looked into purchasing another road grader but made no decision. In the meantime, they accepted a contract to hire the road work at 10 hours a month for $125 per hour. In other business, the council: * welcomed Jennifer Bliss back as city clerk. * heard that the city office would be closed for three days, March 26-28, so Bliss could attend a water conference. * approved the ordinance about fireworks that had been discussed at last month's meeting. The permit will now cost $250. * discussed building permit fees, noting that the current fee is not sufficient. * briefly talked about a pickleball court for the city park. * heard from council member Ariel Krause about the sign at the park. She would like to move it and set it on either rock or concrete. * talked about the revolving loan fund that was used for the water tower. The city will be done with payments for the water tower in 2027. * heard from public works director Karen Dalke that required lead and copper testing had been done, as well as testing for nitrate. She also sent in required sewer samples. * heard of mowing that Dalke had done, as well as water meters that she had installed, and fire hydrant work. She cleared ditches, did locates and did many other duties. * authorized Dalke to purchase trees for the city park as part of a summer library project. * heard about city pump issues. * heard from Dalke that the water fountain at the ball diamond had been vandalized. She ordered a new water fountain for a cost of $500. * was reminded that the city building needs to be wheelchair accessible. No action was taken on the matter at this meeting. * noted a letter from the city's insurance company about new rates and deductible costs. Bliss said that only two insurance companies are available for cities. The wind and hail deductible will now be $25,000. * reviewed various policies and guidelines. * approved the minutes from a number of special meetings that had been mostly executive sessions.

title: Don't have time to get 'round to dinner? Make meatball soup.
author: Lindsey Young
description: I was in such a hurry this week, trying to toss together...
content:
I was in such a hurry this week, trying to toss together a quick dinner for Joey and I before we headed back out the door for more commitments.
In the moments before I headed home, I popped into the grocery store, a new recipe on my phone, grabbing quick ingredients before trying to get food on the table.
But being me, I strayed a bit from the ingredient list, adding this and that to my basket and internally planning the spice mixture I would throw into the soup I was going to make.
Even for a quick dinner, I just couldn't keep myself from playing with the recipe.
The one I tried comes from the blog 'Girl Gone Gourmet' by April Anderson. You can find the original post at https://www.girlgonegourmet.com/italian-meatball-soup/. I changed it quite a bit from the original, adding quite a few ingredients to my version.
Italian Meatball Soup
Ingredients
4 cups chicken broth
14.5 ounce can diced tomatoes
24 ounces marinara sauce (I used a roasted garlic version)
26 ounces frozen Italian-style meatballs
8 ounces fusilli pasta
2 teaspoons dried parsley
2 teaspoons dried oregano
2 teaspoons dried basil
2 teaspoons paprika
2 teaspoons onion powder
2 teaspoons garlic powder
1 teaspoon red pepper flakes, optional
salt and pepper, to taste
grated parmesan cheese, for serving
Directions
In a large pot with a lid, add the broth, diced tomatoes (don't drain them) and marinara sauce, over high heat.
Stir to combine the ingredients, and when they come to a boil, stir in the meatballs. Once the mixture comes back to a boil, add the pasta, parsley, oregano, basil, paprika, onion powder, garlic powder, red pepper flakes, salt and pepper, and stir well.
Turn the heat to medium and place the lid on the pot, letting it simmer for five minutes.
Remove the lid and stir, and continue to let the soup cook at a slow boil for six to seven minutes or until the noodles are cooked to your liking.
If the soup is too thick, add additional broth or water until the soup reaches your desired consistency. When the soup is heated back through, serve topped with parmesan.
This turned out really well. It was thick, hearty and full of great Italian flavor. It was perfect for dinner, but it would have been a great option for lunch with a small cup of soup alongside a grilled cheese sandwich or a big slice of garlic bread, too.
I ended up leaving my soup a bit on the thick side, and as it cooled, it turned into more of a pasta sauce than a soup, so my leftovers will be getting more liquid when I reheat them.
But the main thing is that I managed to quickly get a hot meal on the table that we both enjoyed, even while I kept tossing improvised ingredients into the pot. Sometimes being in a hurry means eating something terrible for dinner, but every once in awhile, it makes for a great meal.
Spice Up Your Life is a weekly recipe column by Lindsey Young, who describes herself as an enthusiastic amateur cook and can be reached through her website at spiceupkitchen.net.

Residents in Hillsboro will have to find an alternate route down Ash while Hett Construction does repairs on a small section of road on Ash between Grand and 1 st Street.
st Street.
Grand will remain open and access to 2S Outdoor Power will be available.
'Traffic should use Main Street as the detour around this area. We are encouraging heavy truck traffic to use Industrial Road to travel north and south. The closure was originally planned to start on Friday, April 12 but was moved up one day. Thank you in advance for your patience and we apologize for any inconvenience during construction,' said a City of Hillsboro Facebook post on Wednesday, April 10.
Street Superintendent Dale Dalke said it should take about two weeks depending on the weather.
'They're removing pavement across the entire roadway there curb to curb for 30 feet or so. There's a bump there. There was a shift in the pavement. A lot of materials in the summer expand because they get hot. This concrete was working against itself, and it would fracture and break itself. And so then there would be holes there. And so we'd fill with asphalt, but the forces were against each other. And then some went up and some went down causing a bump there,' said Dalke.
Dalke said they will also be working on the northeast corner.
'We'll reduce a little bit of sidewalk and the wheelchair ramps to make them ADA compliant,' he said.

title: Hillsboro makes progress in strategic goals
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Progress in the city's strategic plan was the topic of conversation in the April 16 Hillsboro City Council meeting. The council discussed updates in the various sectors they have set goals in. For the…
content:
Progress in the city's strategic plan was the topic of conversation in the April 16 Hillsboro City Council meeting. The council discussed updates in the various sectors they have set goals in.
For the childcare center, City Administrator Matt Stiles told the Council that they now have three bids.
'They're still over the budget but a little bit closer. So there's still a gap in what's been raised and what's available through grant funds and what the project anticipated cost is. So the H4C group is now working to try to figure out how we're going to close that gap,' said Stiles. 'I would anticipate that we'll probably still approve the bid move forward, but they'll probably want to look at some USDA funding, some kind of gap to fill that gap and then try to raise money to repay that. So that's kind of how it's looking right now. It's really interesting that we talked about this as a board from the time we started this one year, it ended up going up almost $600,000 in cost.'
The plan is to award the bid in May with a timeline of about a year for the construction to be completed.
'So we'd be looking at the middle part of next year,' said Stiles.
Housing has also had a good amount of progress.
There will be another public meeting for the Mennonite Housing Project on April 30 at City Hall. If that project is supported there will be 24 units, duplexes, two and three-bedroom models.
'There's some income qualifications on that housing—up to 80% of the level for average income in the area. And then it's based on the number of people in your household what that number actually is,' said Stiles.
Another housing project is the container homes on Third Street.
'We've finalized what the utilities are for that and we'll wait for them to get back with us on what they want to do as far as how to proceed,' said Stiles.
After that, the container homes take six-eight weeks to produce.
306 West Grand is being worked on and made into a rental, and two single family lots on Willow Glen that were sold in the land bank will eventually have custom homes built on them.
'We're moving forward in the housing area. We got a pretty good chunk there. There'd be 10 units on Third Street, 24 over in Mennonite Housing. So 34 there and then you know, we've put one back in service on West Grand, we're gonna have another one there that's converted on South Main and then potentially two more builds. We've got a pretty healthy handful of housing that's got going on,' said Stiles.
For the workforce goal, Stiles told the council that he had a conversation with Dave Mullins from Hutch Community College (HCC) about setting up an internship program though the state and through HCC that would be for childcare.
'We'd tie that back to the childcare center so kind of working two goals on that at once on that,' said Stiles.
The group also discussed progress in the community development and financial stability development goals.
'The Strategic Plan for the last five years has been really successful in my opinion. I was a little skeptical, but it has far exceeded my expectations,' said Councilman Brent Driggers.
'Sometimes these things can end up just sitting on a shelf,' said Stiles.
'That's what I was a little skeptical of,' said Driggers.
For more information, the meetings are available to view on YouTube.
In other business, the council:
*approved vouchers totaling $139,734.52.
*help a public hearing for Ordinance 1390 establishing City of Hillsboro Flood Plain Management. No one spoke at the hearing. Ordinance 1390 was approved.
*heard from Mike King, Republican Candidate for Kansas House District 74
*listened to an annual electric department report from Todd Helmer
*approved Municipal Policy 102 regarding Lightning Arrestors, approved Municipal Policy 103 regarding Vegetation Management and approved Municipal Policy 104 regarding Wildlife Protection
*heard from Stiles about the possibility of doing a city logo redesign.
*learned that Callie Arnold, the new Assistant to the City Administrator, has been hard at work
developing a grant proposal for street light upgrade. That grant is 100% funded and would replace
around 50 streetlights, though the city may look at a full change out which is closer to 300 streetlights. The SEED grant project to replace Dale's Supermarket floor is moving forward; they plan on starting soon. The HEAL grant for 126 N Main is progressing and they should soon clear the final hurdle on their CDBG-CR. The daycare project is going to receive up to $50,000 from KDHE Brownfields to assist with asbestos tile removal.
The next Hillsboro City Council meeting will be at 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday, May 7.

title: Weightlifter focuses on positive body image
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Tiana Gaines has always been focused on fitness and working out, but her fitness focus has shifted from body image to what her body is capable of, especially since having kids. 'Growing up I feel the…
content:
Tiana Gaines competed earlier this month in the USA Master's Nationals Championship in Baton Rouge. Gaines' fitness focus is on what her body is capable of and she loves focusing on nutrition to fuel her goals. Tiana Gaines recently competed at the USA Master's Nationals Championships in Baton Rouge, LA where she took bronze in clean and jerk and competition total. She obtained a qualifying total for the Master's Worlds Championship and will compete in Finland in September. Tiana Gaines has always been focused on fitness and working out, but her fitness focus has shifted from body image to what her body is capable of, especially since having kids.
'Growing up I feel the message was women were to use exercise to be thin instead of using exercise for strength. I love that there is a movement for women to be strong, have positive body image and focus on nutrition to fuel those goals instead of just on appearance. As my kids start to compete in weight-based sports as well, I try to have these same discussions about nutrition, body image, and fueling for performance and health,' said Gaines. 'I hope I am an example to my children to keep developing habits and discipline to chase their goals. Habits that will get you through the times you lack the motivation. And to keep showing up for yourself.'
Gaines, who lives outside of Hillsboro, competed in April in the USA Master's Nationals Championship in Baton Rouge, LA where she took 4th in snatch, bronze in clean and jerk and competition total. With this win she obtained a qualifying total for the Master's Worlds Championship in Finland in September where she will compete against women from all over the world.
'I'm old so I'm in the master's division, which is 35 and older. Your competitions go up by age and weight. I placed third and fourth. In Olympic weight lifting, there's snatch and clean and jerk. Two lifts. You get three attempts on a platform in front of three judges, and they determine if you have a good lift or not. And so you're trying to lift the heaviest you can and then you can place the two lifts and then the total amount of weight that you move,' said Gaines.
The weightlifter, an APRN at NMC Health Orthopedics for her day job as well as married and mom to an 11-year-old boy and six-year-old girl, first fell in love with olympic lifts at CrossFit Old 81 in Newton.
But then it closed about six years ago.
'During that time, I was missing doing Olympic lifts but didn't have any local options. That's when I found The Strength Agenda about 5 years ago. Then due to COVID-19, I started piecing together a home garage gym which was what I needed to be able to balance family, work and my hobbies,' said Gaines.
Gaines was working out on her own but missed having feedback from others.
'I found this coach out of Chicago that does online programming and remote programming with different strength sports. He has athletes who do Olympic weightlifting all over the US. He encouraged me to start competing so I decided to try it. I first did local small meets in Chicago and then I finally qualified for Nationals. I've qualified for Nationals the last three years, but this is the first time I finally placed at Nationals,' said Gaines.
In addition to working out with a coach and in her home gym, Gaines has been doing various fitness activities with her kids.
'My son and I have trained and competed in a Hutchinson Salty Dog/Pup triathlon together last summer. My daughter and I just completed her first 5K at Emma Creek this weekend. It's so fun to watch them set goals, train, and experience them completing their personal accomplishments with them,' said Gaines.
Gaines said her son is also starting to get into weightlifting.
'I bought him a little trainer barbell. The kids come out and I show them how to do the lifts. Not that they're super into it yet, but it's a fun thing that they can join in occasionally,' said Gaines.
'I bought him a little trainer barbell. The kids come out and I show them how to do the lifts. Not that they're super into it yet, but it's a fun thing that they can join in occasionally,' said Gaines. She also likes them to see the nutrition and weight aspect of it all from a healthy perspective.
'With the weight class thing, you have to try to maintain weight. You weigh in two hours before you lift, and you have to make weight or you get bumped. My kids both started wrestling and it's been something teaching them nutrition and maintaining weight and having healthy fuel in our bodies for weightlifting activities and nutrition but in a healthy manner. That's just so important to me when they start doing these weight-based sports,' said Gaines. 'It's what you're able to do with your body versus what the scale says, because I'm trying to stay at a weight where I can maintain that but then also perform the best I can.'
Gaines is ready to compete in Finland in September and represent strong women.
'I feel like women were just taught ‘be skinny' and now there's a whole new movement of women—strong and muscular and sufficient. There's a lot more body positivity. And I love it,' said Gaines.

'I couldn't be more proud of the work they put in to get there,' said Magee.
Leah Brunner (Centre) got to swim at state for the first time.

Hillsboro's Rylie Hein and Austyn Driggers both had solid swims and were able to see the meet and help the team with the 400 Free relay.

title: MSM director has come full circle
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Main Street Ministries (MSM) Director Cheryl Genandt is very familiar with the ministry since she was the first mother to go through the program 33 years ago. 'I was the very first sojourner at Main…
content:
Cheryl Genandt and Barb Shannon meet every morning to do business and pray for the women at Main Street Ministries in Hillsboro. Genandt is the new director there. Main Street Ministries (MSM) Director Cheryl Genandt is very familiar with the ministry since she was the first mother to go through the program 33 years ago.
'I was the very first sojourner at Main Street. I had moved to Hillsboro after a tough divorce with two small children, nine months and four years old, and just through a unique set of circumstances got acquainted with Barb [Shannon]. At the time, they had been praying about this ministry and this building, and they decided to jump into it. When they moved in, they asked if me and my boys would like to move in with them. So we actually lived with them and became part of the family. It was pretty intense but amazing,' said Genandt.
Main Street Ministries is located in Hillsboro and their mission is to provide physical, emotional and spiritual resources in a supportive environment to single mothers and their kids. According to their website, they are a safe place for women and children, a place to practice honesty, forgiveness and responsibility, a place where women are respected, a place where God hears prayers and gives direction for the future.
It was started by Shannon and her then-husband Glen 33 years ago. Shannon left for a long period of time, but she came back about four years ago and now serves as Site Manager.
'I'm here for sure every night from five till eight in the morning so Cheryl can leave. The sojourners know I am here if they need anything or any crisis comes up or anything, then they call me. I usually call her and she's involved if there's a crisis or something, but just trying to give each other breaks. But I am doing this all with Cheryl,' said Shannon.
Genandt credits the program with being a changing point in her life.
'Not that I didn't go down some wrong roads following, but it kind of built a foundation in me that I was always able to return to,' said Genandt.
'Not that I didn't go down some wrong roads following, but it kind of built a foundation in me that I was always able to return to,' said Genandt. She lived with Shannon's family for a year before moving on to get married and have three more children.
'I moved away and did other things, ended up divorced again and finished raising my kids by myself. It was quite a journey,' said Genandt.
She stayed in touch with Shannon over the years. It was Shannon who told her about the director position being available.
'I was not interested, but finally I decided to apply, thinking I wouldn't get it. I prayed that the Lord would do what he needed to do. He did amazing things to get me here—just opened doors that only he could open and made things happen, a place to live, so many things—using people and circumstances to open the door for me to come. And so I came, interviewed a few times, and they offered me the position. So here I am,' said Genandt.
She has been here for a little over two months and has enjoyed being back in the place that helped her out so much so many years ago.
'There's a lot of working pieces to this ministry which is cool. I thrive on challenge. I love to tackle things head-on, and so it's been good. This board is phenomenal,' said Genandt. 'To have all of them here operating in their gifts and being so all in with the ministry, with the ladies that are here, it's just awesome to see. I couldn't do it without them.'
She also credits Shannon with her success as the director.
'She's so integral. It has been amazing how we can work together. We meet every day, every morning, every evening, and we go over what happens during the day and pray about what's next. Her wisdom and her input is invaluable to me. And I just see it as God orchestrating this full circle, someone who held my feet to the fire back in the day, and now I get to walk alongside her,' said Genandt.
Shannon agrees.
'We have a very good partnership. She's grown tremendously, she loves the Lord with a passion and the ladies love her. She's easy to fall in love with. She's going to be really good for this program,' said Shannon.
Benandt credits the Hillsboro community for the success of Main Street Ministries.
'When I moved here the community as a whole was so service-minded and so willing to reach a hand out and reach into people's lives and help them. They are still like that. MSM is a product of that. When somebody steps into your circle, you need all the people reaching into your circle and helping you, and that's community. When somebody steps into your circle, it changes your life. And that's what Barb's family did to me. And what I hope that we can do here is step into these ladies' lives, into their circles with the community continuing in their reaching in which is priceless. That's just so much bigger than me or Main Street Ministries. It's this whole community. It's an honor to be a part of it,' said Genandt.

Janzen survived Nazi Germany, the Russian Red Army and the Polish Army during WWII. She was born in Kansas and moved to Germany as a young girl. She has written a book ‘Surviving Hitler, Evading Stalin'. It recounts her experience as a teenager's peaceful life is upended when Stalin's Red Army captures her family. Chronicling the harrowing events of a family torn apart by war, her book is a poignant account of love and loss, evidence of God's hand in the life of a WWII survivor.
There will be a 20-minute documentary of Janzen's story, followed by a time for questions. It is too painful for her to recount the entire story.
