title: Dealing with chronic disease can be difficult
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: July 10 is Chronic Disease Day and we have an informational article on it this week. I was surprised to learn just how common chronic disease is. As someone who suffers from more than one chronic…
content:
July 10 is Chronic Disease Day and we have an informational article on it this week.
I was surprised to learn just how common chronic disease is. As someone who suffers from more than one chronic disease, I often feel very alone like I am the only one. I may have to follow Dr. Weir's suggestion in the article and find a support group.
I think part of why chronic disease can make you feel alone is that it can be so isolating. You often are so fatigued or sick that you have to go to bed and rest on the bad days which keeps you away from others.
It's also hard for others to understand what you are going through if they don't have a chronic disease. Those who suffer from chronic disease often look fine so it's hard to understand just how sick they can be on their bad days.
Speaking of bad days, those who suffer from chronic disease never know when the bad day is going to hit. Sometimes I can do something one day and be fine but do the very same thing the next day and not be okay. There often seems to be no rhyme or reason to what will trigger my symptoms and cause me to not be able to function normally. And my symptoms/diseases could care less if I have a big day planned or need to be able to function.
For me, it's been difficult because one of my chronic diseases is a result of an accident I was in. As a result of injuries and multiple surgeries, I now will live with the disease for the rest of my life. It happened suddenly and is often a lot. I can remember being 'normal' and not having it just a few short years ago. Now it's my constant reality and always will be.
Another part of the journey that has been difficult that I hadn't considered was finding the right doctors and specialists. And then once you do, finding the right medications and treatments is a whole other battle. It's often trial and error with a lot of error.
And don't even start me on the nightmare of dealing with insurance!
But there are some bright spots I have found. I have learned that a support system is so important and that I have a great one made up of family and friends. Not only are they there to just listen even when they don't understand what I am experiencing, they check in on me when I get quiet and don't feel like talking about what I am going through. I can't eat a lot of things so they show up with something my body is tolerating at the moment or with tea or other items like plants.
I highly recommend a strong support system.
I'm also learning to enjoy the good days when they come and not be so worried about the next bad day. Living in the moment on the good days and being thankful is so important. And being thankful for the positives in life is key on the bad days. It helps shift the negative thoughts that can come so easily.
While I would gladly give up my chronic diseases, I am thankful for the lessons I have learned from them. Hopefully they have made me more empathetic to others who suffer for various reasons. I have for sure learned that we never really know what someone is going through.

title: An ambassador for Tabor retires after a distinguished career
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: Dave Kroeker recently retired from Tabor College. There are many words I could use to describe Dave, but average isn't one of them. Kroeker grew up in Henderson, Nebraska. In high school he played…
content:
Dave Kroeker recently retired from Tabor College. There are many words I could use to describe Dave, but average isn't one of them.
Kroeker grew up in Henderson, Nebraska. In high school he played football, basketball, and summer baseball, as well as running track.
It's no surprise that he attended Tabor. It was in his blood. After all, his mother's younger siblings attended Tabor, and Dennis Fast recruited him to play football and basketball.
Kroeker graduated from Tabor in 1978 with a degree in economics and business administration.
You could say that Kroeker is one of those 'lifers' – someone who was at Tabor for the majority of their professional career. In addition to teaching business classes, he was an assistant football coach to Dan Thiessen, Gary Myers, Tim McCarty, Mike Gardner, Robert Rubel and Mike Gotsch.
He also was an assistant men's basketball coach under Don Brubacher. He was the head track and field coach from fall 2000 through spring 2024.
Kroeker says when I officiated one of the JV college games he coached, I gave him a technical foul for expressing his displeasure with some calls. I don't remember that, but I'll take his word for it. His concern was that I was bending over backward to not favor the home team because I was a Tabor alum, and I didn't want to be accused of being a 'homer.'
Kroeker has many memories of his time as a student, teacher, and coach at Tabor. 'My student experience after a lonely first semester was very special,' said Kroeker. 'I met the love of my life here (his wife, Kim). All of my children were athletes and students at Tabor. I love our mission and have tried to help accomplish that mission.
'It's always been about working for something bigger than myself, and that caused me to come early and stay late, to look forward to the beginning of each new school year, and to be sad when the campus was empty in May.
'I thought I was doing something important, and was where God wanted me to be doing what He wanted me to do,' said Kroeker.
A number of faculty and coaches had a major impact on his life at Tabor, including football coach Doc Kyle, men's basketball coach Don Brubacher, athletic director Del Reimer, and business professor Marvin Sellberg.
When Kroeker returned to Tabor to teach and coach in 1997, he was a full-time professor in the business department. After taking the head track and field job in 2000, he also taught half-time in the business department. About a decade or so later, the track and field job was made a full-time position, and after not being in the classroom for a year, he missed it so much that he asked to teach one class in the fall semester.
'The first year I taught 'Wellness,' and the years after, I taught macroeconomics until this past fall,' said Kroeker.
Recruiting students to a small Christian college in a small city offers unique challenges. 'Bigger is almost always seen as better when it comes to a career, until they (the students) find out about the alumni who are part of large corporations or have made it to the 'big time,'' said Kroeker.
'The upfront cost is also compared to so many other options that students have in their college search, and every school wants high character, high academic, and talented student-athletes on their campuses. Those kinds of student-athletes are 'expensive' on the front end, but I believe they are well worth the investment long-term,' said Kroeker.
Kroeker has been a faithful ambassador for Tabor. 'I love selling our uniquely counter-cultural, Christ-centered approach to student life and academic/sports experience. While we look like many other schools on the Internet, we are truly standing first on the truth of the Bible, and against a number of cultural pressures that many 'faith-based' schools have given in to.
'You become like the people you choose to surround yourself with in life, and I truly believe in what Tabor believes about the unchangeable truth of God's word,' said Kroeker.

title: St. Luke Therapy Clinic shows off newly remodeled space
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: St. Luke Hospital Therapy Clinic in Marion held an open house last week to show off their newly renovated facilities to the public. The expansion and remodel started in October and was recently…
content:
St. Luke Hospital Therapy Clinic hosted an open house last week to show the public their newly renovated space. Guests enjoyed refreshments while checking out the facilities.
St. Luke Hospital Therapy Clinic in Marion held an open house last week to show off their newly renovated facilities to the public.
The expansion and remodel started in October and was recently completed.
'The expansion went to the north of the current building and we added 1,500 square feet to that to provide more of a gym-like feel. Before that we were all in the current space where you had treatment and you're trying to exercise, it didn't work,' said Administrative Assistant Katie Marler.
They also remodeled the space they had been working out of and made bigger offices.
'When they initially remodeled the first time, they only had space for four employees. And we have eleven now. So we now have desks for 15. We extended our office space and then made things a little bit more private on the current side for when we do more manual interventions and such,' said Marler.
The therapy clinic offers physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy. 'Within those we treat post-surgical, generalized strengthening balance, ambulation—so gait, all that stuff that pretty much physical there. We do pediatric as well,' said Marler. 'Speech therapy does a lot of cognition and memory. I do a lot of pediatrics as well with developmental delays. Occupational therapy also does post-surgical, any like trigger finger or carpal tunnel. They also see pediatrics. They see a lot of sensory integration which a lot of people don't realize is a problem.'
Marler said the clinic also treats lymphedema.
'We can do Astym, which is a certified soft tissue massage with some tools that just provide the blood flow to heal properly,' said Marler.
The clinic has an aquatic pool for rehabbing sports injuries. They also focus on women's health at the clinic with things like bladder control, pregnancy, pre-pregnancy, postpartum and more according to Marler.
In addition to serving as an administrative assistant, Marler serves as a rehab technician. She also serves as a physical therapist assistant and treats patients.
She has had to work mostly as administrative assistant right now as the regular Therapy Clinic Director Alex Brooks is gone to Kuwait. He is in the reserves and is currently serving as a physical therapist for the military.
'He got deployed in February of this year and shouldn't be back until October,' said Marler.
While he is gone, Marler and several others have pitched in and helped handle the day-to-day operations of the clinic and more.
'We handled a lot of the construction. We were also in the process of switching over documentation systems. So it's been nonstop. We also just finished covering two maternity leaves this past year. We were full staff for about a month, and then one of our physical therapists left, we hired a new one in January and then Alex left in February. We've just been shuffling things around,' said Marler.
The team has worked well together and made it all work.
'We're very team-oriented, and we do a lot to help each other which is very nice because we're pretty independent, too. There's not a lot of places in our company that a director could leave and they would survive on their own,' said Marler.
The Open House was successful with many from the public attending to check out the new facilities and all the center has to offer.
'We had a wonderful turnout at the Open House for the new Therapy Clinic addition. There were amazing treats and great conversation. Thank you to everyone who joined us. Your presence and support mean the world to us. Together we are building a community of healing, hope and care. We look forward to continuing this journey with you all,' said Marketing and Foundation Director Keri Collett.
To schedule an appointment call 620-382-2863. For physical therapy and occupational therapy, you do not have to have a doctor's referral. Speech therapy does require a referral. More information can also be found on FB at https://www.facebook.com/people/St-Luke-Hospital-Therapy-Services/100083551743116/. St. Luke Hospital Therapy Clinic recently remodeled their existing space and added on an additional 1,500 sq. feet in order to provide more services.

title: Demolition derby part of a point series championship
author: Bill Bush
description: This year's Marion County Fair Demolition Derby, scheduled for Saturday, July 27, at 7 p.m. at the Marion County Fairgrounds, will have a different flavor with new management taking over. Jesse Hamm…
content:
The Marion County demolition derby is scheduled for Saturday, July. 27, at 7 p.m.
This year's Marion County Fair Demolition Derby, scheduled for Saturday, July 27, at 7 p.m. at the Marion County Fairgrounds, will have a different flavor with new management taking over.
Jesse Hamm and his team out of Hillsboro have created a mini-point series for local derbies to give drivers a chance at a points championship. Hillsboro will be the third derby, and Newton will be the fourth and final stop before the championship derby.
The series began in Herington on July 13 and will continue to the McPherson County Fair in Canton (July 21), the Marion County Fair in Hillsboro (July 27) and the Harvey County Fair in Newton (Aug. 11). The championship will take place in Herington on Oct. 19.
Hamm said the idea came from a Canton fall event called the Halloween Hangover, which is something they don't do every year. He agreed to ask around to see if he could rotate the fall derby, and Herington agreed to host it this year.
He said the Points Championship Derby on Oct. 19 is open to all drivers, but those who have competed in at least two of the four derbies in the series will vie for the points championship.
'These drivers can build points throughout these first four derbies, and then the fifth derby in October will be crowning a champion overall for points,' Hamm said.
He said the other advantage of having a series is if drivers have a bad night at one of the shows, they still have three others to compete in.
'Or if they want to build multiple cars, they know what the rules are, and it just kind of gives them more opportunities,' Hamm said.
He plans to offer four classes of demolitions—bone stock compact class, '80s or newer bone stock class, weld class and five-foot rule class.
Hamm, who grew up in and lives in Hillsboro, drove himself for several years. He said that his brother began driving in 1993, and he started in 2000.
He said a lot of what promoting events includes is working social media, fielding phone calls and text messages and searching for sponsors.
'Myself and the team have been working very hard in the past few months of either finding sponsorships or putting on cornhole tournaments to try to raise money for that championship, and so far things have been going good,' Hamm said. 'Still got a lot of work to do, but hoping to get a little bit more money out there for those drivers.'
Last year, his events ranged from 28 to 33 cars. He hopes to reach at least 40 cars for one of his events this year, but won't know until it happens, because he said they don't do pre-registration, so it's hard to gauge what the turnout will be. He said he's received lots of calls from around the area and as far away as Springfield, Missouri.
Hamm hopes the point series will draw attention.
'One thing that I've seen is there's not a lot of locals anymore in these towns, and I'm just trying to come up with ways to maybe make some easier classes for people to, you know, don't have to spend a lot of money. And just trying to get the young kids involved and see if we can get more participants in each one of these derbies,' said Hamm. 'I drove for 16 years, I have a love for this sport and if I'm not allowed to drive anymore, then this is another way that I can keep participating with the derby world.'

title: Author and family adventures to see rocks
author: Shana Thornhill
description: Doubt warred with disgust on my darling son's face. 'But mom,' he whined, 'it's an awful long way to drive just to look at some dumb rocks.' 'Well, yeah,' I agreed. 'But that's pretty much every…
content:
Doubt warred with disgust on my darling son's face. 'But mom,' he whined, 'it's an awful long way to drive just to look at some dumb rocks.'
'Well, yeah,' I agreed. 'But that's pretty much every family vacation we've ever taken.' And so it was. Kansas waterfalls are water flowing over rocks; some near, some far. The Black Hills boasts a wide variety of rocks, both above and below ground, including tree rocks (the Petrified Forest). Devil's Tower is one big rock. South Padre Island isn't known for large rock formations, but they say sand is just a bunch of worn-down boulders, so there's that. Pagosa Springs has a lot of pretty rocks, even if we don't see them because they're covered with snow and we're hurtling over them with pieces of wood strapped to our feet. Heck, even Darling Hubby and I spent our honeymoon admiring and collecting rocks (yes, with a permit from the Parks Service), so the kids ought to have rockhounding in the blood. You wouldn't know it to hear them, though.
Since Darling Daughter has flown the coop in pursuit of an actual grown-up career, it was just the three of us on this adventure. We got up early on Saturday morning, almost as early as we used to for club sports, and pointed the car West. Darling Son was not amused by 'Go West, young man,' and promptly went to sleep in the back seat. Darling Hubby and I spent the trip like we usually do, with frequent stops to see historical markers and admire various indoor plumbing facilities. After a few hours, we were getting close to our first destination, Castle Rock, way out in Western Kansas. Since it had rained earlier that morning, some of the roads through the gorgeous rolling hills were a little, um, interesting. I think we went about two miles at a slight angle to the actual road as we powered through the wet sand and mud.
As we got closer, we saw limestone outcroppings, some with small caves. When we stopped to take some pictures, seashells crunched beneath our feet. Soon, a white spire appeared—seemingly not large at first, but more and more imposing as we got closer. By now, the boy was reluctantly awake and joined us in walking around the monolith. I turned my back for a few seconds, and when I looked again, he was climbing one of the rocks. A huge grin had somehow plastered itself on his face but vanished when he noticed I was taking pictures. We explored a bit of the surrounding badlands, being careful not to damage any of the formations. This is private property, and we wanted to leave it as gorgeous as we found it. Onward through the prairie we went, next stop Monument Rocks.
Much like before, the wide expanse of grassy hills revealed not one, but several large limestone formations. Four adult donkeys and a foal welcomed us to this new vista, again courtesy of private landowners. This one, though, had clear No Climbing signs, so the boy's enthusiasm was slightly dampened. You can walk around and through the stones, even up some higher hills, without having to climb. There were two major groupings, one being the stone arch you might have seen with the sunrise, sunset, or Milky Way framed by the rock. The other was home to a large colony of swallows, and watching them could have been entertainment for hours.
Our third stop was the newly minted Little Jerusalem State Park. This was the only place we had to pay to see, the princely sum of $5 per vehicle. We were treated to more of the limestone spires, but this time, we saw them from the top. When you pull into the parking lot, you can choose between two scenic trails to enjoy the stones. By now, Darling Son had had absolutely enough rocks for one day, and perhaps one lifetime. He stayed in the car while Hubs and I opted to take the longer trail around the rim. It was a stunning hike, with every twist in the path showing a completely different view. It wasn't difficult—I hiked it in my trusty flip-flops, but sturdier shoes might have possibly been a better idea. Extra water was a must. When we got to the end of the trail, we basked for a while on a huge stone that, improbably enough, was still retaining moisture from the rains earlier that day. It was cool and damp, even in the bright sunshine and brisk breeze.
We stayed in Oakley that night and headed home the next morning. If we had taken a little more time, there's the Buffalo Bill Museum in Oakley, the Sternberg Museum in Hays, and a few other nifty sights to see out that way. We stopped in Wilson on the way back to see the World's Largest Czech Egg, and of course, had to hit the Cozy Inn in Salina for a late lunch.
Even if you're not as into rocks as we are, this was a really fun and fairly inexpensive weekend getaway. It was a long way to go to look at rocks, but definitely worth it!

title: Summer Food 4 Kids helps reduce food scarcity in Hillsboro
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Thanks to Summer Food 4 Kids, children in Hillsboro are guaranteed to be able to eat lunch Monday through Friday from 12-12:30 p.m. at First Mennonite Church. 'It's open to anyone 18 and under. We…
content:
Rachel Winter, Aleen Ratzlaff, Tammy Wintermote and Nancy Klaassen place fruit into baggies for sack lunches for the Summer Food 4 Kids program. Thanks to the help of many volunteers, local businesses and the support of local churches, the program feeds almost 100 kids each day Monday through Friday. The program is run out of First Mennonite Church in Hillsboro under the direction of co-coordinators Kayla Gallaway and Norma Duerksen.
Thanks to Summer Food 4 Kids, children in Hillsboro are guaranteed to be able to eat lunch Monday through Friday from 12-12:30 p.m. at First Mennonite Church.
'It's open to anyone 18 and under. We don't check proof of income or anything. If you are hungry and want to eat, you can walk up, bike, ride your skates up or drive up to the hut in the parking lot and get a meal. We just serve everybody who shows up,' said Co-coordinator Kayla Gallaway.
The program began 10 years ago when Co-coordinator Norma Duerksen started it at Trinity Mennonite Church in Hillsboro.
'It started when I heard on NPR that the Wichita food bank had food to distribute to summer kids when they don't have school lunches. But they didn't have distribution centers. If towns would just have places to distribute the food, they would provide the food. And so I said, 'We can do that'. Trinity became the place where the Wichita food bank dropped off the food, and then we served at tables in the Trinity church,' said Duerksen.
Unfortunately they had to pay for the food from the food bank because Hillsboro didn't have a high enough percentage of poverty to meet the qualifications for the program.
'They were supposed to be well-balanced meals, but the kids were just not eating soy butter and raisins and the things that would have made it a balanced meal. And so our people said, 'Hey, we're cooks. We could make hot meat dishes and have fresh vegetables and fruit and cookies',' said Duerksen. 'When I called the school district, they said there were over 200 kids with free and reduced lunches. And that's who we were kind of focusing on—our children who were at risk for food scarcity during the summer.'
The group began cooking and more people and churches started helping out.
'It became citywide. It wasn't just Trinity then. It became all the churches involved,' said Duerksen.
In addition to serving the kids food, they would have a male adult sit at every table to supervise and create conversation.
'I visited with the police department, the school district and the mayor and said, tell me about Hillsboro. Tell me about where the gaps are that a church could fill. The mayor at the time said we need to face that we have poverty here in Hillsboro. We need to admit that. And the superintendent said churches could provide strong male role models for kids who have single-parent homes,' said Duerksen.
But then COVID-19 hit and Summer Food 4 Kids became a drive-by program. Afterward they tried to return to the table model but the numbers dropped.
'After COVID, we realized these parents did not want to drag their kids into the church, have them sit, have them eat, have them do chores of scraping off the plates and cleaning off the tables. They just weren't up to that. We also heard moms with bigger families say they didn't have time to get all six kids in the car to the church on time on a lunch break,' said Gallaway.
The program moved back to the drive by option.
'It was a hard decision. We didn't have that conversation at the table with the kids. We miss that. But drive-by fed 3,000 more people. Our goal was to feed children—families at risk of food scarcity. That was the main goal. And so we decided to go back to feeding people bagged lunches,' said Duerksen.
They now offer the lunches at First Mennonite Church in Hillsboro since Trinity closed last year. And the program continues to be successful and grow. Participants in the Summer Food 4 Kids program pull up at the food 'hut' in the parking lot at First Mennonite Church in Hillsboro to get sack lunches while volunteer Aleen Ratzlaff (standing) and Coordinator Norma Duerksen (sitting) hand out lunches and pool passes to kids 18 and under who participate in the program. The program is put on by local churches to help limit food scarcity for school-aged children in Hillsboro.
'In June, we served 300 more meals than we did last year at this time. So the need is great. The need is still there,' said Duerksen.
The group also gives the adults with the children food.
'We've decided that if the children are hungry, the parents are, too. And so we serve the whole family. We see three kids in the backseat, and mom's driving or grandma's driving, then we give a meal for her, too,' said Gallaway.
Each bag contains a hot meat dish, a bag of fresh veggies and a container of ranch to dip them in, a bag of fresh fruit, a bag of two cookies and a bottle of water. They also get a pool pass for the day.
'They get two different kinds of cookies and almost always homemade by ladies in the community. Thousands and thousands of cookies. Yesterday we served 76 meals so that's 152 cookies. They disappear quickly,' said Duerksen.
The program could not happen without the volunteers. Volunteers help every step of the way from a local farmer donating a cow to other food items being donated. And volunteers show up all week long to help bag the items for the sack lunches.
'We are so thankful to the many people and businesses that help us. We couldn't do it without all of them and all of the churches who donate their time and resources,' said Duerksen. 'I feel like this is a whole community working together to do this project, and it's just such a God thing—to hear it on NPR, start the program, have donations from businesses and churches and individuals—just beyond anything that I could plan or do. It's just so fun to be a part of something beyond my imagination.'
The program is always looking for more help as well.
'We have regular volunteers who come, but sometimes they are gone so we could use subs for them. And we can always use more food items and monetary donations,' said Duerksen.
To donate items, money or time, please contact Kayla Galloway at 620-635-7165 or Norma Duerksen at 620-381-0949.For meals, go to First Mennonite Church at 102 S. Ash St in Hillsboro and pull up to the wooden hut in the south parking lot. Food is served from 12-12:30 p.m. Monday through Friday. Kids of all ages enjoy eating their free lunch from the Summer Food 4 Kids program run out of First Mennonite Church in Hillsboro. The program is run with the help of numerous volunteers and support from local churches in the community.

title: USD 410 BOE approves personnel changes
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The USD 410 Board of Education met for their regular meeting on Monday, Aug. 12 where they approved a number of personnel changes. The board approved a salary increase of of 5.87% for TEEN Director…
content:
The USD 410 Board of Education met for their regular meeting on Monday, Aug. 12 where they approved a number of personnel changes.
The board approved a salary increase of of 5.87% for TEEN Director Lena Kleiner along with a health insurance contribution.
They also approved pay rate changes for Alexis Williams and tutors. Williams will serve as a Marion County Parent as Teachers Program Parent Educator for the 2024-2025 school year and was approved for a pay rate of $20 per hour. Some current USD 410 teachers along with former USD 410 teachers and substitute teachers will be tutoring students this year. The board approved the payment of current USD 410 teachers at their regular hourly rates of pay and payment of others who are not current USD 410 teachers at a rate of $37.04 per hour for tutoring.
David Ediger was approved to serve as Hillsboro High School and Dale Shewey was approved to serve as Hillsboro Middle/High School Assistant Cross Country Coach.
Several new hires were approved as well. The board approved the hiring of Ronald Mueller to serve as the USD 410 Transportation/Custodial Coordinator for 40 hours per week at a training rate of $20.00
per hour effective Aug. 2 increasing to a rate of $25.00 per hour on Sept. 2. He replaces Karen Goossen.
Jayne Smalley was approved to hire to serve as Hillsboro Elementary School Custodian for 40 hours per week at a rate of $14.00 per hour effective Aug. 5. The board also approved the hiring of Ashley Mickel to serve as Hillsboro Middle/High School Custodian for 40 hours per week at a rate of $14.00 per hour effective Aug. 12.
The board also heard a bond project update from Superintendent Clint Corby. He informed the board that half of the roofs have been repaired and a big difference has already been noticed.
'We've had these rains, and we've got no water in our buildings. That's a big deal not having to chase those leaks down,' said Corby. 'If you understood the amount of time that maintenance guys spent tracking down leaks time after time, and to know that we can go in and not have to worry about this is a pretty big deal.'
New doors with safety features have been put in several spots and the rest will be done down the road. The secure entrance doors for the front of HMHS will still need to be done.
'The materials for that one are not in yet. It could be another four to six weeks before that gets in and finished. But they will get the inside secure part, that extra double set of doors will be done for the start of school,' said Corby.
The outsides of the buildings have been cleaned and sealing done and several concrete projects have been done to remove tripping hazards in some locations and to prevent water from collecting in others.
The bleachers have been replaced and look much nicer. The work on those is close to completion but they are still waiting on motors and gear boxes replacements.
'I've had a couple of people ask if we got rid of the backs on the bleachers. We did not get rid of the backs,' said Corby.
Sound and video in the auditorium has also been completed.
There will be more projects continuing into the school year with more projects, including the HVAC system, scheduled for next summer.
In other business, the board:
*accepted a donation of assorted coloring pages, sticker book, crayons and colored pencils for Marion County Parents as Teachers program use. The donation was from Rod's Tire and Service, Inc.
*heard a report from District Activities Director Robert Rempel. Rempel discussed various changes happening in athletics conference-wide. He also explained that Lyons is no longer in the Central Kansas League making the league nine teams. Hillsboro will still compete against Lyons in some non-conference play.
*appointed USD 410 BOE President Jared Jost as the USD 410 delegate for the KASB 2024 Delegate Assembly.
*approved a base bid from DCS Services for bleacher motors and gear boxes replacement using Heartland Seating as the vendor for a cost of $19,602.35.

title: Beautiful pastries are just within your ‘rasp'
author: Lindsey Young
description: Throughout our marriage, one of my side projects with Joey has been figuring out how to make foods he didn't think he liked into something he likes. This has been really easy for tons of vegetables…
content:
Raspberry danishes include decadent sweetened cream cheese, along with tart fresh berries and crunchy puff pastry. They can also be made with pretty much any fresh berry, if raspberries aren't your thing.
Throughout our marriage, one of my side projects with Joey has been figuring out how to make foods he didn't think he liked into something he likes.
This has been really easy for tons of vegetables and mushrooms, but I recently decided to tackle one that I thought might be impossible: raspberries.
I knew it was a difficult assignment for two reasons: 1. He's not much of a dessert guy to start with, and 2. He's tried raspberries several times over the course of our marriage and not really liked them.
Challenge accepted.
I decided to try three different applications for raspberries to see what he might go for, so if you're like Joey and not much of a fan, I'll apologize now for the bombardment of raspberries over the next few weeks.
The good news, though, is this week's recipe can easily be made with any berries, so you still have options.
This comes from the blog 'Vanilla Bean Cuisine' by Molly Pisula. You can find the original post at https://www.vanillabeancuisine.com/raspberry-danish/. I added extra ingredients, including bonus vanilla, in my version.
Raspberry Danish
Ingredients
1 or 2 sheets frozen puff pastry, thawed in the refrigerator (I had about 13 ounces of pastry.)
Flour for rolling pastry
1 egg
8 ounces cream cheese, softened
3/4 cup powdered sugar, plus some for decorating
2 teaspoons vanilla
6 ounces fresh raspberries
Directions
Line a baking sheet or a couple plates that can fit in your freezer with parchment paper, and set it aside.
Lightly flour a cutting board or your countertop, and roll out the puff pastry to a square about 1/8-inch thick. Cut the pastry into about three-inch squares using a knife or pizza cutter.
Prepare an egg wash by beating the egg in a small bowl with a fork. Whisk in a tablespoon of cold water, and set it aside.
In a mixing bowl, beat together the cream cheese, powdered sugar and vanilla until the mixture is smooth.
To assemble, put a scant tablespoon of the cream cheese mixture into the middle of each square, and top it with three or four raspberries.
Fold one corner to the middle of the pastry, and then brush the opposite corner with a little egg wash and fold it on top of the other, pressing it a little to make sure it sticks.
Place the finished danish on the baking sheet. Repeat until all of the puff pastry is used. (There's no need to put the danishes very far apart on the baking sheet at this point, so go ahead and squeeze them on there.)
Place the egg wash in the refrigerator to use later, and place the danishes in the freezer for at least 30 minutes.
When the 30 minutes is nearly up, preheat the oven to 400 degrees.
Line another baking sheet with parchment paper and place the danishes about two inches apart on the sheet. Using the egg wash from before, brush a solid coating all over each danish.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes or until the pastry is golden brown and cooked through. Let them cool fully, and then sprinkle them with powdered sugar just before serving.
Store any leftovers in an airtight container.
I really liked these, and when I took them to the office, Adam declared them one of my better triumphs as of late. Plus, they were pretty to look at while being fairly low effort.
The sweetened cream cheese is a great compliment to the slightly tart berries, and the crisp of the puff pastry sends it over the top.
The real question, though, is how did Joey feel about them? I asked. He gave them an eight out of 10. Not too bad for someone who started out disliking the fruit entirely.
And with that newfound confidence, I was ready to give a few more options a try.
Spice Up Your Life is a weekly recipe column by Lindsey Young, who describes herself as an enthusiastic amateur cook and can be reached through her website at spiceupkitchen.net.

title: Deceased body believed to be missing Peabody clerk
author: Adam Strunk
description: Law enforcement has located a body that they believe to be Jonathan...
content:
Clayton, the interim clerk for the City of Peabody, has been missing since Aug. 3.
Christopher King, husband of Clayton, called a reporter at Harvey County Now/Hillsboro Free Press to inform them of the development. He said he spoke with law enforcement Sunday evening, and they had communicated that his husband's body was located.
'I am sad to hear the news. I love Jonathan very much, and I was hopeful that he would be found alive,' King said.
Sheriff Chad Gay confirmed that the Harvey County Sheriff's Department investigated a report of a crashed vehicle shortly before 3 p.m. Sunday afternoon.
Gay said his office found a vehicle north of U.S. Highway 50, near the Old Trail Road junction, just east of Newton.
He said deputies investigated the scene and believed the vehicle was heading westbound on U.S. Highway 50 toward Newton when it left the roadway and hit a tree. Gay said the location of the vehicle was difficult to see from the roadway. He said the body located was in a state of advanced decay. He said evidence found on the scene indicated the body belonged to Clayton.
Officially, the identity of the vehicle's occupant will be confirmed through medical analysis.
Gay stated that he expected the Kansas Bureau of Investigation to put out a press release later this evening.
Law enforcement, friends and family have been searching for Clayton after he was last seen on Aug. 3. His cell phone was last pinged from a cell phone tower that morning at the Newton Holiday Inn Express, where those working reported Clayton had gone into use the bathroom.
More information will be added to this story when it becomes available.

title: Guests will pound the table for more of this cake
author: Lindsey Young
description: If you've been following my raspberry series the last few weeks, you know that I went on a mission to see if I could make raspberry dishes that my husband, Joey, (a known raspberry hater) would enjoy.…
content:
For a beautiful and lightly sweet dessert, look no further than this raspberry lemon pound cake, which is moist, full of fresh berries and has a light tartness from fresh lemons. It's a great treat for summer or springtime.
If you've been following my raspberry series the last few weeks, you know that I went on a mission to see if I could make raspberry dishes that my husband, Joey, (a known raspberry hater) would enjoy.
The other two recipes I tried received a thumbs up from him, but I wanted to see if I could win with one more.
This one might have been cheating a little because it features fresh lemon juice and zest, and if there's something Joey loves in a dessert, it's a bit of citrus.
But, hey, if you make up your own challenge, I suppose you make up your own rules, too, right?
The recipe I landed on comes from the blog 'The Seaside Baker.' You can find the original post at https://theseasidebaker.com/raspberry-lemon-pound-cake/. I eliminated the glaze from my version and added more raspberries and a smidgeon more lemon.
Raspberry Lemon Pound Cake
Ingredients
1 1/2 cup fresh or frozen raspberries, divided
2 teaspoons cornstarch
1 cup butter, room temperature
1 cup sugar
2 eggs
juice of 1 medium-sized lemon
zest of 1 medium-sized lemon
2 cups flour
1/2 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
2/3 cup sour cream or Greek yogurt
Directions
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Prepare a loaf pan by lining it with parchment paper and spraying it with cooking spray. Set it aside.
In a bowl, gently mix one cup of raspberries with the cornstarch, and set it aside.
In a large mixing bowl, beat the butter and sugar until it's light yellow (about two minutes).
Beat in the eggs, one at a time. Beat in the lemon juice and zest.
Finally, add the baking soda and salt and then alternate adding the flour and sour cream, beating in between, until everything is well combined.
Fold in the raspberry and cornstarch mixture, and pour the batter into the loaf pan, spreading it out evenly.
Lightly press the remaining raspberries about halfway into the top of the batter so you can still see the tops of the berries.
Bake for 50 to 60 minutes or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean.
Let the pound cake cook completely before removing from the pan and slicing.
Store the cake in an airtight container.
I was absolutely head over heels for this recipe. It was moist and buttery and the pops of raspberries, combined with the light tartness from the fresh lemon was fabulous. I could totally picture this on the table for a tea party.
As for Joey, he said he gave the cake a seven out of 10. He said if you're like him and really like lemon, go ahead and add a bit extra to this to make it even better.
Overall, I was pretty happy with my raspberry experiments, and Joey admitted that maybe he doesn't dislike the berries as much as he used to, so it was a win in my book.
Unfortunately for him, that also means I will probably continue to use him as a guinea pig for all kinds of random ingredients, whether he thinks he likes them or not.
Spice Up Your Life is a weekly recipe column by Lindsey Young, who describes herself as an enthusiastic amateur cook and can be reached through her website at spiceupkitchen.net.

title: Writer enjoys demolition derbies with family
author: Shana Thornhill
description: Dear Readers, as some of you may or may not have gathered before now, I led somewhat of a sheltered life as a child. Certain movies and music were off-limits. Certain places were definitely a no-go.…
content:
Dear Readers, as some of you may or may not have gathered before now, I led somewhat of a sheltered life as a child. Certain movies and music were off-limits. Certain places were definitely a no-go. And there were just some things we didn't do . . .like demolition derbies.
I had never been to a demo derby before I met Darling Hubby. I know my mother would hate them—the noise, the smoke, and the dirt would have been intolerable for her. I'm not sure how my Dad would have felt about them. He was definitely a car guy, but not a crashed-up, smashed-up car guy. He was more into Indy cars than NASCAR if you know what I mean.
The first time we took the kids to the derby at the Marion County Fair, I was hooked. Part of me wanted to drive one of the cars . . .at least, that is, until my favorite took a massive hit. That looked painful. A mere spectator I was meant to be, then, with plenty of good memories over the years. This year has been particularly memorable. At one, we brought in our own smoked ribs and corn on the cob to eat in the stands. Darling Daughter's boyfriend got to experience his first demolition derby AND see his beloved scream at the top of her lungs like a crazed banshee at a particularly good hit. He did not run away screaming. Break 'em in early, I always say.
Then there was Harvey County. Usually, I try to get the family to events early, so we can pick good seats. This time, however, we were running far behind. We got lucky enough to find a place to park, but walking to the arena, it looked like standing room only. I'm a pretty tall person, but Darling Daughter is not, so we were trying to inconspicuously drift towards the front of the crowd. I happened to glance up towards the bleachers at the north end of the arena, and someone I didn't know was waving at me. There were empty seats! I couldn't believe it! I pointed at myself: did he mean me? He nodded. I wanted to cheer! I gave him the thumbs up. We headed towards the bleachers and our Good Samaritan In Sunglasses.
As we neared the Promised Seats, I wondered what I'd gotten us into. The seats were on the 6th row up, and everything below them was packed solid with people. As I was wondering how my substantial self was going to get up there, Darling Hubby knelt down before me. Flattered as I was, apparently, I was supposed to use his knee as a step. Reluctantly, I did, visions of bone shattering vivid in my mind as I strained to haul myself up to the seat. The people around us reached over and helped me up. Of course, Darling Hubby and Darling daughter made it up, no sweat, as did Darling Son when he arrived. I was just glad I'd made it up there without putting anyone in the hospital.
Did I mention we were on the north side? The wind was coming out of the south. Within moments, we were all crusted with dirt. So much for the good hair day, I thought. I have had many heroes in my life, but the dude driving the water truck that night is right up there with the best of them. Eventually, the ground was moistened enough so that it didn't form billowing clouds of vision-obliterating dust behind every car.
The people around us in the stands were strangers I'd never met before in my life, but somehow that particular group of people became like family that night. Babies were passed to and fro, we played with some of the smaller children, and even the adults cheered my hooligans on when they decided to line dance on the bleacher seat in between classes. We were all covered in dirt, flashing white smiles in filthy faces. It was hilarious and magical at the same time. And to think, none of it would have happened that way if we'd have been early like usual. When it was time to leave, we all melted into the crowd, a last smile and quick wave before we went our separate ways.
Usually you think of heroes as people who do extraordinary things: feats of unusual strength, bravery or perseverance. In fact, heroes can come from anywhere, like our Samaritan in Sunglasses, or the water truck driver. Sometimes you make more of an impact on someone than you think. Family can be found with just about anyone you have something in common with, if you try hard enough. It's pretty amazing what can happen when you're kind. Some days, you may just be a kind of hero!

title: Hillsboro to take over bowling alley
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Aug. 20 where they approved an agreement for the city to take over the bowling alley. 'As we have discussed since spring, Hillsboro Development Corporation…
content:
The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Aug. 20 where they approved an agreement for the city to take over the bowling alley.
'As we have discussed since spring, Hillsboro Development Corporation wants the city to take over ownership of the bowling alley to ensure that the operations continue. In the agreement the city would receive the bowling alley, all the equipment and existing bank accounts for the sum of $1. There are no outstanding liabilities against the property or operation. The value of the accounts is likely to be more than $20,000 which will be used to support operations at the alley. The city will pay the closing costs and cost of any inspections. There are no stipulations on the use of the alley applied to the sale,' said Hillsboro City Administrator Matt Stiles.
Stiles explained that the intention is to keep the bowling alley as a separate unit from the normal city funds.
'The operations will fall under (Hillsboro Recreation Director) David Ediger. Initially we plan on running the operations as they are currently to evaluate what if anything we'd do differently. There are definitely some ideas to expand the use of the facility, but it's unclear how that will work at this point,' said Stiles.
The alley will continue to operate as Bluejay Lanes.
'Tabor College has opted not to renew its naming rights agreement, and we will be removing 'Tabor College' and the Tabor Bluejay logo from the building sign. The frontage sign needs to be replaced or repaired anyway, and it would be an easy addition to remove those things,' said Stiles.
Stiles said money will be saved by having the alley switch to the city's internal rate for utilities, and it will be able to purchase some items tax-exempt.
'We can also take advantage of grants and tax-exempt donations under city ownership. There is also the potential to collaborate with the CKEC (Central Kansas Entrepreneurship Center) on some projects. With additional activities we hope to build the alley's financial position to pay for capital improvements,' said Stiles. 'Ultimately the goal is to put the alley in a financial position to thrive without city or rec subsidy or be attractive to a private business owner to take over.'
The council also learned of a new job description for a Director of Aquatics/Assistant Recreation Director position.
'With Cara Duell leaving as the Community Engagement Director in September, we have chosen to re-evaluate how her work is being accomplished. The largest and most time-consuming portion of that job is managing the pool. The pool has a large seasonal workforce and a budget of $128,000 per year. It is an asset that requires a lot of attention to keep operational during the summer and work before and after the season to maintain. The management of the splash pad also falls under this position, putting all the aquatic-related items in one place. Though the splash pad is not staffed, it must be managed to make sure it's operational and safe for patrons,' said Stiles.
He explained that the position would also serve as the Assistant Recreation Director helping with programming, marketing, field maintenance and museum management as needed during the off period.
'Those duties are left vague in the description so that David Ediger can assign and adjust depending on the strengths of the individual in the position,' said Stiles. 'It's not as straightforward as some of the other jobs we have, but I think it makes sense. It has all the things you need in there to do the aquatics position which is sort of the important piece of that given how important the pool is and how big a budget it has.'
The largest differences between the current position and the proposed position are the additional recreation focus during the non-pool time and the removal of the specific community engagement items. Stiles explained that many of the community engagement duties are being moved to the Assistant to the City Administrator Callie Arnold, and he will help as well.
The revised position allows more focus on building recreational programming and dedicating more administrative expertise to community engagement items.
Stiles explained that the Director of Aquatics/Assistant Recreation Director is an exempt position with a salary starting at $40,000 depending on experience. The position is currently funded through 2024
and has been factored into the 2025 budget. The current Community Engagement Director position is partially funded from the Industrial Fund and that portion of the funding will be rerouted to support the
Assistant to the City Administrator position in 2025.
The council approved the proposed job description.
In other business, the council:
*approved vouchers totaling $308,093.98.
*appointed Mayor Lou Thurston and Councilman Blake Beyes voting delegates to the League of Kansas Municipalities Conference.
*met as a land bank and approved vouchers totaling $1,475.
*did not make any changes to the 2025 budget. The budget hearing will be at the next Hillsboro City Council meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 3. Councilman Ronald Wilkins encouraged the public to attend the meeting to hear more about the budget and give their input.
*proclaimed Tuesday, Aug. 20 as Trojan Girls Swimming Lauryn Vogt State Champion Day to formally honor the success of the Hillsboro High School girls swimming team for their success in the 2024 season and to recognize the achievement of Lauryn Vogt for winning the 2024 Kansas State High School Activities Association Girls Class 5-1A 50-yard Freestyle and 100-yard Butterfly Championships.
*proclaimed recognizing Public Power Week as Oct. 6-12.
*learned that The Department of Commerce awarded the Community Development Block Grant-Commercial Rehabilitation Grant for $3000,000 for the project at 126 N. Main (Olde Towne building). The building belongs to Eric Driggers.
'Grant funds will pay for tuck pointing, HVAC upgrades, electrical upgrades, ceiling fixtures, basement floor repair, refinishing floors, and window and door replacement. The environmental certification process has already begun. There is a 25% match required that will all be paid by the owner. Much like the daycare project, the city acts as the passthrough for this grant. Ranson Financial is the grant administrator for this project, paid by the building owner,' said Stiles.
