title: Gardner named Coach of the Year
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: WICHITA, Kan. – The Kansas Collegiate Athletic Conference (KCAC) has announced that Mike Gardner has been named as the 2024 KCAC Bissell Division Coach of the Year. Gardner led the Tabor College…
content:
Mike Gardner
WICHITA, Kan. – The Kansas Collegiate Athletic Conference (KCAC) has announced that Mike Gardner has been named as the 2024 KCAC Bissell Division Coach of the Year. Gardner led the Tabor College Bluejays to a 6-5 overall record, a three-win improvement from a season ago, as well as a 4-1 record in Bissell Division play, a two-win improvement from last season. In addition to the turnaround from last season, the Bluejays posted wins over rivals, McPherson College, Bethel College and Sterling College under Gardner's leadership. Under Gardner, 15 Tabor Football athletes earned All-Bissell honors for their efforts this season, a testament to the Gardner's strong leadership and the strong character of the Bluejay Football program as a whole. Two program records were broken during the 2024 season under Gardner's leadership, with Nathan Heilig becoming the career field goal record holder with his 56-yarder in the win over the University of Saint Mary and Brooks Gardner becoming the career leading tackler with 352 total tackles.
The 2024 season marks the 16th winning season in school history, 14 of which came under Gardner while he was either Defensive Coordinator or Head Coach.
Gardner was previously named KCAC Coach of the Year four times ('04, '05, '12 and '15) before earning the award this season.

title: Hillsboro family holds 100th Reunion
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Two immigrants, Martin Jost and Bertha Golbek, immigrated to Hillsboro and married on Nov. 15, 1891, when he was 23 and she was 16. He was born in 1868 in Prangenau, South Russia and she was born in…
content:
Martin and Bertha Jost immigrated to Hillsboro in the late 1800s. Their descendants have met every year in Hillsboro around Thanksgiving to hold a reunion. This year marked the 100th Reunion for the Jost family. Peter Jost (right) and Levi Jost work together to make a spoon at Todd Jost's welding shop Jost's Welding, Inc. on Main Street in Hillsboro on Wednesday. The former blacksmith shop has been in the Jost family for three generations. The Jost family had approximately 230 people for their Thanksgiving meal on Thursday, Nov. 28 during their Jost Family 100th Reunion. The Jost family held a worship service at the Historic Church in Hillsboro on Wednesday night during the Jost Family 100th Reunion. A 35-foot-long Jost family tree covers the wall at the traditional Mennonite dinner on Friday night at the reunion that included Vereneke, Zwiebach and more.
Two immigrants, Martin Jost and Bertha Golbek, immigrated to Hillsboro and married on Nov. 15, 1891, when he was 23 and she was 16. He was born in 1868 in Prangenau, South Russia and she was born in Friedensruh, Ukraine.
Their first child, Bertha May, was born in August of 1892 and their son Peter was born a year and seven months later. They had 12 more children after that for a total of 14 children. These children and their spouses provided 53 grandchildren. Many more great and great-great-grandchildren followed.
In 1924 Martin and Bertha held their first Jost Family Reunion in Hillsboro. The family has continued to hold the reunion every year over the Thanksgiving holiday.
'The family has met every year except for one year during World War II when some of the uncles were gone serving as well as a few aunts who were nurses,' said Todd Jost, who lives in Hillsboro and owns Jost Welding, Inc. which has been in the family for three generations.
This past Wednesday, Nov. 27 through Friday, Nov. 29, the Jost Family 100th Reunion was held in Hillsboro.
'It really is extraordinary when you think about it,' said Marilyn Jost who married into the family and lives in Hillsboro.
The family tree covers 35 feet on a wall and the five generations of descendants span 14 states including Kansas, Wisconsin, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, California, Georgia, Washington, Maine and more. While the original family homestead is located on the corner of Goldenrod and Highway 56 and a handful of Josts live in the area, most of the family has spread out across the country.
Despite living thousands of miles apart, many of the younger cousins have grown up together and formed friendships they look forward to renewing year after year.
Many older cousins have attended for over 60 years while others in the group came for the first time.
'And there were some that we normally see that were unable to come this year for whatever reason,' said Todd.
In addition to welders, the family has other artisans including woodworkers, needleworkers, stone carvers, fine artists, photographers, quilters, metal workers, glassblowers, storytellers, poets and authors. In fact, the family members were encouraged to share their creativity and bring examples of their craft to share with the rest of the family in an arts and crafts fair display they set up of Jost family creations.
They also added some events for newcomers and younger members of the family such as tours of the Hillsboro Adobe House, Kreutziger School House, Friesen Dutch Windmill and Jost Welding, Inc. (formerly Jost Blacksmith Shop).
The family held several meals at various locations throughout the three days including a traditional Mennonite meal and a traditional Thanksgiving meal at noon on Thursday. While attendance varied throughout the three days, there were about 230 people at the Thanksgiving meal which had an incredible amount of food available including 80 pounds of mashed potatoes and three eight-foot-long tables packed tight with desserts.
'How could you not love that gigantic meal? Except for the fact that there was no room on a plate nor in my stomach to try even a small percentage of what was there. I didn't even make it to the dessert table. I love stuffing so I had to try numerous ones,' said Todd.
They also did family photos, a church service and a 'Fireside Conversation' among other activities.
'I really loved the service at the old Historic Church by Tabor. It was beautiful in a way I was not expecting. It really was moving. It was spiritual,' said Todd. 'It was beautiful. The sound in there was great. The singing was—they talk about family harmony. Well, big extended family harmony is a deal.'
The family seemed to enjoy gathering and visiting most of all. The multiple events over several days allowed for many opportunities to do just that.
'There were some people who missed Wednesday, and there were some people who missed Friday. But when you get this many people, you know that not everyone's gonna be able to be there. So if you spread it out over a few days, it just kinda spills over. Everyone gets to talk to somebody. I talked to people I had never talked to before and may never again,' said Todd.
Most of all, the reunion focused on family. There is an analogy in the Jost family about the 14 original Jost children being the 14 spokes of a wagon wheel and there is a poem written about it. Kevin Jost, son of Otto Jost, brought an actual wagon wheel to the reunion with tags for people to write their names on and attach to the spoke of the aunt or uncle they belonged to. The exercise, along with the reunion in general, served as a reminder of the Jost heritage for all who attended.
'Everyone getting together regularly with their whole extended family may be a fragment of something that is old from the past. I think that kind of community that comes from maintaining family ties is something that we as a culture definitely fall short of. So I'm very, very thankful for this family and that we all we love each other. We don't always agree with each other. We don't necessarily socialize sometimes. But when it's important, we pull together. And that has to come from the family lineage that everyone has known that they were loved and that they were supposed to show that love as well,' said Todd.

title: St. Luke Therapy Clinic offers new treatment
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: A new treatment technique called dry needling is now available at the Therapy Clinic at St. Luke's Hospital & Living Center in Marion. Physical Therapy Manager and Doctor in Physical Therapy (DPT)…
content:
Physical Therapists Alex Brooks, DPT, Jennica Carlson, DPT, Karson Taulbee, DPT, and Sheryl Simmonds, DPT, now offer dry needling at the Therapy Clinic at St. Luke's Hospital & Living Center in Marion.
A new treatment technique called dry needling is now available at the Therapy Clinic at St. Luke's Hospital & Living Center in Marion.
Physical Therapy Manager and Doctor in Physical Therapy (DPT) Alex Brooks has been practicing dry needling for years.
'I had been the only one that's done it here. So we actually had three additional people get certified in it, because I was just doing it all the time,' said Brooks. 'I was having to step over and perform the treatments for other therapists because patients were responding very well.'
Dry needling, also known as trigger point dry needling and intramuscular stimulation, is a technique that treats dysfunction of skeletal muscle and connective tissue, minimizes pain and improves or regulates structural or functional damage.
'We use a monofilament needle which means it's a non-injectable so there's nothing that comes out of the needle. They're small in diameter and circumference. So we use it basically to find a trigger point to release any muscle tension,' said Jennica Carlson, DPT. 'It decreases pain and improves mobility because of the decreased pain.'
Carlson says they can also use electrical stimulation(e-stim) along with the dry needling to help the nerves and muscles work better together. This involves the insertion of the needles into specific trigger points or tight muscles which are then connected to a low-level electrical current. The e-stim passes through the needles causing the muscles to contract and relax.
'So we can neuromodulate with it. What I mean by that is every muscle has a nerve that innervates it. So if we hook it up to e-stim, it can neuromodulate, meaning help that nerve make the muscle recruit more fibers to then work correctly. So in some people, they have decreased fiber recruitment and or their muscles just aren't firing correctly especially after surgery or after injury,' said Carlson. 'So we hook their muscles up to the e-stim through the needles to make it work better.'
Dry needling works especially well for many ailments.
'I would say it works well for arthritis pain and joint-related issues. Tendonitis os another big one—tendon inflammation, overuse injuries. And probably what we used it most on is chronic pain like chronic low back pain and chronic cervical pain,' said Brooks.
'I've also used it for muscle recruitment following surgeries like an ACL tear just to recruit those muscle fibers. So we can help after any surgery of a joint,' said Carlson.
The therapist are firm believers in the treatment and want to get the word out about it.
'We want people to understand what dry needling is, what it is used for and that it is available for them here,' said Brooks.
The clinic will work with patients to see if they are eligible for insurance coverage for dry needling treatment.
'Some insurances will cover it based on the diagnosis. Other insurances do not cover it. We always prescreen the patient's insurance before we provide the service so that they're not getting stuck with some bill that they're not going to know is coming,' said Brooks.
For more information, call the St. Luke Hospital Therapy Clinic at 620-382-2863 or visit slhmarion.org.

title: Pilsen Packrats has something for everyone
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: If you are looking for a unique present for that hard-to-shop-for person on your list, Pilsen Packrats may have what you need. The store is located in Hillsboro where Dollar General used to be across…
content:
Tish and Joe Vinduska are the duo behind Pilsen Packrats, a retail space selling antiques, collectibles, furniture, household items and more. They also do auctions.
If you are looking for a unique present for that hard-to-shop-for person on your list, Pilsen Packrats may have what you need.
The store is located in Hillsboro where Dollar General used to be across from its current location.
'We got anything and everything from clothes to movies. We have oil lamps, teacups, jewelry paintings, old books, furniture. A lot of people have been coming in and collecting things from us,' said Tish Vinduska.
Pilsen Packrats is owned by Tish and her husband Joe who live in Lincolnville and have run the business since 2000.
'We started out in Pilsen. And then we had a building in Marion, and now we are in Hillsboro. We have been here for two and a half years now, but a lot of people don't realize what all we have,' said Joe. 'We started out mainly as consignment auctions, and then we also buy and sell storage units. And then we've added on a retail end to the store.'
The store has done well.
'We had to expand it from what we first had in it. We've made it bigger until it could hold more stuff. We just hope to carry on,' Joe said.
The couple says they never know exactly what they will have which makes it fun for some of their regular customers.
'We have a little bit of everything. Through the auction sales and buying the storage units, our inventory changes quite a bit,' said Joe.
Tish said she has people stop in looking for particular items. Sometimes they find them but if not, Tish keeps an eye out and calls them if the items come through.
'I call them up and say, 'Come and look'. I try very hard to find what they're looking for,' said Tish. Pilsen Packrats, in Hillsboro, sells antiques, collectibles, furniture, household items and more. They also do auctions.
While the auctions, storage units and retail store keeps them busy, the couple is always looking to add more. Tish plans to start selling plants and worm castings this spring and Joe would like to add damaged freight at some point in the future.
'We were doing flea markets, too, but we just didn't get the participation so we had to give it up. But if there was enough interest and people would sign up for it, we would probably do it again,' said Joe.
But for now, they have plenty of items for everyone.
'Stop in and see what we're all about. Come in and see us,' said Tish.
Pilsen Packrats is located at 609 Western Heights in Hillsboro and is open 1-5 p.m. on Wednesdays, 10 a.m.-5 p.m. Thursday-Saturday and sometimes on 1-5 p.m. on Sundays during the holidays. For more information, visit https://www.facebook.com/pilsenpackratsauctions or call Joe at 620-323-0249 or Tish at 620-323-0347. Pilsen Packrats, in Hillsboro, sells antiques, collectibles, furniture, household items and more. They also do auctions.

title: Sports stories to help you smile
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: Life today isn't for the faint of heart. There's plenty of bad news going around. Some view the world like a glass half empty, while others see it as a glass half full. In essence, both are true.…
content:
Life today isn't for the faint of heart. There's plenty of bad news going around. Some view the world like a glass half empty, while others see it as a glass half full. In essence, both are true. What's different is our perspective.
Humor helps me balance life's struggles. I find that a good laugh, especially at myself, helps me keep things in perspective.
As another year comes to an end, here's an amusing (I hope) look at some of the sports headlines and stories. Enjoy, and maybe even smile, at the headlines and story summaries courtesy of the satirical website 'The Babylon Bee.'
Yankees Defeat Yankees In World Series
The 2024 Major League Baseball season ended in historic fashion, as the New York Yankees successfully defeated the New York Yankees in the World Series.
Key strategies employed by the Yankees to defeat the Yankees included having Aaron Judge drop a routine fly ball, messing up a simple throw to third, and Gerrit Cole not covering first base as though he were playing for a AAA Little League team.
Though disappointed to come up short, Yankees players were quick to give credit to the team that defeated them. 'You've got to hand it to us,' said star New York slugger Aaron Judge.
'We were clearly able to stop every attempt we made to win this series. It hurts. But, hey, you've just got to tip your cap to us for beating us out there on the field tonight. We'll just rest up during the offseason, come back next spring, and make another run at it. Hopefully, we don't run up against us in the playoffs next year.'
To Save Time, Announcers Will Now Only Mention When There's Not A Flag On the Play
In a move designed to save time and lessen the stress on broadcasters' voices during games, the NFL revealed that announcers will now only mention when there's not a flag on the play.
The NFL hopes that this change will keep announcers from losing their voices before games are over by not having them mention every one of the approximately 732 penalty flags that are thrown in each game.
'This is a game-changer,' said CBS broadcaster Jim Nantz. 'With so many penalties these days, my voice couldn't hold up through a four-quarter game. With this new policy, I'll still be able to speak by the time the game ends. Honestly, since we're only mentioning when flags aren't thrown on a play, viewers will hardly hear from me at all.'
In NBA First, LeBron And Bronny Execute Synchronized Father-Son Flop
History was made on the basketball court last night when fans witnessed a once-in-a-lifetime moment as LeBron James and his son Bronny executed the NBA's first perfectly synchronized father-son flop.
The younger James joined his legendary father on the court last night for a few minutes of playing time, which culminated with both LeBron and his son simultaneously flinging themselves to the floor and crying for several minutes for no apparent reason.
'He's a chip off the old block, that's for sure,' Lakers Head Coach J.J. Reddick said following the game. 'There's been a lot of talk about whether Bronny belongs in the league, but when you see him execute a perfect flop like that alongside his father, you see the potential. You can tell LeBron has been teaching him the important things.'
In Interest of Fairness, Chicago White Sox To Be Allowed To Use Batting Tee
With a disastrous season nearing its end, Major League Baseball announced that in the interest of fairness, the Chicago White Sox would now be allowed to use a batting tee.
'If this doesn't help them score some runs, we don't know what will,' said MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred. 'We spoke with the other 29 ball clubs and reached an agreement that the White Sox should be allowed to hit from a tee. It's the least we could do, bless their hearts. If it doesn't work, we'll experiment with letting them start each inning with the bases loaded, or maybe each game they can have one player from the opposing team.'

title: Area Sports Roundup 12-18-24
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: Goessel Boys basketball – The Goessel Bluebirds hosted the 18th Annual Bluebird Classic Dec. 9-14. The boys played Little River on Tuesday, Dec. 10 and lost with a final score of 55-22. The Bluebird…
content:
Goessel
Boys basketball – The Goessel Bluebirds hosted the 18th Annual Bluebird Classic Dec. 9-14. The boys played Little River on Tuesday, Dec. 10 and lost with a final score of 55-22. The Bluebird boys next played Canton-Galva on Friday, Dec. 13 and lost with a final score of 73-33.
Coming—The Bluebirds will next play on Dec. 20 at home against Douglass.
Girls basketball – The Goessel Bluebirds hosted the 18th Annual Bluebird Classic Dec. 9-14. The girls played Little River on Tuesday, Dec. 10 and lost with a final score of 60-24. The Bluebird girls next played Canton-Galva on Friday, Dec. 13 and won with a final score of 37-31.
Coming—The Bluebirds will next play on Dec. 20 at home against Douglass.
Hillsboro
Boys basketball – The Trojan boys competed last week in the Moundridge Tournament. They played on Tuesday, Dec. 10 against Lyons and won 60-49. Next they played Inman on Thursday, Dec. 12 and won 67-27. They finished up on Friday against Moundridge losing with a final score of 53-40.
'We finished second in the Moundridge Tournament. We were able to take care of business against Lyons and Inman. On Friday we played a tough Moundridge team for the championship. During the first quarter, we played some very good defense. Moundridge was able to gain a lead, because of some costly turnovers and missed shots. I was proud of the boys for battling all night. Our effort was there. We need to clean up something offensively and defensively, but we continue to improve each practice,' said Coach Kyle Kroeker.
Coming—The Trojans will play Thursday at home against Southeast of Saline before heading into Christmas break.
Girls basketball – The Trojan girls competed last week in the Moundridge Tournament. The girls started the tournament off playing against Lyons on Tuesday, Dec. 10 and won 53-22.
'It was a good win against a really scrappy team. We struggled to get into any rhythm offensively the first half. Second half we were able to play much better. We shot the ball much better and held Lyons to six points in the second half. I was pleased with how we finished the game,' said Coach Micah Ratzlaff.
On Thursday the Trojans played Inman and barely lost with a final score of 53-51.
'I thought we did some really good things on both ends of the court but came up short in the end. The girls played hard but turnovers really hurt us down the stretch. We will continue to work and get better,' said Ratzlaff.
The tournament wrapped up Friday night when the Trojans played Moundridge and lost 31-28.
'Our girls played really hard against a very talented Moundridge team. We struggled out of the gate and found ourselves down double digits at halftime. The second half we continued to defend and work our way back into the game. We out scored Moundridge 15 to 3 in the 4th quarter and lost by three with a chance to tie it. Tough loss, but I was proud of the girls effort,' said Ratzlaff.
Coming—The Trojans will play Thursday at home against Southeast of Saline before heading into Christmas break.
Wrestling – The Hillsboro/Canton-Galva Trojan Wrestlers competed last week.
The girls participated in the Chase County Women's Jamboree on Thursday, Dec. 12. Both Aimee Kelley and Claire Morey placed 3rd and each scored 9 team points in their individual weight classes.
'In order to pick up more competition experience for our girls before Christmas break, we added the Chase Co. Girls Jamboree to our schedule on Thursday. Unfortunately, due to various circumstances, only two of the girls were available to compete. It was a great opportunity for Aimee and Claire to get some quality mat time and both were able to pick up a win,' said Coach Scott O'Hare.
The boys participated in the 2024 Railer Round Robin on Friday, Dec. 13.
Jaxon Chrislip placed 3rd and scored 11team points.
Sutton Redger placed 4th and scored 9.5 team points.
Logan Rogers placed 6th and scored 4 team points.
William Andreas placed 6th and scored 3 team points.
Lucas Sorenson placed 7th and scored 2 team points.
On Friday our boys team took the long trip out west to compete in the Railer Round Robin Scramble Tournament at Ellis. This tournament provides a great early season challenge for our wrestlers every year as we see several quality teams from central and western Kansas. It proved to be a stout challenge for our young, experienced team, but they gained some valuable experience. Our two most experienced wrestlers in sophomore Jaxon Chrislip and junior Sutton Redger did earn trips to the medal stand earning third and fourth place, respectively in two of the deepest and toughest weight classes in the tournament. In the championship bracket, Chrislip lost a tough match to the #4 ranked wrestler in 3-2-1A as well as a 9-8 heartbreaking loss to Balthazor from Hill City. He also earned an exciting win over the #6 ranked wrestler in 3–2-1A, Wilkens from Council Grove. Redger picked up three straight dominant wins by fall before dropping his first match of the season to Stephen from Hill City, currently ranked #3 in Class 3-2-1A. Although our less experienced guys did not find a lot of success as far as wins and losses, they did pick up some great experience and three of them came away with earning their first varsity wins in their young careers,' said O'Hare. 'Hopefully the wrestlers use the experiences from this tournament as motivation and get a better feel for the areas they need to improve in. We hope to get in a good week of practice before co-hosting the Marion Co. Dual Tournament this Friday.'
Coming—The Trojans will co-host the Marion County Dual Tournament Invitational on Friday at home before heading into the Christmas break.

title: Area Wide Sports Roundup 12.25.24
author: Hillsboro Free Press

Hillsboro's Ella Potucek out maneuvers the Southeast of Saline players to score for the Trojans in the Thursday, Dec. 19 game which the Trojans won 44-25.
Hillsboro
Boys basketball – The Hillsboro boys beat Halstead on Tuesday, Dec. 17.
'From the tip, it was a very fast-paced game. Both teams were on fire from the field. The first quarter score was 31-20 and at the end of the first half was 49-42. The game slowed down a little in the second half and the final was 77-66. Easton Shahan and Lincoln Wichert had an incredible scoring night with 29 and 23, respectively. We had a team season-high 24 assists led by Seth Driggers with 10 assists,' said Coach Kyle Kroeker.
On Thursday, Dec. 19, the Trojans ended their semester play with a home game against Southeast of Saline. They won 62-43.
'Our defense was solid against Southeast of Saline. We were able to play great team defense. We moved the ball really well on offense and the boys were able to find great shots all night. Lincoln Wichert and Nash Dickinson led us in scoring with 18 and 17, respectively. Noah Beavers and Anders Weisbeck did a great job cleaning up the boards,' said Kroeker. 'We are competing hard every single game. This team is getting better every time they step on the court whether in practice or game. Our shot quality is improving and we're playing really tough on defense. It will be exciting to see what we can do after Christmas break.'
Coming—The Trojans will compete after the holidays on Tuesday, Jan. 7 at Trinity.
Girls basketball – The Trojan girls played their last game for the year on Thursday, Dec. 19 where they defeated Southeast of Saline with a final score of 44-25.
'I was very pleased with our effort tonight against another tough opponent. Coming off a tough week at the Moundridge tournament and again on Tuesday facing a very talented 3A team at Halstead I was hoping we had enough gas in the tank to show up and execute and compete at a high level against another tough opponent with SE of Saline. From the jump, I could tell the girls were locked in and ready to go. We struggled early offensively, but our defense kept us in the game through the first two quarters down by two at half. I challenged the girls to dig deep and play with confidence and just trust in each other and play with confidence. They did just that in the second half. We were able to play with good pace and get back defensively and get stops holding SE of Saline to eight points in the second half,' said Coach Micah Ratzlaff. 'On offense, we had good ball movement and we were patient enough and confident enough to not settle for bad shots, take care of the ball, and execute really well in the second half. We were also able to keep up our defensive intensity and contain the drive, contest shots, and get stops on defense. We definitely got better tonight and as a coach it's always fun to see how excited the girls were about the win! We have played a really tough schedule and that will continue after the Christmas break. Our goal is to enjoy the game of basketball and to compete at a high level and accept every challenge in front of us! I am proud of my team and my amazing coaches on a daily basis. We are all looking forward to a chance to take a quick break and get back into it after the Holidays. Merry Christmas everyone from the Trojan girls basketball team.'
Coming—The Trojans will compete after the holidays on Tuesday, Jan. 7 at Trinity.

Survivors include sister-in-law Ruby (Greg) Wilkinson, nephews Brian (Jan) Scharping and Jeff (Julie) Scharping. Great nephews Andrew (Emma) Scharping, Robert Scharping, Eric Scharping, and Nicholas Scharping. Great nieces Heather (Cody) Baldwin, Elizabeth (Seth) Boswell, and Megan (Forrest) Jenkins. Great-great nephews Joseph and Paul Boswell, Charles Scharping, and great-great niece and nephew, Aspen and Leif Jenkins as well as many other relatives and friends. Memorial service will be held on Friday, December 27 at 11 a.m. at First Mennonite Church in Hillsboro, Kansas. Private family burial will take place at a later date, Lehigh Mennonite Cemetery.
Memorial: First Mennonite Church, 102 S. Ash St., Hillsboro, Kansas, 67063.

title: KDOT, KHP and KTA stress the impact of impaired driving during the holidays
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: The holiday season often brings people together to celebrate. The Kansas Department of Transportation, Kansas Highway Patrol and Kansas Turnpike Authority remind all drivers to understand the impact…
content:
The holiday season often brings people together to celebrate. The Kansas Department of Transportation, Kansas Highway Patrol and Kansas Turnpike Authority remind all drivers to understand the impact of impaired driving during their celebrations.
Impaired driving is illegal and deadly. Last year from Dec. 19, 2023-Jan. 1, 2024, KDOT records indicate nine people died in Kansas crashes. Impairment including drugs and alcohol was involved in 19 crashes where 12 people were injured.
'We're reminded of the value of our relationships with others during each holiday season,' said KDOT Transportation Secretary Calvin Reed. 'Everyone should do their part to make sure they arrive at their holiday celebrations safely.'
Drivers will see increased law enforcement presence on Kansas roads during the holiday season, as part of the national campaigns Drive Sober or Get Pulled Over and If you Feel Different, You Drive Different. Drive High, Get a DUI.
'During this Christmas and New Year's holiday, law enforcement officers across the state are determined to prevent impaired driving crashes that lead to injury and fatal crashes,' said KHP Superintendent Colonel Erik Smith.
The average cost of a DUI is about $10,000 in attorney's fees, fines, court costs, lost time at work, higher insurance rates and more. Offenders can also lose their driver's licenses.
'Driving impaired is a choice,' said KTA CEO Steve Hewitt. 'It's essential for everyone to take responsibility, plan ahead and ensure their celebrations don't end in tragedy.'
KDOT, KHP and KTA want all drivers to make traffic safety a priority throughout the year as well as during the holidays. Before the celebrations begin, make a plan. Use a designated driver, a rideshare or a cab. If a friend is leaving a holiday celebration impaired, take the keys. If you see an impaired driver on the road, contact law enforcement.
For more information on impaired driving: www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drunk-driving.
For the latest updates on road closures and conditions, visit KanDrive.gov, call 511 in Kansas or 866-511-5368 outside Kansas. Travelers who need assistance on the highway can dial *47 for the KHP or *582 while on the KTA. If it's an emergency, call 911.

title: Improvements and more improvements are coming to city rec
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: Either a program moves forward or backward. It rarely stays the same. In the midst of changes at the top of Hillsboro's recreation program, with a new director at the helm since July, the recreation…
content:
Either a program moves forward or backward. It rarely stays the same.
In the midst of changes at the top of Hillsboro's recreation program, with a new director at the helm since July, the recreation program is definitely moving forward.
It helps that new director David Ediger is no stranger to leading a program. It's hard to imagine how Hillsboro could be more fortunate than to have Ediger make the transition from athletic director at Tabor College to being Director of Parks and Recreation in Hillsboro.
To be fair, this isn't Ediger's first rodeo as head of Hillsboro's rec program. He was the director in 1994-95 when he was finishing up as a student at Tabor College, before graduating in 1995. That was shortly before Hillsboro opened the Sports Complex, so facilities have greatly changed since then.
In his new role, Ediger oversees the sports complex, recreation department, swimming pool, splash pad, golf course, bowling alley, park, and museums. Ediger is quick to credit others for any initial success he's had in his new role, saying, 'I have really good people that I oversee, who do a great job in all of these areas.'
It's easy to look at a rec program in terms of how many people, especially school-age kids, benefit from participating in different sports or activities. But during the late fall and winter months, the number of program offerings are usually slim because there are school programs that fill the void.
If you think that means nothing is happening during these months, think again. A lot is happening under the radar. For example, since Ediger took the helm of the rec program, he and other city employees have been busy making improvements to the facilities.
'One improvement is that we enclosed more of the pavilion at the complex to allow us to store all of our equipment in one place so we can better account for what we have,' said Ediger. 'We also are moving in the fence on the field that the high school softball team plays on. This will give them a quality field to play on with a real fence.
'Other improvements we are looking at are giving Memorial Field an upgrade, exploring adding pickleball courts (currently the only pickleball courts are on Tabor's campus), sand volleyball courts, a dog park, and a wiffle ball field to the complex, along with a few other minor items.
'We are also working on improvements to the playground area at the sports complex, and some upgrades in the park,' said Ediger.
One thing I especially appreciate about Ediger is his desire to grow the rec program to benefit more people. Granted, it's easy to say that's a goal. It's another thing entirely to make it happen. I, for one, believe Ediger takes that goal seriously.
'I want the rec program to continue to grow,' said Ediger. 'I am always looking at how to build upon and improve what we currently have.
'We hosted area rec directors in November to share ideas and talk about how we can improve our programs individually and as surrounding communities as we compete with each other.
'We want to give the kids a really good experience. Adding such programs as bowling, a junior golf league and as an after-school program are some of the ideas we are trying to get into practice.
'We also discussed what programs for adults we all have and how we can improve and add those into our programs. We have a lot of youth programs, but not many for adults. I will need to get creative and find ways to give our adults opportunities as well,' said Ediger.
The city has a rec director with a servant's heart and attitude. While there's a limit to how much anyone can do given how much time, and/or money is available, it's nice to have someone in this role who truly wants to make a difference.
We are blessed to have many good employees across the spectrum of city departments working on our behalf. You can add David Ediger to the list of employees who take their responsibility, and how to best use our tax dollars, seriously.

title: Hillsboro to increase rates
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council voted to increase utility rates in their last meeting of the year on Tuesday, Dec. 17. The new rates will be effective in January. 'But we won't actually see it on a bill…
content:
The Hillsboro City Council voted to increase utility rates in their last meeting of the year on Tuesday, Dec. 17. The new rates will be effective in January.
'But we won't actually see it on a bill until February. That's just how it falls on the billing cycle,' said Hillsboro City Administrator Matt Stiles.
For water, the base rate went from $29 to $34 for residential and $36 for commercial.
The conservation tier increases for residential are $6.71 for 0-7,000 gallons; $6.85 for 7,001-15,000; $6.98 for 15,001-30,000; and $7.12 for 30,001 +. The conservation tier increases for commercial uses are $6.71 for 0-15,000; $6.85 for 15,001-40,000; $6.98 for 40,001-80,000; and $7.12 for 80,000 +.
For trash, the monthly service charge per residential user for one trash poly cart within city limits is $16.75 and outside city limits is $18.25. Additional trash poly carts, subject to availability, may be provided upon request for an additional charge of $7.50 per cart. There are a variety of options available for commercial users.
For recycling, the minimum monthly service charger for residential users for one recycling cart up to 95 gallons is $5 within city limits and $5.35 outside city limits. An additional monthly charge of $1.75 will be charged for a second recycling cart up to 95 gallons, subject to availability. Service charges apply to all residential users regardless of use of recycling.
There are a variety of options available for commercial users. See the city website or call the city office for more information if needed.
The council approved a contest for the public to name the bowling alley. The city will be accepting submissions from Jan. 3 – 31. Submissions can be left in person at the city office at 118 E. Grand Ave or the bowling alley at 121 S. Main St. or through a QR code that can be found on flyers around town and on the city's Facebook page.
Submissions will be evaluated based on creativity, originality, relevance and memorability. A panel made up of Stiles, Mayor Lou Thurston, Director of Parks and Recreation David Ediger and current bowling alley staff Jackie and Becky Gage will review the entries and choose a winner to be announced at the Feb. 18 council meeting.
The prize for the winner will be a year of free bowling.
Stiles told the council that the Hillsboro Fire Department has a Firefighters Relief Organization (FRA) that all volunteers become members of when they are accepted into the department.
'The FRA collects dues and fundraises and provides a combination of insurance policies for death, dismemberment, incapacitation and injury. The FRA provides monetary support to firefighters in need through various programs,' said Stiles.
He explained that the FRA administers the annuity funded by the Kansas State Insurance Department's 2% premium tax on all fire and lighting policies written in the state, allowing members who serve for
20 years or more to retire and receive a cash payment based on years of service. The FRA has a life insurance policy through USAlliance for $25,000 for all active members.
'As part of the fire station project, we have talked a lot about design that reduces the risk of cancer. Exposure to chemicals and smoke raises the risk of cancer in firefighters by 9% and death from cancer by 15% compared to the non-firefighter population. In response to that, the FRA has asked the city to consider providing premium assistance for a cancer policy,' said Stiles.
Stiles went over the quotes provided by the FRA for policies for Cancer and critical illness that includes cancer, heart attack and stroke and explained that if a covered person is diagnosed with cancer within certain definitions, they will receive a payout.
He said like most insurance of this type, it is age banded, meaning the older you are the more the cost.
'A $15,000 Cancer only policy—the middle coverage amount—for the current group would be $2,766.96. If the Council were to consider contributing to an additional FRA cancer policy, I would suggest an amount up to $2,800. Providing up to $2,800 in premium support would allow for the purchase of a $15,000 cancer coverage policy or be used to reduce the cost of a higher level of coverage, the difference being paid by the FRA. Given that there are a lot of options to consider, members of the FRA may want to fund a policy in addition to the $2,800 offered by the city. Funds for this policy would be taken from the fire department budget,' said Stiles.
The council approved purchasing the cancer insurance policy.
In other business, the council:
* approved vouchers totaling $246,034.94.
* approved an estimate of $14,122.18 to repair the Peterbuilt trash truck
* approved adopting the amended 2024 budget
* approved the renewal of cereal malt beverage licenses for Casey's, Ampride, Dollar General, Pizza Hut, Pueblo Viejo and the city golf course.
* heard an update on the fire station open house the council held to discuss the fire station project with the community. Stiles reported that 14 community members attended. 'I know there were several conversations with those community members. Some specific questions I heard were about the inclusion of the living quarters to the project, how the project will be paid for, what would happen to the current station along with more technical questions about the station itself. The overall response was positive and supportive. I'm sure there have been more community members offering their opinions outside of the meeting. Most of the people I've spoken with are little intimidated by the price but understand that the project will not get cheaper and have generally been supportive,' said Stiles.
The council voted to move forward on the project and begin the process for the USDA loan and assemble the needed procurement and environmental documents.

title: Where have all the student athletes gone?
author: Joe Kleinsasser
description: What is going on with high school sports – in particular, basketball? Is it my imagination or are fewer student athletes participating than previously? Let's not draw any hasty conclusions, but…
content:
What is going on with high school sports – in particular, basketball? Is it my imagination or are fewer student athletes participating than previously?
Let's not draw any hasty conclusions, but anecdotally, one area school has only eight girls playing high school basketball. Even Hillsboro High School, with its traditionally successful basketball program, has only 11 girls playing the sport this season.
In an effort to better understand the situation, I sought and received input from a number of people either currently or formerly involved in high school athletics. The general consensus is that overall, the number of student athletes participating in basketball is down.
While there are multiple reasons why that's the case, there was some agreement on the major challenges affecting the number of student athletes participating in high school sports. One such factor is club sports – specifically club softball, volleyball, track, and swimming.
Some kids and their parents believe it is advantageous to focus on one sport instead of playing multiple sports. In fact, one high school coach heard a junior college volleyball coach tell a high school athlete that they needed to play club volleyball all winter or he wouldn't recruit them. That same high school girls basketball coach emphatically said club volleyball is destroying high school basketball.
Basketball is tougher and more work than volleyball, according to one coach, and some girls choose the easier route. Club volleyball supporters want athletes to play year round, which has contributed to more arm injuries than ever before, due to overuse.
One basketball official observed that some of today's student athletes are soft, which doesn't mean they aren't capable and talented. It means they aren't as committed or devoted to working hard to be the best they can be while playing a sport.
While some high school coaches of fall sports prefer that student-athletes focus on their particular fall sport and not basketball, focusing on one sport runs counter to what many college coaches preach, which is a preference that student-athletes play multiple sports.
Then again, sometimes the lack of student participation in team sports is simply basic math. It's a numbers game. There are cycles where there aren't as many male or female students available to play high school sports, particularly in schools with lower enrollments.
It's hard to conceive of a shortage of players when witnessing so many young kids playing sports. But it seems that many students stop participating after junior high, which is unfortunate, according to one former coach. Many boys are late bloomers physically, and if they'd stick with it, they might develop into a decent to very good student-athlete in high school. Instead, some kids figure they won't ever play on the varsity high school team, so why bother going out?
Others are playing so much summer basketball at a young age that they are burned out before high school, according to one former coach.
Playing sports takes a time commitment, which is a challenge for some students. Those students may also be involved in music and other things like church and youth activities. Meanwhile, some kids would rather have a job and make some money. An understanding coach might still be able to work with them, but not all do.
Some area activity directors say one challenge is the length of a sports season, and some students see it as too much work. Interestingly, there also seems to be a general disinterest in the sport of basketball by some student athletes.
It seems the number of student athletes participating in two or three sports a year is declining, which reduces the number of participants in some sports.
So, is this a problem or not? It largely depends on your perspective and position on specializing in a single sport versus participating in multiple sports.

title: Hillsboro discusses convenience fees
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Jan. 7 which began with...
content:
The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Jan. 7 which began with the swearing-in of re-elected council members Byron McCarty and Jeff Jorgenson.
Mayor Lou Thurston congratulated both on their re-election and said he looks forward to a great year with them on the council.
Hillsboro City Administrator Matt Stiles reminded the council that the new credit card convenience fee system for electronic payments transitioned on Jan. 1. He explained that there were initial issues making the switch to the new system, but all is working well now.
'While there were some complaints about the fee itself, the primary issue's been technical—has some issues with the card readers and the credit card processing terminals didn't work correctly on Jan. 2. It took over a day to resolve the problems, but the system is now functioning as expected,' said Stiles.
Thurston addressed comments from the public on social media that the city was trying to make more money with the new system.
'This action increases no revenue to the city other than it keeps us from having to pay the associated costs that go along with credit card fees. It's more a way to avoid costs, because it was costing us over $30,000 in credit fees annually. The city is not making a dime on this. We're just trying to stop us from losing money,' said Thurston.
The convenience fees apply to credit card, debit card, eCheck, and ACH payments, including utility autopay customers. These fees are set by the payment processor, Forte, and are not retained by the city. Card payments are 2.5% of the transaction (minimum of $1.95) and eCheck payments are $1.75 per transaction.
Stiles told the council that the city has been awarded a KDOT Transportation Alternatives grant to install a hike/bike trail on Orchard Drive, connecting Ash Street and Hickory Street near Sonic.
'An unexpected benefit of this grant is the inclusion of funding for engineering services—a rare addition, as KDOT typically does not cover engineering costs in these projects. To access the engineering funds, the city is required to conduct a competitive selection process for engineers,' said Stiles. 'It will be advertised on the city website and sent directly to at least three engineers from KDOT's prequalified list. Proposals are due by Jan. 31 with the engineer selection scheduled for the Feb. 18 meeting. EBH, the city engineer, is a prequalified KDOT engineer and will be invited to submit a proposal.'
Stiles explained that including engineering services in the grant saves the city approximately $90,000, covering design, administration and inspection costs.
Stiles informed the council that the Recreation Department has decided to pilot an annual bowling membership program to increase usage of the bowling alley.
'This program is modeled similarly to the annual membership programs for the city golf course and the Delores Dalke Family Aquatic Center (DDFAC). For an annual fee, members can access the bowling alley during public hours. Membership categories include Single, Family and Youth levels. Benefits include free bowling during open hours (excluding private parties and league fees), a 10% discount on facility rentals, complimentary house ball and shoe rentals and one exclusive 'Members Only' night at the alley,' said Stiles. 'This membership model is being tested for 2025 as staff have limited data on expected participation.'
Membership pricing is as follows:
• Family Membership (includes all IRS dependents in the household): $250 annually
• Single Membership: $125 annually
• Youth Membership: $125 annually
To promote membership participation and support employee wellness, the city will provide all regular full-time and part-time employees, as well as volunteer firefighters on the Hillsboro Fire Department, with a 50% reduction on their chosen annual membership fee at Bluejay Lanes. This discount applies only to the membership tier selected by the employee or firefighter and is non-transferable. The council approved the policy.
In other business, the council:
* approved vouchers totaling $352,151.98.
* discussed a pay estimate of $245,036.29 for the Adams Street project. The pay estimate was approved.
* approved a no-cost change order for the daycare project, adding five days to the project due to weather.
* heard about the appointment of Dale Shewey to the Recreation Commission.
* heard a report from Stiles of a 4% drop in sales tax collections for the year.
* again discussed moving council meeting times with council members expressing their availability and flexibility for meeting times. The council decided to revisit the topic at the next meeting.
* heard public and council comments expressing gratitude for the support and dedication of first responders and city staff during recent snow events.

title: Celebration of a career: Brubacher calls it a day, transitions to dean of enrollment
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: HILLSBORO, Kan.– Except for a couple of years, there has been a...
content:
HILLSBORO, Kan.– Except for a couple of years, there has been a Brubacher in the Tabor College athletic department since the 1970s, but that fact will soon change. Grant Brubacher has been involved in Bluejay athletics in some sort of way since before he could remember but now enters the academic realm as he takes on the title of Dean of Enrollment at Tabor College.
Brubacher is no stranger to Tabor, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts in business administration with concentrations in accounting and finance management in 2006. While excelling in the classroom, Brubacher competed as a three-sport athlete for the Bluejays, earning KCAC All-Conference honors in Baseball, Men's Basketball, and Men's Soccer, as well as KCAC Academic All-Conference and NAIA All-America Scholar Athlete honors in each sport. Brubacher was named KCAC Men's Soccer Offensive Player of the Year in 2004 and named an NAIA Men's Basketball Honorable Mention All-American that same season.
Brubacher played that success as a student-athlete into his first head coaching role, or more appropriately roles, as he was named the Assistant Baseball Coach for the Bluejays in 2006. Additionally, he took over both Bluejay Men's and Women's Soccer programs in the fall of 2007, leading both programs until 2013, when he stepped down from the Women's Soccer program and continued to lead the Men's squad.
Grant picked up his 100th career win during the 2020 season in a 2-nil decision over conference foe Avila University. The following season, the Bluejays earned their first NAIA Men's Soccer Tournament berth since the 1961 season.
Brubacher was inducted into the Tabor College Athletic Hall of Fame in 2018.
As much as Brubacher loved coaching, when the Dean of Enrollment position was created, he knew it was the perfect time to make the transition.
'It's been an honor to serve as the men's soccer for the last 18 seasons,' said Brubacher. 'I am grateful for the players who trusted Tabor and our program enough to study and play here. The relationships formed with these young men is what I will miss the most.'
The next big task following Brubacher's transition into the academic world was to find a worthy successor, which seemed like a no-brainer to Brubacher and the Tabor College administration, as they had the perfect candidate in mind, enter Rafael Marins.
Rafael Marins stepped foot in Hillsboro for the first time in the fall of 2010 as a Freshman from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil and made an immediate impact for Coach Brubacher and the Bluejays, earning a starting spot his first year and scoring his first career goal in a win over Saint Gregory's University (Okla.). Marins went on to start the remaining three seasons of his career before serving as a Student Assistant under Brubacher during the 2014 season while he finished his degree.
Marins moved to the Pacific Northwest following graduation, settling down in Washington and securing a job as a coach for Fuerza FC, a women's elite adult amateur team in Marysville, WA. In 2017, Marins was hired as the Head Women's Soccer Coach at Everett Community College in Everett, WA., a job he held until 2021 when he was named as the Head Men's Soccer Coach at Everett. Following his stint at the junior college level, Marins served as a coach for Everett FC Premier Youth Soccer Club from 2022-24.
In May of 2024, Marins got the call from Tabor about potentially returning to his alma mater to serve as the program's first Associate Head Coach. Marins agreed and moved his family from Washington back to Hillsboro and spent the 2024 season coaching alongside his mentor, Grant Brubacher.
With the book closing on the 2024 campaign almost two months ago, Marins now has the chance to make his mark on the Bluejay Men's Soccer program. Grant Brubacher is excited for his protégé to take the reins.
'I am excited for the program's future with Rafa stepping into the Head Coaching role. It is rewarding to see a former player take the reins, and I am confident he will continue to grow the program. I look forward to watching them play in the fall,' said Brubacher.

title: Local pharmacies push for reform
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Many area pharmacies will be closed on Wednesday, Feb. 5 to advocate for pharmacy benefit managers (PBM) reform. 'Pharmacy benefit managers are powerful corporations that act as middlemen between…
content:
Many area pharmacies will be closed on Wednesday, Feb. 5 to advocate for pharmacy benefit managers (PBM) reform.
'Pharmacy benefit managers are powerful corporations that act as middlemen between pharmacies, insurance companies and drug companies. While they claim to lower drug costs, their business practices often have the opposite effect. PBMs decide which pharmacies can be part of their networks, limiting patient choice. They reimburse pharmacies less than the cost of the medication, driving many small, independent pharmacies out of business. They pocket the spread—the difference between what they charge insurers and what they pay pharmacies—raising costs for patients and taxpayers,' said Traci Lanning, owner of Lanning Pharmacy in Marion.
Eric Driggers, owner of Hillsboro Hometown Pharmacy, explains that PBM reform is more critical than it has ever been as roughly eight retail pharmacies close every day due to a lack of reimbursement.
According to Lanning, without PBM reform, the consequences will ripple across communities causing: Reduced access: patients may need to travel longer distances for medications and essential healthcare services.
Higher costs: PBM practices increase premiums and out-of-pocket costs for everyone.
Healthcare strain: Hospitals and clinics will face increased pressure as patients struggle to manage their medications effectively.
According to Hesston Pharmacy, if nothing changes this year, closures of Kansas pharmacies will continue at a terrifying rate. They stated in a Facebook post that pharmacies that do not stay open can't safely take care of all the extra prescriptions from other pharmacies closing. And mail-order services often take too long or don't keep medicine safe, which could hurt patients.
So all three pharmacies will be closed all or most of the day on Feb. 5. And many pharmacists will use that time to attend the Kansas Pharmacists Association (KPhA) Advocacy Day in Topeka that day.
'Our pharmacy will be closed until 3 p.m. on Wednesday, February 5th to allow our staff to head to Topeka to stand up for our pharmacy and our patients! We'll work with lawmakers to make sure people can get their medicines, stop pharmacies from closing, and fix unfair PBM rules,' said Hesston Pharmacy on their post.
'I apologize for any inconvenience this may cause, but it is now or never for many Kansas pharmacies's ability to serve their communities. For emergencies, HHP will be available after 2 p.m.,' said Driggers.
'By closing together we are hoping to raise public awareness of PBM abuse and show lawmakers and patients that we are committed to protecting our future,' said Lanning.
And customers can help as well.
Driggers says to help ensure local retail pharmacies remain in business, tell lawmakers that PBM reform is needed.
'Contact lawmakers and urge them to protect medication access, stop pharmacy closures and support PBM reform now. Share your story about why access to a local pharmacy matters. Advocate for fair treatment of pharmacies to ensure continued access for our communities. We have an example letter from KPhA that we have given to many of our patients. The letters are available at our pharmacy and can be emailed to people as well,' said Lanning.
For example letters, call the pharmacy at 620-382-2135, email lanningrx@yahoo.com or stop by at 217 E. Main in Marion.
A federal bill to reform pharmacy benefit managers was introduced in the Senate in April of 2023 that establishes requirements for pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) with respect to services provided to health insurance plans.
According to the bill, PBMs must report annually to the plan sponsor certain information about the PBM's services, including the amount of prescription drug copayment assistance funded by drug manufacturers, a list of covered drugs billed under the plan during the reporting period and the total net spending by the health plan on prescription drugs. PBMs also must provide plan sponsors with a supplementary report every six months with specified information about drugs that were dispensed under the plan by pharmacies that are wholly or partially owned by the PBM.
The bill also prohibits spread pricing. Under the bill, spread pricing occurs when a PBM charges an insurance plan (or an insurance plan charges plan participants) a price for a prescription drug that exceeds the price paid to the pharmacy for the drug.
Finally, PBMs must remit to the plan sponsor all rebates, fees, alternative discounts and other remuneration received from a drug manufacturer. The bill establishes civil penalties for violations of these requirements and provides funding for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and the Department of Labor to implement the provisions of this bill.
As the pharmacists and KphA wait for the bill to pass, they are taking action on Feb. 5.
And while it is a serious issue and there is a need for action, Driggers does not want to scare people.
'It is not as bad at Hillsboro Hometown Pharmacy as many other rural pharmacies. It is more of a concern that I am monitoring vs. a crisis that others are experiencing. I am trying to balance the fact that change is needed but not strike fear in the community that the pharmacy is about to go out of business. That is NOT where we are at,' said Driggers. 'Up to this point I have been able to accept pretty much everything insurance and network. Without change, I am not sure that will always be the case. This is my main concern. Some network's reimbursement is so bad that I could see us not being able to participate. This is a really hard decision. If we are not in the network, we wouldn't be able to process prescriptions for people with that insurance. That is not how I want to serve the community.'
Lanning is in the same situation.
'We are fortunate that PBM tactics have not had a huge impact on us yet, but each year there are reimbursement changes and people switching to Medicare D plans so there is always a little bit of unknown at the beginning of each year. We are hopeful that our lawmakers pass the reform that is needed so in the future we are not having to make the difficult decisions that many other pharmacies in the state are having to make now,' said Lanning.

title: National Stalking Awareness Month: shining a light on a pervasive crime
author: Hillsboro Free Press
description: January is National Stalking Awareness Month (NSAM), a time dedicated to raising awareness about the serious and often misunderstood crime of stalking. Stalking involves a pattern of behavior directed…
content:
Safehope staff wore something sparkly on Jan. 18 as a reminder to shine a light on stalking for Stalking Awareness Month. Stalking is a serious issue that affects millions each year and often goes unnoticed.
January is National Stalking Awareness Month (NSAM), a time dedicated to raising awareness about the serious and often misunderstood crime of stalking.
Stalking involves a pattern of behavior directed at a specific person that would cause a reasonable individual to feel fear or concern for their safety.
Stalking affects millions across the United States. Projectrest.org states that nationally, it is estimated that 1 in 3 women and 1 in 6 men will be stalked sometime in their lifetime. This translates to millions of individuals who have experienced the fear and distress associated with stalking behaviors.
In 2023, Kansas had 867 reported cases of stalking. The highest percentage was in the 30-34 male/female age bracket. 85% of the victims reported their stalker was someone they had known according to a report by the KBI.
And stalking happens here in Marion County as well as in nearby McPherson and Harvey Counties.
Safehope, a non-profit, serving Harvey, Marion and McPherson counties provides advocacy and support to all survivors and secondary victims of domestic and sexual assault, mass violence, and stalking; while seeking social change through awareness, education, and prevention. They have been working with victims of stalking and compiled these interesting statistics on stalking cases in 2024: Marion County, a population of 11,690, had 18 people served by Safehope.
McPherson County, a population of 30,091 had 8 people served by Safehope.
Harvey County, a population of 33, 504 had 21 people served by Safehope.
And these are just the number of cases that have been reported to Safehope. Many may go through police departments, may file an order of protection online or choose to not report at all.
Recognizing and Responding to Stalking
Recognizing stalking is crucial for prevention and support. Common behaviors exhibited by stalkers include: Following or spying on the victim
Unwanted phone calls, texts, or messages
Showing up uninvited at places frequented by the victim
Sending unwanted gifts or letters
Monitoring the victim's computer or phone usage
Using technology, such as GPS, to track the victim's location
If you or someone you know is experiencing stalking, it's important to take all threats seriously and seek help immediately. Contact your local law enforcement, reach out to an advocate at the Safehope Helpline available 24 hours a day 7 days a week at (316) 283-0350 or (800) 487-0510, or reach out to trusted family and friends for support.
Keeping a detailed log of all incidents can also be helpful in building a case against the stalker.
Safehope's services are free, confidential and voluntary. The Resiliency Center by Safehope, located at 104 W 17th Street in Newton, offers free therapy to Safehope participants by licensed therapists. Therapeutic services include trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, play therapy, sand therapy and mindfulness. Safehope's Helpline is available 24 hours a day 7 days a week providing supportive services by professionally trained staff offering crisis intervention, advocacy and support to address the needs of victims and their children.
Support Provided by Safehope in 2024: 17,979 services to 783 survivors
3193 helpline calls
45 survivors and 1,436 nights in shelter
Assisted with 108 protection orders
834 therapy appointments
The Marion Safehope office is located at 422 E. Main Street and the Newton office is located at 316 N. Oak.
National Stalking Awareness Month serves as a vital reminder of the prevalence and seriousness
of stalking. By increasing awareness, providing education and supporting victims, communities can work together to prevent stalking and ensure the safety and well-being of all individuals.

title: Hillsboro City Council discusses snow removal
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Jan. 21 where they heard from City Administrator Matt Stiles that he and his staff are working on revising the snow and ice ordinance. 'If you go back and…
content:
The Hillsboro City Council met on Tuesday, Jan. 21 where they heard from City Administrator Matt Stiles that he and his staff are working on revising the snow and ice ordinance.
'If you go back and look at it, it's a little bit out of date and there's a few things that need to be changed on that. So we're going to be making some adjustments with that,' said Stiles.
Stiles explained that they had some complaints with how the city handled the snow removal with the recent storms, but that most people are really good about it.
'There's just a few things that can be adjusted,' said Stiles.
Stiles said he met with Dale Dalke, Hillsboro Street Supervisor, who gave suggestions as well for the snow and ice removal from the streets.
Mayor Lou Thurston mentioned that he had comments made to him regarding snow and the clearing of sidewalks.
'It is actually the responsibility of the property owner and not the city to clear your sidewalks. I would like to throw out that reminder to everybody that our sidewalks are still part of our property owner's responsibility. And this one has been particularly tough, first of all, because of the large amount of snow we got to start and then the extreme cold temperature. So it's been a challenge,' said Thurston.
Thurston went on to say that the Hillsboro Police Department has helped with code enforcement for snow in the downtown area to try to keep the sidewalks cleared off.
'That was a little tougher this year than I think it's been in past years. I just commend our city crews for the hard work they do in making sure we can get around, but also we have a responsibility as individuals,' said Thurston.
The council adopted Ordinance 1402 which corrects a few accidental errors made in Ordinance 1401 that previously adjusted utility rates. According to the new ordinance, the city will charge $10 to pick up car tires, $15 for truck tires and $20 for tractor tires.
Stiles explained to the council that Harvey County will replace a large box culvert on Indigo Rd/ the 13-Mile Road, north of US-50, starting Feb. 3.
'The project is anticipated to last until the end of April. Due to the culvert's location, viable detour options are limited. The southernmost open street appears to be 70th Street. Harvey County has installed detour signs within the city to alleviate confusion, and we encourage residents to use K-15 as an alternative route,' said Stiles.
The council also voted to change the council meeting times from 6:30 p.m. to 4 p.m.
The next meeting will be on Tuesday, Feb. 4.
In other business, the council:
* approved vouchers totaling $458,728.10
* approved CDBG vouchers totaling $9,450
* met in a land bank meeting and reviewed 2024 activity and current property
* learned that Carolyn Ray, a member of the Hillsboro Golf Course Pro Shop team since 2015 died on Jan. 15 due to complications from a stroke. Funeral arrangements have not yet been announced.
* heard that the KPP PACE solar project is set to begin in March with the facility expected to be fully operational by early February 2026.
* learned that Marion County Emergency Management has requested to rent space in the AMPI building to store equipment currently housed at the former Building Center location. A draft lease agreement has been sent to the county for review.
* heard that the RHID application for the Mennonite Housing Project has been approved by the State Department of Commerce. A resolution will be included on the Feb. 4 agenda. Following this, there will be a protest period for other taxing entities.
'We are working with Mennonite Housing on finalizing their design and plan, which should be completed by February. If all proceeds as planned, groundbreaking will take place in late March or early April,' said Stiles.

title: Goessel's Voth releases children's book
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Gayle Voth has always worked with children in one way or another. Voth, who has lived in Goessel her entire life, ran a preschool in town for 37 years. 'I also worked for a number of years at the…
content:
Gayle Voth recently wrote Through the School Doors -Tales of Recess, Math, and Mop Buckets. She will be holding a signing for the book this weekend at Faith & Life Bookstore in Newton.
Gayle Voth has always worked with children in one way or another. Voth, who has lived in Goessel her entire life, ran a preschool in town for 37 years.
'I also worked for a number of years at the Bethesda Nursing home here in town and tried to bring in children for various things. That's how I gravitate. I think about how you can involve children. When I decided to retire from Bethesda, I decided to do some subbing. That's what I've been doing for the past two and a half years,' said Voth.
In addition to substitute teaching, she has taught in various capacities such as Bible school and Sunday school.
'Then when I retired I just thought it would be really fun to write a children's book,' said Voth.
So about nine months ago, she started working on her book.
'I made a couple of false starts and then I latched onto this topic of school. I use poems to tell individual stories about things that happen in the school,' she said.
Voth said the book covers topics children might commonly encounter in school.
'Most of them have a little bit of a problem that the main character has to solve. For instance, there's a poem called School Lunches. There's one about a backpack, one about the janitor's closet and one about recess. Those are some of the titles,' said Voth. 'I think most people will find it amusing, especially with the illustrations.'
The illustrations are done by a cousin, Aaron Ratzlaff, who also grew up in Goessel.
'It was a lot of fun to see Aaron's illustrations. I knew the style of his illustrations and that they would likely be on the humorous side. We both come from a bloodline where humor has been pretty important, and I think that's why our ideas fit together so well. He was able to perfectly capture the essence of each poem through his illustrations,' said Voth.
According to Voth, the book is geared toward second to fifth-graders.
'But I think some younger kids could get some value out of it, and I think all the way into adults can enjoy it as well. I think adults and older kids will be able to kind of relate to a lot of the topics in there, too,' she said.
The author found her favorite part of the experience was writing in poem format.
'I liked trying to find words that would be descriptive and would tell the story that I was getting at,' she said.
For Voth, the hardest part was having to pay for it all.
'I self-published and it's not cheap to do that,' she said.
But even that couldn't dampen her amazing experience of writing and publishing her first book.
'It was all really more or less quite a bit of fun. I really thought it was a fun process,' she said.
Will the author be writing more books in the future?
'I probably will wait and see. I would love to, but we'll have to see how things play out. I do have more ideas. We'll see what happens,' said Voth.
The book is available at Faith & Life Bookstore at 606 N. Main Street in Newton and at Goessel Grocery & Deli on East Main Street in Goessel. Or contact Voth directly in person or through Facebook at https://www.facebook.com/gayle.voth. Voth may try to get the book into more bookstores or on Amazon but is still looking into those options.
To get a signed copy and meet the author, head to the book signing from 10 a.m. to noon on Saturday, Feb. 8 at Faith and Life Bookstore in Newton.

title: Hanschu headed to study in Tasmania
author: Laura Fowler Paulus
description: Hillsboro's Jaxxon Hanschu has been working at Dale's Supermarket for the last few months, but he is preparing for quite the adventure this semester. 'On February 10th, I will be flying to Hobart,…
content:
Annabella Diaz and Hillsboro's Jaxxon Hanschu will spend a semester at the University of Tasmania. They leave Feb. 10.
Hillsboro's Jaxxon Hanschu has been working at Dale's Supermarket for the last few months, but he is preparing for quite the adventure this semester.
'On February 10th, I will be flying to Hobart, Tasmania—an island state of Australia— as part of a study abroad exchange program through Missouri State University (MSU). I will attend the University of Tasmania as I continue my college education until I fly back home on July 6th,' he said.
Hanschu, who graduated from Hillsboro High School in 2022, has been attending MSU in Springfield, MO. He also interned last summer as a conservation technician at Maxwell Wildlife Refuge near Canton.
Hanschu will not be going to Tasmania alone.
'My girlfriend, Annabella Diaz and I will be flying together, and two other students from MSU will be attending the University of Tasmania as well. I actually owe a lot of credit to Annabella for this opportunity of traveling abroad,' said Hanschu. 'Personally, as someone who is generally more introverted, I never would have followed through with this opportunity by myself. Having her by my side and supporting me to dream big and take advantage of the opportunity to travel while in school is something I am grateful for beyond words.'
Hanschu finds that he is more excited than nervous about his trip.
'I am surprisingly not very nervous about my adventure—yet. I obviously hope the journey of getting there goes smoothly since the whole flying process will take 24 hours. I believe all the nerves will hit me at different times, whether if that is as I am boarding the plane or if I get homesick while I am abroad. Luckily I have been filled with excitement rather than nerves or anxiety during the planning process,' he said.
Hanschu explained that Tasmania is in the southern hemisphere so he will be experiencing summer there compared to our winter here. There is also a 17-hour time difference between Tasmania and Kansas.
He is most looking forward to experiencing an entirely different education system along with seeing what university life there is like.
'I am also really excited to experience the culture of Tasmania, along with the natural, dynamic beauty of the island, the unique wildlife and artisanal foods. Half of the island is nationally protected land, making it one of Australia's most protected regions. My days could be spent hiking in a mountainous rainforest, relaxing along the coastline's white sand beaches or experiencing the city life of downtown Hobart,' said Hanschu.
He will return to MSU in the Fall. He plans to graduate in May of 2026 with two Bachelor of Science degrees in Wildlife Conservation and Forestry, along with a Geographical Information Systems (GIS) Certificate.
After graduation, Hanschu plans to further his education through the pursuit of a Master of Science degree related to ecology, forestry and conservation.
'I am still in the process of deciding exactly what I want my emphasis to be or what university I want to attend. Several universities I have considered include Montana University, Oregon State University, Colorado State University and Wageningen University in the Netherlands,' said Hanschu. 'A few interests I have include biodiversity conservation, ecosystem forest ecology and community ecology— specifically predator-prey relationships and how they affect ecosystem stability and animal behavior. Recently, I have developed a passion for research and ultimately want to spend time in nature and think scientifically about conservation and ecological challenges.'
